item.title: [SCMP] Eye on China: Japan reopens taboo debate over nuclear-powered submarines
item.description:
With China flexing its naval power across the Pacific and bilateral tensions running high, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is weighing a move long viewed as taboo – nuclear-powered submarines for the Maritime Self-Defence Force fleet.

“We will seriously consider [the possibility] in a concrete and realistic manner,” Takaichi told the Japanese parliament on October 14.

Yet with Tokyo set to revise its core security documents by year’s end, the proposal is dividing the ruling coalition.
item.content:encoded:
With China flexing its naval power across the Pacific and bilateral tensions running high, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is weighing a move long viewed as taboo – nuclear-powered submarines for the Maritime Self-Defence Force fleet.

“We will seriously consider [the possibility] in a concrete and realistic manner,” Takaichi told the Japanese parliament on October 14.

Yet with Tokyo set to revise its core security documents by year’s end, the proposal is dividing the ruling coalition.

The Japan Innovation Party – the junior coalition partner – wants nuclear propulsion introduced quickly, while some lawmakers from Takaichi’s Liberal Democratic Party are asking whether the military benefits justify the high costs and legal hurdles.

At issue is whether Japan needs nuclear-powered submarines when it already operates an advanced conventional submarine fleet and is developing uncrewed maritime capabilities.

Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi told parliament last December that Japan’s pacifist constitution did not prohibit nuclear propulsion for military vessels.

But the country’s Atomic Energy Basic Act restricts nuclear energy to peaceful purposes. Successive governments have interpreted this as ruling out military nuclear propulsion, a position Takaichi’s cabinet reaffirmed later that month.

Beijing has criticised the controversial proposal, with Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning on October 16 accusing Tokyo of seeking to gradually loosen its nuclear restrictions and linking the proposal to the wider debate over Japan’s nuclear policies.

Such moves threatened regional peace and stability, Mao warned.

The debate comes amid growing concern in Tokyo about the People’s Liberation Army’s expanding operations in the western Pacific.

On October 16, Koizumi said China’s military operations were expanding while Japan’s Pacific intelligence-gathering and surveillance capabilities remained limited, making stronger defences urgent.

The defences include underwater assets. Japan’s conventional submarines are particularly well-suited to defending the maritime chokepoints around its southwestern islands, where operating quietly at low speeds makes them effective in ambushes.

Nuclear-powered submarines could also defend these chokepoints, but their advantage lies in speed and range.

Conventional submarines can only travel at high speeds underwater for a limited time before their batteries need recharging. Nuclear-powered boats can sustain high underwater speeds over much longer distances.

That could help Japan reach Chinese naval forces in the western Pacific with greater speed, shift between patrol areas or interception points as they change course, and retreat more quickly from dangerous waters after an attack.

Such mobility and endurance would be costly.

Eric Heginbotham, a Massachusetts Institute of Technology security scholar, told The Japan Times in January that nuclear-powered submarines could cost roughly two to three times as much to buy and four times as much to operate as conventional boats, depending on design.

A June study by Hudson Institute researcher Masashi Murano and four colleagues estimated that, for similar expenditure, Japan could acquire and maintain six nuclear-powered attack submarines (SSNs) or 10 large conventional missile submarines, supplementing a baseline fleet of 22 conventional boats.

The researchers also estimated that an average of one or two nuclear-powered boats would be deployed at any given time, compared with three of the large conventional missile submarines.

They concluded that conventional missile submarines combined with underwater drones would be likely to offer Japan better value for conventional warfare.

In an interview, Murano said: “Nuclear propulsion extends a submarine’s reach, but a single boat on station cannot search blindly for Chinese SSNs across the vast Pacific.”

While nuclear propulsion becomes more valuable further from home, he questioned whether Japan should prioritise such missions, noting that “distant open-ocean operations are where the US Navy is strongest”.

Despite its sophisticated submarine-building industry and civilian nuclear expertise, Japan would need entirely new military infrastructure for nuclear-powered submarines.

Defence Minister Koizumi highlighted the financial and technical demands of nuclear propulsion on October 9, noting that nuclear reactors were expensive, required larger submarine hulls and demanded specialist expertise for their operation and maintenance.

He said nuclear-powered submarines were generally considered noisier than conventional boats, although their acoustic performance was improving.

Another pivotal question is how Japan would obtain naval reactor technology.

Tokyo would have to develop its own propulsion system or get help from countries such as the United States or France, with the choice affecting submarine design, construction costs and long-term dependence on foreign suppliers.

American nuclear-powered submarines use highly enriched uranium, which Japan cannot currently produce, while French designs use low-enriched uranium that is closer to the fuel used in civilian reactors.

Japan would also need specialised shipyards, maintenance facilities, nuclear-safety systems and trained naval reactor personnel.

A US Virginia-class nuclear-powered submarine requires about 140 crew members – roughly twice the complement of a Taigei-class boat.

Additional personnel would be needed for maintenance, technical support and nuclear safety, placing further pressure on Japan’s already overstretched military.

The transition would take considerable time as well.

Murano estimated that even if development began now, Japan would need “a decade or more” to field its first nuclear-powered submarine – “realistically not before the late 2030s and more likely the 2040s”.

Establishing a sustainable operational fleet would therefore take even longer.

That raises an immediate question for Tokyo: whether investing billions in nuclear-powered submarines would deliver greater military value than expanding its existing conventional submarine force and further developing its uncrewed maritime capabilities.

Christopher Hughes, a professor of international politics and Japanese studies at the University of Warwick, questioned whether countering the PLA Navy was necessarily the “prime function” of Japan’s interest in nuclear-powered submarines.

Tokyo might instead be seeking a more survivable conventional counterstrike capability, he suggested.

But this would not necessarily require nuclear propulsion. Japan is studying how to integrate vertical missile-launch systems into future submarines.

Jeffrey Hornung, Japan lead for the think tank Rand Corporation, said that if he were a Japanese lawmaker, he would seek an assessment of whether nuclear-powered submarines would close “an important gap” in Japan’s capabilities.

If conventional submarines, underwater drones and advanced mines could meet those needs, that should give policymakers “reason for pause” before rushing into acquisition, he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore tells suppliers to ‘honour commitments’ amid Indonesia’s gas cut
item.description:
Singapore expects all parties who have signed commercial contracts for gas supplies to “honour their commitments”, said Prime Minister Lawrence Wong on Sunday after Indonesia cut its exports.

Speaking at the People’s Action Party (PAP) convention, Wong added that Singapore’s gas importer will take the necessary steps to protect its rights and interests.

Indonesia began reducing natural gas exports to Singapore on Saturday. Indonesia’s upstream oil and gas regulator SKK Migas said the move was to divert more supplies to domestic electricity needs.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore expects all parties who have signed commercial contracts for gas supplies to “honour their commitments”, said Prime Minister Lawrence Wong on Sunday after Indonesia cut its exports.

Speaking at the People’s Action Party (PAP) convention, Wong added that Singapore’s gas importer will take the necessary steps to protect its rights and interests.

Indonesia began reducing natural gas exports to Singapore on Saturday. Indonesia’s upstream oil and gas regulator SKK Migas said the move was to divert more supplies to domestic electricity needs.

Singapore’s Energy Market Authority said the reduction of 31 million standard cubic feet of gas a day amounts to less than 2 per cent of Singapore’s total daily gas demand.

About 95 per cent of Singapore’s electricity is generated using natural gas and it imports a significant amount of this gas through pipelines from Indonesia.

“The gas supplies are covered by commercial contracts. We expect all parties to honour their commitments and Singapore’s gas importer will take the necessary steps to protect its rights and interests under these contracts,” Wong said.

Singapore has been readying itself for such risks, the prime minister added. It has invested in liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminals to import natural gas from different countries, without having to rely on pipelines, providing more options to manage any disruptions to supply.

However, Singapore must look beyond natural gas to cleaner sources of power that can provide reliable electricity around the clock, Wong added.

This is why authorities are studying the potential of nuclear energy, he said.

“Understandably, there are concerns about the safety of nuclear power in a small and densely populated country like Singapore. We take the concerns very seriously. Safety must come first,” Wong said.

“But we should not rule out an option simply because it is difficult or controversial. We must assess the risks and trade-offs carefully, engage Singaporeans, and eventually make the right decision to secure our energy future.”

From 2027, Singapore will be embarking on an assessment by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to gauge the country’s ability to make an informed decision on adopting nuclear energy.

Known as the IAEA’s Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review, each phase comes with key milestones that have to be reached to guide countries in their understanding of the commitments and obligations associated with developing a nuclear power programme.

Wong said: “Dealing with today’s concerns is only part of our job. We must also prepare Singapore for tomorrow – that means looking ahead, anticipating problems and acting before they become more difficult to solve.

“Consider the economy of the future. It will still be driven by ideas and talent, but computing power will become increasingly important and that requires enormous amounts of energy.”

In his speech, Wong noted that the world has become more “dangerous and troubled”, with harder challenges, but Singapore faces these difficulties from a position of strength, he added.

“We remain a trusted partner and an attractive place for businesses and investors,” the prime minister said.

In addition, Singapore is proactively strengthening partnerships across different regions of the world, with office-holders travelling more frequently to build relationships and deepen cooperation.

In the past week, President Tharman Shanmugaratnam made a state visit to Sweden, while Wong recently returned from Qatar and the United Arab Emirates.

“These countries are in different parts of the world, but they all see value in working closely with Singapore,” Wong said. “That reflects the trust and goodwill we have built over many years.”

Singapore is known as a reliable partner, a trusted hub and a country that delivers on its commitment, Wong said.

“This reputation is a vital asset, especially in today’s fragmented and troubled world. It helps us attract high-quality investments,” he added. “And the investments support growth, create jobs and enable incomes to rise.”

Some challenges are harder to tackle as they cross national borders – these include online scams or haze.

Singapore is grappling with its worst haze episode since 2015. It has sent notices to 10 Singapore-based firms and 10 Indonesian firms under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act.

“We cannot solve these problems through our own efforts alone. We need cooperation from other countries,” Wong said.

“But that does not mean we stand by and do nothing. We are doing everything we can within our power to protect Singaporeans, strengthen our own response and work with partners to tackle these problems at source.”

Touching on governance, Wong said that the Singapore we want cannot simply be delivered by the government to Singaporeans, and has to be “built with Singaporeans”.

“That is the partnership we strive for: a PAP government that listens, acts and delivers. A people who step forward and contribute and a society where everyone looks out for one another.”

While Singaporeans have given the PAP a strong mandate to govern for another term, this mandate is not an “entitlement”, Wong said.

“It is a responsibility to deliver what we promised, tackle the difficult issues facing our country and prepare Singapore for what lies ahead. That is why we must never take the trust of Singaporeans for granted. After all, no political party has a permanent claim on that trust,” Wong said.

“Every generation of PAP leaders and activists must earn it afresh. We know what is expected of us. We must listen and deliver. We must hold ourselves to high standards and we must always put Singapore and Singaporeans first.”

Wong noted that while some sectors of Singapore’s economy are doing well, others are facing pressures.

Some workers are benefiting from new opportunities, but others are struggling to keep up. Lower-wage workers worry about keeping pace with rising costs, while Singaporeans in their 40s and 50s who lose their jobs worry about finding work again.

“We understand these concerns and we will respond to them. Our task is not just to keep the economy growing. It is to make sure that growth translates into better lives for all Singaporeans,” he said.

The government is also doing more to ease the burdens on parents and give families greater assurance, as seen by measures introduced at this year’s National Day Rally, he added.

Wong acknowledged that the government has a “full agenda”, such as continuing to tackle the cost-of-living pressures and helping Singapore secure better jobs.

Ultimately, the government will do its part, but everybody has a part to play too, the prime minister said.

“We will create opportunities and support workers through change, but workers must be prepared to learn and adapt,” Wong said.

“We will reduce the emphasis on exams and broaden education pathways, but parents must give their children space to grow at their own pace.

“We will strengthen support for families and seniors, but all of us must also look out for one another.”

This story was first published by CNA

item.title: [SCMP] Will China’s 4 peace principles for tackling African conflicts work?
item.description:
Beijing has a formula for tackling African conflicts and hot-button issues, and during a meeting this month with Togolese leader Faure Gnassingbe, Chinese President Xi Jinping outlined it in four principles linking peace to development.

The principles entail focusing on African-led security free from outside intervention; upholding sovereignty and UN Charter principles; rejecting force and sanctions and favouring ceasefires through dialogue; and focusing on both immediate security concerns and long-term development.

Asked on Monday whether the principles could be applied to northern Ethiopia and heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said they offered “practical guidance” for the Horn of Africa.
item.content:encoded:
Beijing has a formula for tackling African conflicts and hot-button issues, and during a meeting this month with Togolese leader Faure Gnassingbe, Chinese President Xi Jinping outlined it in four principles linking peace to development.

The principles entail focusing on African-led security free from outside intervention; upholding sovereignty and UN Charter principles; rejecting force and sanctions and favouring ceasefires through dialogue; and focusing on both immediate security concerns and long-term development.

Asked on Monday whether the principles could be applied to northern Ethiopia and heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said they offered “practical guidance” for the Horn of Africa.

Days later, a joint statement following a meeting between Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and his Djiboutian counterpart, Abdoulkader Houssein Omar, said China would continue to play a constructive role in mediating regional disputes through its existing Horn of Africa peace-and-development initiative, subject to the wishes of the countries concerned.

Beijing has financed major infrastructure projects in the region under the Belt and Road Initiative, its China-centred trade and investment scheme. These include the Addis Ababa–Djibouti Standard Gauge Railway, as well as oil, fishing and maritime interests across Sudan, South Sudan, Somalia and Djibouti.

Yet, Beijing remains reluctant to intervene directly, opting instead to support African-led diplomacy to preserve its long-standing doctrine of state non-interference.

As conflict in Ethiopia’s Tigray region threatens to destabilise the Horn of Africa, China seeks to strike a delicate diplomatic balance advocating for peaceful, African-led solutions that align with Xi’s conflict-resolution principles.

The idea is to safeguard China’s billions in regional infrastructure and economic investments while carefully maintaining its core foreign policy pledge of non-interference.

But experts said lasting peace would ultimately depend on regional actors addressing internal factionalism, respecting state sovereignty and fostering inclusive dialogue alongside broader international peace efforts.

Yun Sun, a senior fellow and director of the China programme at the Stimson Centre, a Washington-based think tank, said Beijing’s response reflected concern about what renewed fighting could mean for its interests in the Horn of Africa.

“I think it first and foremost points out China’s concern and aversion to instability,” Sun said. “War and conflicts fundamentally undermine China’s interests on the ground.”

China also faced a diplomatic constraint, she added, saying it seeks to influence how conflicts are resolved without abandoning its stated principle of non-interference in other countries’ affairs.

Rather than lead a peace process itself, Beijing tends to support approaches led by countries in the region and their regional organisations.

“The balance they strike is through siding [with] and supporting [a] regional approach and the involvement of regional organisations,” Sun said. “That confers legitimacy and credibility to the Chinese approach.”

Ethiopian federal forces and fighters from the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) are battling again in northern Ethiopia, putting the 2022 Pretoria Peace Agreement under severe strain.

Ethiopian federal forces entered Mekelle, Tigray’s capital, in early October after advancing on the city and prompting TPLF fighters to withdraw.

Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government announced a six-month caretaker administration in the Tigray region to restore services, return displaced people and prepare for elections.

The conflict has also escalated Ethiopia–Eritrea tensions, with Addis Ababa accusing Asmara of backing the TPLF and occupying its territory.

Eritrea denies the claim and accuses Ethiopia of threatening Red Sea access, critical for landlocked Ethiopia, which relies on Djibouti’s port.

According to Seifudein Adem, a visiting professor at Doshisha University in Kyoto, Ethiopia must address its internal divisions if it is to resist outside intervention.

“President Xi Jinping is correct to suggest that Ethiopia should put its house in order by resolving internal disagreements through dialogue because disorder is the ultimate justification for external intervention in Africa,” he said.

Adem argued that the obstacle was not an inability to resolve disagreements peacefully.

“Rather, these disagreements often take the form of militarised factionalism,” he said. “This, in turn, is because the Ethiopian state does not enjoy a monopoly over the means of violence in the society.”

“The problem is that some of these neighbouring countries seem to view their interference as a kind of African solution to African disorder, consistent with an ‘African-led’ solution,” Adem added.

Xi’s emphasis on sovereignty shifted the focus from Africa as a whole to the rights of individual states, he said.

According to Costantinos Berhutesfa Costantinos, a public policy expert at Addis Ababa University and former United Nations policy adviser, China has an interest in calming the fighting but must use its influence carefully.

“China is a friend and major trade partner and investor in the Horn,” Costantinos said, citing Beijing-backed roads, power-generation and transmission projects, and industrial estates in Ethiopia.

Those investments could not deliver their intended economic benefits without peace, he added.

Costantinos said China’s diplomatic initiative, together with its influence through the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation, raised expectations that Beijing would engage with countries in the region to help resolve their long-standing conflicts.

China appointed Xue Bing as its first special envoy for the Horn of Africa in 2022 and convened a conference on peace, governance and development in Addis Ababa that year.

By November last year, Hu Changchun succeeded Xue. Hu has continued to promote Beijing’s regional initiative.

Costantinos said governments in the Horn should put Xi’s principles into practice through diplomacy to reduce tensions, protect trade routes and secure local ceasefires.

“No conflict can be considered resolved if any group whose interests are affected has been left out of the negotiation or mediation,” he added, observing that the parties would not enter talks with equal influence.

As Costantinos saw it, China should work alongside existing peace efforts.

“China will only add to the praiseworthy efforts by the [African Union], UN, US and [European Union],” he said. “Its initiative will in no way gainsay the work of these venerable institutions and countries.”

item.title: [SCMP] Fandom vs flag: why young Chinese embrace Japanese pop culture but reject war-era symbols
item.description:
Young Chinese people enjoy Japanese pop culture such as anime and music, but many draw a firm line at symbols of Japanese militarism.

That line was tested recently at Moscow State University, where Chinese students confronted a classmate wearing Japan’s rising sun flag in class and called for his repatriation, state-run newspaper Global Times reported on Sunday.

Many countries, including China, view the flag as a symbol of Japanese militarism and aggression. Japan’s Self-Defence Forces still use the flag today.
item.content:encoded:
Young Chinese people enjoy Japanese pop culture such as anime and music, but many draw a firm line at symbols of Japanese militarism.

That line was tested recently at Moscow State University, where Chinese students confronted a classmate wearing Japan’s rising sun flag in class and called for his repatriation, state-run newspaper Global Times reported on Sunday.

Many countries, including China, view the flag as a symbol of Japanese militarism and aggression. Japan’s Self-Defence Forces still use the flag today.

The October 14 incident sparked an online backlash against the Chinese student and praise for those who reported him, following commentaries by People’s Daily, the Communist Party’s official newspaper, and the People’s Liberation Army.

“A disgrace to the Chinese people,” read one of the top comments under a post by Jun Zhengping, a social media account run by the PLA.

Among those condemning the student were people who enjoyed Japanese pop culture, including Lucy Huang, 24.

The Japanese anime fan began watching the medium in primary school, watching more than 200 anime series and reading manga – Japanese comic books and graphic novels.

“Japan in anime cannot really be called Japan but is an idealised utopia,” Huang said, adding that she drew a clear distinction between Japan in reality and the country as depicted in anime.

She said it was “unforgivable” for a Chinese person to wear the rising sun flag.

Japanese anime began appearing on Chinese television in the 1980s and gradually gained a larger audience over the following decades.

According to a 2018 report by Chinese consultancy iResearch, China had more than 200 million online anime users in 2018, with nearly 80 per cent of 803 surveyed anime consumers expressing a preference for Japanese animation.

Yet, for many young Chinese like Huang, an interest in Japanese pop culture does not mean an embrace of Japan as a whole.

Lillian Liu, a final-year university student in China’s Fujian province, echoed Huang’s anger over symbols associated with Japan’s wartime aggression against China.

Liu boycotted a September collaboration between WEGO – a popular Japanese fashion brand known for its anime merchandise and clothes – and Japanese anime series My Hero Academia.

Chinese platforms dropped the anime in 2020 after a character linked to Japan’s Unit 731, which conducted human experiments during World War II, appeared in the series.

“I really like Japanese anime and manga, but as Chinese people, we cannot allow our country’s political stance to be violated,” said Liu, who began watching Japanese anime in kindergarten.

In a September commentary, Beijing Daily, the official newspaper of the Communist Party’s Beijing Municipal Committee, described the collaboration as “an act of support for Japanese militarism”.

“This is shameful. I won’t buy anything from the store again,” said Liu, who estimated spending up to 20,000 yuan (US$2,995) a year on Japanese pop culture merchandise and bought three transparent bags showing anime merchandise from WEGO before the incident.

WEGO Harajuku, the brand’s China subsidiary, later issued an apology, saying its Japanese parent company had cancelled the collaboration and removed related promotional posts.

But Yuki, 24, an anime fan who gave only her first name, said she had noticed a shift in how young people around her viewed Japan.

“The spread of anime has, to some extent, helped young people today avoid viewing all Japanese people as bad,” Yuki said.

Once a fan of My Hero Academia, Yuki stopped following the series after the 2020 controversy.

“Culture itself is also a form of politics. After the incident, I no longer engage with [My Hero Academia],” said Yuki, who regularly attends anime conventions where fans dress up as characters from animation and manga.

She has also seen how political tensions can affect the anime scene.

“The popularity of Japanese anime seems to rise and fall with China-Japan relations and political tensions,” she said, observing that a convention organiser had removed booths related to Japan after Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s contentious remarks on Taiwan.

In November last year, Takaichi told Japan’s parliament that a Taiwan contingency could trigger the deployment of the Self-Defence Forces, eliciting heavy criticism from mainland Chinese officials and state media.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States and Japan, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

China and Japan have long had a complex and evolving relationship, shaped by more than 1,000 years of exchanges in writing, religion, art and technology.

During several dynasties including the Tang, Japan sent envoys to China to study its political system, Buddhism, written culture and urban planning. The island country drew heavily on Chinese civilisation in shaping its own institutions and culture.

But Japan’s industrialisation and military expansion in the late 19th century led to war with China. Japan defeated the Qing dynasty in the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894-95, forcing it to cede lands including Taiwan.

After Japan’s 1945 surrender at the end of World War II, China and Japan moved towards diplomatic relations, normalising them in 1972. Since then, ties have improved at times, only to be repeatedly strained by historical and territorial disputes.

Orna Naftali, an associate professor in the Department of Asian Studies at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said both recent geopolitical tensions and historical factors had contributed to hostility towards Japan in China.

“Every now and then, there is some kind of geopolitical tension about different issues, which is because of reasons including history,” Naftali said.

As for popular culture, she thought it did not necessarily lead people to “develop more positive attitudes” towards a country’s government or its policies.

Naftali said young people’s views of Japan were shaped by domestic influences and interactions with the country’s people and family members.

“What to think of a certain country [is shaped] not just through textbooks but also different rituals and ceremonies and whatever the teacher says,” she added.

Naftali observed that relatives’ memories of the war, whether young people had in-depth conversations with Japanese people and socioeconomic background also played an important role in shaping their understanding of the country.

Although “there is a constant sort of animosity towards Japan in terms of the nationalist rhetoric”, young people’s views were more complex, she said, adding that some held more favourable attitudes towards Japan, while even those with negative views had nuanced perspectives.

Shin Kawashima, professor in the University of Tokyo’s Department of International Relations, said young people in both China and Japan had shown considerable interest in one another’s cultures.

“In that sense, in the distant future, as the current younger generations come into contact with one another, Japan-China relations may take on a form different from what they are today,” he said.

However, Kawashima voiced pessimism about the prospects for building stable, positive ties between Chinese and Japanese societies through youth exchanges, noting that the “Chinese government has currently suspended most official exchanges with Japan”.

“At present, the influence of the political sphere on the economy and society is increasing, and such possibilities are not expected to expand,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Clashes flare at Paris protests as more than 400,000 march across France
item.description:
Protests across France were largely peaceful on Saturday, despite heightened tensions and sporadic clashes between protesters and the police, but authorities remained on high alert as night fell.

The French Interior Ministry counted 410,000 people who hit the streets across the country on Saturday, down from the 550,000 who protested last weekend.

The October 17 demonstrations descended into looting and the worst urban rioting France had seen in years.
item.content:encoded:
Protests across France were largely peaceful on Saturday, despite heightened tensions and sporadic clashes between protesters and the police, but authorities remained on high alert as night fell.

The French Interior Ministry counted 410,000 people who hit the streets across the country on Saturday, down from the 550,000 who protested last weekend.

The October 17 demonstrations descended into looting and the worst urban rioting France had seen in years.

A total of 249 protests took place in France on Saturday, just over half of the 430 protests that were recorded on October 17, according to French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, who added that police had detained close to 1,000 people by about 7.30pm on Saturday, with that number expected to go up.

“The marches unfolded well” despite the presence of certain “radical groups”, Nunez said.

In Paris, around 110,000 people took part in Saturday’s protest, according to Paris Police Prefecture, which said the situation across the city remained mostly “calm”.

The march started in the afternoon in a festive but uneasy mood at the southern edge of the city.

Towards Porte de Vincennes, the end point of the route, police clashed with groups of masked protesters dressed in black, an identity-hiding tactic known as the black bloc, firing tear gas and water cannon as the demonstrators set off fireworks and threw projectiles at officers.

Police also fired tear gas in Lyon and Nice, where demonstrations had been banned, and in Lille and Marseille, where a single march had been authorised in each city.

For many young students who gathered in Paris on Saturday, the main message was for the government to understand their struggle, their demand for better education and the general population’s suffering amid the rising cost of living.

Many of the protesters shared similar sentiments: they condemned the violence from looting and rioting, but also expressed anger at police conduct.

“Obviously I don’t support any kind of violence,” said Manon, a student.

“But we shouldn’t blame everything on the troublemakers who came from an underprivileged background and who probably suffer from more invisible forms of violence in their everyday life.”

Three friends had told Manon to be careful – not of the troublemakers, but of the police.

“It’s easy to see things burning, but people too have been burning on the inside,” she said.

Tensions surrounding Saturday’s demonstrations, already high, escalated further following a shooting of a “racist nature” in the western Paris suburbs of Trappes and La Verriere on Friday, which left one person dead and five injured.

The Paris police prefecture cited the attack as a primary reason for altering the authorised protest route late Friday afternoon, ordering the march shifted away from Place de la Bastille in central Paris to Porte d’Italie on the city’s outskirts.

Trade unions accepted the change after a failed legal challenge, but criticised the government for attempting to divide the movement and create chaos.

Police began clearing Place de la Bastille around noon, directing demonstrators towards Porte d’Italie, where some local residents learned only from journalists on the scene that their neighbourhood was now along the march route.

The abrupt re-routing deepened anxiety among local officials and businesses bracing for renewed unrest, with one official telling the South China Morning Post that the protest risked being “all over the place” and turning into “a mess”.

With 70,000 police and gendarmes deployed nationwide and soldiers also mobilised to protect public buildings and infrastructure, the government faced intense pressure to prevent a recurrence of the widespread violence and looting seen the previous weekend.

“A fiasco like this, two weekends in a row, I don’t know what explanation we could give the French. We really cannot afford to get this wrong,” an adviser to Interior Minister Nunez told broadcaster BFMTV on Saturday.

Across France, authorities moved to ban most demonstrations following French President Emmanuel Macron’s intervention on Thursday, in which he stated that “the general recommendation is to hold no demonstrations in the coming days”.

Protests were prohibited outright in regional cities including Bordeaux, Lyon and Nice, with only a single demonstration approved for each of Paris, Lille and Marseille.

In Paris, local businesses took aggressive security precautions.

Along Rue Beaurepaire and surrounding streets, storefronts were closed behind thick sheets of plywood.

Burn marks on the road and paper signs reading “Fermeture pour cause de sinistre” (Closed due to unforeseen circumstances) remained visible reminders of the previous Saturday’s riots, during which a bar was torched and multiple retail outlets were ransacked.

The few cafes and shops that chose to open planned to close by early afternoon.

Even luxury boutiques in the west of the French capital, located far from the designated protest route, boarded up display windows and reinforced entryways against potential roving bands of vandals. Major cultural landmarks including the Louvre and the Musee d’Orsay were also closed.

Sweeping restrictions have intensified national debate over civil liberties and the constitutionally protected right to protest as the French government tries to maintain social order.

“I want the interior minister to carry out his primary mission: guaranteeing the exercise of individual freedoms and the right to protest, and protecting people first and property second,” the green party mayor of Paris’ 11th arrondissement David Belliard told the SCMP. “That is simple and basic in a great democratic country.”

Belliard’s district encompasses both Place de la Bastille and Place de la Republique – covering some areas hardest hit by last Saturday’s riots and the exact corridor where organisers had originally planned to march.

France is the most prominent flashpoint in a wider wave of demonstrations over the cost of living, housing and government spending rippling across Europe this weekend, with rallies planned in Italy, Portugal, Spain, Belgium and Albania.

In Italy, a coalition called the “October 17 Movement” called protests across eight cities on Saturday.

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni reinforced police and military deployments in Milan, one week after violent clashes and looting hit the country’s financial and fashion capital.

item.title: [SCMP] Will AI-powered open-door vending machines reshape Hong Kong’s retail landscape?
item.description:
Sherry Shum has embraced a new shopping routine after finding a smart vending machine near her home in Chai Wan.

The 37-year-old retail worker uses her phone to scan a QR code, opens the smart machine’s door, picks up a bottle of Coca-Cola, an oolong tea and a pack of potato chips, closes it and walks away with HK$60 (US$7.70) worth of goods. The whole process is so seamless that the only time she spends is deciding what to buy.

The moment Shum takes an item from the shelf, the machine detects the product based on its appearance and debits her account. Once she shuts the door, the bill is settled via the payment method she selected before opening it.
item.content:encoded:
Sherry Shum has embraced a new shopping routine after finding a smart vending machine near her home in Chai Wan.

The 37-year-old retail worker uses her phone to scan a QR code, opens the smart machine’s door, picks up a bottle of Coca-Cola, an oolong tea and a pack of potato chips, closes it and walks away with HK$60 (US$7.70) worth of goods. The whole process is so seamless that the only time she spends is deciding what to buy.

The moment Shum takes an item from the shelf, the machine detects the product based on its appearance and debits her account. Once she shuts the door, the bill is settled via the payment method she selected before opening it.

“I buy things basically every day … I can grab multiple items at once after just opening the door,” she said. “The open-door machines are more convenient because you do not have to wait for items to drop one by one from traditional machines that sometimes get stuck.”

For decades, vending machines have evolved from simple dispensers of bottled or canned drinks into smart retail points that combine digital payments and data-driven consumer insights. They now offer a low-cost retail channel for third parties such as local charities, selling products like flowers and daily necessities – from disposable underwear to sanitary towels.

These artificial intelligence-powered open-door vending machines have been growing in popularity in Shenzhen in the past couple of years, but they remain a minority in Hong Kong.

Some operators have pledged to install more of them across the city in the coming months, with one reporting higher sales revenue during the trial stage.

IVM Technology is one of Hong Kong’s largest operators, managing around 800 AI vending machines alongside 1,500 traditional ones in Hong Kong, the firm’s founder and managing director Leo Lui told the South China Morning Post.

Hong Kong currently has an estimated 15,000 to 17,000 vending machines, with the number expected to increase as the lower capital costs of AI machines attract new market entrants, Lui said.

“It will not surprise me if there are 30,000 to 40,000 machines later,” he said.

Lui pointed to Hong Kong’s exorbitant logistics, labour and parking costs – such as paying HK$200 just to park a delivery van for restocking at major commercial sites – as a major bottleneck.

Unlike mainland Chinese operators who could rely on low delivery expenses to sell low-margin goods, Hong Kong vending businesses faced fixed transport costs of about HK$2 per item, forcing them to focus on higher-priced, premium inventory, Lui said.

While the new open-door models generated 20 to 30 per cent more revenue in closed environments such as offices, traditional machines still outperformed them by 30 per cent in transient public spaces like bus stops, Lui said.

“On the streets, some consumers might find the new machines are too slow, whereas with an Octopus card on a traditional machine, the product drops in a second after a purchase is made,” Lui added.

While nearly 90 per cent of new vending machines deployed on the mainland were AI open-door models, Hong Kong’s adoption remained significantly slower due to distinct local economic factors, said Rex Leung, general manager of IVM Technology.

The offline nature of the Octopus card contactless payment system presented a significant hurdle for AI machines, which required post-purchase settlement after the door was closed, Leung said.

“The physical Octopus card is an offline payment method where users tap and leave immediately, which is incompatible with this machine that charges users only after they finish shopping,” Leung added.

To resolve this issue, Octopus Cards was expected to launch an integration allowing users to scan a quick response (QR) code and settle payments online via the Octopus application, Lui said.

Leung added the company aimed to evolve into a platform that allowed a wider range of organisations to sell goods in their machines.

FreshUp, another local vending machine operator with a network of more than 5,000 machines, had deployed more than 500 smart coolers that allowed customers to open the door, take products and be charged automatically through visual recognition technology, said David Lam, the group’s founder and CEO.

The smart models were generating 10 to 20 per cent more revenue per transaction than traditional push-button machines because the open-door design encouraged consumers to buy multiple items at once, Lam said.

“People might have pressed buttons for individual items in the past, but now, since they have already opened the fridge to buy a drink, they might take chocolate or potato chips if they find them interesting, increasing the overall basket value or unit items per transaction,” Lam added.

The AI models required an upfront hardware cost of HK$20,000 to HK$30,000, which was similar to the price of traditional machines, Lam said.

While the local smart retail sector was projected to grow steadily at an annual rate of 5 to 10 per cent, Lam said operators had to note a recurring fixed backend computing fee to software providers for data processing every time the cabinet door was opened.

Beyond commercial retail, the elimination of mechanical coils and rigid size restrictions has allowed open-door cabinets to serve as low-cost “micro-retail platforms” for non-governmental organisations and local brands seeking physical exposure without traditional overheads.

The new technology provided a low-cost retail alternative for charities such as Po Leung Kuk, which sold products made by people with disabilities, said Choi Kai-yin, a social worker and service manager at the organisation.

Listing items in physical retail stores incurred high rental and administrative costs, making it difficult for charities to generate sufficient revenue to support their disabled creators, Choi said.

“Renting a shop is [costly], as we are selling bottled drinks for about HK$10 each, and it is hard to calculate how many bottles we need to sell to cover the rent,” Choi added.

By selling bottled tea at HK$12 through vending machines, Po Leung Kuk hoped to retain a reasonable profit margin, which would directly benefit individuals with disabilities in recognition of their contributions and participation in vocational training, Choi said.

Swire Coca-Cola has been rolling out smart vending coolers on the mainland for several years, as retail formats incorporating digital payments increase in popularity following the pandemic. Its Hong Kong bottling business has now begun introducing these coolers, which allow customers to open the door and select drinks, adapting technology and operating processes proven on the mainland.

These coolers are easy to operate: shoppers select a payment method before opening the door, choose their products and close the door. When the door is closed, the bill is settled.

“Consumers today expect to see it, want it and get it almost instantly, and Hong Kong is no exception. People want a cold drink close to where they live, work, study and play, and they want paying for it to be quick and simple,” said Hunter Jin, Greater China CEO of Swire Coca-Cola.

“Smart vending coolers meet that expectation by combining cashless payment with product-recognition technology, so the whole purchase feels seamless.”

Swire Coca-Cola has deployed more than 150 coolers across sports and entertainment venues, workplaces, residential communities, educational institutions and industrial settings to reach locations unsuitable for conventional machines.

These new coolers would not completely replace the company’s network of around 6,000 conventional vending machines in Hong Kong, but would serve as a smart alternative offering a seamless digital experience, Swire Coca-Cola said.

“As Hong Kong continues to welcome major events and visitors, vending can do more than sell drinks,” Jin said. “We are exploring Hong Kong-themed vending and digital experiences at venues, transport hubs and tourist destinations that showcase local culture and add to the city’s vibrancy.”

item.title: [SCMP] Ukraine’s Starlink woes should be a wake-up call for Taiwan, analysts say
item.description:
Taiwan should not rely on a single foreign satellite provider for critical wartime communications, analysts have warned, after sudden restrictions on the use of Elon Musk’s Starlink disrupted Ukrainian drone operations.

The episode has renewed debate in Taiwan over the risks of entrusting essential communications to foreign commercial operators whose services could be restricted for political, military or business reasons.

Analysts said this was particularly relevant as Taipei was trying to strengthen the resilience of its communication networks against potential mainland Chinese attacks while simultaneously expanding its use of drones and other unmanned systems.
item.content:encoded:
Taiwan should not rely on a single foreign satellite provider for critical wartime communications, analysts have warned, after sudden restrictions on the use of Elon Musk’s Starlink disrupted Ukrainian drone operations.

The episode has renewed debate in Taiwan over the risks of entrusting essential communications to foreign commercial operators whose services could be restricted for political, military or business reasons.

Analysts said this was particularly relevant as Taipei was trying to strengthen the resilience of its communication networks against potential mainland Chinese attacks while simultaneously expanding its use of drones and other unmanned systems.

“The lesson from this incident is that we cannot become overly dependent on satellite navigation services provided by a single company,” said Shu Hsiao-huang, a senior analyst at Taiwan’s government-funded Institute for National Defence and Security Research.

SpaceX this month imposed new speed restrictions on terminals in Ukraine connected to its Starlink satellite internet service, disrupting some Ukrainian drone combat operations.

The restrictions cut a terminal’s link to the internet when it travels faster than 160km/h (100mph), a speed often exceeded by Ukrainian drones equipped with Starshield, the military version of Starlink.

The restrictions forced some drones to fly more slowly, making them easier for Russian forces to target or evade and prompting Kyiv to seek changes to the limits.

Conflicting accounts have emerged over who was responsible for the restrictions and why they were introduced.

Musk suggested that US President Donald Trump had decided to implement the limits because the US government owns and controls Starshield. Trump denied this, but said he doubted Musk was responsible, while the Pentagon also denied it was involved.

Regardless of who made the decision, the episode showed the dangers of depending on a system ultimately controlled by an external provider, according to Zivon Wang, a military analyst at the Chinese Council of Advanced Policy Studies in Taipei.

“Even the military-grade Starshield system funded or heavily supported by the US government could still potentially be disconnected or have its speed restricted at a critical moment because of political considerations or commercial interests,” Wang said.

He said the risks could be more complicated for Taiwan because Musk has substantial commercial interests on the Chinese mainland, including Tesla’s Shanghai factory.

While Taiwan’s military does not currently use Starlink, its legislature has eased rules that previously restricted foreign satellite communications companies from entering the local market, although detailed implementation arrangements have yet to be announced.

Taipei has already struck deals with providers willing to work within its restrictions, including Eutelsat OneWeb, while pursuing indigenous low-Earth-orbit satellite capabilities.

But analysts warned that replacing dependence on terrestrial and submarine networks with a single satellite constellation would merely exchange one vulnerability for another.

Wang called for a “multi-orbit, multi-provider” strategy combining indigenous satellites with commercial constellations from different international suppliers.

Taiwan should accelerate development of what he described as a “Taiwanese version of Starlink” to retain a communications channel beyond the control of foreign companies, while expanding cooperation with alternative operators such as OneWeb and Luxembourg-based SES.

He said the approach could also support Taiwan’s defence industry by encouraging the development of unmanned systems that did not rely on the US government-operated GPS as well as communications links less dependent on satellites.

Shu said redundancy would become increasingly important as Taiwan incorporated more unmanned systems into its armed forces.

Satellite systems support positioning, navigation and timing – or PNT – which are essential to operations ranging from unmanned aircraft and precision weapons to telecommunications and electricity networks.

Taiwan therefore needed alternatives to GPS as well as backup communication networks, Shu said.

The options include inertial navigation systems that can calculate an object’s position without external signals and AI-based visual navigation and terrain matching.

“The essence of satellite navigation redundancy is not putting all your eggs in the GPS basket,” Shu said, adding that weapons and critical infrastructure needed to remain functional during periods of “digital darkness”.

Developing unmanned systems capable of navigating without GPS would further reduce Taiwan’s dependence on satellite services, he added.

James Yifan Chen, a Taipei-based international relations and strategic studies scholar, said Taiwan’s situation differed from Ukraine’s because Taipei had “chosen not to depend on Starlink or Starshield because of its concerns about Musk’s close business ties with China”.

But that did not eliminate its reliance on foreign technology. Much of Taiwan’s advanced military equipment comes from the United States, meaning Taipei still needed to consider the possibility that externally supplied capabilities could be restricted during a conflict, he said.

Another challenge was whether “Taiwan’s own satellites could eventually provide sufficient connectivity and withstand electronic warfare and jamming by the People’s Liberation Army”, Chen added.

Beijing regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

Analysts also cautioned against treating Ukraine as a direct template for a Taiwan Strait conflict.

Wang said Taiwan’s potential battlefield would be much smaller, while drones operating across the strait would face different geographical and weather conditions.

Many Taiwanese drones would probably operate around the island or in coastal areas, where microwave links and other terrestrial communications could provide alternatives if satellite connections failed, he said.

The controversy also raised a broader question about the reliability of US support, according to Huang Huei-hua, director of the Taiwan Global Talk think tank.

“If Taiwan found itself in Ukraine’s predicament during a cross-strait conflict, it could end up the biggest loser,” she said. “Like Ukraine, Taiwan could face the risk of being abandoned.”

Huang said relying too heavily on any single foreign partner, including the United States, carried considerable risks.

“Taiwan needs to prepare a range of contingency plans, or it risks becoming expendable when the interests of larger powers change,” she said.

“The crisis of trust between Ukraine and the United States should serve as a wake-up call: there is no permanent comfort zone, even between allies.”

item.title: [SCMP] China’s next generation of leaders waiting in the wings for more senior roles
item.description:
Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. In the fourth part of this series, William Zheng looks at how the next generation of the party is being formed.

When China’s political elites gather behind closed doors in Beijing for the Communist Party’s fifth plenum on Monday, much of the attention will be on the quiet preparations for allocating hundreds of pivotal roles in next year’s 21st party congress.

At the heart of this transition is the rise of the party’s seventh generation – often referred to as the 7G – who were born in the late 1960s and the 1970s and whose ascent will be critical in shaping China’s political trajectory.
item.content:encoded:
Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. In the fourth part of this series, William Zheng looks at how the next generation of the party is being formed.

When China’s political elites gather behind closed doors in Beijing for the Communist Party’s fifth plenum on Monday, much of the attention will be on the quiet preparations for allocating hundreds of pivotal roles in next year’s 21st party congress.

At the heart of this transition is the rise of the party’s seventh generation – often referred to as the 7G – who were born in the late 1960s and the 1970s and whose ascent will be critical in shaping China’s political trajectory.

Xie Maosong, a senior researcher at Tsinghua University’s National Institute of Strategic Studies, said the party was looking for cadres who had “absolute political loyalty, integrity, fighting spirit, technological or ‘hard science’ expertise, grass-roots experience and hardship resilience”.

“Just like their predecessors, they must demonstrate unquestioned loyalty and integrity. But given China’s technological advancement into uncharted areas, the new leaders will have to know emerging technology and hard science as China can no longer copy from others.”

However, recent patterns within the party suggest that Beijing is giving age less weight when it comes to promotions, while the far-reaching anti-corruption campaign is hitting this generation as hard as any other.

The 7G

Regardless of whether Xi Jinping, now 73, chooses to stay in charge beyond the 2032 party congress, he will still need a deep bench of loyal and talented younger officials to carry out his policies.

In recent decades, candidates for Politburo seats have usually been identified many years ahead.

Most candidates for membership of the key decision-making body in 2032 will currently be members of the party’s Central Committee or will be selected as alternate members at next year’s party congress.

Traditionally, most Central Committee members, who have a ministerial-level rank, are required to step down at the age of 65.

Meanwhile, Politburo members observe an informal rule known as “seven up, eight down”, in which those under the age of 67 may serve another five-year term, while those aged 68 or older must retire.

Xi broke these precedents for some key figures in 2022, including top diplomat Wang Yi, then aged 69, who was seen as indispensable for managing China’s foreign relations amid escalating competition with the United States.

He also kept the country’s top general Zhang Youxia, then aged 72, in place to manage the country’s military modernisation programme, but Zhang later fell from favour and was detained earlier this year on suspicion of corruption.

Roughly two-thirds of the current Central Committee will have reached the statutory retirement age by the time of the party congress in October next year.

Consequently, the seventh generation, currently about 8 per cent of the party’s central leadership body, is expected to become the biggest cohort.

Only 7G officials who are already members of the Central Committee or those who have been newly appointed as ministers and provincial leaders – who will get their Central Committee seat in 2027 – are likely candidates for leadership roles beyond 2032.

The leading candidates

Some of these contenders have already taken over top regional and ministerial roles this year.

They include Zhu Zhongming, born in April 1972, who was appointed as mayor of Shanghai late last month, a role that puts him in line to become the city’s next party chief.

Zhu, 54, is a career finance official who spent much of his working life in his native province of Zhejiang, where he worked under Premier Li Qiang while he was governor.

Other regional government chiefs of a similar age include Zhejiang governor Liu Jie, Jiangsu governor Liu Xiaotao, and Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region’s government chairman Wei Tao – all born in 1970 – as well as Shanxi governor Lu Dongliang, who was born in 1973.

Other leading candidates, including Beijing mayor Yin Yong and Hubei party secretary Guan Zhiou – who outranks the regional government chiefs – are just a few months older and also considered leading candidates to take on senior national roles.

Other contenders from that generation hold central government and party roles, including A Dong, who leads the Communist Youth League Central Committee, Zhang Chengzhong, the Minister of Emergency Management, and Cheng Fubo, the director of the state-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission.

Most of these 7G officials are full or alternate members of the Central Committee. Shanghai mayor Zhu and emergency management minister Zhang, both appointed only recently, are expected to be made full members of the Central Committee at next year’s party congress.

Xie from Tsinghua said “resilient officials”, who had cut their teeth in difficult, under-resourced environments – mirroring Xi’s own formative years – or demonstrated versatile and effective problem-solving skills would be put on a faster track to promotion, as they will have to manage more emergencies caused by extreme weather.

“The preferred style for next-generation leaders is quiet, efficient execution of central mandates rather than high-profile self-promotion or experimental local diverging policies. They must also show the ability to integrate economic development with security considerations, ensuring that local industrial policies adhere to broader central directives regarding supply-chain resilience and social stability,” Xie added.

Chinese born in the late 1960s and 1970s have often been described as “the luckiest age cohort” on social media because they were too young to experience the political turmoil of the Cultural Revolution or the physical hardship experienced by “sent-down youths” who worked as farmers in rural areas.

They also avoided the starvation endured by previous generations and grew up as the country’s economy started to boom.

An analysis published by Li Cheng, director of Hong Kong University’s Centre on Contemporary China and the World, said half of the leading 7G cadres had doctorates – making them the most highly educated cohort in party history – and often had experienced life outside the party system, including overseas study.

Li found that around one-third of them were trained in engineering, while economics and finance represented their other primary fields of study.

There was also a significant proportion that had experience of managing state assets, financial institutions or complex industrial projects, reflecting Beijing’s demand for officials capable of navigating economic headwinds and technological competition.

Yin, the mayor of Beijing, is a prominent example. He holds a master’s degree in public administration from Harvard University and previously served as vice-governor of the People’s Bank of China.

Another example is 1970-born Guo Ningning one of the few high-ranking female contenders for higher office. She was appointed party chief of Fujian’s provincial government on Saturday, paving the way for her appointment as governor.

She spent more than a decade leading operations for state banks in Hong Kong and Singapore before entering provincial governance.

Meanwhile, Hubei’s deputy party chief Zhuge Yujie, born in 1971, was named as the new party secretary of the Qinghai government, also putting him in line to become the province’s next governor.

No more fast track

However, these officials have climbed the ladder more slowly than some previous generations.

For example, the 2002 party congress saw dozens of officials in their late 30s or early 40s being given vice-ministerial posts, some of whom achieved full ministerial rank three years later, including Sun Zhengcai, who became agriculture minister at the age of 42, or Hu Chunhua, who became head of the Communist Youth League aged 43.

At the time, these promotions were seen as filling a skills gap caused by a lack of administrative skills and economic experience among older officials.

But since Xi came to power in 2012, fewer younger cadres have been given senior posts as the leadership prioritised performance and experience.

The youngest members of the Central Committee were in their mid to late 40s when they were appointed and the average age of new members of the last two Politburos – around 62 – was much higher than in the previous three, where it was well below 60.

Xi and other senior leaders have warned that fast-tracked young bureaucrats sometimes lack real-world experience.

As early as 2011, the Central Organisation Department explicitly warned of the problem caused by “three-door cadres” – a term used to mock young civil servants who moved directly from their family’s doorstep to university and then into government offices.

Xi has also introduced the concept of “letting seedlings develop firm roots”, dunmiao in Chinese, mandating that up and coming cadres spend extended periods in complex, frontline postings – such as poverty alleviation, disaster response and industrial restructuring – before being eligible for senior command.

Those who crashed out

An additional challenge for the 7G cadres is the country’s ongoing anti-corruption drive, which has already led to the downfall of some high-profile figures.

The latest case involves Beijing’s executive vice-mayor Xia Linmao, who was placed under investigation last week.

Born in 1970, Xia, who has a doctorate from Tsinghua University and held a variety of top-tier technocratic postings in the capital’s urban planning and government operations, epitomised the demographic cohort that rose swiftly through the sub-provincial ranks.

His downfall is just the latest warning that rising cadres face intense and constant scrutiny and will be judged strictly on political compliance and administrative conduct rather than their potential.

Other once-promising 7G officials who have fallen foul of the anti-corruption drive include former Urumqi party boss Yang Fasen, who was jailed for life last October for accepting more than 147 million yuan (US$20.7 million) in bribes, and Fei Gaoyun, who held a similar role in Hefei and was placed under investigation in May.

Li Yunze, the former head of the National Financial Regulatory Administration, who was celebrated as the first official born in 1970 to achieve full ministerial rank, provides another cautionary tale.

He was abruptly demoted and stripped of his seat in the national legislative body in May over disciplinary violations, underscoring that a temporary lead in the political marathon provides no immunity against tightened scrutiny.

item.title: [SCMP] Overseas Filipinos feel heartache over missing parcels for loved ones, demand answers
item.description:
At this time of year, Fatima Ramos would normally be preparing her balikbayan boxes. Overseas Filipinos typically fill these boxes with gifts, clothes, food and household items to send to their loved ones back home in the Philippines for Christmas.

Ramos has previously sent the tax-exempt parcels to her family and Philippine charity organisations from Abu Dhabi, where she is a domestic worker.

Now back in the Philippines, Ramos is seeking answers about the parcels she sent last year, some of which arrived severely damaged while others remain missing.
item.content:encoded:
At this time of year, Fatima Ramos would normally be preparing her balikbayan boxes. Overseas Filipinos typically fill these boxes with gifts, clothes, food and household items to send to their loved ones back home in the Philippines for Christmas.

Ramos has previously sent the tax-exempt parcels to her family and Philippine charity organisations from Abu Dhabi, where she is a domestic worker.

Now back in the Philippines, Ramos is seeking answers about the parcels she sent last year, some of which arrived severely damaged while others remain missing.

“I got one of my boxes, and it was completely soaked. The clothes were faded and mouldy. The items and the box were all crushed. It was heartbreaking. The food, such as the chocolates, had melted because it got wet,” Ramos told This Week in Asia.

Ric, an engineer in Saudi Arabia who asked to be identified only by his first name, has suffered a similar experience with a balikbayan – a compound word in Tagalog meaning return to a country – box.

According to him, he sent a balikbayan box from Jeddah in June, and a delivery company’s representative told him in July that the parcel was still awaiting shipment. When he followed up in September, his emails and calls went unanswered.

For many overseas Filipinos, balikbayan boxes often represent weeks or months of careful selection of items paid for with their hard-earned savings, and an expression of their love from afar. Their tax-exempt status reflects the Philippine government’s recognition of the role overseas Filipinos play in supporting their families.

But thousands of these boxes have been left in limbo as the Christmas season approaches, with some abandoned in shipping containers at Philippine ports and others stranded in their countries of origin amid problems involving cargo forwarding companies.

The boxes sent by Ramos and Ric were handled by Makati Express Cargo, a forwarding company serving customers in the United States and the Middle East.

The Philippines’ Bureau of Customs (BOC) revoked the company’s licence in January and filed criminal complaints against it in May over nearly 40,000 boxes left unclaimed at ports, involving more than 30 million pesos (US$1.6 million) in unpaid duties.

Ramos sent eight boxes between January and March before returning to the Philippines for good because of a heart condition that she said had worsened following Iran’s attacks on the United Arab Emirates, including Abu Dhabi.

She found out about the mounting complaints against the forwarding company only after she returned home.

“At first, I didn’t want to believe it. But then I started following up with my package online and through the company’s website in March. By April, I still couldn’t get an answer to verify whether my boxes had already arrived. They should have been in the Philippines by now,” she said.

This Week in Asia has reached out to Makati Express Cargo for comment.

On Sunday, the BOC said it had discovered 29 abandoned shipping containers holding at least 10,000 of the boxes at various ports in the Philippines, some of which had arrived in May.

In June, the BOC had earlier filed complaints against five cargo forwarding companies over 3,176 abandoned boxes.

Some of the boxes had already been opened, rummaged through and “slaughtered”, Ramos claimed.

This Week in Asia has also reached out to the BOC for comment.

Ramos, who has been gathering complaints from at least 300 overseas Filipinos in the Middle East over their unclaimed boxes, said she had spoken to officials from the BOC and the Department of Migrant Workers to help resolve the matter.

Labour of love

For migrant Filipinos, the unaccounted balikbayan boxes are a sore point as they symbolise their love and sacrifice, according to analysts.

Over 2 million Filipinos work as overseas Filipino workers (OFWs), part of a larger global diaspora of between 10 million and 15 million.

“Some Filipino families who decided to migrate to other countries may consider sending balikbayan boxes as a means of extending love and care to relatives in the Philippines. A balikbayan box could be viewed as a sustenance of relational closeness or to communicate thoughtfulness,” said Lenis Aislinn Separa, an intercultural communication researcher based in New Zealand.

“Each item they buy that fills a space in a balikbayan box has a backstory of how they struggled in prioritising between what they need to survive living abroad and providing what they believe their family needs back home.”

Hannah Nario-Lopez, an assistant professor at the University of the Philippines Diliman’s sociology department, said each box was a labour of love from migrant workers, who would curate items carefully over weeks or months.

“This simple, small, menial act converts the physical distance and the time spent abroad into tangible care, allowing the worker to remain present in the everyday life of their household,” she said.

The box also complements regular cash remittances from OFWs by offering items for household needs such as groceries, toiletries, school supplies, bags and shoes. For some, its loss could disrupt daily routines, such as health supplements for family members who were elderly or ill, Nario-Lopez said.

As such, the loss of the box would become a source of trauma for a family, according to Nario-Lopez.

“The non-arrival of a box feels like a broken promise, leading to guilt for the sender, and disappointment or a feeling of abandonment for the family,” she said.

Ramos said in one meeting with the Bureau of Customs, an OFW shared that she had sent a balikbayan box containing medicines for a family member, who later died. The box was lost along the way.

“The medicine never made it. The commissioner [of the bureau] was moved, because he had not realised how severe the impact had been,” she said.

Nario-Lopez said every loss of a balikbayan box would erode trust in Philippine institutions involved in its safe delivery, citing cases of looting at warehouses that stored such parcels.

“We have to remember that the balikbayan box is actually a grant to Filipinos working overseas. It’s tax-free because they’re sustaining the country through their remittances. So because of this, it becomes a manifestation of distrust in our logistics and governance,” Nario-Lopez said.

She warned that OFWs also faced unscrupulous scammers looking to exploit them.

“OFWs searching for cheap shipping alternatives become valuable targets for predatory forwarders. It seems like it gives an opening to people with bad intentions,” she added.

Nario-Lopez urged Philippine authorities to tighten regulations and online tracking of box movements to protect OFWs and their families.

“We could pressure the state through social media, for example, to have a more systematic or universal database to actively track container ships, expose fraudulent consolidators and [praise] lobby officials or leaders who would genuinely advocate for OFWs,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] Big dreams, growing pains in Indonesia: Prabowo’s turbulent 2 years in power
item.description:
When 35-year-old Bekasi resident Ika Kartika voted for Prabowo Subianto in Indonesia’s 2024 presidential election, she hoped the former general would restore a “Suharto-like” era of stability, when everyday essentials were affordable and life felt more predictable.

Growing up, she had often heard her parents reminisce about the “good old days” under the late strongman, whose rule had brought a sense of order to their lives.

Two years into his presidency, however, rising food prices have left Ika questioning whether Prabowo, who was once Suharto’s son-in-law, can deliver on that vision.
item.content:encoded:
When 35-year-old Bekasi resident Ika Kartika voted for Prabowo Subianto in Indonesia’s 2024 presidential election, she hoped the former general would restore a “Suharto-like” era of stability, when everyday essentials were affordable and life felt more predictable.

Growing up, she had often heard her parents reminisce about the “good old days” under the late strongman, whose rule had brought a sense of order to their lives.

Two years into his presidency, however, rising food prices have left Ika questioning whether Prabowo, who was once Suharto’s son-in-law, can deliver on that vision.

“I thought he would turn things around. Now I feel cheated and disappointed,” Ika said.

Her disillusionment reflects a broader loss of confidence in the 75-year-old former special forces commander – a sharp reversal from the position of strength he enjoyed after finally winning the presidency on his third attempt.

Taking office with virtually no parliamentary opposition after bringing former rival parties into a sprawling governing coalition, Prabowo rode a post-inauguration honeymoon that saw his public approval rating hit 79 per cent at the start of his term as he began implementing his blueprint to transform Southeast Asia’s largest economy and elevate its global standing.

At home, he staked his legacy on eradicating child malnutrition through his universal free nutritious meals programme – initially projected to cost 450 trillion rupiah (US$25 billion) a year at full scale – and reviving rural economies through Red and White Village Cooperatives, a state-backed network of retail and logistics hubs.

For investors, his pitch was that these and other state-led initiatives would create millions of jobs and propel annual GDP growth to 8 per cent, with sovereign wealth fund Danantara central to his plan to put state assets to work in strategic industries and accelerate development.

Abroad, he championed Global South diplomacy in the Brics bloc alongside a pledge to remain a stabilising anchor in Southeast Asia.

Yet as Prabowo marked his first 24 months in the top job on Tuesday, those lofty ambitions have collided with harsh realities on all three fronts.

An October survey by Saiful Mujani Research and Consulting (SMRC) found that Prabowo’s approval rating had fallen to 44.5 per cent, below the 50 per cent mark for the first time. A separate survey by the Centre of Economic and Law Studies (Celios) found that 75 per cent of respondents felt stressed by government policies, with high prices for basic necessities and a lack of job opportunities among their chief concerns.

Simultaneously, a looming global index downgrade has triggered a bruising stock market rout, while raging forest fires have blanketed the region in toxic smog, choking neighbours Malaysia and Singapore.

In the face of those challenges, analysts say Prabowo has oscillated between reactive damage control and stubborn resolve.

Rather than fundamentally rethink his agenda, he has made adjustments, such as slashing the budget for the free meals programme but refusing to abandon it, and repeatedly reshuffling his cabinet. His government has also sent confusing signals abroad, approving foreign firefighting help to battle the haze before subsequently putting the offers on hold.

While ruling party allies defend his adjustments as “dynamic moves” to protect fiscal stability, observers argue they merely paper over the deeper structural flaws of his administration.

The question now is whether Prabowo can genuinely change course or whether the setbacks of his second year will define the rest of his term.

Prabowo himself remains publicly defiant. Brushing off economic pessimism at a nickel-processing project launch on October 8, he pointed to robust state-backed investments as proof that his administration was succeeding.

“Every month, they predict that we will collapse. But today, I have come here and I see a bright future for Indonesia,” he declared.

Fraying mandate

At the heart of the public mood shift is the troubled roll-out of the signature welfare schemes that once anchored Prabowo’s popularity. The SMRC survey showed that 61 per cent of citizens familiar with the free meals initiative were unhappy with its execution, while 71 per cent doubted the village cooperatives plan would succeed.
