Saidiman Ahmad, a researcher and programme manager at SMRC, said the poll exposed a broad defection of supporters across all demographic groups, pinpointing mismanagement of the president’s flagship initiatives as the main cause of public censure.

Both the free meals initiative and village cooperatives plan “were significant factors”, Saidiman said.

Those missteps are glaring to voters like Lugas Limojoyo, 31, a resident of Purwokerto in Central Java who backed Prabowo in 2024 among the three presidential tickets.

Lugas, a former hotel chef, described the free meals programme and the cooperatives as Prabowo’s “main red flags”.

Pointing to recurring mass food-poisoning cases, he noted a lack of basic food safety protocols – an observation echoed by Indonesia’s food and drug agency, which has repeatedly cited poor sanitation and untrained staff as the primary causes behind thousands of students falling ill.

Lugas saw a similar lack of coordination in the village cooperatives initiative, noting that many state-funded warehouses “have already been built but aren’t operational, sitting there like empty husks”. Reuters has also reported concerns from analysts about the scheme’s top-down approach, the commercial viability of some locations and whether the cooperatives can respond to local needs.

Still, the programmes retain pockets of support. Anissa Fadhilah, a 29-year-old greengrocer in Surabaya, said she remained satisfied with Prabowo’s performance and would vote for him again in 2029 after her daughter received school meals and her business landed supply commissions from the scheme.

“I think [the free meals initiative] has the desired effect of lifting ordinary people economically, so I’m for it,” Anissa said.

Officials also defended the administration’s two-year track record.

Jasmine Herawan, a spokeswoman for Indonesia’s Government Communications Agency, said the administration had expanded the social safety net, with its free meals programme reaching 57 million recipients, while nearly 1.5 million people had been lifted out of extreme poverty within a year.

She also cited gains in food security, saying Indonesia produced 34.71 million tonnes of rice in 2025 without importing any that year.

On the extractive sector, Jasmine said: “We’ve also affirmed our mineral sovereignty by setting up a single-door export system for our key commodities.” The system is intended to give the government greater oversight of mineral exports and make it harder for companies to understate the value of what they sell overseas, potentially depriving the state of tax revenue.

Market reckoning

Costly spending commitments, however, have raised broader concerns about fiscal sustainability. Earlier this year, the government cut 67 trillion rupiah from the free meals programme before imposing further spending curbs across ministries in the final quarter to help keep the budget deficit within its legal ceiling of 3 per cent of GDP.

But fiscal tightening did little to reassure investors. On October 16, index provider MSCI warned that Indonesia could be downgraded from “emerging” to “stand-alone” market status over concerns about opaque corporate ownership and trading manipulation, triggering a bruising sell-off in Indonesian assets. The Jakarta Composite Index plunged 11.6 per cent and the rupiah fell to 18,050 per US dollar.

Despite emergency regulatory fines against market manipulators and bourse officials pledging swift governance reforms during a meeting with MSCI on Monday, the benchmark index hit a six-year low this week, as investors continued to digest the warning and the risk of billions of dollars in passive capital outflows.

Siwage Dharma Negara, co-coordinator of the Indonesia Studies programme at Singapore’s ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute, said regional investors continued to view Prabowo’s economic policy as unpredictable.

“He will not give up his populist programmes, like the free meals and rural cooperatives, but it is not clear what the economic benefit for the country will be,” Siwage said.

Siwage noted that the recent fiscal correction was too small to satisfy investors, many of whom viewed the free meals as a waste of state resources that should be redirected towards education, health or struggling regional governments.

“Prabowo fundamentally does not trust anyone else to advise him on economic direction,” Siwage said, warning that such moves were creating a poor investment climate. “If we want to restore market confidence, the most urgent fix is reducing this state intervention in the economy.”

Inside Prabowo’s ruling Gerindra party, lawmakers reject assertions that the administration’s economic agenda is faltering. Gerindra spokesman Sugiat Santoso dismissed Celios’ two-year study as “over the top” and “deliberately dramatised” to create mass panic.

Defending the village cooperatives as a path to financial independence for disadvantaged communities and the free meals as an ongoing investment in future generations, Sugiat added, “The president is definitely not here to please analysts, but to bring about real changes for the welfare of the people.”

Musical chairs

Unwilling to abandon his core populist pledges, Prabowo has instead turned to frequent personnel changes to tighten his grip on the bureaucracy – reshuffling his cabinet or installing new officials three times in the first two weeks of October alone, bringing his total number of cabinet shake-ups to eight in two years.

Arya Fernandes, head of politics and social change at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies Indonesia, said these shake-ups stemmed from the president’s underlying political vulnerability – specifically Gerindra’s lack of parliamentary dominance and the lingering influence of his predecessor, Joko Widodo.

This has forced Prabowo to consolidate power by accommodating a wide political spectrum, Arya noted. But the high cost of maintaining that stability – through an oversized cabinet and increased military budgets – has driven up fiscal pressure and forced the central government to slash local funding.

“In sum, Prabowo has secured elite support and lost mass support,” he said.

Yoes C. Kenawas, a researcher at Lembaga Survei Indonesia, said this dynamic reflected a leader whose authoritarian instincts make him insecure about elite loyalty.

“He remains deeply paranoid about elite betrayal and being backstabbed by coalition partners,” Yoes said. “Even with an 80 per cent parliamentary majority, he does not feel secure.”

Siwage said swapping out officials would not solve the administration’s deeper flaws: “We have seen many cabinet reshuffles so far, and he will likely continue shuffling officials, thinking a new person will fix the problem. But the real issue is that the entire system of governance is currently ineffective at implementing sound economic policy.”

Fanning flames

Nowhere has that administrative strain spilled beyond Indonesia’s borders more visibly than in the transboundary haze crisis.

Since August, severe forest and peatland fires across Sumatra and Kalimantan have sent thick smoke across the region, forcing school closures in Malaysia, prompting diplomatic protests and leading Singapore’s prime minister to warn of action against errant companies.

Siwage linked the resurgence of the fires directly to Prabowo’s domestic fiscal squeeze, which he said left local governments “without enough operational funds to fight the fires”.

For months, Jakarta resisted regional offers of firefighting help, while public remarks by officials only inflamed tensions – most notably when the newly appointed communications agency head suggested neighbours should remember Indonesia’s forests “send oxygen” when there is no haze.

Rifki Dermawan, an international relations lecturer at Universitas Andalas in West Sumatra, says the episode highlights a stark contrast: while Prabowo frequently travels globally, “Asean does not seem to be a priority”.

Pointing to the president’s failure to apologise or engage with regional counterparts over the pollution, Rifki said it suggested the bloc “might not be among Prabowo’s interests”. He attributed Jakarta’s reluctance to accept outside help to Prabowo’s suspicion of foreign involvement and repeated rhetoric blaming “foreign agents”.

A diplomatic thaw seemingly arrived on October 15 when Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir announced Prabowo had approved regional firefighting help. But the administration later abruptly backtracked when security chief Dudung Abdurachman put the offers on hold, declaring Indonesia was “still capable” of managing the blazes.

Prabowo then railed against “countries that like to insult” his nation over the wildfires, amid growing public anger and calls for Indonesia to be treated as an “outcast” in the region.

“Indonesia is a polite and patient nation. Our country is often insulted, but believe me, our nation does not want to be insulted all the time,” Prabowo said on Wednesday.

⁠⁠Prabowo also told his cabinet ‌on Wednesday that MSCI was trying ⁠to “scare us”, adding ‌that Indonesia was “not afraid” ‌and would not ⁠buckle, Reuters reported.

Despite plunging approval ratings, a market sell-off and diplomatic fires, Yoes warned Prabowo might not feel compelled to change course because the pain of his second-year slump had not hit his immediate political centre.

“The crisis is fragmented,” Yoes said. “The toxic haze chokes Sumatra and Kalimantan, but it does not blanket Jakarta or Java.”

Because the distress was clustered outside the capital, it looked manageable on paper, he added, “but underneath the surface, this is a crisis in the making”.

Defiance or adaptation

Analysts say moving beyond short-term diplomatic firefighting to rebuild his popular mandate and calm financial markets over the remaining three years of his term could depend on Prabowo’s willingness to look outside his inner circle.

So far, however, the president has framed mounting resistance not as a symptom of policy missteps but as a manufactured campaign by entrenched elites bankrolling paid protesters and online influencers – known locally as “buzzers”.

“We have no doubts. Even if they have hundreds of trillions of rupiah, they pay buzzers, they pay for algorithms, they attack us on social media, and they finance demonstrations, we are not afraid. We stand with the people, we are ready to die for the people,” Prabowo said during a fiery speech on October 6.

That defiant posture worries observers who believe Prabowo must adapt his approach to meet the challenges he is facing.

SMRC’s Saidiman argued that reversing the polling slide would require structural reform – starting with shrinking the cabinet, pulling back from the ongoing militarisation of the civilian sphere and conducting a “radical review of the administration’s costly yet ineffective populist programmes”.

“The president needs to step up and enact fundamental changes to how he governs the nation,” Saidiman said, adding Prabowo “should let opposition forces fulfil their function as a democracy should”.

Siwage warned that without an effective parliamentary opposition to check the president’s instincts, financial market tremors could eventually spiral into a wider political reckoning.

“Prabowo currently controls most of the government coalition and the parliament. With essentially no opposition, why would he change course when nobody dares to oppose his policies?” he said.

Outside Jakarta’s corridors of power, voters who helped put Prabowo in the presidential palace say he still has a window to turn things around – if he starts listening to ordinary Indonesians.

In Central Java, Lugas urged the president to break out of his palace echo chamber.

“My suggestion for Prabowo is to cross-check the reports he gets from those closest to him, because obviously he is only being fed information on the good things,” he said.

And in Bekasi, despite feeling let down by rising living costs, Ika said she was not ready to give up on Prabowo’s presidency just yet.

“Maybe these are growing pains for us,” she said. “I’m still optimistic about Prabowo’s leadership and I pray he won’t prove me wrong.”

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore embraces AI for cyber defence, with one caveat: breach transparency
item.description:
Singapore is turning to major technology firms to strengthen its cyber defences, even as it presses them for greater transparency over security breaches – a balancing act facing regional governments as they seek to harness artificial intelligence while guarding against the risks it introduces.

Those risks were highlighted by an AI agent linked to OpenAI that gained unauthorised access to files on an Australian government website earlier this year, raising questions over how quickly companies disclose security incidents as AI systems become more capable and autonomous.

At a summit earlier this month, Singapore launched a refreshed cybersecurity strategy that would see it progressively deploy AI across its cyber defence operations and work with industry partners to accelerate adoption, as it seeks to bolster protection for its critical infrastructure.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore is turning to major technology firms to strengthen its cyber defences, even as it presses them for greater transparency over security breaches – a balancing act facing regional governments as they seek to harness artificial intelligence while guarding against the risks it introduces.

Those risks were highlighted by an AI agent linked to OpenAI that gained unauthorised access to files on an Australian government website earlier this year, raising questions over how quickly companies disclose security incidents as AI systems become more capable and autonomous.

At a summit earlier this month, Singapore launched a refreshed cybersecurity strategy that would see it progressively deploy AI across its cyber defence operations and work with industry partners to accelerate adoption, as it seeks to bolster protection for its critical infrastructure.

The city state would take a “pragmatic” approach to AI adoption, allowing it to choose between the “best available” models, K. Shanmugam, coordinating minister for national security, said during a speech at Singapore International Cyber Week on October 13.

“We will not need to develop our own AI models for every use case. What we really need is the capability to evaluate the best available models and to adapt them to our own needs.”

Anthropic’s Claude is among the models Singapore is exploring as it seeks to strengthen its cyber defences. The US technology firm signed an agreement with Singapore on the sidelines of the summit, setting out areas of AI cooperation, including safety, security, responsible adoption and research into the impact of adoption.

“Singapore has been a leader in responsible AI, with a long track record of investment in model testing and evaluation,” said Anthropic co-founder Benjamin Mann at the signing on October 13, a day before the firm opened its fifth Asia-Pacific office in the city state. Anthropic already has offices in Japan, India, South Korea and Australia.

“With this [memorandum of understanding], we’ll partner with Singapore to help ensure the transition to powerful AI goes well here, across Asia-Pacific, and around the world,” Mann said.

Safety and transparency concerns

The partnerships offer governments access to emerging technologies and technical expertise, but also make transparency and oversight increasingly important as AI systems become more capable and autonomous.

On the sidelines of the event, Shanmugam told the media that Singapore had sought greater transparency from major technology companies, following meetings with firms including Anthropic, Google, Amazon and OpenAI.

“They need to notify us early on when something happens, taking a leaf from the experience in Australia and what happened there,” he said. “Generally, the companies have expressed an attitude of cooperation. But I would say it’s work in progress. It’s something that we are talking to them about.”

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese criticised OpenAI in September over what he called an “unacceptable” breach involving an AI agent that infiltrated a government health website and accessed public and non-public files in June. Albanese accused the firm of taking “way too long” to tell Canberra about the incident.

The San Francisco-headquartered company, which said it learned of the breach in August, apologised and acknowledged that its handling of the incident was “not enough”.

In July, open-source AI platform Hugging Face said it had been hacked by autonomous AI agents. Less than a week later, OpenAI revealed that the “unprecedented cyber incident” was driven by a combination of its models after it lost control of them during a security test.

Singapore had yet to encounter another attack like those attributed to cyberthreat group UNC3886, Shanmugam said. Last year, he revealed that the group had been targeting the city state’s critical infrastructure.

“We haven’t come across another attack like what we have heard from other countries,” he said. “But, you know, also, we don’t know what we don’t know.”

Gatra Priyandita, a senior analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, said closer cooperation with technology companies did not necessarily increase the risk of such breaches and could help mitigate threats through information-sharing and technical evaluation.

He warned, however, that expanding AI use in governance could create new vulnerabilities that existing cybersecurity arrangements might not address.

“AI agents could inadvertently access unauthorised systems, expose sensitive information or be manipulated through malicious inputs,” he said, urging the establishment of clear boundaries on AI autonomy and the use of controlled environments during deployment.

The partnerships could also make it harder to determine who was responsible when disruptions or breaches occurred, Gatra said.

“If an AI system makes a mistake that disrupts government services, who is accountable? The government agency deploying it, the company developing it, or the officials who authorised its use?”

Asean cooperation

Other Southeast Asian nations have also begun drawing on resources from major technology companies to strengthen their cyber defences, but industry experts warn that a widening digital divide could leave smaller states behind.

The Philippines and Google announced the expansion of a multi-year partnership in June aimed at strengthening Manila’s cybersecurity and subsea cable systems to ensure resilient digital connectivity. The country’s cyber-monitoring hub has also deployed Google Cloud’s security framework, which provides AI-driven cyber defence.

Last year, Thailand announced plans to adopt the Google framework, with the aim of enabling its cyberdefence centre to coordinate responses more effectively to online threats targeting government bodies and infrastructure.

But less developed states might lack the technical resources or negotiating leverage to secure timely disclosures from major technology firms through bilateral arrangements, said Gatra, who urged greater cooperation among members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

“Singapore could work with Asean partners to develop common expectations around incident notification and cross-border information-sharing,” he said.

The city state has said it wants to strengthen the bloc’s collective cyber resilience by deepening practical cooperation and capacity building when it assumes the Asean chairmanship next year.

Shanmugam told the media that Asean already had a framework for dealing with cyberthreats but acknowledged that it remained a “work in progress”. The Asean cybersecurity cooperation strategy outlines five pillars, including strengthening readiness, advancing regional policy coordination and building capacity.

“We are all catching up on this issue of AI, and each country is focused on its own issues,” he said. “Asean collectively has some work to do in trying to deal with it together too. So, these are discussions that have to carry on.”

item.title: [SCMP] Novel idea: Thailand, Vietnam take books on the road in reading drive
item.description:
Tran Dai Thang spotted two young people who had picked up their drinks at a pop-up cafe beside his travelling bookstore and were about to leave, so he called them over.

One of them said they did not read books, Thang recalled. But he kept the conversation going and eventually persuaded the visitor to buy a book for 10,000 dong (US$0.40) – heavily discounted from its original price of 45,000 dong.

For Thang, an artist and publisher, the small sale mattered far less than the fact that someone who said they did not read had chosen to pick up a book.
item.content:encoded:
Tran Dai Thang spotted two young people who had picked up their drinks at a pop-up cafe beside his travelling bookstore and were about to leave, so he called them over.

One of them said they did not read books, Thang recalled. But he kept the conversation going and eventually persuaded the visitor to buy a book for 10,000 dong (US$0.40) – heavily discounted from its original price of 45,000 dong.

For Thang, an artist and publisher, the small sale mattered far less than the fact that someone who said they did not read had chosen to pick up a book.

“Who knows, it might be the start of a new habit,” he said.

Thang, 53, is spending a year travelling across Vietnam in a truck with his “Books To Every Home” project, also known as “Roaming Turtle”.

In neighbouring Thailand, a similar book truck named “Somelee” (Cotton) is pursuing an equally ambitious mission: visiting all 77 provinces to take literature beyond Bangkok and the country’s other urban centres.

Their goal goes beyond selling books. By taking their trucks beyond the big cities, the two projects hope to spark curiosity, build connections through storytelling and turn chance roadside encounters into lasting reading habits for people who might otherwise never enter a bookshop.

But bringing books to the provinces comes at a cost – from fuel and accommodation to staff wages – and neither truck can guarantee a crowd at every stop.

‘Come with me for a year’

Thang’s decision to start Roaming Turtle followed the closure of the last branch of his Ca Chep bookshop chain on Ho Chi Minh City’s Vo Van Tan Street in June. Customers were increasingly buying online, he said, and he no longer had the time or focus to run the store.

As its closure approached, a former employee offered to help him sell books.

“Then come with me for a year,” Thang recalled replying.

With no advance plan, the truck set off on July 15 from Ho Chi Minh City on a journey scheduled to last until July 2027. By mid-October, Thang said the Roaming Turtle had reached its 27th stop – Nam Dinh in the Red River Delta – with Thai Binh next on the itinerary.

“The Ca Chep Bookstore may have closed its fixed location, but we don’t want the story of Ca Chep to end there,” he said, noting that Ca Chep means carp in Vietnamese. “Ca Chep only temporarily paused, but never stopped swimming.”

Growing up in mountainous Hoa Binh province, Thang loved reading and drawing. After graduating from the University of Industrial Fine Arts in 1995, he designed book covers at a state-owned publisher before establishing Dong A, his own book company.

On the road, those skills come together. Together with a driver and a sales assistant, Thang introduces readers to Dong A’s titles and hand-draws book covers upon request. Bystanders even help unload boxes, arrange displays and manage sales.

His autobiography has become a particular attraction. He initially brought five copies to sell at each stop, illustrating every cover differently. When those sold out, readers began ordering copies online and bringing them to his truck to be illustrated. In Da Nang, he hand-illustrated 22 covers.

“Each book cover is a unique illustration, connected to a person and a memory from my journey,” he said.

Other encounters have triggered deeper personal memories. In Quy Nhon, he met an unemployed mother who used her limited savings to buy books for her child – a scene that reminded him of his own childhood and mother.

Beyond the capital

In Thailand, the team behind the Somelee book truck began with a similar problem of access.

Bookshops and literary fairs were concentrated in Bangkok and other major urban centres, according to Yasawath Chuthivisitrathikul, a project manager at P.S. Publishing. The publisher was previously affiliated with Somewhere Bookshop and Home Cafe in Bangkok’s Yai district, which closed its doors on Sunday.

“We saw this as an opportunity to reach everyone – both readers and people who have never read books before,” Yasawath said.

Founded by Borisat Pongwat, or “Turk”, Somelee aims to reach regular readers and non-readers alike.

So far, the five-person Somelee team, including Yasawath and Borisat, has visited about 25 venues and plans to cover all 77 Thai provinces within two years.

Jarungdach Phosri, or “Ton”, who drives the truck, said journeys had grown rapidly, from three cafe visits in Nakhon Ratchasima (Korat) to a single tour covering 15 provinces over nearly three months.

Somelee’s inventory initially focused on Thai novels, short stories and poetry, before expanding into children’s literature. However, the team discovered reading preferences varied widely by region.

Jarungdach said some stops showed strong demand for translated literature, while others preferred short stories or Thai works. Unfulfilled reader requests are logged as feedback to guide future stock selection.

“What makes it worthwhile, beyond selling books, is meeting readers,” Jarungdach said. “Some are people we have only spoken to through a keyboard. We get to meet and exchange ideas.”

One reader travelled three hours on a motorcycle from another province just to visit the truck, Yasawath recalled.

At Natit Coffee and Crafts in Nong Khai province, proprietor Raviya Wongsathitana said the cafe connected with Somelee through a local community page on social media while taking part in the first Nongkhai Reading Week.

The cafe hosted activities alongside the truck, including a workshop on making simple handmade books or 'zines. Most visitors were existing customers, Raviya said, although the event also attracted wider local interest.

“I see Somelee as a living mobile bookstore,” she said. “They share stories of their travels and tell people who they’ll meet and where, allowing visitors to be part of an experience beyond simply buying books.”

Keeping things moving

Behind these encounters is a complex mobile supply chain. To keep inventory stocked, Somelee posts book shipments ahead to hotels along their route, while local cafe owners offer travel tips and help arrange accommodation.

Nevertheless, operational costs are a constant burden. Fuel, lodgings and equipment add up quickly, while turnout at remote stops can be unpredictable. Unfavourable weather, particularly heavy rain, can easily disrupt operations for days.

“We want to promote a reading culture, so we started driving out to meet people in the provinces, far from Bangkok,” Yasawath said. “Both readers and people who have never read books before are welcome, and we continue to stay in touch with them online.”

In Vietnam, Thang financed his truck with a bank loan of around 1.2 billion dong (US$46,360). Sales cover everyday living and operating expenses on the road, while Dong A handles staff salaries and vehicle loan repayments.

Both projects sometimes lower prices to keep books accessible. Somelee offers reductions of 15 to 30 per cent – sometimes exceeding 50 per cent for students – while Thang focuses sales in cities so he can give books away for free at schools in more remote locations.

For Thang, a year on the road has sharpened his approach to publishing.

“Making good, beautiful books remains important, but prices must allow them to reach people with different means,” he said. “People who truly want to read should not have to give up a book they love just because they lack money.”

item.title: [SCMP] What will China’s fifth plenum mean for the root-and-branch corruption drive?
item.description:
Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. In the third part of this series, William Zheng and Alcott Wei examine how the fight against corruption is shaping the party’s future.

When China’s political elites gather for a key conclave in Beijing later this month, the increasingly empty auditorium will speak loudly to the event’s theme – the ruling Communist Party’s strict self-discipline and its never-ending fight against corruption.

The fifth plenum of the party’s 20th Central Committee will also serve as an important venue for the political momentum of next year’s quinquennial leadership transition and ratify disciplinary verdicts against dozens of fallen cadres.
item.content:encoded:
Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. In the third part of this series, William Zheng and Alcott Wei examine how the fight against corruption is shaping the party’s future.

When China’s political elites gather for a key conclave in Beijing later this month, the increasingly empty auditorium will speak loudly to the event’s theme – the ruling Communist Party’s strict self-discipline and its never-ending fight against corruption.

The fifth plenum of the party’s 20th Central Committee will also serve as an important venue for the political momentum of next year’s quinquennial leadership transition and ratify disciplinary verdicts against dozens of fallen cadres.

The four-day closed-door meeting comes roughly one year ahead of the 21st National Party Congress in late 2027 and is poised to formalise one of the most extensive turnovers of senior party, state and military personnel in modern Chinese political history.

According to a tally by the South China Morning Post, 20 full and seven alternate members are facing corruption investigations and await formal expulsion from the Central Committee.

The SCMP’s research also shows that about 35 full and alternate members who did not appear at last year’s plenum have made no public appearances in the current cycle, indicating potential trouble for their political careers.

The fifth plenum, from October 26 to 29, is also set to endorse a key document outlining a long list of measures by the party to maintain internal discipline, ensure political loyalty and fight corruption.

Xie Maosong, a senior researcher at the National Institute of Strategic Studies at Tsinghua University, noted that this focus on the party’s governance came seven years after a similar document that zeroed in on modernising the nation’s governing capacity.

“In 2019, the focus was on how to run the government and manage society better. Now, the focus is on the party ruling China,” Xie said.

“The reason is simple: China’s overall governance starts from the ruling party. The party’s successful and effective self-governance is a prerequisite for China’s long-term governance.”

Cutting down sick trees

As the countdown to 2027 begins, the fifth plenum is set to see a fresh push to cement better party governance control and ensure uncompromised loyalty ahead of the next party congress.

Beijing issued a series of blunt warnings via the script of a January speech by President Xi Jinping, published in the party’s top theoretical journal Qiushi on October 15. It was the first time some of the details had been made public.

In the speech, Xi argued that internal regulations had long been too vague. He demanded systemic reforms to prevent “using a cattle pen to confine a cat” – a traditional idiom for lax rules that fail to restrain misbehaviour.

Emphasising that corruption remained widespread and prone to recurring within the party, Xi pledged to uproot or cut down “sick trees” wherever necessary.

The metaphor, from ancient Chinese poetry, suggests that new life will flourish beyond decaying trees, with the new replacing the old.

Fighting corruption is also a major focus of “Xi Jinping Thought on Party Building”, a new addition to the paramount leader’s expanding theoretical canon that was made public just months ahead of the plenum.

Officially introduced to the party in June, the political doctrine is aimed at building a “Marxist party with long-term governance”.

Besides the relentless drive to ensure officials “do not have the audacity, opportunity or desire to commit corruption”, the doctrine calls for the party’s centralised leadership to avoid divisions that will weaken the party.

It insists on comprehensive and rigorous self-governance to enforce discipline and continuous self-reform across all levels, as well as solid political and theoretical bases to enhance loyalty and avoid weakening the party’s ideological foundations.

The doctrine also demands a robust organisational system to train and select high-calibre officials who strictly follow party directives.

According to Xie from Tsinghua, strict and comprehensive party governance is a “key pillar” of Xi’s party building thought, especially at the juncture of the transition period for leading officials.

“With the party’s self-governance system in place, the next batch of leading cadres will have a unified code of conduct and they can have a cleaner start,” he said.

A Nanjing-based analyst said that while Xi’s sustained, hard-hitting efforts may address the symptoms, the plenum’s agenda suggested he was willing to go deeper and wider to address the causes of China’s chronic corruption problems, but in his own way.

The political analyst, who asked not to be named as his school required him to seek approval when speaking to media, detailed some of the opportunities for corruption that the country still faced.

“In China, areas like promotion of officials, public projects, military equipment acquisition and natural resources development remain highly lucrative black boxes in which one or a few key persons can dictate the decisions involving billions of dollars, despite the relentless anti-corruption fight,” he said.

“While Western analysts would suggest the scrutiny of the public and the media to be part of the equation, it will not be the party’s priority as Xi firmly believes strengthening the party’s self-governance is sufficient.”

Expected absences

At the 20th party congress in October 2022, 205 full Central Committee members were appointed, along with 171 alternate members. Four years later, the number of empty seats at next week’s conclave could highlight an extraordinary level of attrition.

The anti-corruption campaign has taken a heavy toll on the committee, with 35 of its full members either under investigation or stripped of their seats in the National People’s Congress, China’s top legislature.

The precedent for mass adjustments was set during last year’s fourth plenum, which confirmed the expulsion of 14 full and alternate members – including former senior generals He Weidong and Miao Hua – and elevated 11 alternates to full membership.

The party is set to appoint a cascade of replacements to the vacant or compromised seats as it deals with the large backlog of the remaining 21 full members and seven alternate members who are facing investigation but are yet to be expelled from the committee.

The vacancies reflect a sprawling anti-corruption and political disciplinary campaign that is cutting across both party and government systems as well as the People’s Liberation Army.

The SCMP’s tally shows that Xi’s anti-corruption machinery clearly accelerated after 2020, when 19 “tigers” or senior officials were caught. The number of top officials facing investigation has been on a rising trend, reaching a new high of 65 last year.

Most officials in the group, supervised directly by the party’s top anti-graft body, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI), belonged to a pool of officials known as “centrally managed cadres”, meaning they typically ranked at deputy ministerial level or above.

A smaller number held slightly lower ranks but occupied sensitive positions in important sectors.

Unlike their subordinates, who are managed and supervised by local branches of the party’s organisation and disciplinary agency, senior officials are under the direct management of the Central Organisation Department, its top personnel body.

The Central Committee has yet to confirm the expulsion of a slew of prominent former ministerial and regional chiefs occupying full member seats who were snared in corruption investigations over the past few months or are facing legal procedures.

Among them are Jiangxi’s former party chief Yi Lianhong and provincial governor Ye Jianchun, former Inner Mongolia party secretary Sun Shaocheng and government chief Wang Lixia.

They include Hu Henghua, who was mayor of Chongqing, Lan Tianli, former Guangxi government chairman, Yi Huiman, who chaired China’s securities regulator, and emergency management minister Wang Xiangxi.

Several lower-ranked alternate members are facing investigations but have yet to be formally removed: ex-mayor of Shenzhen Qin Weizhong, as well as the former Xian and Hefei party bosses Fang Hongwei and Fei Gaoyun, respectively, and ex-railway chief Fei Dongbin.

And with just a week to go before the plenum, Xia Maolin, vice mayor of Beijing and an alternate member of the Central Committee, has come under investigation.

Bijie party secretary Wu Shenghua, who was expelled from the party and dismissed from public duties in January, became a target of name-and-shame campaigns in September when Beijing made him an exemplary case of failing to address local government debts incurred by predecessors.

Missing generals

There was even more turbulence in the PLA, where the anti-corruption and political rectification campaign has reached the pinnacle of its command structure, the Central Military Commission (CMC).

The CMC’s former deputy chairman Zhang Youxia and member Liu Zhenli were both accused of severe political disloyalty and factionalism.

A broad swathe of CMC, theatre-command and service-branch chiefs holding Central Committee seats were also implicated. Many were expelled from the national legislature before their term ended, usually a sign of serious career setback.

They included Wang Peng, who was director of the CMC’s training department, its political and legal affairs committee chief, Wang Renhua, as well as the head of equipment development, Xu Xueqiang.

Logistics Support Department chief Zhang Lin, General Office director Zhong Shaojun and Ju Qiansheng, who commanded the PLA’s Strategic Support Force, were also removed from their positions.

Other senior expulsions included ground forces commander Li Qiaoming and four political commissars: Li Wei, from the information support force, Western Theatre Command’s Li Fengbiao, Zhang Hongbing from the armed police and the air force’s Guo Puxiao.

Wang Kangping, the former commander of the Joint Logistics Support Force who was removed from the national legislature in June, is the only uniformed alternate member waiting for the Central Committee’s decision.

The vanished ones

There are also civilian officials who have disappeared from the public eye without explanation, which could suggest some career hiccups or that they have quietly stepped down from their positions.

Among the most prominent abrupt departures was ex-agriculture minister Han Jun, who was unexpectedly removed from his position in April.

Also noteworthy was the sudden exit of former international liaison department head Liu Jianchao, who vanished from public view following an overseas trip last summer. He was subsequently replaced by Liu Haixing.

Two critical positions bridging Beijing’s military-civilian fusion statecraft were left vacant with the departure of Jin Zhuanglong, former industry and information technology minister, and Lei Fanpei, who chaired state-owned conglomerate China State Shipbuilding Corporation. Beijing has made no announcements about their status.

The replacement dynamic

Under party statutes, vacancies on the Central Committee are filled by alternate members, who are ranked based on votes received at the previous congress.

However, recent sessions indicate that promotions are no longer strictly aligned with the ranking of alternate members and could even become the latest indicator of further downfall.

During last year’s fourth plenum, as alternate members were promoted to fill vacancies, several were bypassed – including Wang Jiayi, Shi Yugang and Fang Hongwei, with the latter subsequently expelled from the party.

Any candidate skipped in the line-up at this year’s event is likely to face intense scrutiny regarding their political standing.

The round of replacements in the previous plenum did not strictly follow the established ranking of alternate members. Instead, four military and three civilian alternate members were “skipped over”.

The military alternates were Wang Liyan, then-deputy commander of PLA Rocket Force, Wang Kangping, who commanded the Joint Logistics Support Force, Fang Yongxiang, ex-head of the CMC’s General Office, and Shi Zhenglu from Northern Theatre Command.

The skipped-over civilian officials were the then deputy education minister Wang Jiayi, former Xian party secretary Fang Hongwei and Shi Yugang, deputy chief of the provincial political advisory body in Yunnan.

Several of the skipped alternate members were later officially confirmed to be facing disciplinary investigations.

Wang Kangping was stripped of his seat in the national legislative body while Xian’s Fang Hongwei was detained by the CCDI just days after the fourth plenum and expelled from the party and public office in July.

item.title: [SCMP] The West’s double standard on global unrest
item.description:
In the early days of the student protests in France, mainstream Western media took the protesters’ claims about poor school facilities and declining resources at face value. Only when the violence spread across the country, and to some of its European neighbours, did people begin to ask whether deeper causes were at play.

Leftists blame social problems, from the cost-of-living pressures linked to the war in Ukraine to rising unemployment, especially among the young. Right-wing critics blame Islamists, antifascists, radical environmentalists and, of course, immigrants.

A Financial Times report said: “EU regulators are examining possible foreign interference and disinformation campaigns around the French riots and outbursts of violence and looting in other European countries. According to security officials, pro-Russian and far-right social media accounts linked to previous disinformation campaigns have spread violent videos in an attempt to sow more chaos. Iran and Algeria are also suspected of being behind some of the messaging, experts said.”
item.content:encoded:
In the early days of the student protests in France, mainstream Western media took the protesters’ claims about poor school facilities and declining resources at face value. Only when the violence spread across the country, and to some of its European neighbours, did people begin to ask whether deeper causes were at play.

Leftists blame social problems, from the cost-of-living pressures linked to the war in Ukraine to rising unemployment, especially among the young. Right-wing critics blame Islamists, antifascists, radical environmentalists and, of course, immigrants.

A Financial Times report said: “EU regulators are examining possible foreign interference and disinformation campaigns around the French riots and outbursts of violence and looting in other European countries. According to security officials, pro-Russian and far-right social media accounts linked to previous disinformation campaigns have spread violent videos in an attempt to sow more chaos. Iran and Algeria are also suspected of being behind some of the messaging, experts said.”

As I follow the unrest unfolding in Europe, I find it uncanny how closely it parallels the 2019 anti-government riots in Hong Kong. Such mass disturbances almost always have many causes, including underlying social malaise and long-standing grievances. There is no single causal factor, only, perhaps, a single trigger.

In Hong Kong, the trigger was a proposed extradition bill. The protests then broadened into demands for immediate democratic transition. I, and many others, have extensively documented foreign government and semi-government involvement. The players included the US Congress, the US National Endowment for Democracy, the National Democratic Institute for International Affairs, the US Agency for Global Media and the Open Technology Fund.

In fact, we didn’t have to dig much. They were rather proud of their handiwork, with some testifying in Congress that they could not continue because of funding cuts by the first Trump administration.

To this day, many Western media outlets still claim it was all a fight for democracy, later suppressed by the national security law.

I don’t deny that democratic demands played a significant role in the 2019 riots. But they were not the sole or even the underlying cause, just as poor facilities alone cannot explain the social breakdown we are witnessing in France, even though they first led high school students into the streets.

Yet mainstream Western media instinctively reach for mono-causal explanations, usually a struggle for democracy, however they define it, when mass unrest breaks out in non-Western countries. Only when similar breakdowns happen in allied or friendly countries do they allow for nuance and deeper social analysis.

One reason is, of course, simple ignorance of those other societies. “Democracy” is the one-size-fits-all explanation when you need to write a column about an unfriendly country you know nothing about.

I recently watched an amusing French TV news programme in which the moderator asked professional pundits to name two other living Chinese persons besides Xi Jinping, and they all had difficulty doing so. It was reminiscent of George W. Bush, while running for president, being embarrassingly unable to identify foreign leaders.

Ukraine was similar to Hong Kong in this respect. The so-called Maidan revolution of 2014 is seen in the West, especially now, as a democratic revolution. Never mind that the governments that followed were as corrupt as the pro-Moscow one before. The rest of the world mostly sees it as a coup, or is at least neutral about it.

At the very least, it triggered the Russian aggression that has continued ever since. Many Ukrainians may now be rethinking the wisdom of poking the bear and – for heaven’s sake – of trying to join Nato.

A recorded telephone conversation between Victoria Nuland, then US assistant secretary of state, and Geoffrey Pyatt, then US ambassador to Ukraine, was leaked in February 2014. They discussed political strategy, which leaders to support and the composition of a post-Yanukovych government amid the Euromaidan protests. In the leak, she famously said, “F*** the EU”, signalling a readiness to act unilaterally.

Indeed, American scholars such as John Mearsheimer and Jeffrey Sachs have argued that the 2014 uprising was a coup. Of course, everyone knows there were many causes. But everyone has an ideological axe to grind.

I, for one, would argue that the world would be more peaceful today without the 2014 coup. But to each their own.

While ignorance and strategic opportunism helped explain how social unrest is portrayed differently in mainstream Western media, the biggest motivation is probably ideological.

What happened to Hong Kong now seems almost comical, though quite tragic for the Hongkongers who left

Between 2010 and 2020, data-tracking projects recorded nearly 7,000 protests across 153 countries, at least 900 of them major, each involving more than 10,000 participants.

Naturally, Western pundits and politicians, especially those in Washington, would focus on those affecting antagonistic China and Russia. Exploiting internal opposition and unrest in unfriendly countries has long been Washington’s default playbook, followed sometimes, but not always, by its Western counterparts.

But it is short-sighted. An unstable Hong Kong or China would be terrible for the world economy and, by extension, for the US. A successor state to the current Putin regime – should it collapse from losing the war in Ukraine – would probably be neither pro-Western nor democratic, but even more bent on revanchism.

What happened to Hong Kong now seems almost comical, though quite tragic for the Hongkongers who left. Several Western governments bought into their own propaganda and, from 2020, offered them exits, as if they were fleeing persecution like Ukrainians and Yemenis. Many have had difficulty adjusting to their new lives; some have returned to Hong Kong.

Those same Western countries are now beset by anti-migrant populism, resulting in a brutal migrant crackdown, as in the US, or the rollback of easy access in the migrant application process, as in Canada and Australia.

Meanwhile, some Hong Kong and mainland officials remain under US sanctions. Perhaps Beijing should sanction some top officials in Washington and Paris for their own brutal domestic police and military crackdowns.

Of course, China has never been so petty and ridiculous.

item.title: [SCMP] Gulf economies accelerate diversification as recession looms over Iran war
item.description:
Before the outbreak of the war triggered by the US-Israeli attack on Iran in February, the Gulf monarchies were living the prosperity dream that was the envy of the world.

Their hydrocarbon-fuelled economies were glitzy oases of growth, inoculated from the conflict in Gaza that had rocked other parts of the Middle East for several years.

Underpinned by decades-old US security guarantees and conflict mediation by billionaire sheikhs, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar cultivated images as peaceful lands of opportunity as they invested staggering amounts of money in economic diversification programmes.
item.content:encoded:
Before the outbreak of the war triggered by the US-Israeli attack on Iran in February, the Gulf monarchies were living the prosperity dream that was the envy of the world.

Their hydrocarbon-fuelled economies were glitzy oases of growth, inoculated from the conflict in Gaza that had rocked other parts of the Middle East for several years.

Underpinned by decades-old US security guarantees and conflict mediation by billionaire sheikhs, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar cultivated images as peaceful lands of opportunity as they invested staggering amounts of money in economic diversification programmes.

Backed by sovereign wealth funds with trillions of dollars invested mostly in the West, these leading states of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) embarked on transformative programmes to reposition their economies amid the global transition away from oil and gas. Similar diversification initiatives were also happening in Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain, the other three GCC members.

Such a shift towards long-term economic stability is important in maintaining the political legitimacy of the Gulf monarchies in the eyes of their burgeoning young populations, especially amid mounting public anger at the carnage in Gaza, according to analysts.

The GCC states, as well as other Muslim-majority governments such as Pakistan and Turkey, eventually persuaded US President Donald Trump to end the Gaza war in October 2025, renewing optimism about the Gulf economies.

However, everything changed soon after the Gaza ceasefire, when Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu managed to convince Trump to go to war against Iran.

Rather than just retaliating against Israel, Iran has also vented its fury against the GCC states, attacking energy infrastructure, airports and ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz.

With Trump weighing his options, including both another military escalation and a politically inconclusive end to the war with Iran after midterm congressional elections on November 5, uncertainty reigns in the Gulf region.

The eruption of war between Saudi Arabia and Tehran’s Houthi rebel allies in Yemen last month has exacerbated these anxieties.

Driven by necessity, GCC governments have unveiled plans to stabilise their economies. The two largest in the bloc – Saudi Arabia and the UAE – are on the verge of a potential technical recession caused by the Iran war, while Qatar is already in a recession.

In the second quarter of this year, Saudi Arabia’s economy – the largest in the GCC – fell by 4.8 per cent from 3 per cent growth in the first quarter. The UAE’s economy – the Gulf’s logistical hub – decreased by 2.1 per cent from an expansion of 3 per cent over the same period.

Qatar’s economic outlook worsened, with its GDP declining by 15.7 per cent in the second quarter, accelerating from a drop of 7 per cent in the first quarter.

According to the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) projections published on October 13, the UAE is expected to record a 3.9 per cent drop in its GDP in 2026 from a pre-war forecast of 3.1 per cent growth, while Saudi Arabia is projected to fall by 3.3 per cent this year from an earlier predicted 4.6 per cent growth.

Bahrain, Kuwait and Qatar are set to record double-digit GDP contractions in 2026.

Like the IMF, the World Bank has forecast the GCC economies to rebound in 2027 if hostilities end this year and unhindered passage through the Strait of Hormuz is restored by next March.

Tim Callen, a former chief of the IMF’s GCC division, expected the Gulf states to step up their economic diversification plans.

The development of new industries would move ahead with some adjustments, including “a new focus on diversifying and better protecting energy and transport infrastructure”, Callen said.

Karen Young, a senior research scholar at Columbia University’s Centre on Global Energy Policy in New York, said Gulf governments would continue to prioritise investments in natural gas production and its export in liquefied form, as well as the acquisition of such assets overseas.

They would also focus on other “essential” areas such as more localised defence manufacturing, AI and other technologies.

Young said the diversification of the power sector in the GCC to include nuclear and renewables would be crucial to reviving its economies, while other sectors like tourism could continue to come under pressure.

Sovereign wealth funds like Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, the UAE’s L’imad and the Oman Investment Authority would provide much of the funding and impetus needed to get the Gulf economies back on track, according to analysts.

“Those funds have already demonstrated a propensity to play a greater domestic role. But these funds can’t do it all alone,” said Robert Mogielnicki, founder of Paris-based Polisphere Advisory.

The involvement of foreign partners would be critical because of the considerable investments that would be needed to revive and grow the GCC economies, Mogielnicki said.

Analysts predict GCC members will spend hundreds of billions of dollars to expand infrastructure across major sectors in the coming years as part of their economic transformation.

One such initiative is a planned cross-GCC oil pipeline bypassing the Strait of Hormuz to be co-funded by all six members, which a report published by Rice University’s Baker Institute for Public Policy estimated earlier this year to cost US$55 billion.

HSBC, Hong Kong’s biggest lender, recently projected the value of ongoing infrastructure projects in the UAE at US$190 billion.

The government of Dubai – one of the country’s seven emirates and its business centre – announced a US$572 billion pipeline of projects on October 13, including a massive new suburb and the construction of the world’s biggest airport.

Mognielicki said the GCC’s ambitious infrastructure roll-out was both expensive and complex. “For the moment, most Gulf governments see a compelling justification for paying the price.”

Callen said that despite these undertakings, it was far from certain whether the confidence of foreign investors in the GCC economies could rebound any time soon.

Investors would be assessing the post-war demand for both energy and non-oil goods and services from the Gulf states, as well as the outlook of their tourism, conference, logistics and aviation sectors, according to Callen.

“This is a very complex strategic project both because diversifying away from oil is anyway extremely difficult and to add to that now is the regional uncertainty,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Vietnam’s 2045 vision faces a reality check as capital squeeze tests growth ambitions
item.description:
Since coming to power in August 2024, General Secretary To Lam has emphasised his ambition to turn Vietnam into a high-income country by 2045. Towards this goal, a National Assembly resolution in April set a target of average annual growth of 10 per cent through 2030, with infrastructure building expected to serve as a major growth engine.

However, Vietnam is struggling to mobilise sufficient capital to finance this ambitious agenda because of both domestic and external constraints. Hanoi therefore faces a choice: align its growth targets with the capital it can raise at a reasonable cost or accept considerably greater economic risks.

The projects illustrate the scale of the challenge. The North–South high-speed railway is projected to cost US$67 billion, while the two Ninh Thuan nuclear power plants, with a combined capacity of 4,000 megawatts, are expected to cost at least US$22 billion. Financing Vietnam’s high-growth plans for 2026–2030 is estimated to require about US$297 billion annually, or 40 per cent of nominal GDP.
item.content:encoded:
Since coming to power in August 2024, General Secretary To Lam has emphasised his ambition to turn Vietnam into a high-income country by 2045. Towards this goal, a National Assembly resolution in April set a target of average annual growth of 10 per cent through 2030, with infrastructure building expected to serve as a major growth engine.

However, Vietnam is struggling to mobilise sufficient capital to finance this ambitious agenda because of both domestic and external constraints. Hanoi therefore faces a choice: align its growth targets with the capital it can raise at a reasonable cost or accept considerably greater economic risks.

The projects illustrate the scale of the challenge. The North–South high-speed railway is projected to cost US$67 billion, while the two Ninh Thuan nuclear power plants, with a combined capacity of 4,000 megawatts, are expected to cost at least US$22 billion. Financing Vietnam’s high-growth plans for 2026–2030 is estimated to require about US$297 billion annually, or 40 per cent of nominal GDP.

Domestic banks carry most of this burden. Bank lending accounts for about 83 per cent of Vietnam’s financing mix, compared with 13 per cent for bonds and 4 per cent for equity. By late June, outstanding credit reached 19,970 trillion Vietnamese dong (US$760 billion), up 18.1 per cent year on year. Credit expanded by 7.41 per cent in the first half, while deposits grew by only 5.02 per cent, pushing the loan-to-deposit ratio to about 112 per cent.

Banks have responded by competing more aggressively for funding. Posted six- to 12-month deposit rates are generally 5.0 per cent to 6.5 per cent, in line with the State Bank of Vietnam’s efforts to keep rates low. In practice, however, depositors are reportedly offered effective yields of 8.5 per cent to 11.0 per cent through private negotiations.

Scarce credit is also distributed unevenly. In June, 18 major projects requiring 752 trillion dong were exempted from standard credit-growth limits. Developers include large and well-connected conglomerates like Vingroup, Sun Group and Masterise. By contrast, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which account for 98 per cent of Vietnamese firms, receive only about 20 per cent of bank credit. They face lending rates of 10 per cent to 12 per cent, while 93.5 per cent of loans require collateral. Yet SMEs account for most employment and household incomes.

The strain is already visible: new business registrations fell 13.9 per cent year on year in July, while completed dissolutions rose by 270 per cent. This writer’s recent field trip to Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City revealed that many SMEs are struggling because they cannot access the credit needed to sustain or expand operations. This is happening despite stellar headline GDP growth of 9 per cent in the first nine months of 2026.

High interest rates have brought the property market close to a standstill. Average home-loan rates have reached 14 per cent to 16 per cent, while the number of residential property transactions nationwide fell by 36 per cent year on year in the first half. This has cooled speculation and reduced the risk of a property bubble.

However, the high rates have also created new vulnerabilities. Developers depend heavily on property sales for cash flow, while their average bond issuance rate has risen to 11.4 per cent, and their debt-to-equity ratio has climbed to 74 per cent, against an average of 54 per cent during 2022 to 2025. Disrupted cash flows increase the risk that repayment difficulties will translate into higher bank bad debt. As China’s experience illustrates, a prolonged property slowdown can also weigh on household confidence, consumption, public finance and economic performance.

The logical response is to look abroad, but external options remain limited. The international financial centres in Da Nang and Ho Chi Minh City, launched in January and February, have issued certificates to only a few dozen investors, while credit-rating requirements exclude some major foreign banks. Sovereign bond issuance is constrained by Vietnam’s credit rating, which is one notch below investment grade from S&P and Fitch and two from Moody’s.

The government aims to achieve investment-grade status by 2030, which analysts estimate could cut borrowing costs by as much as 1.5 percentage points. But that benefit would come too late for many projects beginning now.

International capital markets are also becoming less welcoming to Vietnamese firms and banks. The US 10-year Treasury yield is about 5 per cent, while the Federal Reserve raised its target range to 3.75 per cent to 4 per cent in September. Surging global demand for capital, particularly to finance AI and related technologies, is intensifying competition for funding. Meanwhile, geopolitical pressures, including the US-led war against Iran and the Russia-Ukraine conflict, are pushing up the risk premium that emerging markets like Vietnam must pay.

Looking ahead

There are three key implications here.

First, Vietnam may need to align its growth ambitions with what it can finance at a reasonable cost, to ease funding pressures and put expansion on a more sustainable footing.

Second, if Hanoi maintains its targets while domestic interest rates remain high, the wider economy will bear the strain, with SMEs likely to feel it first. High borrowing costs could produce more closures and discourage private investment, leaving the economy more fragile even as infrastructure spending sustains headline GDP growth.

Third, Vietnam will increasingly need international funding, creating opportunities for foreign banks and other credit institutions. But greater reliance on debt carries risks. Much public infrastructure does not generate direct returns sufficient to service the borrowing used to fund it. In an environment of prolonged high interest rates, excessive debt-financed investment could weaken the repayment capacity of both the government and Vietnamese enterprises.

Vietnam can still build the roads, railways, airports and energy infrastructure it needs, but not necessarily at the pace envisaged. Ambition must be matched by affordable capital, and the two are increasingly moving apart. A more calibrated growth target would reduce financing pressures and the risk of a costlier debt adjustment later.

Le Hong Hiep is a Senior Fellow and Coordinator of the Vietnam Studies Programme at ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. This article was first published by ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute’s commentary website fulcrum.sg.

item.title: [SCMP] China’s humanoid robots hunt for work in South Korea as Seoul bets on physical AI
item.description:
This article was first published by The Korea Times in a partnership with the South China Morning Post.

Chinese humanoid robot makers are accelerating efforts to gain a foothold in South Korea, moving beyond dance performances and showroom displays to factory trials and commercial deployments, as Seoul ramps up investment in physical artificial intelligence.

A growing number of Chinese robotics companies – including Hong Kong-listed UBTech Robotics, start-up Anyverse Dynamics, Shanghai-based AgiBot and leading robot maker Unitree Robotics – have flexed their muscles or announced projects in South Korea this year.
item.content:encoded:
This article was first published by The Korea Times in a partnership with the South China Morning Post.

Chinese humanoid robot makers are accelerating efforts to gain a foothold in South Korea, moving beyond dance performances and showroom displays to factory trials and commercial deployments, as Seoul ramps up investment in physical artificial intelligence.

A growing number of Chinese robotics companies – including Hong Kong-listed UBTech Robotics, start-up Anyverse Dynamics, Shanghai-based AgiBot and leading robot maker Unitree Robotics – have flexed their muscles or announced projects in South Korea this year.

“China’s new generation of robot companies has global DNA and naturally looks overseas, and South Korea is one of the most important markets in the Asia-Pacific region,” said Ethan Qi, an associate director covering robotics at Counterpoint Research. The lack of locally built humanoid robots available at scale had created an opening for Chinese suppliers, he added.

Commercial foothold

Representatives of Galaxy Robot Park, a robot-themed entertainment venue in Seoul, agreed to buy UBTech’s lifelike U1 model after seeing its debut in Shenzhen in June, according to Sean Qin, overseas head of the company’s commercial robots division.

The robot, designed with a female appearance and standing 1.68 metres tall, cost around 170,000 yuan (US$25,000) and was delivered to the park last month, Qin said. UBTech entered the South Korean market as early as 2019 and had since sold more than 10,000 robots to dozens of corporate and government customers, he added.

In July, UBTech, headquartered in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, also announced plans to trial humanoid robots on a South Korean automotive parts production line with local partner Duksan JM Robotics and parts maker Ajin Industrial. Several UBTech models were undergoing on-site operational tests in the country, Qin said, without providing details.

“As a manufacturing powerhouse, South Korea already makes extensive use of robotic arms, autonomous mobile robots and other conventional systems,” he said. “The next step is to help workers become more productive in tasks that demand greater flexibility. That makes Korea a key market for UBTech and for humanoids more broadly.”

Zhang Yufeng, founder and CEO of Anyverse Dynamics, who previously worked with SK Telecom and Hyundai Motor, said South Korea was “one of our most important overseas markets”.

The Beijing-based start-up teamed up with South Korean coffee chain Hollys at the World Robot Conference in Beijing in August to test robots that serve drinks, clear tables and reset seats. The robots were currently undergoing trial operations at a cafe in Beijing, Zhang said.

South Korea ranked as China’s third-largest export market by value for “intelligent bionic robots” in the first nine months of 2026, behind the United States and Japan, according to Chinese customs data. Exports to South Korea totalled US$19.99 million, or 9.7 per cent of the US$206.95 million China shipped globally. China exported 16,559 robots to 108 countries and regions under the customs category, introduced this year, which covers humanoids and robot dogs.

Eight of China’s 10 top-selling humanoid robot makers had been testing the waters in South Korea through product certification, trademark filings and sales channels, according to a report by industry research platform Labsdeep that was cited by Electronic Times this month.

“We plan to begin trials in Korean cafes and other commercial service settings in the fourth quarter, before expanding into manufacturing,” Zhang said, noting that the company had been working on product certification for the market.

Seoul’s stringent Korea Certification requirements prompted UBTech to adapt its communications modules and radio frequency settings for local use, Qin said.

Factories as main testing ground

China’s robotics boom has spawned a wave of unicorn firms over the past two years, some of which have already begun shipping products at scale, backed by an extensive supply chain at home. Their push to find commercial applications to justify the investment and hype surrounding humanoid robots coincides with South Korea’s drive to deploy physical AI across its industrial base.

Seoul is prioritising the technology to strengthen manufacturing as its working-age population shrinks and potential economic growth slows. The government has proposed 3.1 trillion won (US$2.3 billion) in physical AI funding for 2027, more than triple this year’s level.

The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources’ Manufacturing AI Transformation programme, dubbed M.AX, supports AI adoption and factory trials involving robots, including humanoids, with a target of 500 AI factories by 2030. The ministry has budgeted 1.1 trillion won for AI transformation this year.

Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said in August that the government would support factories operated by AI and robots, helping South Korea become “a global leader in manufacturing AI transformation by 2030”.

South Korea’s industrial heavyweights are also moving quickly.

LG Electronics is building its Data Factory in Seoul to train robots for industrial and household applications, while testing robots on its own production lines. Samsung Electronics established its Robotics eXperience division in July, targeting manufacturing before expanding into homes and retail. A bipedal robot designed to operate round the clock in manufacturing and logistics could debut at the CES annual consumer electronics trade show in Las Vegas in January 2027, JoongAng Ilbo reported on Tuesday.

Hyundai Motor Group has begun training Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoids at its factory campus in the US state of Georgia, ahead of a planned 2028 deployment in manufacturing. Doosan Robotics has unveiled AI-powered sanding and palletising systems and is developing robot-control software, with support from Nvidia.

South Korea’s start-up ecosystem is also drawing fresh capital. AI and robotics accounted for 45 per cent of third-quarter investments tracked by The VC, a local start-up and venture capital investment database platform. Within physical AI, funding is flowing to robot makers as well as start-ups developing foundational models for robots and supplying training data.

The country offered a broad range of potential deployment sites in carmaking, shipbuilding and semiconductor manufacturing, Counterpoint’s Qi said. But gaining access was difficult for Chinese suppliers because they needed local customers willing to participate in proof-of-concept trials.

Partners and rivals

The growing presence of Chinese firms has stirred political debate. At a parliamentary audit on October 6, lawmaker Lee Jeong-heon of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea brought robots from China’s Unitree and AgiBot to challenge the government over South Korea’s competitiveness in physical AI.

Lawmaker Ahn Cheol-soo of the main opposition People Power Party questioned whether the robots had undergone security checks and accused the National Assembly of providing a stage for Chinese technology.

Deputy Prime Minister Bae Kyung-hoon, who is also the Science and Information and Communications Technology minister, urged South Korea to ramp up physical AI investment and development, pointing to China’s growing deployment of humanoids.

“China is also deploying more humanoid robots in the field and collecting data,” he said during a Physical AI Tech Week round table in Seoul on October 13, according to news outlet MoneyToday.

Bae questioned whether Korea’s plans were bold enough and called for higher targets to avoid regretting insufficient investment in the future. Companies also needed to shoulder greater responsibility because the government could not support every initiative, he said.

Park Young-hoon, head of the Korea Trade-Investment Promotion Agency’s Shenzhen office, said he also saw room for cooperation.

“Companies need to explore new business opportunities using Shenzhen’s local supply chains and innovation capabilities while competing with Chinese technology companies,” he told local media outlet Newspim in October.

Anyverse Dynamics’ Zhang said he saw the two countries’ industrial strengths as “highly complementary”. South Korea combined global leadership in advanced manufacturing with a capacity for AI innovation, while China offered a comprehensive supply chain, a deep pool of engineering and AI talent, and rapid product iteration, he said.

For UBTech’s Qin, policies favouring domestic companies have not deterred Korean customers from considering Chinese suppliers. “The Korean customers we have dealt with are open to working with Chinese robot makers,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] China’s private firms are fighting for profits. Are regulations adding to the burden?
item.description:
Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. This month’s edition, the fifth plenum, is attracting even more attention as the world’s second-largest economy takes on a more prominent role in global affairs. In the second part of this series, Emma Ma speaks to businesspeople as they adapt to stepped up regulatory enforcement and deal with other economic issues the government has pledged to solve.

Six years after China Evergrande Group started to show signs of insolvency – the beginning of a downward spiral that would eventually lead to the property developer’s bankruptcy and its founder sentenced to life in prison – Zhu Yinfen is still waiting to recover money the company owes to her Shanghai firm.

“Evergrande still owes us 500,000 yuan (US$74,885),” Zhu said, adding that the worst problem was not the unpaid debt, but the many other clients who routinely failed to settle their bills on time.
item.content:encoded:
Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. This month’s edition, the fifth plenum, is attracting even more attention as the world’s second-largest economy takes on a more prominent role in global affairs. In the second part of this series, Emma Ma speaks to businesspeople as they adapt to stepped up regulatory enforcement and deal with other economic issues the government has pledged to solve.

Six years after China Evergrande Group started to show signs of insolvency – the beginning of a downward spiral that would eventually lead to the property developer’s bankruptcy and its founder sentenced to life in prison – Zhu Yinfen is still waiting to recover money the company owes to her Shanghai firm.

“Evergrande still owes us 500,000 yuan (US$74,885),” Zhu said, adding that the worst problem was not the unpaid debt, but the many other clients who routinely failed to settle their bills on time.

“I was quite anxious at first, but I’ve grown accustomed to it. Payment delays are rampant in the construction sector,” said Zhu, whose company supplies water-purification equipment for construction projects.

While government data shows China’s private sector accounts for about 80 per cent of urban employment and 90 per cent of new jobs, its performance has become increasingly uneven.

Though emerging industries such as technology and advanced manufacturing benefit from government support and attract investment, firms in traditional industries, including construction and manufacturing, have borne the brunt of an economic slowdown.

Delayed payments rank among the biggest concerns of Chinese entrepreneurs. At the same time, compliance costs are rising rapidly as tax authorities step up enforcement of rules and scrutinise the collection of social insurance premiums.

Some local governments simply cite audits as excuses. We have a project in a small city ... payments for it have been held up for a decade

Wang Xianhui, Shanghai

“Dented by weaker profit expectations and faltering investment confidence, private‑sector enterprises have stepped up deleveraging,” wrote Zhang Xiaojing, a researcher at Beijing-based National Institution for Finance and Development, in a July note.

The government has not ignored these issues. President Xi Jinping personally pledged to address arrears owed to private companies in a high-profile address to the country’s leading entrepreneurs in February 2025.

The central government has since rolled out measures designed to help businesses weather the storm. But some businesspeople said that while the policies appeared promising in theory, they remained challenging in practice.

Now, attention is turning to the fifth plenum of the Communist Party’s Central Committee, to be held from Monday to Wednesday. The committee will focus on “strictly governing the party,” including measures to enforce party discipline and combat corruption.

Xi has repeatedly said such efforts are needed to ensure Beijing’s policies, including those intended to benefit the private sector, are properly implemented.

Payment delays evolve

Wang Xianhui runs a medium-sized firm on the outskirts of Shanghai. It mainly works with local governments and major state-owned construction enterprises.

According to him, a 12‑month payment cycle is considered normal for the sector, yet delays stretching beyond that time frame can also occur. Before 2020, he said, receipt of payments typically took only three to six months.

“Some local governments simply cite audits as excuses. We have a project in a small city in [central China’s] Hubei province, and payments for it have been held up for a decade,” Wang added.

With the property market yet to recover from a prolonged slowdown catalysed by Evergrande’s default, the construction sector remains the epicentre of overdue payments. In the years since the slump, the problem has only evolved, industry insiders said.

Over the past two years, Zhu said she has watched the situation shift from payment delays to debt settlement via unsold flats.

“One of my clients is a major Shanghai-based developer. Starting in 2024, they began settling out contract obligations with unsold apartments in the suburban areas,” Zhu said.
