She added that the properties were part of the developer’s unsold inventory, and the firm offset her construction payment at the original sales price – far higher than current market rates.

“Housing prices have kept falling over recent years. Local authorities set pricing for new apartments, and it is common for new-home prices to stand well above resale values – a 10 per cent to 20 per cent premium is typical in Shanghai,” Zhu said.

That means if Zhu took ownership of these flats and tried to sell them, she would incur losses. On top of that, her firm would also be required to cover transaction-related taxes.

“And it is not a choice between cash or property – it is either accept the apartment, or keep waiting,” she said. “It’s not limited to just one developer.”

According to China’s National Bureau of Statistics, total accounts receivable of China’s industrial enterprises above a designated size hit 29.48 trillion yuan (US$3.9 trillion) by the end of August, up 9 per cent year on year and outpacing the 6.6 per cent growth in revenue.

To address the issue, Beijing has reiterated that state-owned enterprises (SOEs) must settle payments in cash. At a mid-September press conference, an official with the State-owned Assets Supervision and Administration Commission said cash payments to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) “must be enforced as a hard rule”.

The government has also set up a website where SMEs can report delayed payments. Still, some private business owners said that while the initiative was well-intentioned, it lacked practical effectiveness.

“I can sense the government’s resolve to fix these issues through the website. But we would only file a complaint there if we no longer wanted to do business with those SOEs,” Wang said.

“Besides, our firm is a lower-tier contractor. That means even if we chose to submit a complaint via the website, we lack many key contracts and supporting documentation. The reality is far too complicated.”

Problems with delayed payments are not unique to China, however. In Europe, business-to-business transactions generally face a 60-day deadline for fulfilment. Late payments carry statutory interest set at least 8 percentage points above the European Central Bank’s reference rate.

Zhang Lin, deputy director at the research centre of Shanghai-based Far East Credit Rating, wrote in a May column for financial media outlet Caixin that Beijing could draw on Europe’s measures to impose tangible financial costs for payment delays.

“What awaits settlement is not merely individual invoices, but better liquidity and stronger confidence across the economy,” he said.

I’ve heard of several larger firms getting calls from the tax authorities recently

Richard Zhu, Shanghai

Paying in full

This summer, Shanghai entrepreneur Richard Zhu began ensuring full social security payments are made for his employees, a process he jokingly described as “window dressing”. He heads a medical-device contract manufacturer generating 20 million yuan in annual revenue.

Previously, his company had been remitting most social security contributions at the statutory minimum – more than 7,500 yuan a month for Shanghai as of this year – even though over half of his staff earned higher salaries.

At his firm, he said, workers in their 20s were willing to accept lower insurance premiums to boost their take-home cash. For his older, core employees, he has always made full social security contributions, he added, as they were mature enough to understand the value of social security benefits.

The informal practice is widespread among China’s SMEs as they deal with heavy operational burdens.

Combined employer and employee social insurance contributions in China can reach as high as 38 per cent of an individual’s wage, a higher share than in some developed economies, including the US at 15.3 per cent and Japan at 30 per cent.

Social security premiums have emerged as a significant source of public revenue. According to figures from the Ministry of Finance, national social insurance premiums hit 9.12 trillion yuan in value in 2025, outstripping the 6.89 trillion yuan in proceeds from value-added tax.

“I’ve heard of several larger firms getting calls from the tax authorities recently. Officials flagged mismatches between their social-security contribution bases and actual payroll, ordering them to get their social-security contributions into line with regulations,” Richard Zhu said.

Even though he has not received any notification from the local tax authority, he said he proceeded with the adjustments as a precautionary step – though he remains worried that non-compliance might derail his company’s partnerships with large pharmaceutical firms.

A professor with close ties to the State Taxation Administration, who requested anonymity over the sensitivity of the matter, said that enforcement has ramped up this year, and that provincial governments have established specific performance targets stipulating what proportion of local enterprises should achieve social security compliance.

After the change – made without reducing the pay of younger staff members to compensate – the combined outlay for social security contributions and the mandatory housing fund at Richard Zhu’s firm has surged to nearly 40 per cent of the expanding wage base, eating into the company’s profit margin.

He and others in the private sector are asking a similar question: why step up enforcement of premium collection when the economy is losing momentum?

“As China’s population is ageing at an accelerating pace, rigid expenditure pressures on the pension fund have risen steeply,” said Tony Peng, an independent researcher who has studied the domestic social security system for more than 10 years. “The domestic pension fund is confronted with heightened real-world pressures to balance its current-year revenues and outlays.”

Those pressures compound as local governments’ fiscal positions grow strained with less revenue from land sales, he added. In the past, fiscal resources have served as a backstop for social insurance accounts whenever premium collections came up short.

The fallout

Peng said he believed tightening enforcement was still the correct policy direction. However, he added, “with weak domestic demand and extremely thin profit margins among private firms, a tighter enforcement ramp‑up would exacerbate their difficulties and could trigger wage cuts or lay-offs.”

The repercussions already appear to be manifesting in the job market, insiders said.

Confronted with narrowing profit margins, Richard Zhu opted for the simplest solution – scaling back new hiring. This summer, he slashed his recruitment quota, dropping from eight positions for engineers and office-based staff to two.

Research from 2025 by Ye Jingjing, a professor at Zhongnan University of Economics and Law in Hubei province, found that heavier social security contributions led to a decline in new job postings.

Beginning in 2019, China’s tax authorities took over collection of social insurance premiums, an institutional shift that triggered an earlier round of tighter regulatory enforcement.

Ye’s research showed that average new job listings on one major domestic online recruitment platform dropped by 7.2 per cent in the post-2019 period relative to the 2017-19 baseline. At the same time, total social security contributions from surveyed companies climbed by 16.22 per cent.

“Conditions differ from one firm to another. Labour-intensive enterprises that carry relatively high wage-to-cost ratios are more vulnerable to changes in the social security contribution base,” Ye said.

Peng, the independent researcher, suggested that authorities carefully consider the pace of implementation and design of transitional arrangements.

He proposed that local governments provide rebates or interest subsidies for those firms that remit full social-security contributions and have avoided staff lay-offs. This kind of “targeted compensatory support” would help incentivise some enterprises to abide by the law more willingly, he said.

Richard Zhu, meanwhile, said he was choosing to stay positive.

“Having spent 23 years in this business, I’ve learned it’s all about cycles. There have been ups and downs. Perhaps in another five years, all these problems will be absorbed during an economic upturn.”

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong’s 700-year-old oyster industry goes hi-tech with ‘super’ specimen
item.description:
Out on Deep Bay, between Hong Kong and Shenzhen, the first thing you notice is what doesn’t seem to belong there.

Many of the oyster-farming rafts here are old. Weathered wood, greyed by salt and sun – the kind that has floated in these waters for generations. A few look abandoned, but this is inevitably the appearance a 700-year-old industry takes on when it is running out of time.

And then, there are the newcomers – bobbing buoyantly in a bright, unmistakable shade of blue – made of fibreglass. Pacing back and forth on one in a pink shirt and dark trousers is Professor Thiyagarajan Vengatesen, a marine biologist from the University of Hong Kong (HKU) who is better known as Professor Rajan.
item.content:encoded:
Out on Deep Bay, between Hong Kong and Shenzhen, the first thing you notice is what doesn’t seem to belong there.

Many of the oyster-farming rafts here are old. Weathered wood, greyed by salt and sun – the kind that has floated in these waters for generations. A few look abandoned, but this is inevitably the appearance a 700-year-old industry takes on when it is running out of time.

And then, there are the newcomers – bobbing buoyantly in a bright, unmistakable shade of blue – made of fibreglass. Pacing back and forth on one in a pink shirt and dark trousers is Professor Thiyagarajan Vengatesen, a marine biologist from the University of Hong Kong (HKU) who is better known as Professor Rajan.

Born in India’s Tamil Nadu state, Vengatesen came to Hong Kong in 2001 to take up seven years of advanced research into larval biology at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology. His interests lay in how oyster larvae were struggling with environmental adaptation and building their shells at a time of increased ocean acidification.

Vengatesen’s mentor at the time predicted that oysters would become vulnerable to climate change, but the gravity of the situation only sank in when he witnessed it first-hand. After Vengatesen joined HKU, in 2008, a colleague connected him with an oyster expert, who took him to Zhanjiang, in Guangdong province, in 2009, and showed him an industry suffering without scientific involvement. Vengatesen became one of the first scientists in the region to study how climate change would affect oyster farming, but meeting the growers in Zhanjiang – seeing how their livelihoods depended on a species they could not protect – convinced him this was worth a life’s work.

Little did he know he would spend the next decade and counting looking for a solution to save Hong Kong’s oysters.

Lau Fau Shan sits on the northwestern edge of the New Territories, a rural neighbourhood of narrow strips of small businesses and stalls pressed between the hills and the bay. Its main street smells of dried seafood, salt and the mustiness of oyster shells left in the sun. Stacks of prized golden oysters – semi-dried bivalves, with a soft texture – line the shopfronts, along with bottles of oyster sauce and oyster-shell crafts.

Oyster cultivation is part of Lau Fau Shan’s cultural, historical and economic tapestry. Abutting Deep Bay, this area has been farmed for these molluscs for centuries, the local species itself named after the city: Magallana hongkongensis – the Hong Kong oyster.

In the 1960s and 70s, this area was the heart of Hong Kong’s booming oyster-farming industry. Hundreds of families worked the rafts through the “off-bottom” aquaculture technique, growing oysters on ropes or in suspended cages, with the resulting products being shipped across the region and the world. Lau Fau Shan’s seafood restaurants drew crowds from across the city. Feasting on a banquet here was a status symbol.

Walk the alleyways of the neighbourhood today and ask who farms oysters, and the answer is almost always the same: “My father used to”, “My grandfather used to” or, occasionally, “I used to”.

But oysters are serious business, and not just for Lau Fau Shan growers. Hong Kong-based food giant Lee Kum Kee, founded nearly 140 years ago, built its brand on oyster sauce as an indispensable pantry staple. Beyond mere ingredient, the bivalve represents identity and tradition. So influential is Lee Kum Kee’s flagship condiment as a cornerstone of Cantonese cuisine that the craftsmanship that goes into making it was inscribed as an intangible cultural heritage of Guangdong province in 2022. For a story that began with oyster sauce in 1888 and has since spread to more than 100 countries and regions globally, Hong Kong’s declining oyster industry represents a loss not just for producers, but for a unique food culture.

Most of the oyster products sold in Lau Fau Shan’s shops now come from across the water, grown in mainland China and shipped to the town that popularised Hong Kong oysters as a trade. The Hong Kong industry is still around, but mostly as a memory. A statue of an oyster overlooks the rafts at the end of the main street, its paint washed in the sun.

Even before climate change took its toll, the industry was in decline, beset by an ageing workforce, outdated methods and young people leaving.

And then, the oysters started dying.

Chan Kwok-leung remembers the winter of 2007, when the water in Deep Bay did not get cold enough. “Brother Leung” had grown up in the 70s and 80s, when the winter water was “cold as melted snow”. The chill helped the oysters build up their flesh, leaving them plump and sweet in time for the Chinese New Year market. It was how it had always worked.

But that year, almost all of the oysters withered.

“I felt so lost,” he says. “In an instant, a whole year’s livelihood was gone.”

With his crop devastated, Brother Leung left the industry and went to work in construction, saving until he could afford to buy new oyster spats and start again the following year. It was not the last time his oysters would die.

Historically, oyster rafts in Deep Bay tended to cluster to the east of the Shenzhen Bay Bridge, in zones that are further from the ocean, with moderate salinity levels. Hong Kong oysters are adapted to these estuarine conditions, to the brackish area where the Pearl River meets the sea, growing for centuries in water that is neither fully fresh nor fully salty.

But over the years, more growers moved in, triggered in part by Shenzhen’s ban on oyster aquaculture, in the early 2000s. Rafts crowded Deep Bay, numbering around 5,000 by the mid-2010s, and most of the new arrivals were to the west of the Shenzhen Bay Bridge, in saltier water.

Oysters struggle to survive prolonged periods of high salinity. As they expend energy trying to balance the salt in their bodies, less is left for growth.

Climate change only made it worse.

“Warmer winter conditions now last more than 15 days longer than usual,” Vengatesen explains. Prolonged warmth disrupts the oysters’ biological clock, prompting them to prepare for reproduction earlier, diverting energy from building up their flesh to developing their gonads. It is a fatal combination: poor meat quality, then death.

But figuring out how science could help was only half the battle. When Vengatesen first started visiting Lau Fau Shan, the farmers were wary and kept their distance. Vengatesen is an Indian scientist who could not speak Cantonese, while the locals had generations of experience and a lunar calendar that had steered them for centuries. What could this man possibly know about their oysters?

Unconvinced, the farmers would not let him near their rafts. Only licensed boats are allowed out to the oysters, and the growers control access.

Vengatesen recalls the time he tried to swim out to the rafts: “I wasn’t successful, but it showed them that I was serious about wanting to help.”

Personal scepticism was only one obstacle. Negative public image was another concern. By the late 2000s, local media reports of bacterial contamination and heavy metals had eroded consumer confidence in Hong Kong-grown oysters. In 2013, the Shenzhen government threatened to ban sales of the shellfish as unfit for consumption.

“Local oysters have a limited market,” says Vengatesen. “People still perceive them as contaminated”; the stigma “has to be broken down scientifically”.

Brother Leung, meanwhile, kept an open mind and said yes to Vengatesen’s involvement in 2010. He had returned to Lau Fau Shan after the 2007 die-off, and knew the old ways no longer worked. “I was one of the first oyster growers to talk to Rajan,” he says. “Also, because I was one of only a few who could speak English.” (He had picked up the language during stints working in the seafood industry in Fiji and Australia.)

In 2016, something shifted. A South China Morning Post article covered Vengatesen’s collaboration with the growers – “the first positive report in a very long time”, he calls it. It outlined plans to revive Lau Fau Shan’s oyster industry, with scientists assisting in its recovery, a purification system in the works and a hatchery on the horizon.

While the story did not solve everything, it changed the atmosphere. As Vengatesen puts it, it made things easier for him.

First, Vengatesen had to address food safety. Farmers needed a way to prove their oysters were safe to eat. He helped them secure a government loan to establish Hong Kong’s first commercial depuration plant in Lau Fau Shan. Opened in 2018, the plant is said to have the capacity to process 10,000 oysters a day. At the facility, harvested oysters sit for up to four days in seawater sterilised by ultraviolet light to reduce bacteria levels to meet safety standards – though the government still advises cooking local oysters before eating.

Chan Shu-fung – a third-generation oyster farmer and the chairman of the Deep Bay Oyster Cultivation Association – invested more than HK$1 million (US$127,430) of his own money in the project. His depurated golden oysters are stocked in City’super and Sogo, the first locally farmed oysters to reach Hong Kong’s high-end supermarkets. He has become one of the industry’s most vocal advocates, as he is familiar with the difficulties of operating in this field. Running the depuration plant costs, on average, four to five times more than ordinary oyster production. He now primarily powers it up based on orders he receives, rather than on a regular basis.

Next problem: the oysters themselves. Because the local species could not adapt to the rapidly changing climate, Vengatesen set out to breed a hardier version that could survive. Vengatesen and his team at HKU developed a genomic tool – the SNP (single-nucleotide polymorphism) chip – that allows them to scan an oyster’s genetic material for markers linked to stress tolerance, disease resistance and growth. Instead of waiting years to see which oysters would survive in current conditions, they could identify the strongest ones in the larvae stage, breed them and repeat the process to further refine the selection for the ultimate stock.

“It used to be like a slow, careful family-tree project,” says Vengatesen, describing the old strategy. “Now, we have a short cut: we look at the oyster’s DNA – its instruction manual – to scan for tiny markers that are like ‘good-luck charms’ in the genes, which tell us which oysters have [already developed] natural protection against sickness and stress.”

Each oyster is given a rating based on how many “good” markers it has, and the team then picks the highest-scoring individuals and conditions them to spawn.

Finally, after years of trials and tests, came the result: the HKU Super Oyster, bred by Vengatesen and his team, is a climate-change-tolerant strain of Magallana hongkongensis tough enough to survive the mass mortalities that wipe out regular oysters.

Vengatesen made significant breakthroughs in the lab, but scaling up production and testing the oysters under real-world conditions would require the right facilities and support. Enter the Hong Kong Oyster Hatchery and Innovation Research Unit, the first such hub in the city dedicated to developing sustainable aquaculture solutions. Opened in 2022, the HKU Oyster Hatchery – established through funding from Lee Kum Kee and the Sustainable Fisheries Development Fund – cultivates resilient HKU Super Oyster seed stock and supplies them to local growers.

For Lee Kum Kee, backing the project was a clear-cut decision.

“It gives us an opportunity to contribute to the long-term sustainability of an industry that is closely linked to our own history,” says Clarence Chung Shiu-cheong, director of technical and procurement at Lee Kum Kee.

As a business that is deeply rooted in “oysters and the communities behind them”, he says, “the challenges faced by local farmers” affect not just the producers, but the legacy of local food culture.

“Preserving Hong Kong’s oyster-farming traditions is about much more than preserving an industry. It is about preserving generations of knowledge, craftsmanship and a way of life that forms part of Hong Kong’s unique food heritage, built over generations through the experience and dedication of local oyster farmers,” Chung explains.

“It is important not only to respect that heritage, but also to help create the conditions for it to continue.”

A sea of blue rafts out in Deep Bay is what that safeguarding work looks like today – physical proof that the bivalves Vengatesen has bred in a Petri dish can survive in the same waters that have been killing their ancestors. One man believed in Hong Kong’s oysters when the city had written them off as a sunset industry.

Vengatesen is also developing a triploid version – oysters with three sets of chromosomes instead of two. “With that extra set, the cells get confused and can’t divide properly to make sperm or eggs,” he explains. “So, these oysters give up on reproduction altogether. Instead of pouring 80 per cent of their body into making babies, they put all their energy into growing meaty bodies, year-round. And they handle heat and stress better.”

Millions of seeds are produced per year at the HKU Oyster Hatchery, and the blue rafts are home to the first field test for Vengatesen’s triploids, estimated to be ready by next summer.

In the summer of 2025, Brother Leung and other farmers stocked more than 30,000 ropes with HKU Super Oyster seeds, which will take 18 months to mature. In Zhanjiang’s high-salinity waters, where regular oysters tend to die, the survival rate of this new strain was 40 to 50 per cent, he had been told. In Deep Bay, they hope for a similar outcome this winter.

“We were very surprised by this,” says Brother Leung of the Zhanjiang experiments. “We truly believe that Professor Rajan’s research and the HKU Super Oysters may become our lifeline in the near future.”

“When oysters can thrive despite these [environmental] pressures, it strengthens the entire industry and helps preserve Hong Kong’s oyster-farming heritage for future generations,” adds Chung.

Besides, the science isn’t simply making a positive impact on people – the benefits also ripple out to the broader marine ecosystem. “Oyster reefs provide habitat and shelter for fish and other marine life, and they play a role in maintaining the biodiversity of coastal waters,” he says.

Whether the HKU Super Oysters will be introduced into large-scale production lines, such as at Lee Kum Kee, remains to be seen. First, the science and cultivation practices must be allowed to mature, Chung asserts, “but, naturally, as a company whose heritage began with oyster sauce, we would be pleased to see these efforts one day come full circle”.

In the meantime, Brother Leung is already requesting more HKU Super Oyster seedlings for the next round. He and his fellow farmers are exploring the possibility of building their own hatchery, so they can produce the seeds themselves.

What Vengatesen has achieved has also reshaped the industry’s governance. For years, the number of rafts in Deep Bay had grown unchecked, reaching more than 14,000, according to a survey conducted by the Hong Kong government in May 2023. After his research identified overcrowding as a contributing cause of mass mortality among local oysters, the government commissioned him to evaluate raft management. He recommended cutting the total by nearly half.

“We strongly support the government’s proposal to reduce the number of oyster rafts to 7,000,” says Chan. “Professor Rajan’s research helps us understand what a reasonable number of rafts should be in Deep Bay.”

A new management framework was introduced, beginning with a registration system in 2023 and moving towards a licensing structure, overseen by a committee drawn from the industry itself.

Hong Kong’s Tang clan has held farming rights in Deep Bay since 1667, when the imperial government granted them a deed to rent out the oyster beds to farmers. For centuries, anyone wanting to cultivate oysters along the Lau Fau Shan coast paid rent to the Tang pioneer settlers, and later to the Tang ancestral hall, the Yau Kung Tong. Under the new licensing system, the age-old organisation is taking on a formal management role. “It is functioning like a property-management company,” says Tang Yu-kei, the association’s general manager.

He, too, is a convert. Having witnessed how the old method has failed, with fewer farmers and dwindling incomes, he sees the new approach as offering the clan a more sustainable role than collecting rent from a trade in decline. “I don’t fully understand the details, but we’re beginning to believe in science,” he says.

Vengatesen’s ambitions go further still, extending beyond the bay: he wants to build a “Made in Hong Kong” oyster brand, one that can compete with the major mainland producers. With seeds bred in the city, oysters grown in Hong Kong waters and processing and purification carried out locally, the brand would be owned and exported from here. Right now, most farmers still buy their spats from the mainland. Vengatesen wants the whole chain to be local.

“Oyster farming in Hong Kong carries over 700 years of history,” he says, “and this deep-rooted heritage must be preserved and leveraged. Hong Kong’s golden oysters are a unique speciality that has already become a recognised local brand.”

Hong Kong’s reputation for quality and trust, he argues, is an asset that cannot be replicated. “Why not build on this reputation to promote Hong Kong oyster cultivation and exports under a ‘Made in Hong Kong’ label?”

Vengatesen also believes that the brand cannot be built by scientists and farmers alone. It will only work if Hongkongers themselves start believing again, if they stop reaching for imported oysters and start asking for local ones.

For Deep Bay oysters to succeed, “we have to change their image in the eyes of Hong Kong people”, says Chan. Part of that is answering a simpler question: can these new oysters taste like the old ones?

At a Lau Fau Shan cha chaan teng, an oyster omelette arrives, its edges crispy and golden. A local classic served for generations, this version is made with HKU Super Oysters, freshly shucked by Brother Leung and brought to a diner that usually sells imported molluscs from the mainland. Under the expectant eyes of the scientist and the farmer, I take a bite: the HKU Super Oyster tastes almost identical to the regular kind, but is slightly less rubbery, with a distinct, metallic flavour.

All in all, there is nothing remarkable about it – and, for an industry trying to prove it can still compete, that might be precisely the point. Vengatesen’s HKU Super Oyster does not need to be a revelation. It needs to survive the winters that killed its predecessors, grow fat in water that once starved them and taste like something a Hong Kong family would be happy to order.

It will take until next summer for the triploid, the next generation, to be ready. Tang has his doubts about those. “We’ve only encountered triploids from the Pacific Ocean,” he says. “I’ve personally eaten them and I didn’t like them. But if it’s triploids from Hong Kong oysters, it could be promising.”

Vengatesen offers a practical take. While some in the industry worry that the triploids will taste worse than wild oysters, quality aside, he says, they need the triploid to survive – because “almost all of [the farmers] are jobless in the summer”. More than just tasty seafood, it is a lifeline for those who still depend on the industry to put food on their own table.

In the waters between Hong Kong and Shenzhen, tradition is learning to believe in science. Although the verdict is still out on what comes next, for the first time in years, there might be something worth believing in.

item.title: [SCMP] ‘Incisive’ final report on Tai Po blaze singles out 4 government bodies
item.description:
An independent committee investigating Hong Kong’s deadliest fire in decades has submitted its findings to the government, with a source saying the “incisive” report has singled out four government bodies for accountability.

It is understood that the 12-chapter report found that among the four government bodies named, the Housing Bureau’s Independent Checking Unit should bear the greatest responsibility for a lack of oversight of renovation work at the Wang Fuk Court residential estate, which contributed to the heavy death toll from the inferno.

But the insider said on Thursday that the report did not name any bureau secretaries in connection with the blaze that broke out at the Tai Po estate on November 26 last year, killing 168 people.
item.content:encoded:
An independent committee investigating Hong Kong’s deadliest fire in decades has submitted its findings to the government, with a source saying the “incisive” report has singled out four government bodies for accountability.

It is understood that the 12-chapter report found that among the four government bodies named, the Housing Bureau’s Independent Checking Unit should bear the greatest responsibility for a lack of oversight of renovation work at the Wang Fuk Court residential estate, which contributed to the heavy death toll from the inferno.

But the insider said on Thursday that the report did not name any bureau secretaries in connection with the blaze that broke out at the Tai Po estate on November 26 last year, killing 168 people.

The judge-led panel submitted its final report to Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu after holding 30 public sessions and hearing from 80 witnesses, including residents, firefighters, government officials and experts.

“With the evidence and materials received as the factual framework, the committee has completed its inquiry work on the matters set out in its terms of reference, and prepared the report accordingly,” the committee said.

The panel, ordered by Lee, ceased operating following the submission of the report, its website showed.

Lee thanked the committee members for their efforts, saying the panel had provided a comprehensive review of the causes of the fire and recommendations on large-scale building maintenance and renovation projects.

“The government will make comprehensive reforms in areas including the supervision of building maintenance works, building management and the regulation of fire service installations,” he said.

“We will carefully study the committee’s report, actively follow up on its recommendations and shortly announce plans for comprehensive reforms and pursuing accountability.”

The government said it would seek legal advice on how best to publish the report at the “earliest possible juncture” without prejudicing court proceedings. Charges have been laid against seven individuals and two companies for their alleged roles in the tragedy.

A redacted version of the report could be made public next week at the earliest.

The source told the South China Morning Post that the report contained 12 chapters detailing the committee’s findings on the causes of the fire.

He described the report as “incisive”, refuting speculation the tone was mild, but without providing additional details.

The report singled out four government bodies for accountability – the Fire Services Department, the Buildings Department, the Labour Department and the Independent Checking Unit – as well as some civil servants named during the hearings, the insider said.

The Labour Department was deemed to carry a smaller share of responsibility for failing to act promptly on residents’ complaints about workers smoking at the site.

The source added that the report also included recommendations on construction material standards and measures to combat bid-rigging.

The blaze engulfed seven of the estate’s eight blocks and became Hong Kong’s deadliest fire since 1948.

The committee’s lead counsel, Victor Dawes, identified six “human failures” that led to the tragedy. These included the use of non-fire-retardant scaffolding mesh, the widespread installation of combustible polyfoam boards over windows, the deactivation of the fire alarm system and the suspension of the fire hosepipe reel system.

The other failures involved temporary openings in emergency staircases, where fire-rated windows had been replaced with movable boards, and workers’ smoking habits.

At the final hearing, the committee’s legal team presented a 627-page closing statement, blaming the “litany of failures” for the disaster.

The statement said the government bore “unshirkable responsibility” for the tragedy and singled out the four government bodies.

Lau Siu-kai, a consultant for the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said it was premature to pre-empt the government’s response as the report had not yet been made public.

However, he called on the administration to gauge public sentiment before taking any follow-up actions, adding that he expected Beijing and the government would act to strengthen support for the revamped political system under the “patriots administering Hong Kong” principle.

“I believe the central government and the chief executive will consider the matter from the perspectives of the government’s credibility, governance effectiveness, political stability and the unity of the governing team,” Lau said.

“It has to assure the public that the government is accountable and handles the matter in a fair and impartial manner.”

Veteran political commentator Sonny Lo Shiu-hing said the public expected not only civil servants but also ministers to be held accountable. But he noted that with a government transition next July, the administration might decide against a cabinet reshuffle so close to the end of its term.

Lo also suggested that the government publish a report outlining its reform measures to deepen public understanding of its follow-up actions.

The committee counsel’s closing remarks criticised the Fire Services Department for failing to detect that the fire alarm system had been deactivated at the estate and for avoiding its statutory duties.

Following the blaze, the department stepped up inspections of fire services installations and put forward legislative proposals to strengthen regulation of such equipment.

During a check of 1,500 old buildings across Hong Kong, the department found 64 of them had not carried out annual inspections, with malfunctioning fire alarm systems found in 13.

The department extended the checks in April, aiming to inspect 5,000 blocks in two years.

Among its legislative recommendations, the department has proposed amending the Fire Services Ordinance so contractors and technicians would be legally required to obtain prior approval before shutting down fire safety equipment.

Lawmaker Peter Shiu Ka-fai, chairman of the Legislative Council’s security panel, declined to comment on the accountability of the department, arguing that the full picture would only be available after the report was released.

He expressed confidence in the department for “discharging its duty with integrity”.

“The Wang Fuk Court fire was an occasion to remind us that some regulations will have to be updated,” he said. “Many lawmakers agreed that doing so would enhance public safety. I believe when these amendments are submitted for vetting, they will be passed.”

item.title: [SCMP] China is moving past a GDP-first mindset. Can local officials get with the programme?
item.description:
Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. This month’s edition, the fifth plenum, is attracting even more attention as the world’s second-largest economy takes on a more prominent role in global affairs. In the first part of this series, Frank Chen and Alice Li track the ways top-level policy decisions flow down to local officials – and the challenges those officials face in balancing a wide set of priorities.

When many took time off to enjoy China’s National Day holiday earlier this month, stories from media outlets in the eastern province of Jiangsu showed the region’s Communist Party chief, Xin Changxing, hard at work.

He started the day by conducting a safety inspection at a metro station, then visited local shops to see how sales were faring over the holiday. Later, he observed a fire drill before spending the rest of the day checking in on crowd control measures at major tourist hotspots.
item.content:encoded:
Plenary sessions of the Central Committee, the upper echelon of China’s ruling Communist Party, are major events on the country’s political calendar. This month’s edition, the fifth plenum, is attracting even more attention as the world’s second-largest economy takes on a more prominent role in global affairs. In the first part of this series, Frank Chen and Alice Li track the ways top-level policy decisions flow down to local officials – and the challenges those officials face in balancing a wide set of priorities.

When many took time off to enjoy China’s National Day holiday earlier this month, stories from media outlets in the eastern province of Jiangsu showed the region’s Communist Party chief, Xin Changxing, hard at work.

He started the day by conducting a safety inspection at a metro station, then visited local shops to see how sales were faring over the holiday. Later, he observed a fire drill before spending the rest of the day checking in on crowd control measures at major tourist hotspots.

As China’s economy continues its transition to an era of lower absolute growth figures but greater sophistication, Beijing has expanded its to-do lists for local officials like Xin who are on the front lines of implementing policy.

Once tasked almost solely with stimulating economic growth, these political cadres are now juggling a set of increasingly complex – and sometimes competing – priorities.

To name a few, officials are taking steps to fight corruption, maintain national security, improve public safety, reduce debt, create jobs, nurture China’s home-grown tech and keep the economy growing.

But under the weight of weak domestic consumption and a tepid property market, gross domestic product figures have been fluctuating. Earlier this year, Beijing said it would aim for 4.5 to 5.0 per cent GDP growth for 2026 – the lowest target since 1991.

Caution wins over initiative ... A mistake could cost them more than doing nothing

Alfredo Montufar-Helu, Ankura

While concerns grew about meeting that benchmark after a 4.3 per cent growth rate was reported in the second quarter, a 4.5 per cent rate recorded in the third quarter suggests the lower end of that range remains in sight, pushing the rate up to 4.6 per cent for the first nine months of the year.

All eyes are now on the fifth plenum of the party’s Central Committee, to be held from October 26 to 29. The meeting comes roughly one year before the party’s twice-a-decade national congress, a session expected to feature an extensive personnel reshuffle, including the formation of a new decision-making Politburo.

The plenum is an occasion for Beijing to clarify its policy goals. But analysts said the focus of this edition of the high-stakes gathering might be on the party’s self-improvement and strengthened rule.

Some observers expressed worries that Beijing’s shifting, sometimes contrasting priorities could divert local officials’ attention away from growth.

Alfredo Montufar-Helu, China managing director at consulting firm Ankura, said while economic development still mattered, Beijing’s definition of it had changed.

“Growth [is] increasingly judged by its contribution to security and tech self-reliance,” he said.

Local officials, typically risk-averse, would be paying close attention to the party’s signals, Montufar-Helu added.

“Caution wins over initiative,” he said. “A mistake could cost them more than doing nothing.”

Broadening priorities

While the policy juggling act expected of local officials is not a new phenomenon, analysts said more targets are being set.

“Every day, they might have different orders cascade down to them,” said Zhu Jiangnan, an associate professor of politics at the University of Hong Kong. “So what are the real priorities? Those emphasised more by the topmost leaders would become the ones to work on.”

But what localities are told to prioritise today is drastically different from the growth-centric mandate handed down decades ago.

Then, the binding principle was “economic construction”, shaped by China’s paramount leader Deng Xiaoping after he came to power at the end of the 1970s. Successive leaders such as Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao largely adhered to a similar policy.

But Xi Jinping, Communist Party general secretary since 2012 and president since 2013, has broadened what Beijing viewed as critical, analysts said.

First, there was his instruction to “coordinate economic development and security”, enshrined into the party constitution at its 20th national congress in 2022.

At the previous congress in 2017, he coined the term “high-quality development”, introducing another overarching principle to inform decision-making and indicate growth was no longer the only benchmark at play in policy work.

China’s intensifying rivalry with the US has also prompted Beijing to make self-reliance in tech another high-level mandate as it seeks to break the West’s chokehold on advanced products and components, with localities urged to coalesce their resources in this effort.

After Xi visited Shanghai twice this year – trips that were centred around tech – the city’s government gazetted two documents to supercharge basic research and innovation and promote the use of artificial intelligence, observers noted.

To help cadres at all levels tackle the new priorities, Beijing has been pushing to install a “correct” understanding of what constitutes good performance among officials since February, eyeing a strong start to its 15th five-year plan.

The move was seen as a pivot away from focusing on raw GDP growth and “at-all-costs” development as the sole criterion for promotion, placing the debt, fraud and vanity projects that sometimes resulted from this mindset in the crosshairs.

“Nowadays, the focus is on politics and party doctrine,” said the head of a government agency in Zhejiang province who declined to be named. The official, who oversees financing for small and medium-sized enterprises, said she and her colleagues were beginning to make decisions with more caution, weighing the political dimension alongside the economic realm.

“We study political theories and top leaders’ directives and apply them to our work,” she added.

Growth not out of focus

However, this shift in perspective has not left the problems plaguing the economy without a response. When momentum appeared to be waning in the second quarter despite a strong start to the year, Beijing held a succession of meetings, seminars and inspections dedicated to diagnosing and tackling the most pressing issues.

Larry Hu Weijun, chief China economist at Macquarie, said Beijing tended to take a dynamic and adaptable approach.

“Having multiple goals doesn’t mean growth is not important,” he said. “Rather, the importance of growth diminishes once the target is within reach, but rises sharply when the target is under threat.”

Recent actions bear this logic out. Last month, policymakers unveiled a series of measures in quick succession to resuscitate the economy: cutting policy interest rates, offering mortgage interest subsidies for homebuyers and unlocking 550 billion yuan (US$82.18 billion) in local debt quotas to boost investment.

At a meeting of the party’s Politburo in July, Beijing pledged to accelerate the pace of fiscal spending, promptly roll out incremental policies and speed up the transition of growth models for the remainder of the year amid rising volatility in global markets and the second-quarter GDP downturn.

Among these efforts, top economic planner the National Development and Reform Commission, the Ministry of Finance and the People’s Bank of China have set up a 100 billion yuan fiscal-financial coordination fund to boost domestic demand.

Policymakers have resisted letting loose a stimulus “flood”, saying their intent has been to focus on countercyclical adjustments and the precise targeting of priority areas, including private and small-scale enterprises, domestic demand and the green energy transition.

Putting officials on notice

However, local officials are frequently reminded on what their priorities are – and how they must deliver. Beijing is unafraid to name and shame as it admonishes deviations in the understanding and implementation of its directives.

One area that has been given extra attention in recent years is public safety, particularly in the wake of several natural disasters. Central authorities have stepped up scrutiny of local governments this year over safety issues and tightened accountability.

Since September, over 400 officials across four regions – Hainan and Jiangsu provinces, as well as the Guangxi Zhuang and Xinjiang Uygur autonomous regions – have been held responsible for safety risks and lapses in local oversight following evaluations by central government inspectors.

Beijing has also taken a closer interest in localities that have been instructed to fire up their economic engines, examining the results of their efforts in detail and doling out penalties for ill-fated or extravagant projects.

In June, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection – the party’s chief anti-corruption organ – named and shamed officials in Jiangxi, Sichuan and Hebei provinces, as well as the Guangxi and Inner Mongolia autonomous regions, for chasing development that increased debt risks and using public funds for projects that did not return a profit.

Businesses get reality check

As local officials work to navigate Beijing’s shifting requirements, they may in turn alter their practices as they deal with businesses, particularly the private and foreign firms operating in the country.

While some firms have acknowledged the need to curb debt and move away from a GDP-first mindset, others have voiced concerns about mixed, even conflicting signals and structural mismatches in policy implementation.

The American Chamber of Commerce in China flagged some of these issues in its annual white paper.

“Central directives prioritising hi-tech self-reliance and domestic national security controls often clash directly with local-level efforts to rebuild foreign business confidence and revive consumer spending,” the chamber wrote in April.

The business advocacy body called on policymakers to create a “proportionate, predictable balance” between national security and economic openness, warning sudden shifts or conflicting signals could lead multinationals to defer long-term investments.

A heavier focus on national security and public safety has been cited by some business figures as complicating their operating environment.

One common complaint, for instance, centres on frequent safety inspections and red tape disrupting firms’ normal operations and adding to their costs. A report published last year in an online content platform run by the Chongqing municipal committee of the Chinese Communist Party noted that some companies were subjected to four or five safety inspections in a single week.

Ankura’s Montufar-Helu said Beijing’s increasing emphasis on security and party discipline has made local officials more risk-averse as they choose which projects and businesses to support with incentives.

“Local governments will steer resources towards the sectors Beijing has flagged as strategic and away from anything that looks risky … Officials will be slower to back projects that could draw scrutiny, including those involving foreign and private companies,” he warned.

“For them, getting things done with local authorities is likely to be harder.”

item.title: [SCMP] Is Washington misreading Beijing? Decline in US visits to China sparks concern
item.description:
When Grant Newsham, a retired US Marine colonel and security analyst, sat down for an interview that aired last month, he called China’s economic rise illusory and said there were “600 million Chinese at least who live on US$5 a day or less”.

His remarks quickly drew online criticism as well as accusations that he was using outdated figures from 2020 while ignoring differences in purchasing power.

Some commenters argued that uneven development was common across countries. Others questioned how much on-the-ground China experience Newsham had before making the statement to the Epoch Times, a right-wing outlet associated with Falun Gong and banned in China.
item.content:encoded:
When Grant Newsham, a retired US Marine colonel and security analyst, sat down for an interview that aired last month, he called China’s economic rise illusory and said there were “600 million Chinese at least who live on US$5 a day or less”.

His remarks quickly drew online criticism as well as accusations that he was using outdated figures from 2020 while ignoring differences in purchasing power.

Some commenters argued that uneven development was common across countries. Others questioned how much on-the-ground China experience Newsham had before making the statement to the Epoch Times, a right-wing outlet associated with Falun Gong and banned in China.

However, the debate went beyond a dispute over China’s living standards: it highlighted a need for Americans – including policymakers and academics – to gain first-hand experience of China, while drawing attention to their shrinking opportunities to gain that exposure.

A report issued by the Washington-based Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) last month documented a sharp decline in congressional delegations to China between 2010 and 2026, a period marked by persistent bilateral tensions.

A separate analysis published by the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) later in September highlighted a parallel downturn in American students studying in China and the erosion of programmes designed to train future China specialists.

Observers warn that the loss of direct, on-the-ground exposure could threaten America’s ability to assess and engage its primary rival, particularly as China’s strategic importance to US foreign policy continues to grow.

A broad retreat

According to the CSIS report, visits by congressional delegations to mainland China and Hong Kong have fallen since the late 2010s as bilateral relations deteriorated.

Tensions deepened during US President Donald Trump’s first term from 2017 to 2021, marked by a full-blown trade war, intensifying technological rivalry and recurring military stand-offs in the contested South China Sea.

The report showed that visits plunged at the onset of the Covid-19 pandemic and had yet to return to earlier levels.

Congressional travel to Taiwan has also dropped since 2022. The report attributed the decline to lingering fallout from then-House speaker Nancy Pelosi’s 2022 visit to Taipei – which triggered major People’s Liberation Army drills – and subsequent caution in Washington around such delegations to avoid further provoking Beijing.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

The ripple effects will spread from academia into government, media and business, heightening the risk of miscalculation

Sun Chenghao, Chinese academic

CSIS found that only 32 per cent of the 535 sitting US lawmakers had travelled to mainland China, Hong Kong or Taiwan, based on its tracking of congressional delegations between 2010 and 2026.

The report expected that share to shrink further as veteran members left office and newer lawmakers arrived without that first-hand experience.

US Senator Steve Daines is among the few lawmakers who still make such trips. He concluded his most recent visit to China in late August, just weeks ahead of President Xi Jinping’s trip to Washington from September 23 to 25.

After Daines visited artificial intelligence and space firms in China’s tech hub Hangzhou and the southern city of Guangzhou, he told Bloomberg the US risked underestimating “both the quality and the scale of the tech innovation ecosystem in China”.

Isabella McCallum, co-author of the CSIS report, noted that the small 32 per cent share – the 172 current lawmakers who have visited mainland China, Hong Kong or Taiwan – suggested on-the-ground engagement was becoming less common among the people responsible for shaping US policy towards China.

“With less direct experience of China, Congress will become more reliant on second-hand information for one of the country’s most consequential relationships,” McCallum said in an interview.

Meanwhile, lawmakers continued to introduce legislation concerning Beijing, creating a growing gap between how much Congress acted on China and how well its members knew the country, she added.

To Beijing, the concern is not simply that US lawmakers may hold unfavourable views of China. It is that their assessments may be made without enough contact with the people, businesses and institutions affected by their decisions.

Sun Chenghao, a senior fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy, said limited direct experience could make American policymakers more likely to rely on political labels and a narrow security-focused view of China.

“This could lead them to overestimate certain threats while overlooking opportunities for cooperation,” Sun said.

The decline in congressional visits is part of a wider retreat in exchanges between the two countries.

According to the CSIS report, fewer than 2,000 Americans are estimated to be studying in China, compared with a peak of about 11,000 in 2019.

Likewise, the number of Chinese students enrolled at US universities had continued to fall from its 2019 peak of 372,532 amid tightening visa restrictions and curbs on research exchange, the report said, without stating current figures.

According to the Institute of International Education’s most recent annual survey, nearly 266,000 Chinese students were in the US in 2024.

The drop in academic exchange was also underscored in an analysis released by CFR on September 23.

It highlighted the suspension in China of US government-backed exchange projects, including the Fulbright programme and the Critical Language Scholarship. The author, political scientist Rush Doshi, noted that these programmes had helped to cultivate generations of specialists equipped to study China through its language, society and political institutions.

Meanwhile, some study-abroad programmes at US universities have been halted following a Pentagon directive in August instructing institutions to review relationships with foreign counterparts over national security concerns.

The loss of these opportunities could have consequences beyond universities.

Doshi noted that American government agencies and businesses largely relied on China expertise to interpret China’s actions, from geopolitics and security to trade and supply chains.

“A United States that no longer trains people who can read Chinese primary sources, sit in Chinese classrooms, track policy implementation on the ground, is hardly more secure and is substantially less capable,” he wrote.

Sun said the decline in China expertise could also hurt Beijing, depriving the country of interlocutors who could accurately interpret its intentions.

“In the long run, the ripple effects will spread from academia into government, media and business, heightening the risk of miscalculation and narrowing the scope for cooperation,” he said.

Rebuilding channels

The CSIS report called for renewed congressional travel, arguing that visits could help lawmakers understand how China’s policies and economic decisions affected their constituents.

McCallum said such trips could give Congress members a better understanding of issues they raised with Chinese officials, connecting foreign policy with practical concerns at home.

She cited Daines, whose home state of Montana is a major beef producer. Daines has used his visits to press for restored Chinese market access for American beef producers.

But visits must go beyond carefully arranged itineraries showcasing economic development, the CSIS report noted. McCallum said Beijing should allow visitors to have greater access to China’s economy and society, and make room for frank conversations with a range of counterparts.

She also identified Chinese sanctions against US officials as a possible deterrent to congressional travel.

“Sanctions on even a limited number of members can discourage others from travelling,” McCallum said, adding that expanding congressional travel took effort from both sides.

Sun similarly argued that Beijing should ease visits by lawmakers from both parties and chambers of Congress, including their staff.

“Exchanges should directly address constituency concerns, including agriculture, jobs and trade, while establishing follow-up mechanisms to turn single visits into sustained dialogue, preventing communication from snapping whenever the political climate cools,” he said.

The need for sustained, first-hand engagement with China extends beyond Congress to education and academia.

The CFR analysis called for Washington to rebuild funding and institutional support for China studies, while clarifying federal rules so that non-sensitive academic activities, such as language learning, could continue.

The report also urged Washington and Beijing to protect educational programmes from the wider tensions in their relationship.

Diao Daming, a professor in international studies at Renmin University of China, said efforts to strengthen Americans’ first-hand understanding of China would also benefit Beijing.

“They would help both sides develop a clearer, more objective and accurate understanding of each other, deepen their appreciation of the vital importance of stable China-US relations to both countries and the wider world, and ultimately contribute to greater stability in bilateral ties,” he said.

There have been signs of renewed interest in exchanges, but the larger question is whether these efforts can help rebuild American expertise on China.

At his summit with Trump in September, Xi invited 100,000 young Americans to visit China for exchange or study programmes in the coming five years.

The initiative doubles an earlier target announced in 2023 – to bring 50,000 young Americans to China by 2028. Chinese authorities said that target had been reached ahead of schedule.

Diao said the 2023 initiative’s early completion showed strong demand for youth and people-to-people exchanges between the two countries.

“These efforts incrementally build goodwill in a subtle, quiet way,” Diao said. “They lay a solid foundation for people-to-people ties and play a crucial role in stabilising the broader bilateral relationship.”

Sun, while echoing Diao’s view, cautioned that short-term visits alone could not reverse the decline in American expertise on China.

Developing specialists required sustained engagement with the country, rather than brief exposure through organised exchange programmes, Sun noted.

He said visits should be connected to longer-term opportunities, including Chinese-language courses, semester exchanges, graduate study and field research.

Sun added that credit recognition, scholarships and academic supervision could help participants continue their studies after returning home.

item.title: [SCMP] ‘Poster child’: why more Chinese firms have Thailand in their expansion plans
item.description:
With domestic profits narrowing and production capacity expanding, China’s firms are continuing to widen their overseas footprints in search of new, more lucrative markets. In this series, we examine China Inc.’s next phase of “going global” and the complex, challenging international environment its companies have chosen to enter.

A subtle shift is taking place among Chinese businesses as they adopt a “China plus one” outlook and redirect domestic investments to neighbouring economies – a strategy largely designed as a hedge against tariffs and geopolitical risks.

Vietnam, popular for much of this period, is beginning to lose some favour as firms look to Thailand as another alternative destination. The latter country has gained the edge on its competitor in the post-trade war 2.0 era, attracting billions of US dollars in outlays last year.
item.content:encoded:
With domestic profits narrowing and production capacity expanding, China’s firms are continuing to widen their overseas footprints in search of new, more lucrative markets. In this series, we examine China Inc.’s next phase of “going global” and the complex, challenging international environment its companies have chosen to enter.

A subtle shift is taking place among Chinese businesses as they adopt a “China plus one” outlook and redirect domestic investments to neighbouring economies – a strategy largely designed as a hedge against tariffs and geopolitical risks.

Vietnam, popular for much of this period, is beginning to lose some favour as firms look to Thailand as another alternative destination. The latter country has gained the edge on its competitor in the post-trade war 2.0 era, attracting billions of US dollars in outlays last year.

But the influx has also made Bangkok more mindful of risks, particularly those related to US measures intended to limit Chinese transshipment.

“Thailand is hailed as a new poster child of the ‘China plus one’ strategy of the new era,” said Donald Low, professor of public policy at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.

As tech-intensive Chinese manufacturers flock there while the sun sets on export re-routing via Vietnam, the Land of Smiles may gain further ground over its neighbour.

“Thailand has a reasonably mature, sophisticated manufacturing base that is more advanced than Vietnam’s,” Low said.

From Vietnam’s perspective, “manufacturing saturation” and a perception change – aggravated by US trade scrutiny, including punitive tariffs of 40 per cent on Chinese goods found to have been diverted through the country – mean it may have run its course as a popular destination, the scholar added.

Thailand in, Vietnam out?

In 2025, Thailand attracted US$5.33 billion in Chinese investment, compared with Vietnam’s US$2.46 billion, according to data from the Chinese Ministry of Commerce.

Thailand’s location and established industrial infrastructure have allowed China-funded factories to plug straight into supply chains that are being extended from China to members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), Low said.

“For tech-intensive manufacturing – like electronic components and machinery, electric vehicles [EVs] and solar panels – Thailand has the requisite capabilities to attract investments. BYD, for instance, runs an EV plant there,” he said.

In a success story now touted by Thai officials, the first EV made by BYD in Thailand rolled off the production line in 2024 in Rayong, the location of a US$490 million factory with an annual capacity of 150,000 units and a Thai workforce of 10,000.

On the other hand, BYD’s plan for a similar factory in Vietnam, unveiled in 2024, remains stuck in the slow lane, with construction delayed.

“Even before the US imposed tariffs on transshipped goods, there were already signs Vietnam was ‘saturated’ with manufacturing from China, especially in assembly,” according to Low.

“It was becoming less attractive to assembly manufacturing due to infrastructure bottlenecks and rising labour costs … American levies added to the pressures facing Chinese firms there.”

Some again see Thailand as the next Vietnam … They need a ‘Made in Thailand’ label

Thai trade official

Perception in Vietnam is also becoming less favourable towards Chinese investment. “A growing view is that Vietnamese domestic manufacturers weren’t benefiting from Chinese firms investing there for avoiding US tariffs,” Low said.

“There was little technology transfer, the investments weren’t helping the economy upgrade and worse, they may also squeeze out Vietnamese firms.”

In contrast, Thailand is anticipating a growing influx.

In the first half of 2026, Thai authorities approved 321 mainland China-funded investment projects for government incentives, representing one-quarter of the total. These projects brought in 45.7 billion Thai baht or 9.7 billion Chinese yuan (US$1.4 billion), according to Thailand’s Board of Investment (BOI).

Between 2021 and 2025, total investments from mainland China reached 132.5 billion yuan, with an average year-on-year growth of 56 per cent.

Thailand has also entered the top four recipients of Chinese foreign direct investment in Asean, alongside Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia.

Thailand not becoming another Vietnam

Though more Chinese firms are making their way to Thai shores, their motives may still differ substantially, according to a trade official with Thailand BOI’s office in China, adding that some still sought only to divert exports.

“Some again see Thailand as the next Vietnam … They need a ‘Made in Thailand’ label,” she said, declining to be named as she was not authorised to speak to media.

The official said Bangkok’s relatively favourable trade ties with Washington presented an opportunity for companies looking to establish themselves in Thailand – as well as less scrupulous exporters searching for tariff loopholes.

She pointed to Bangkok’s 17 free trade agreements covering 24 partner economies, which would enable “broad export access”, as well as Bangkok and Washington’s reciprocal trade agreement, which included possible zero-duty treatment for certain products.

This stands in contrast with Vietnam’s higher US duty exposure, thanks to stricter transshipment rules and its trade surplus with the US – two times the size of Thailand’s.

Thailand, though also subject to rules of origin verification, experiences “relatively lower US scrutiny”, the official said.

These considerations are likely to have influenced Chinese manufacturers’ plans.

In a December stock exchange filing, Shandong Bailong Chuangyuan Bio-tech, one of China’s largest food ingredient producers, said it had raised 748 million yuan to expand its Thai operations.

“This is a strategic move … The Thai facility will not only boost profitability by leveraging low-cost raw materials and tariff advantages there … It can also circumvent trade barriers,” said the company.

Some analysts warned that a rush by Chinese manufacturers into Thailand could eventually turn the country into another Vietnam, with those seeking a new tariff haven getting squeezed all over again.

“With tools like Section 301 probes, Washington is looking through the map,” said Dan Martin, a Vietnam-based international business adviser with global consultancy Dezan Shira & Associates.

“Other countries like Thailand can also come under scrutiny, just like Vietnam. Exporters should stop hunting for the next loophole.”

But Thailand is not sitting idle, and appears to be heeding lessons from Vietnam’s experience over punitive measures targeting transshipment and “origin fraud”.

Minimal processing or simple relabelling before re-exporting has been under heavy scrutiny by the Thai Department of Foreign Trade, with the department heightening monitoring for products of Chinese origin and formulating watch lists for sectors vulnerable to tariff circumvention, according to Thai media reports.

To avoid US retaliation and access restrictions, and to protect legitimate local producers, Bangkok is collaborating with Washington to inspect suspected supply chains and mandate strict rules of origin certification.

Last year, Thailand’s Anti-Dumping and Subsidy Consideration Committee said it had determined certain Chinese steel pipe imports were slightly altered or transshipped through the country to bypass tariffs, a practice it deemed an evasion of anti-dumping rules.

In February, the US Department of Commerce also determined imported pipes, completed in Thailand but using steel billets from China, circumvented anti-dumping duties.

Thailand still beckons

As Bangkok takes steps to combat re-routing and other tariff avoidance practices, Thai diplomats in China stressed their country still “fully embraces” Chinese investments, adding that Bangkok was committed to helping companies tap Thailand’s potential.

Siwadee Suksawate, commerce consul with the Thai consulate in Guangzhou, said there were immense opportunities for Chinese firms who “invest local and sell local”.

“We have a huge domestic market of 66 million people. In areas like electronics and automotive, especially EVs, we are positioned to attract manufacturers seeking diversification and localisation,” she said.

“Rather than viewing Thailand as [only] for export, more Chinese firms now have long-term commitment and localised production and management.”

Unlike many in Vietnam, prominent Thai voices are continuing to call for infusions of Chinese capital. “Thailand is not wrong to welcome Chinese investment. The capital is real, the factories are being built, and the technology is arriving,” read a May editorial by the Thailand Business News.

“For a developing economy seeking to industrialise rapidly, that is not a relationship to squander.”

New era, new playbook

Underpinning their warmer economic ties after last year’s peak tariff levels, Beijing and Washington have extended their trade truce and pared back tensions, particularly after this year’s summits between President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump.

New Chinese investments coming to Thailand are lured by our real advantages, less likely for transshipment

Siwadee Suksawate, Thai commerce consul

The US has agreed to identify US$30 billion worth of “non-sensitive goods” from China, like toys, fireworks and daily necessities, for tariff exemption under the new Board of Trade mechanism. Beijing has agreed in principle to a similar exemption.

Officials and business leaders from Thailand, Vietnam and China said the friendlier atmosphere could reduce the incentive to divert exports.

“This means new Chinese investments coming to Thailand are lured by our real advantages, less likely for transshipment,” Suksawate said.

One type of Chinese investment being courted heavily is in hi-tech electronics, she said, adding that Bangkok had optimised tax and other incentives for them, particularly for those setting up shop in Thailand’s Eastern Economic Corridor, a special economic zone close to the Chinese border.

Liu Quanlei, chairman of the Chinese Enterprises Chamber of Commerce in Thailand, observed a similar shift towards local sales.

“Notably, more [Chinese firms] are going local, prioritising sales in Thailand and Asean … This is particularly evident in the tech and digital sector, led by Huawei and ZTE, in the home appliance sector represented by Haier, Midea and TCL, as well as EV makers like BYD and Chery,” Liu said at a business seminar held in September at the 23rd China-Asean Expo in Nanning.

He added some Chinese investors were shipping finished products and components back home, including rice, rubber and non-ferrous metal.

Liu said this demand was expected to bring more positive spillovers to Thailand, Vietnam and other countries in China’s periphery, including Chinese producers based there, in the form of more imports.

Though Thailand has gained a considerable lead on Vietnam, it is not all gloom in Hanoi, even as the momentum wanes for export re-routing.

“Vietnam is no longer a low-cost, low-income economy. It’s naturally looking to upgrade industrial structure and technology capabilities, rather than attract low-end manufacturing,” Low said.

At the China-Asean Expo in September, Vietnamese exhibitors occupied 170 booths spanning 3,000 square metres (32,290 square feet).

While attending the expo, Vietnam’s deputy prime minister Pham Gia Tuc made no reference to export re-routing, but said Hanoi would welcome Chinese trade and investment in artificial intelligence, smart manufacturing and industrial estate development.

Meanwhile, China’s launch of the massive river-to-sea Pinglu Canal in September, a waterway connecting southwest China with the Gulf of Tonkin – and several nearby Vietnamese ports – could again redraw trade in Hanoi’s favour.

The canal is expected to slash tens of billions of yuan in annual logistics costs and spur more two-way flows between China and Asean, potentially positioning Vietnam as the beachhead for trade between the bloc and the world’s second-largest economy.

item.title: [SCMP] Why foreign companies are still betting on Hong Kong’s culinary reputation
item.description:
Despite a downturn in Hong Kong’s food and beverage sector, foreign enterprises are still betting on the city as a fine-dining destination, with a South Korean hydroponic ginseng grower and a 123-year-old Japanese confectioner choosing it for their first overseas ventures.

Jack Kwon, founder and CEO of Seoul-based Biofx, signed a deal with Hong Kong hydroponics firm Farm66 last Thursday to grow Korean gourmet ginseng in the city and sell it to local consumers and restaurants.

The deal marks the first time the Korean company has expanded hydroponically grown ginseng operations overseas.
item.content:encoded:
Despite a downturn in Hong Kong’s food and beverage sector, foreign enterprises are still betting on the city as a fine-dining destination, with a South Korean hydroponic ginseng grower and a 123-year-old Japanese confectioner choosing it for their first overseas ventures.

Jack Kwon, founder and CEO of Seoul-based Biofx, signed a deal with Hong Kong hydroponics firm Farm66 last Thursday to grow Korean gourmet ginseng in the city and sell it to local consumers and restaurants.

The deal marks the first time the Korean company has expanded hydroponically grown ginseng operations overseas.

Hydroponics is an indoor cultivation technique in which plants are grown not in soil but in mineral- and nutrient-infused water under LED lights, typically using a method that allows crops to be planted vertically on shelves to optimise space.

“We had several choices: Japan, Singapore, Vietnam and so on, but we made the decision to go to Hong Kong because Hong Kong is the number one fine dining market in Asia,” Kwon told the South China Morning Post.

The group also hopes to use Hong Kong as a springboard to other markets in the region, such as Singapore, Vietnam and Japan, he said.

He added that the process of opening a company in the city for his international ambitions was also the most flexible and that he had strong relationships with an accounting firm in Hong Kong, which provided support.

Kwon said all of the ginseng plant, including the stems and leaves, could be turned into products, unlike traditional ginseng harvested just for the roots. He aimed to bring that expertise, as well as marketing materials, to a Hong Kong urban farm.

Kwon said he had used ChatGPT in August last year to find Farm66 for his first overseas venture. The company will provide infrastructure and technologies for his operation in Hong Kong.

Gordon Tam Chi-ho, founder and CEO of Farm66, said his firm was currently looking for a site to house a container farm for hydroponic ginseng, and was confident that it could secure a place within a year.

“We learned a lot from them because from their research, the leaves are higher in nutrients and could also become products,” Tam said.

The leaves could be harvested every two months and used to make pesto, served in salads or brewed as tea, he added.

Victoria Wang, the farm’s chief information officer, said Farm66 used cameras linked to artificial intelligence and real-time data analytics, allowing Kwon to keep a close eye on the plants in Hong Kong while he was in Seoul.

Wang added that manipulating the LED lights could also help grow more, larger leaves, with adjustments done electronically.

Bringing in foreign capital has been a top priority for Hong Kong. The city’s investment promotion arm, InvestHK, has helped set up or expand 516 overseas and mainland Chinese companies in the city in the first eight months of the year, Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Algernon Yau Ying-wah told the SCMP in an interview earlier this month. He believed they tapped the Hong Kong market because the city was “stable, safe and free”.

The investment came despite restaurant receipts and purchases remaining flat, with 0.8 per cent growth in value offset by a 0.1 per cent reduction in volume in the first six months of this year, compared with the same period last year.

Another newcomer to Hong Kong is Okaman Honpo, a 123-year-old producer of wagashi, or Japanese confectionery, from Tokushima.

The company recently launched its first overseas outlet in Hong Kong in collaboration with local brand Master Gift, owned by 78-year-old Hong Kong chef Wan Tat-kong, who has lived and worked in Japan for more than 30 years and whose food has received accolades there.

Kenji Okada, the 79-year-old fourth-generation owner of Okaman Honpo, said he had not thought about expanding the company beyond Japan but decided to do so after being persuaded by Wan, a friend.

The pair jointly developed wagashi that combined Chinese and Japanese influences for the Hong Kong market, in a project initially planned to run for five years.

“There is a limit to the [amount of] ingredients we have, such as sugar from cane, because we grow them on our farm, and cannot scale too much. So the company will focus on its Hong Kong business first,” Okada said through an interpreter.

Okada said he would have retired had it not been for Wan’s proposal to collaborate. But now he hopes that whoever takes over the family business will continue with the joint venture.

Wan said he would visit Okada’s workshop in Japan three to four times a year to jointly produce the wagashi, which would be delivered to Hong Kong at a more affordable price than what was currently available on the market.
