“This is also a form of people-to-people cultural exchange between two countries,” Wan said.

Gary Ng Cheuk-yan, a senior economist at Natixis Corporate and Investment Bank, noted that both businesses had partnered with Hong Kong firms to enter the market, adding that such synergy benefited both local and overseas enterprises.

“If the economy were great, perhaps they [foreign businesses] could just set up here on their own. In reality, it’s not as easy to do so, so this allows them to share risks and achieve a win-win scenario,” Ng said.

These collaborations demonstrate that businesses are exploring new growth avenues, from creating tailored products to reach customers more effectively to offering fresh dining choices, according to Ng.

Ng also pointed out that the target market segment for both the Japanese and Korean businesses, though smaller, appeared to be more premium and niche, which could present unique opportunities in Hong Kong.

Another factor prompting Korean and Japanese businesses to venture overseas is weakness in their domestic markets, even as specific sectors – such as semiconductors in South Korea and tourism in Japan – continue to perform well.

As a result, many enterprises were looking to export products to sustain growth, and Hong Kong presented targeted opportunities for those seeking expansion, Ng said.

Vera Yuen Wing-han, a lecturer in economics at the University of Hong Kong, noted that despite shifting consumption patterns, with many local residents heading across the border to mainland China for food and entertainment, the city still retained strong spending power.

“If there are special enough offerings, Hongkongers are willing to pay a premium,” Yuen said. “If it’s a concept backed by good promotion, a rich story, quality, and unique selling points, it can become very popular.”

She pointed out that Hongkongers’ penchant for all things Japanese and Korean significantly boosted market receptivity for products from the two countries while frequent cultural exchanges and tourism further facilitated business collaborations.

“It’s more special when these are brands from overseas, not affordable products or those that you could secure from the mainland, as many people already have access to those by spending time across the border,” Yuen said.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong’s Huanggang crossing absorbs 366% surge as travellers stream back
item.description:
Inbound crossings at Hong Kong’s revamped Huanggang Port surged by 366 per cent on Monday afternoon over comparable periods in September, as the first long weekend since its reopening came to a close, with authorities expecting an even greater rush later in the evening.

A steady stream of travellers returned to Hong Kong through the checkpoint on Monday, with crowds growing noticeably by 5pm, peaking at around 6.15pm, and tapering off by 7pm, as observed by the South China Morning Post.

Unlike Sunday, when departing travellers complained on social media about long wait times during peak hours, Monday’s inbound flow remained orderly.
item.content:encoded:
Inbound crossings at Hong Kong’s revamped Huanggang Port surged by 366 per cent on Monday afternoon over comparable periods in September, as the first long weekend since its reopening came to a close, with authorities expecting an even greater rush later in the evening.

A steady stream of travellers returned to Hong Kong through the checkpoint on Monday, with crowds growing noticeably by 5pm, peaking at around 6.15pm, and tapering off by 7pm, as observed by the South China Morning Post.

Unlike Sunday, when departing travellers complained on social media about long wait times during peak hours, Monday’s inbound flow remained orderly.

“It’s a very nice port – the bathrooms are clean, it’s huge and spacious … what a great thing to see in our lifetime,” said 66-year-old retiree Adam Ko, who was with his wife, Mary.

The couple said they were aware of the large crowds at the crossing over the weekend.

“It’s still early in the night, so we decided to come here hoping to skip the peak hours. It was very smooth and we just breezed through,” said Ko.

However, he noted minor traffic congestion while approaching the port by taxi in Shenzhen at around 4.30pm. “We were stuck on the roads for maybe 10 minutes. Acceptable, but I’d think twice if it was any later in the day.”

A Shenzhen resident in her forties who works in the garment industry and gave only her surname, Tang, said she preferred the revamped port for its convenience.

“This new arrangement saves me about 20 minutes crossing the border,” she said.

According to the Security Bureau, 9,401 travellers entered Hong Kong via Huanggang Port between 2pm and 4pm on Monday, a 366 per cent surge from the average number of inbound crossings through the former Huanggang/Lok Ma Chau control point during the same hours across the four weekends in September.

It expected the number of inbound travellers to rise further in the evening.

With the expected surge in crossings, all immigration clearance channels were opened, while authorities prepared crowd-control measures and designated waiting areas for passengers using public transport.

The holiday marked the first major test for the revamped crossing between Hong Kong and mainland China, which reopened on October 12 with a new joint immigration clearance system designed to cut processing times from about half an hour to as little as five minutes.

Travellers can complete clearance by presenting a single identity document and passing through an automated channel with three gates.

Yung Ka-wai, deputy commander of the Immigration Department’s Lok Ma Chau Division, said clearance at Huanggang had been smooth on Monday and expected the afternoon-to-evening period to be the busiest for foot traffic.

“We will continue to monitor the situation at the control points in real time and flexibly deploy manpower according to passenger flows to speed up the clearing of crowds,” Yung said.

“Travellers are advised to plan their journeys early, choose a suitable control point and avoid crossing the border during peak hours.”

He also reminded eligible residents to register in advance if they wished to use the new clearance model.

Commissioner for Transport Winnie Tse Wing-yee inspected Huanggang Port on Monday morning, instructing officers and public transport operators to closely monitor passenger and traffic flows and deploy resources flexibly. She also asked bus companies to run additional short-haul special services to clear travellers more quickly.

The Transport Department said about 120 franchised buses, 40 minibuses and 130 cross-border buses had been deployed for service and standby on Monday.

Headways for franchised buses would be shortened to two to three minutes during peak hours, and to three to four minutes for minibuses and cross-border buses.

Huanggang handled more than 152,000 crossings on Sunday, with some travellers waiting up to two hours amid congestion that lawmakers attributed to unfamiliarity with new clearance procedures, a surge in traffic and computer system reboots.

Immigration Department figures showed the port handled 152,068 crossings, the highest daily total since it opened on October 12. These comprised 77,166 outbound trips and 74,902 inbound journeys.

Hongkongers accounted for 133,265 crossings, while mainland visitors made 16,832 trips.

The facility is designed to handle up to 300,000 travellers and 15,000 vehicles a day, with daily passenger numbers initially expected to range from 100,000 to 200,000.

As the Chung Yeung Festival break fuelled a surge in cross-border travel over the weekend, the Security Bureau issued a “busy” advisory for Huanggang on its “Easy Boundary” portal on Sunday afternoon, warning that clearance could take up to 45 minutes. Some mainland visitors, however, reported queuing for as long as two hours.

Lawmaker Ben Chan Han-pan, chairman of the Legislative Council’s transport panel, said travellers’ unfamiliarity with the new “collaborative inspection and joint immigration clearance” model was the main cause of congestion on Sunday, with some attempting to use the automated channels without registering beforehand.

He added that the sudden surge in passenger numbers had also overwhelmed the control point.

Chan said computer systems at the immigration counters had slowed after running for extended periods and needed to be rebooted, further lengthening queues.

Lawmaker Chong Ho-fung said the long queues at the newly reopened port over the weekend were inevitable given the large number of travellers crossing the border during the Chung Yeung Festival peak.

He said that close to 40,000 people crossed at Huanggang between 10am and 2pm on Sunday, averaging nearly 10,000 an hour, and even with each passenger taking just a minute to complete clearance, queues could easily result in an hour-long wait.

“The government’s projections and my own both forecast this would happen. It is a chaotic situation that was within expectations,” Chong told a radio programme.

He urged authorities to step up publicity about registration procedures and eligibility requirements for the new “joint clearance” automated channels.

Children under seven cannot use the automated channels and must be accompanied by their parents to staffed counters to complete clearance. Those aged seven to 17 can use the “joint clearance” channels once their parents have registered them.

Chong said clearer information would help prevent families with young children from reaching the front of the queue only to discover they were ineligible and had to move to staffed counters, adding to their clearance time.

“There were too many different reasons why a passenger could not complete clearance, and staff on the ground may not be able to identify the exact reason immediately, causing a chaotic situation,” he said.

He also suggested designating more clearance lanes for use by both foreign travellers and Hong Kong residents to speed up the process.

Chong said he had also observed system reboots on Sunday in the “joint one-stop” vehicle clearance lane because of mismatches between Hong Kong and Shenzhen data.

But he said the congestion was unlikely to persist, as clearance should become smoother once more travellers had registered properly.

item.title: [SCMP] Katie Zacharia and Mao Ning – a study in contrasts in US and China media strategies
item.description:
Katie Zacharia may have lasted just five days as the White House press secretary but still managed to set off a diplomatic incident with China.

In an interview with a conservative commentator on Thursday, Zacharia referred to China as a place that “doesn’t even have proper toilets”.

Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning responded a day later with a smile and a brief, pointed invitation.
item.content:encoded:
Katie Zacharia may have lasted just five days as the White House press secretary but still managed to set off a diplomatic incident with China.

In an interview with a conservative commentator on Thursday, Zacharia referred to China as a place that “doesn’t even have proper toilets”.

Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning responded a day later with a smile and a brief, pointed invitation.

“We welcome her to visit China more often when she has the opportunity,” said Mao, a veteran diplomat.

Like Mao, Zacharia was – if only for less than a week – the highly visible public face of her government, speaking on issues that could shape how her country was perceived.

But Mao and Zacharia are the products of vastly different systems and took contrasting paths to the podium, using very different ways to tell two very different stories.

Worlds apart

Zacharia’s debut – and final – official White House briefing lasted fewer than 15 minutes on Tuesday, with much of her presentation delivered from a prepared script.

By then, questions had surfaced about her legal credentials after she had presented herself as a lawyer in media appearances.

According to her LinkedIn profile, Zacharia worked as an associate at Zhong Lun Law Firm, one of China’s biggest, in Beijing from 2011 to 2013.

Before joining the White House, she was a frequent commentator on conservative networks Fox News and Newsmax, where she defended US President Donald Trump and his agenda. She had also briefly held a communications role at the Department of Homeland Security.

As she stepped into one of the most visible communications positions in the US government, Zacharia found herself becoming the story.

Asked about her legal credentials, she said she had received them “when I moved to China”, before later saying she had misheard the question.

By the weekend, she was no longer in the White House job.

In China’s foreign ministry spokesperson system, officials generally have extensive diplomatic experience and undergo substantial preparation before taking on the position.

Another difference is in the scope of their roles.

A foreign ministry spokesperson is among the Chinese government’s most prominent and regular public-facing representatives, communicating Beijing’s positions on diplomacy and international affairs.

By contrast, the White House press secretary’s responsibilities extend beyond explaining domestic and foreign policy.

As a presidential appointee, the spokesperson is also expected to defend the president’s agenda and respond to political criticism on their behalf.

Zacharia was appointed to the role just three weeks before the midterm elections, at a politically sensitive time with Trump’s approval ratings at near-record lows. Her debut briefing on October 13 combined praise for Trump and his “America first” agenda, taking questions from just three reporters before wrapping up.

She left a question about Ukraine unanswered, saying she would have to return to it, prompting further doubts about her readiness for the position.

Her predecessor, Karoline Leavitt, had also used her first briefing to frame a major development involving China through the lens of US domestic politics.

Describing the emergence of Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) company DeepSeek as a “wake-up call” for the US AI industry, she blamed the previous Joe Biden administration for allowing China to develop the technology so rapidly.

Different paths

China’s foreign ministry formally established its spokesperson system in March 1983, during the country’s reform and opening-up drive.

A year earlier, Qian Qichen had held what is regarded as the ministry’s first press conference. He later rose through the diplomatic ranks to become foreign minister and vice-premier.

The ministry’s spokespersons are career diplomats who typically gather years of experience in foreign affairs before taking on the high-profile role.

Mao became the ministry’s 33rd spokesperson in September 2022 and was appointed director general of its information department in January 2025.

Before taking on the chief spokesperson role, Mao had spent more than 27 years in diplomatic service, focusing mainly on Asian affairs. She had also briefly served in a local government position as deputy mayor in 2020.

Qin Gang, who was later removed from office, also served two stints as a ministry spokesman before rising to become foreign minister in 2022.

By contrast, White House press secretaries often come from political communications, campaign work or media backgrounds.

Leavitt, for example, worked in Trump’s first administration, served as communications director for Republican congresswoman Elise Stefanik and was national press secretary for Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign before taking the White House job in January 2025.

The contrast reflects the different institutional functions of the two positions.

The White House press secretary speaks mainly for the president and his administration, defending its policies while responding to domestic political scrutiny.

China’s foreign ministry spokesperson, by comparison, communicates the government’s positions on international affairs through regular briefings, which have been held each weekday since 2011.

Method and manner

For Beijing, public communication is part of a broader effort to shape how China is understood abroad, with the foreign ministry enlisted to “tell China’s story well”.

To this end, Chinese spokespersons’ comments are measured and carefully scripted, sometimes using subtle and indirect language.

A 2022 commentary in Shanghai news outlet The Paper defended this style of communication as a strategic buffer, saying that avoiding definitive statements left room for manoeuvre without boxing officials into a position that could prove difficult to defend.

That is poles apart from the more combative style associated with some US White House press secretaries. Leavitt, for instance, became known for her sharp retorts and rapid-fire responses, which also won praise from some Chinese social media users impressed by her verbal agility. Her language was direct and combative, consistent with the political messaging that had defined her work on Trump’s campaign.

But the Chinese spokesperson is usually more measured – something Mao in particular is known for.

Nevertheless, China’s roster of spokespeople has also included more controversial figures, most notably Zhao Lijian, who became a prominent face of the Wolf Warrior style of diplomacy.

The style, named after a Chinese nationalist action-film franchise, is commonly used to describe an assertive and confrontational approach to defending China’s interests and responding to foreign criticism.

Critics argue that such confrontational messaging risks damaging China’s diplomatic relationships, while supporters see it as a forceful response to Western criticism.

item.title: [SCMP] The AI promise was automation. The reality? Managing digital workers
item.description:
When artificial intelligence agents first arrived, they came with a tantalising promise: autonomous “digital workers” that would finally free humans from corporate drudgery. As businesses across Asia are discovering, however, the reality is quite the opposite – more work, new friction and a whole new layer of management.

When Xiao Mengjie, an AI product marketing manager at a Big Tech firm in Shanghai, recently assigned two AI agents what she described as a simple task, she expected efficiency. Instead, she got corporate gridlock.

Rather than dividing the workload, her agent and her supervisor’s agent locked in a prolonged discussion over responsibilities, debating who should verify details and which one should take ownership of different tasks, in a spectacle not unlike the human bureaucracy they had been hired to replace.
item.content:encoded:
When artificial intelligence agents first arrived, they came with a tantalising promise: autonomous “digital workers” that would finally free humans from corporate drudgery. As businesses across Asia are discovering, however, the reality is quite the opposite – more work, new friction and a whole new layer of management.

When Xiao Mengjie, an AI product marketing manager at a Big Tech firm in Shanghai, recently assigned two AI agents what she described as a simple task, she expected efficiency. Instead, she got corporate gridlock.

Rather than dividing the workload, her agent and her supervisor’s agent locked in a prolonged discussion over responsibilities, debating who should verify details and which one should take ownership of different tasks, in a spectacle not unlike the human bureaucracy they had been hired to replace.

“It became very formal and cumbersome,” Xiao said. “Agents can create communication overhead too.”

Across Asia, businesses have eagerly bought into the pitch of autonomous software capable of planning and executing multistep workflows with limited human intervention. But from Singapore’s hotels and insurers to Hong Kong’s service sector and mainland China’s tech giants, enterprises are confronting a sharp reality check.

The surge in regional adoption reflects a broader global frenzy for autonomous software.

Meta Platforms’ personal agent, Muse, launched in September, drew an estimated 2.8 million downloads in its first two weeks.

In mainland China, enthusiasm for OpenClaw, an open-source agent, sparked a craze known locally as “raising lobsters”, prompting hundreds of people to queue outside Tencent Holdings’ headquarters in Shenzhen earlier this year for help installing the software.

Tech titans including Tencent, Alibaba Group Holding, owner of the South China Morning Post, and Baidu have all introduced agent-focused enterprise products.

Yet the rush to deploy AI agents has exposed a gap between what the technology can do and how effectively organisations can manage it.

Why some businesses struggle to put AI to work

At times, users find that seemingly straightforward workflows become challenging puzzles once they are handed over to autonomous agents.

At Singapore-based hospitality technology start-up Conzi, chief operating officer Mark Wee wants AI agents to handle the multi-departmental, behind-the-scenes work that often pulls hotel staff away from guest care.

For example, when a hotel guest leaves a scathing review, the complaint can trigger a lengthy chain of work behind the scenes. A receptionist must respond, a manager investigates what went wrong, and a supervisor checks records to determine who was responsible. The hotel might even revise its operating procedures.

But deploying AI agents to manage complex hotel operations is easier said than done.

A single guest complaint could involve multiple departments, from housekeeping to hotel management, requiring agents to navigate fragmented systems and determine when human intervention was needed, Wee said.

The challenge is compounded by operational knowledge that is often scattered across spreadsheets, paper records and the heads of experienced employees.

Wee said Conzi was working to consolidate this information so its agents could coordinate tasks across departments, but he stressed that technology alone was not enough.

“If you don’t get the buy-in from the people who are supposed to use the systems the most, any system in any organisation will fail,” Wee said.

Similar obstacles confronted Asia’s travel industry, where differing regulations, technical standards and disconnected platforms complicated AI deployment, according to Prabu Sangar, director of technology operations and integration at FCM Travel Asia, a corporate travel management company.

“Even if the AI is as capable as it is, the surrounding environment may not be ready for it,” he said.

In Hong Kong, companies were trying to accelerate AI adoption while contending with “legacy” technology systems and organisational resistance, said Robert Hah, Hong Kong office lead at consultancy Accenture Greater China.

Only 10 per cent of Hong Kong companies surveyed had integrated generative AI across multiple business functions, compared with about 21 per cent of mainland Chinese enterprises, according to Accenture.

Leo Wong, co-founder of Hong Kong-based business communications platform imBee, said demand for AI agents had grown among customers across Hong Kong, Singapore and Malaysia, but concerns over data security were slowing adoption, especially in Hong Kong. The company provides AI-powered tools that help businesses manage customer communications across WhatsApp, email and other messaging platforms.

Wong said banks, insurers and other financial services companies were particularly cautious, with deployment decisions taking longer as they worked through their AI strategies and security requirements.

Organisations wanted to build confidence in the technology before deploying it, he added.

I already have lots of ideas, and AI makes more of them feel achievable, so I start more projects. Then every project is waiting for my judgment, and I end up being the busiest person

Xiao Mengjie, AI product marketing manager

Wang Jiangyu, professor of law and associate dean at City University of Hong Kong, said the institutional mechanisms needed to govern autonomous agents had struggled to keep pace with their technical development.

“The governance challenge today is less about creating more powerful AI and more about ensuring that increasingly capable systems remain accountable and aligned with human objectives,” he said.

While AI systems had become more capable of executing tasks autonomously and coordinating with one another, questions including how decisions should be reviewed and who bore responsibility for those decisions remained unresolved, he said.

Too many agents?

In their eagerness to automate, some enterprises are discovering that more agents do not automatically translate into higher productivity.

At imBee, a company with around 50 to 60 employees, at least several hundred AI agents helped staff perform tasks ranging from software development to internal communications, according to Wong.

Wong, who described himself as non-technical, said he personally managed more than 20 agents, which in turn coordinated other agents.

While imBee used quality checks and verification procedures to avoid major errors, according to Wong, other workplaces reported that stacking agents simply duplicated existing corporate bloat.

“The market is over the phase of ‘agent maxing,’” said Raunak Mehta, co-founder and CEO of Singapore-based insurance technology company Igloo.

Operating across Southeast Asia with about 230 employees, Igloo uses software workers for customer service, software development, claims processing and financial reconciliation.

Mehta said total agent count was no longer a meaningful measure of operational success. Instead, the focus had shifted towards “agent harnesses” – control frameworks that coordinated agents, regulated their access to internal tools and allowed human oversight.

Leading AI agents – including Meta’s Muse, Tencent’s Xiaowei agent, and Manus 2.0 – increasingly rely on such harnesses to better understand users and drive long-term platform adoption.

Without proper harnesses, companies faced what Sangar of FCM Travel Asia called “agent sprawl” – a chaotic proliferation of autonomous software across departments with conflicting permissions, overlapping data sources and unintended interactions.

Uncoordinated agents can also compound mistakes across entire workflows.

“One agent might report that a task is complete when it has merely produced a draft,” AI product marketing manager Xiao said. “Another agent could mistake that output for an approved decision and act on it, allowing errors to spread.”

Compounding the risks, hotels and financial institutions must expose vast amounts of proprietary data to extract the full value of AI, increasing their exposure to cyber threats. “There is definitely a risk of rogue actors approaching us and trying to maliciously extract information,” Conzi’s Wee said.

Teaching people how to brief, review and correct an agent matters as much as the technology itself

Lionel Sim, The AI Capitol

Recent incidents have highlighted the risks of giving AI agents access to sensitive information and the authority to act without human approval.

Last month, Chinese AI start-up Z.ai said it had temporarily disabled certain features of its ZCode coding assistant after developers reported that the software was uploading local code repositories to cloud servers without their consent. The company, also known as Zhipu, apologised and patched the vulnerability.

A Reuters investigation published last month found that AI agents from Alibaba, DeepSeek and Moonshot AI systematically lied, hid failures and fabricated results during controlled tests. Alibaba, DeepSeek and Moonshot did not respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.

In another high-profile case, an OpenAI agent undergoing security evaluation broke out of its sandbox environment and breached systems at AI platform Hugging Face.

The risks have drawn the attention of regulators. Singapore’s Infocomm Media Development Authority has recommended that businesses restrict agents’ access to sensitive systems, define limits on their autonomy and establish mechanisms to shut them down when they malfunction.

The Cyberspace Administration of China has also mandated that companies complete mandatory algorithm filings and pre-deployment security assessments before rolling out agents, particularly those handling sensitive data or customer-facing operations.

Rise of the AI middle manager

Li Jiahao, a researcher specialising in global AI development at the Guangzhou Institute of the Greater Bay Area, said China had issued several AI regulatory documents quite rapidly over the past year, but these did not immediately translate into accountability mechanisms.

In both China and the rest of the world, “AI’s technical capabilities are iterating on a quarterly basis, regulations are iterating yearly, and liability is being determined case by case”, he said.

“These three curves are moving at completely different speeds, and the gap between them is still growing.”

As digital agents multiply, the fundamental operational bottleneck is shifting from computing power back to human supervisors.

Lionel Sim, founder of AI research firm The AI Capitol, said AI agent adoption in Asia was outpacing management. Employees were deploying agents “on their own initiative”, which was “great for momentum”, but companies did not have oversight of access, ownership and active tools, he said.

The adoption of AI agents has also resulted in a “skills shift”, pushing employees into management roles. “Teaching people how to brief, review and correct an agent matters as much as the technology itself,” Sim added.

For workers like Xiao, managing AI agents can be intensely stressful. While agents can work continuously and at a rapid pace, humans do not gain more hours in the day to supervise them.

“I already have lots of ideas, and AI makes more of them feel achievable, so I start more projects,” Xiao said. “Then every project is waiting for my judgment, and I end up being the busiest person.”

Mehta of Igloo warned that growing reliance on agents could create a longer-term problem: companies might eventually struggle to find employees with the experience needed to supervise them.

Li, the Guangzhou researcher, said AI might not suddenly cause mass unemployment, but it was likely to narrow the door for young people entering the workforce as companies scaled back hiring.

“Strong AI management capability means finding ways to turn the efficiency gains from AI into more new jobs, and weak management capability may simply mean companies save on labour costs while society bears the cost of youth unemployment,” he said.

Despite the growing pains, industry experts believe there is no turning back.

Chen Bo, a senior research fellow at the East Asian Institute of the National University of Singapore, described the current stage of AI development as “a wild growth phase”, with significant risks emerging around coordination, accountability and other areas.

“But when a major technological revolution comes along – when everyone is facing the AI revolution – the only real option is to ride its development while limiting the downsides, not to hold it back because of them,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Abby Choi’s partner tells murder trial she hid ex-in-laws’ financial reliance on her
item.description:
Slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung’s partner told a court this week she initially misled him about her former in-laws’ wealth before describing them as horrible and ungrateful after a bitter family dispute.

Chris Tam Fong-chun’s testimony also shed light on his complex relationship with Choi and his former classmate Alex Kwong Kong-chi. The three remained connected through their four children, as Choi had two with each man.

During the third week of the murder trial, Tam told the High Court that the 28-year-old model had initially portrayed her former in-laws as financially independent and comfortable. She feared her two children from her first marriage would be looked down on in their new home because of their background, the court heard.
item.content:encoded:
Slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung’s partner told a court this week she initially misled him about her former in-laws’ wealth before describing them as horrible and ungrateful after a bitter family dispute.

Chris Tam Fong-chun’s testimony also shed light on his complex relationship with Choi and his former classmate Alex Kwong Kong-chi. The three remained connected through their four children, as Choi had two with each man.

During the third week of the murder trial, Tam told the High Court that the 28-year-old model had initially portrayed her former in-laws as financially independent and comfortable. She feared her two children from her first marriage would be looked down on in their new home because of their background, the court heard.

After an acrimonious row over parenting in mid-2022, Choi allegedly told Tam for the first time that she had been supporting the Kwong family financially and urged him and his father to cut ties with them.

But Tam said he and Choi had kept up a friendly facade in front of her former in-laws while seeking to sell a HK$72 million (US$9.17 million) home registered in Kwong’s father’s name.

He acknowledged he had been “a bit sneaky”, but said this was unavoidable as the couple tried to recover what belonged to them gradually and through diplomatic means.

Asked whether he still viewed his former classmate in the same way after the dispute, Tam said: “I would say the friendship was no more.”

Kwong, 31, is standing trial on a joint count of murder alongside his father, Kwong Kau, 68, and elder brother, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35.

The elder Kwong, a retired police sergeant, has also denied preventing the lawful burial of Choi’s body. His two sons pleaded guilty to that offence before the trial began last month.

Prosecutors argued that the murder stemmed from a family feud over the proposed sale of the luxury flat at the upmarket Kadooria residential estate in Ho Man Tin.

They said Choi had registered her former father-in-law as the owner to avoid paying HK$9 million in double stamp duty but had never intended to give the property to her former in-laws.

The court heard that Choi had a heated argument with her former mother-in-law, Jenny Li Sui-heung, at the Kadooria flat in June or July 2022, when the influencer’s elder daughter had a fever.

Li allegedly told her son Alex to stay away from the child because she could infect him, prompting Choi to accuse her of favouring sons over daughters.

Kwong Kau allegedly joined the row, twice attempted to attack Choi, swore at her and called her a “birthing machine”.

The elder Kwong was subsequently barred from visiting the flat and seeing his two grandchildren, the court heard.

But the children were allegedly taken to see him and his girlfriend while Choi was attending a fashion event in France during the Chinese New Year holiday in 2023, much to her dismay.

Tam became friends with Alex Kwong in 2008, when they were studying at Concordia International School in Kowloon Tong, the court heard. Tam later continued his studies in Australia, while Kwong moved to Sear Rogers International School, where he met Choi, the court was told.

Tam appeared surprised when Kwong’s counsel, Andrew Raffell, suggested he had wanted a “romantic and sexual relationship” with his client when they were schoolmates.

“Definitely disagree,” the witness said.

Tam said he first met Choi in late 2013 or early 2014, during a brief holiday visit to Hong Kong to see Kwong, who was then married to her.

He said his relationship with Choi changed after Kwong “totally disappeared” one day in 2015. That year, Kwong began divorce proceedings and absconded from a trial over his alleged involvement in a HK$6.3 million theft case.

Tam and Choi began dating in December 2015 and held a wedding banquet a year later, although they never registered their marriage, the court heard. Their daughter was born in September 2016 and their son three years later.

“After Abby and I were together, I knew through Abby that Kwong Kong-chi was fine with our relationship and sent us his blessing. I also know his relationship with Abby was something in the past,” Tam said.

He added that he and Choi would meet Kwong during leisure trips to mainland China. The three saw one another more often at family gatherings after Kwong returned to Hong Kong in 2022.

Asked whether they had remained close until Choi’s disappearance, Tam said it was reasonable for them to do so because of their children.

He said the Kwong brothers and their mother appeared calm and unconcerned after Choi disappeared on February 21, 2023.

Li allegedly suggested that her former daughter-in-law had been abducted and that they should delay reporting her disappearance to police until the supposed kidnappers made their demands.

Anthony Kwong, who was working as Choi’s stand-in driver at the time, allegedly evaded questions about her whereabouts and pretended to help by driving Tam around to look for her.

Parts of Choi’s dismembered remains were found at a rental flat in Lung Mei village, Tai Po, on February 24.

The trial also shed light on the Tam family’s wealth and financial dealings with Choi and her former in-laws.

Tam’s father, Tam Chak-kwan, founded the popular restaurant chain TamJai Yunnan Mixian and received a share of the proceeds from its HK$1 billion sale to a Japanese company.

In 2019, the family moved into their current 4,000 square foot home on Begonia Road in Kowloon Tong, which the elder Tam bought for HK$168 million.

He said he had given his previous home, a 1,800 square foot flat valued at HK$41 million at the Manhattan Hill private estate in Lai Chi Kok, to Choi in 2018. But he had not expected his de facto daughter-in-law to live there, as he wanted to share a home with his grandchildren.

The court heard that the elder Tam gave Choi at least HK$200,000 a month to cover living expenses for her and his son. He also gave her more than HK$80 million in total to invest.

Chris Tam said Choi had made money investing in luxury watches, although he was unsure whether she had done so through her ex-husband.

Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, accused Alex Kwong of failing to repay any of the more than HK$70 million her daughter had given him to invest. She also called him a “brute” and dismissed his claim that he had supported her financially as “a pack of lies”.

Choi also allegedly put money into the Kadooria flat and an egg waffle shop run by Anthony Kwong, but Chris Tam said both had proved poor investments.

The court also heard how Kwong Kau had helped settle a dispute over a HK$5 million gambling debt Chris Tam incurred in Macau in August 2021.

The younger Tam said he had refused to repay the loan because he knew the casino, run by SunCity Group, was about to close following the arrest of its founder and CEO, Alvin Chau Cheok-wa.

Tam’s father said he had approached Kwong Kau for help because he wanted to resolve the dispute.

He said he had transferred HK$5 million to Kwong Kau’s personal bank account in March 2022 and paid him a further HK$450,000 in gratuities for people with triad affiliations who had stopped debt collectors from harassing his family.

The elder Tam said Kwong Kau later asked him for a HK$400,000 loan, saying police had frozen his account. Tam agreed to lend him HK$250,000, which had yet to be repaid, the court heard.

He added that he had ignored Kwong’s request for help with legal fees after the former officer was remanded in custody in connection with the case.

The trial continues on Tuesday before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia’s shoppers love Chinese e-commerce. But is the bargain worth it?
item.description:
In hindsight, it was only a matter of time before Esha Yusof joined the growing ranks of Malaysian shoppers being drawn to Chinese e-commerce giant Pinduoduo.

Esha is a relative newcomer. She signed up in July, more than half a year after the platform launched in Malaysia – and has been smitten with it ever since.

Rock-bottom prices, a vast range of products and seamless payments through a popular local e-wallet make it easy for the 32-year-old to spend an average of 500 ringgit (US$122) a month on everything from home decor and kitchen supplies to fashion and stationery.
item.content:encoded:
In hindsight, it was only a matter of time before Esha Yusof joined the growing ranks of Malaysian shoppers being drawn to Chinese e-commerce giant Pinduoduo.

Esha is a relative newcomer. She signed up in July, more than half a year after the platform launched in Malaysia – and has been smitten with it ever since.

Rock-bottom prices, a vast range of products and seamless payments through a popular local e-wallet make it easy for the 32-year-old to spend an average of 500 ringgit (US$122) a month on everything from home decor and kitchen supplies to fashion and stationery.

“Most items are much cheaper than in the Malaysian market. It’s hard to compare because they come directly from factories or warehouses in China,” said Esha, who works for a competing e-commerce site.

Delivery takes at least two weeks, far longer than many of the app’s local rivals. But that delay has had the opposite effect to the one you might expect.

“With the long wait, it makes more sense to buy almost every week, so the wait feels shorter when parcels keep arriving every week,” Esha said, adding that she still used local platforms for urgent orders.

Many Malaysians are now doing the same. Since the app’s launch in the country last December, social media has been awash with delighted shoppers showing off their hauls, from smartphones to sofas, rolls of toilet paper and even bags of cement.

But surging demand for goods shipped direct from China through the likes of Pinduoduo often comes at the expense of local retailers and manufacturers that struggle to match their Chinese rivals’ deep discounts.

Meanwhile, the millions of parcels flooding into Malaysia and the waste they create are testing the limits of the country’s ability to collect and dispose of it all.

Disappearing margins

Pinduoduo is far from the only e-commerce platform active in Malaysia. Small local businesses, especially in physical retail and manufacturing, have already seen their margins shrink amid intense competition from earlier entrants like Lazada and Shopee.

Still, the app’s arrival has prompted an outcry from local businesses, who complain that direct shipments from far larger competitors in China have unfairly priced them out of their own market.

Shipping direct from China is the strategy that has powered Pinduoduo’s growth since its founding in 2015, giving more established e-commerce players such as Taobao and JD.com a run for their money. Lazada and Taobao are subsidiaries of Alibaba Group, which also owns the South China Morning Post.

Pinduoduo built its empire on a simple premise: allow consumers to pool their purchases into bulk orders directly with factories and wholesalers to get better deals.

“The influx of low-priced products from foreign e-commerce platforms is putting tremendous pressure on Malaysian retailers, wholesalers and manufacturers, particularly micro and small businesses,” said Chin Chee Seong, president of the SME Association of Malaysia, an umbrella body for the country’s small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

Chin said operational costs had shot up by 80 per cent or more this year, citing an SME Association survey in April that found 76 per cent of respondents reported being hit hard by rising fuel and energy costs, with 45 per cent bracing themselves for a cash-flow crunch over the next six months.

“Malaysian SMEs are being squeezed from both sides – rising operating costs and increasingly aggressive price competition. Many simply cannot afford to keep reducing their prices,” he said.

A widespread slump in SME activity would be disastrous for the economy. Micro, small and medium-sized enterprises account for nearly 97 per cent of all registered businesses in Malaysia and employ around 8 million people, roughly half the entire workforce.

“As local shops and businesses lose sales or cease operations, they will reduce hiring and reduce demand for supporting services such as banking, advertising, accounting and other business services,” said Lee Heng Guie, executive director of the Socio-Economic Research Centre, a Malaysian think tank.

“Closed shops result in commercial and retail outlet vacancies, and the landlords may be forced to reduce rents to attract fewer available tenants, reducing property income.”

Retailers of imported consumer goods, from fashion to general merchandise, are likely to be the most immediate and visible casualties. Yet economists warn that the greater danger is that posed to Malaysia’s all-important manufacturing sector.

The rapid shift to buying electronics, apparel, footwear, cosmetics and furniture from overseas sellers could cause local factories to permanently lose their share of the domestic market, said economist Yeah Kim Leng of Sunway University.

“The distinction matters because retail displacement can be transitional as traders pivot to services or niche products, whereas manufacturing capacity, once lost, is far harder to rebuild,” he said.

Trashy dilemma

E-commerce began taking root in Malaysia in the mid-2010s, but demand truly exploded during the Covid-19 pandemic, when strict movement restrictions forced millions of people to do their shopping online between 2020 and 2022.

That habit has become even more deeply ingrained in the years since. An estimated 900 million parcels were delivered across Malaysia in 2025, according to the latest available government data, a multifold increase from the 52 million a decade earlier.

The appeal for e-commerce players is clear. A February note from equity and market analysts at Kenanga Research forecast that the value of e-commerce merchandise in Malaysia would reach 1.5 trillion ringgit in 2027, up from 1.2 trillion ringgit in 2024 (US$268.9 billion).

But this penchant for hyper-consumption could overwhelm the country’s capacity to deal with the vast amounts of rubbish generated.

Malaysia’s 135 landfills are already close to capacity, handling an average of 39,000 tonnes of solid waste daily, according to government figures from last year. Any increase in e-commerce shipments will almost certainly add to the growing trash pile.

The government has also pointed to a low recycling rate of 37.9 per cent of recoverable materials and poor waste separation practices at household and local council levels.

“The growth of online shopping, driven partly by competitive prices and convenience, has increased the volume of packaging waste,” said Randolph Jeremiah, vice-president of the non-profit Environmental Protection Society Malaysia.

“Although some online platforms, retailers and manufacturers have begun reducing packaging and switching to more recyclable materials, such as paper filling instead of polystyrene, these efforts may not be sufficient to keep pace with rising consumption.”

A raft of government policies has been introduced in an attempt to modernise solid waste management, broaden the use of sustainable plastics and materials, encourage recycling and reduce waste generation.

But grand plans meant little if the problem was not addressed at the source, said Jeremiah, adding that efforts to reduce unnecessary packaging by a handful of platforms, retailers and manufacturers needed to be extended across the entire supply chain.

“At the same time, consumers should make more informed purchasing decisions and practice proper waste separation and recycling,” he added.

Fair play

The overseas e-commerce blitz is not all bad news for Malaysia, however. For some, losing business in one area opens up opportunities in another.

“We had a 40 per cent drop in demand over the past few months for small parcel deliveries because a lot of people can just get their items delivered straight to their homes,” said a local courier operator who asked not to be named.

“But demand has gone up for shipments of bigger items like furniture and kitchenware and even machinery for factories and construction.”

An early investment in warehouse space in Guangzhou, China’s outbound shipping hub, made all the difference for them in securing a steady stream of clients, the operator said, adding: “A lot of our customers nowadays buy direct from factories in China, so having our own warehouse there makes it easy to arrange shipments for them.”

Even entrepreneurs worried about the fallout from direct-to-consumer sales from overseas enjoy the savings as shoppers.

“You must also look at the other side [of the coin]. The consumer is very happy. I’m very happy that I can buy my socks for just 12 ringgit,” said the SME Association’s Chin.

What local businesses wanted was not to stop Pinduoduo and other foreign e-commerce giants selling in Malaysia, he said, but a level playing field.

Under Malaysian law, a 10 per cent sales tax on low-value goods took effect in 2024 to cover imported items worth 500 ringgit or less. But trade groups say many direct overseas shipments slip through untaxed, giving foreign sellers an edge.

Local industries have also warned that directly shipped items such as electronics and toys are not subject to Malaysian safety regulations and may endanger consumers.

“Malaysian businesses should not be disadvantaged simply because they pay local taxes, employ Malaysian workers and comply with our laws and regulations,” Chin said. “We must protect consumer interests without sacrificing Malaysian businesses, jobs and our domestic manufacturing ecosystem.”

When unveiling next year’s budget on October 9, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said the government would introduce an e-commerce bill at the next parliamentary sitting to close legislative and enforcement loopholes and protect local businesses from unfair competition.

But the government must do more than just draft a new law, said Muar MP Syed Saddiq Syed Abdul Rahman.

“Malaysian entrepreneurs are not asking for government handouts. They are not asking for competition to be shut down entirely. They only want fairness, so that competition is fair,” he told parliament during the budget debate.

“[Foreign e-commerce sites] need to establish a local presence. Work with local businesses, open offices and hire workers in this country … I am proposing a middle ground, not shutting them down entirely.”

item.title: [SCMP] Susan Thornton on US-China ties, post-midterms and averting a new balloon crisis
item.description:
Susan Thornton is a former American diplomat who for decades worked on US policy in Eurasia in the State Department before becoming acting assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs during the first Trump presidency. She is the director of the Forum on Asia-Pacific Security at the National Committee on American Foreign Policy and a senior fellow at the Paul Tsai China Centre, Yale Law School. She spoke to Orange Wang about keeping the lines of China-US communication open.

For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

What do you think overall of the summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping?
item.content:encoded:
Susan Thornton is a former American diplomat who for decades worked on US policy in Eurasia in the State Department before becoming acting assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs during the first Trump presidency. She is the director of the Forum on Asia-Pacific Security at the National Committee on American Foreign Policy and a senior fellow at the Paul Tsai China Centre, Yale Law School. She spoke to Orange Wang about keeping the lines of China-US communication open.

For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

What do you think overall of the summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping?

The summit was necessary. Leader-level meetings are the only guardrail we really have in US-China relations right now. It is very important that these meetings happen.

I’m probably more positive on this than other people because I do think that leader-level meetings in US-China relations are always difficult to put together. And the fact that Trump has done this twice with Xi – once in Beijing and once in Washington – may help regularise such high-level meetings, which we absolutely need to keep the relationship on track right now since we don’t have much else.

I’m not surprised by the negative coverage. The US-China summits are always held to a higher bar when it comes to outcomes of the meeting.

There have been expectations built up over many decades that US-China summits are always a big deal when they happen because they’re very hard to mount, and then they always have to have these long lists of outcomes.

We need to try to normalise these meetings between the US and Chinese leaders if possible. If you have to have a long list of accomplishments all the time, it’s going to be very hard to hold these meetings.

Some argue that the prospect of multiple face-to-face summits this year has put constraints on both sides, especially when it comes to sensitive issues. How could the two sides avoid a repeat of disruptions to bilateral relations, such as the balloon incident in 2023 and the fallout from then-House speaker Nancy Pelosi’s visit to Taiwan in 2022?

What you’re getting at here is exactly the issue of whether we can have constructive strategic stability.

In the US, I believe that constructive strategic stability – to the extent that people who agreed to that were really understanding what the Chinese side was talking about – is really about avoiding these worst-case scenarios. Avoiding conflict, avoiding a crisis that leads potentially to a conflict, et cetera.

The key is for both sides to understand what those issues are that could lead us there. And I do think we have been making progress in this administration on those issues.

President Trump is not new to this. He did this before for four years, and it ended quite badly under Covid-19. But I think whenever I’ve heard him speak about that time, it seems to me that he has thought about it and understands what the dynamic was that led things to get so out of hand and doesn’t want to see that happen again.

I think others in the administration also understand this. I think [Treasury Secretary] Scott Bessent and [Secretary of State] Marco Rubio definitely understand that this is what they’re trying to accomplish.

You put that strategic stability on top of all of these areas of difference that we have, and it does make it quite difficult to manage. But I do think with those high-level cabinet officials understanding what the boundaries are, there are additional touch points.

Marco Rubio and [Chinese Foreign Minister] Wang Yi have been speaking more than previously. Scott Bessent has a lot of things on his plate, so it may not be as easy for him to engage regularly with his counterpart, but he has been managing to meet [Chinese Vice-Premier] He Lifeng frequently. And you’ve got a number of economic and trade officials under him and under [US Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer who are plugged in together and talking.

I don’t think the crisis will come in the economic sphere. We can work through those questions and not have a crisis. We’ve really been doing this for quite a long time now.

The crises will come in the security area, most likely, and in a way those are harder because the security bureaucracies in both countries aren’t very connected to one another and don’t really have regular dialogue mechanisms.

We’ve always been talking about having some kind of military-to-military mechanisms for communication hotlines. There’s been a little bit of that in this administration and it’s got a bit improved, but it seems always very unstable. So, I think that’s the potential area that has to be guarded against.

President Trump does know where [Beijing’s] red lines are on Taiwan. That has been a learning curve probably for him. But he has a pretty firm view on that issue now, and I feel like Beijing has been reassured that he understands what the mainland’s position is.

It seems to me that the tension over Taiwan has abated, but the one question that Beijing keeps bringing up concerns Taiwan arms sales. I’m hopeful that the US side can find a way to manage that effectively. We’ve managed it in the past and should be able to do it again. And I think Trump will focus on it and try to take care that it gets done in a way that doesn’t cause a crisis.

How do you view the role of this summit in potentially helping address difficulties and challenges ahead in the US-China relationship?

I see US-China bilateral ties as being in a state of fragile stability.

During the summit in Beijing in May and since then, many Chinese colleagues have been excited about the notion that we’ve been able to put a name on the relationship, so we have a framework within which we can know what we’re working towards, which is a constructive relationship of strategic stability.

Looking at this summit, it’s important that they could meet and normalise that, but it’s also important that we be able to see them meeting in the future. We don’t have those kinds of mechanisms set up yet.

In addition to the leader-level meetings, what would be important to maintain this constructive stability is the institutionalisation of the relationship, which we’ve lost over the last 10 years. We need to start building that back to maintain stability.

The summit in September was the start of an institutionalisation of things that were agreed upon in May in Beijing.

For example, the Board of Trade, which was announced in May but really didn’t do much between May and now because of the summits, was actually pressured to meet, set up working groups and talk to one another. There are groups of people under Jamieson Greer and under [Greer’s Chinese counterpart] Li Chenggang who are meeting and talking through these things. You need a lot more connectivity among professionals if you’re going to have stabilisation of this relationship in any way.

The other area maybe that will move forward is AI, which was also announced in May. Scott Bessent announced that there would be an AI dialogue, and maybe that will meet in Shenzhen.

So, we can start to see the institutionalisation of these things. It’s still not nearly enough between the US and China.

I hope we’ll remember how hard it is to get mechanisms restarted because institutionalisation is a big job and it doesn’t happen overnight.

Trump gave Xi a very high-level reception, breaking some traditional protocols, and that triggered a lot of questioning and even criticism in the US. How do you view that?

Trump wants to appear welcoming and hospitable but also strong, so there was a jet flyover during the military review. A lot of this is just Trump’s personal way of thinking about how he wants to stage events. It doesn’t have as much to do with diplomatic protocol.

There were previous occasions when a president went to meet someone at Joint Base Andrews, so it does have some diplomatic precedent.

But I would hesitate to attach a lot of significance to the protocol.

Think of all of the things that they did that are highly unusual for a presidential visit. Walking out to look at the presidential helicopter, going over to see the construction of the White House ballroom. All these things are very much a signature of Trump’s way of handling the visit. I think a lot of people just don’t understand this.

That’s the main criticism: it’s very, very long on symbolism, pageantry, pomp and circumstance, and short on outcomes. This may signal a change in US-China summitry.

We used to try to, in diplomacy, trade diplomatic protocol issues and ceremonial issues, which were very high on the Chinese agenda for a visit, for concerns on the US side, for substantive outcomes.

But it’s no longer the case that we can expect that the Chinese are going to make concessions for only protocolary and ceremonial kinds of considerations. I think that is a change in the relationship that we’re seeing.

Both sides offer high levels of protocol and neither side really gets any trade for that. Maybe we can dispense with the ceremony of a state visit in the future and focus more on substantive issues at regular leader meetings.

Do you think that this summit has laid a proper foundation for Trump and Xi to meet at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in November and Group of 20 (G20) in December? The Chinese side has called 2026 a “big year” for bilateral relations, with the two countries’ leaders having the chance to meet face to face four times. But what about next year? How could the US and China keep up this head-of-state diplomacy?

They will have to make a big effort. This is why I think it is positive that President Trump seems to really value his meetings with President Xi and really wants to continue to communicate with him directly either via face-to-face meetings or other ways.

I hope we’ll take advantage of that because that hasn’t always been the case with US leaders in the past. That is an important advantage that Trump offers in this very difficult time in US-China relations. He’s open to talking to President Xi anytime, I think.

I would like to see if they could connect more on the phone.

Next year they are probably not going to travel as much as they did this year. And that’s another reason the relationship has to be institutionalised in the way that we’ve been talking about. There’s such a thin layer of professional expertise in the government that is plugged in to the other side, and that is probably not going to change too much over the next couple years.

The other thing we have to worry about is that if we institutionalise the relationship under this administration, what’s going to happen in the next administration? I hope the next administration would keep whatever institutionalisation has been started and build on that, not just try to always do their own thing. That’s not going to be a good way for us to proceed with the relationship.

There has been discussion that the Apec gathering in November could open scheduling windows for a US-Russia, China-US-Russia or Trump-Kim Jong-un summit. How do you view the likelihood of these potential bilateral or multilateral meetings taking place?

It definitely raises possibilities for dramatic diplomacy that could certainly appeal to President Trump.

President Trump has already invited [Russian President Vladimir] Putin to come to Miami for the G20 summit, and it’s likely that he’ll attend. It’s creating some ripple effects in Europe because they may or may not be too pleased that he’s coming, but I think that will all be worked out.

President Trump still sees himself as a broker of peace, and so he wants to create these opportunities for dramatic things to happen and big changes in some of the problem areas that we see. Certainly the Russia-Ukraine war is one of them, but North Korea is another one.

We know that he wants to meet again with [North Korean leader] Kim Jong-un, and that has not happened yet. If that could happen in Shenzhen during Apec – several people have mentioned this as a possibility, or that Trump could do it on his way to China – those would be dramatic opportunities.

We were talking earlier about the calendar for next year, and then Trump is getting towards the end of his term. It seems like he might want to do something in this area.

It might make it more attractive for Trump to actually go to Shenzhen and for Xi to come to Miami if there is an opportunity for progress on Ukraine or the North Korea nuclear issue.

It’s very hard to see the preparation going far enough between now and November or December to make dramatic successes out of such a meeting, however. Usually, such things take a lot more preparation, so I would be sceptical on that score. But I have heard a lot of people talking about such possibilities, so perhaps they will materialise.

You mentioned the AI dialogue. The US and China appear to be taking different approaches to developing this technology. There is also debate within the US over whether the development of advanced models should be slowed. Given these international and domestic differences, how do you view the prospects for the bilateral AI dialogue?

I do think it’s going to be extremely difficult.

I participated in US-China discussions on mechanisms to report cyber incidents. The AI dialogue is not exactly the same as that, but in the area that the US is concerned about, I think it’s quite similar and also just as difficult, if not more so.

The US and China have different concerns, and it’s very hard for the two of them to talk to each other because they’re just coming from completely different vantage points.

The Chinese government – and Chinese interlocutors that I’ve talked to reflect this – seems to be quite confident in its ability to control its AI operators and make sure that things that it doesn’t want to have happen in the AI sphere will not happen. Is it overconfident? I am concerned they are not really thinking about the possibilities of loss of control on the Chinese side with AI.

They’re mostly worried about what’s happening on the US side and the possibilities of loss of control, the fact that the US government doesn’t control these private companies, that the companies themselves are reporting a lot of things that are somewhat hair-raising and fear-inducing. The US government seems to be thinking that China is going to have the same concerns it has, whereas it really doesn’t.

And also, the two systems don’t match up in terms of reporting, transparency and other things that you would need to talk about if you were going to try to share best practices or discuss a strategy for keeping incidents from getting out of control.

Trump said that the line for AI safety in the US is the Department of Justice, in other words, the legal system, and that is just not the way the Chinese are going to operate in terms of AI safety.

It’s going to be very hard from an institutional and bureaucratic set-up perspective, this security-to-security bureaucracy mistrust. The Chinese system is just not given to being transparent about these things. Chinese media have focused on various US AI operators who are trying to do the right thing by self-reporting accidents that have happened.

In the Chinese system, these things would not be publicly reported. China has been criticising the US AI labs and taking advantage of this moment to make itself look like a more responsible actor, when I’m not sure that is fully justified.

It’s also very hard to understand how the US and Chinese governments would put together delegations that would look at all similar and have the same kind of expertise. So, I find it a little bit head-scratching as to how this is going to go ahead.

It’s important to get some of these people in the room together and have regular discussions. Maybe they can build up a little bit of personal familiarity that will help us at some point in the future when we hit a real problem. I think that would be an advantage.

Xi has invited 100,000 young Americans to visit China over the next five years. You travelled to China this year and last year to attend events on subnational cooperation between the two countries. What is your read on the state of bilateral local and people-to-people exchanges? Are they still constrained by factors such as visas and flights? There have been recurring calls to reopen the US consulate in Chengdu and the Chinese consulate in Houston. How possible do you think that would be?

This area is still a source of difficulty, even though the two governments have pledged to make improvements.

I noticed that they did mention the number of flights. Certainly, they talked about students. But the question is how to make this happen. There’s still extreme suspicion in local-level, people-to-people exchanges, mostly coming from, to be honest, local-level politicians. There are some organised groups that are also pushing against people-to-people exchange between the US and China.

I don’t see much change in this. I don’t know, if the US midterm elections in November see a huge shift in the Congress, what might happen there. Most of the local anti-China legislation is coming from Republican states, so it depends a little bit on domestic politics.

I don’t know if the Democrats will focus on this as an issue, but in general Democrats have been much more open about people-to-people travel back and forth. I don’t know if they can affect the atmosphere on this issue. It is something to watch.

Certainly, the downturn in Chinese students is noticeable. I work at Yale University, and we’ve got a number of Chinese students who were unable to come for the start of the semester because they didn’t get their visas in time.

Visas are still an issue on both sides. I know people who are having trouble getting visas to go to China, so it’s a two-way thing, and it’s very unfortunate. But it’s really hard to see where a push is going to come from in the US to fix this problem.

We should keep pressuring both sides to make improvements here. And again, the devil’s in the details. These two security bureaucracies have a deep, deep level of mistrust.

Treasury Secretary Bessent said China and the US had agreed to extend the trade truce for two months, until January 10 next year. Why only two months rather than a longer period? What could the two sides achieve during this time frame?

To me, it is a bit surprising that the extension of the Busan trade truce was so minimal. I think two months is about the minimum that they could have agreed.

What that says is they did not want the truce to end because neither side is prepared for what might happen or the consequences of ending that truce. But they couldn’t come up really with any agreement to extend it, so they’ve just basically rolled over the agreement from last year.

Both sides were probably hoping that they would be able to extend the truce and improve it, but apparently that didn’t happen. It’s probable that they didn’t have enough time to do that, because these kinds of negotiations take quite a bit of time and preparation. And you can’t just have a meeting on a Sunday in New York between top officials and expect to hammer these things out in that kind of time frame. So, my suspicion is that they did not manage to agree on any of the improvements in the rollover that they wanted, and they didn’t want to roll over the current truce, which is kind of minimal, for too much of an extended period of time because they still hope to get something better.

Probably the January time frame is not much time to do anything either. But at least if there is a meeting in November, then that gives another forcing function, and there’s also the G20 summit in Miami in December, that’s a lot of connectivity between now and January 10. So, there is a possibility of getting something done there, although it will be difficult.

And then we’ll hit January 10, and the truce will probably roll over one way or another. They won’t want to lose this truce, I don’t think, in January either.

The one factor that probably was pushing on the US side is the midterm elections coming up in early November. I think the US side wanted to get something that would get us past the midterm elections and give some comfortable margin after that to assess where things are going.

Observers in both countries argue that China is becoming more confident and increasingly sees itself as Washington’s equal, while perceptions of continuing US decline are growing globally. The narrative of “the East is rising and the West is declining” continues to surface in public discussions. What do you think about this? Before the September summit, some argued that China was in a stronger position at the negotiating table because of the war on Iran. If that is the case, how long could that last?

I do think China is more confident, reasonably so. And certainly, the US has been losing influence on the international stage for a period of time. In the wake of the war in Iran, that has accelerated, probably.

The question, really, is whether China is making gains from the losses that the US is inflicting on itself. I think China has made some gains, but it is not a slam dunk yet that China has made equal gains to the US’ losses. In other words, I don’t see that China is somehow displacing the US.

The interesting thing to watch is we’ve seen President Xi go to the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan and the Brics summit in India, talking in many of his speeches about China being a responsible player, that China stands for a continuation of globalisation, openness and free trade, and I think what people see China doing in practice is somewhat different from that. Or at least they are sceptical that this is what China is standing for and what China is all about.

In fact, a lot of countries, especially in China’s neighbourhood, continue to have concerns about China and are actually threatened by China. And China hasn’t really done much to reassure those countries that they shouldn’t be afraid of China. I think this is the dilemma China has.

It wants to take advantage of this moment when the US is on the back foot, clearly, in Iran and elsewhere, and it has taken some advantage, but it has not managed to really convince people of what its ambitions and intentions are. I think that is going to continue to be a tough balancing act for China.

I hope China will start to show in its actions more what it’s actually thinking about for the long term, and I think that will be important in terms of the narrative too out there in the world.

The US is clearly in a transition period. Domestic politics are at a turning point, and we’re going to have to work through that. So, it’s going to be a period of time. Whether China can take advantage of our domestic transition is really a question for China’s own policy and diplomats to work out.

US allies such as Japan and the Philippines are strengthening their security ties, while tensions with Beijing continue to simmer in the South China Sea, the East China Sea and the waters east of Taiwan. Would this make it more challenging for Beijing and Washington to manage their bilateral relationship?

As for the South China Sea, some Chinese experts have said that Beijing’s goal is not to expel US influence from the region and that it could consider opening certain island infrastructure to US vessels to help ease tensions. Do you think this is realistic?

I don’t know about that specific proposal, but certainly China can’t be happy about what it’s seeing in terms of its immediate neighbours linking up in tighter coalitions for their security.

China hasn’t been doing much to reassure them that they shouldn’t be worried about China, and so that’s going to produce this natural kind of build-up of defence and military capability and trying to link with other countries in the region to strengthen their posture. It’s exactly what you would expect. And it can’t be something that China sees as a good development.

I have to say that it’s really hard for these countries to see in the future how China is going to not behave in a very kind of domineering way towards them. This is how things have been playing out in the region, which is why they seem to be so eager to have US engagement stay in the region.

I think that’s a big question mark right now, which is making people in the region even more worried about the future. How to assure these countries about their future security, their relationship with China? How is China going to treat these countries? That’s a huge question. And right now, it’s not going so well.

Taiwan has, of course, always been at the centre of relations between Washington and Beijing. That issue is a bit special and separate from some of these other issues.

But the same dynamic is really at play there, the fear of what the relationship with Beijing would be like in the future. I think Beijing hasn’t given very clear or positive signals about that to anybody yet.

Confidence is one thing, but how you wield your confidence is very important.

item.title: [SCMP] Six legendary libraries, where architecture and academia meet
item.description:
Libraries are hard drives containing the memory of the world in an ancient form. Less pocketable than anything digital, but in many cases far prettier, these buildings are also sometimes works of art in their own right and cathedrals of humanism, whether erected four centuries ago or by a still-living architect of global acclaim.

Their beauty is inessential to their function but celebrates the knowledge they contain, the power and wealth or taste and intellect of those who commissioned them, or plays a role in preserving the essence of cultural identity.

You might visit one to see the masterful carpentry of ornate shelving, elaborate spiral staircases and walkways, stained glass, trompe l’oeil frescoes, carved marble and art, in addition to displays of rare and ancient books, maps, treaties, manuscripts and other historic documents. To the atmospheric silence and the smell of wax polish found in churches is added the warm aroma of ancient leather bindings.
item.content:encoded:
Libraries are hard drives containing the memory of the world in an ancient form. Less pocketable than anything digital, but in many cases far prettier, these buildings are also sometimes works of art in their own right and cathedrals of humanism, whether erected four centuries ago or by a still-living architect of global acclaim.

Their beauty is inessential to their function but celebrates the knowledge they contain, the power and wealth or taste and intellect of those who commissioned them, or plays a role in preserving the essence of cultural identity.

You might visit one to see the masterful carpentry of ornate shelving, elaborate spiral staircases and walkways, stained glass, trompe l’oeil frescoes, carved marble and art, in addition to displays of rare and ancient books, maps, treaties, manuscripts and other historic documents. To the atmospheric silence and the smell of wax polish found in churches is added the warm aroma of ancient leather bindings.

You might enter for some relief from the haste, heat and hustle of a big city, or because the libraries themselves have become popular meeting places, with cafes and places to sit.

Here are six institutions whose collections or buildings should not be overlooked, whatever reason you have for being in town.

The Real Biblioteca del Monasterio de San Lorenzo de El Escorial, Madrid, Spain

Philip II of Spain (1527-98) ruled one of the greatest empires in human history and did so much of the time from El Escorial, creating here the national library of the Kingdom of Spain in a room intended to be one of the most magnificent in the palace, and a rival for the richest libraries elsewhere in Europe, particularly cultural competitor Italy.
