First of all, there is a real interest in what some people call traditional thought, or pre-modern thought, which includes the Confucian tradition but also lots of other areas, such as Taoism.

The Chinese government has been sponsoring publication of China’s canon of official writings, with the parts that suit contemporary politics tending to be stressed.

For instance, Confucian thinking does have an interest in proper hierarchy and this is something that is obviously very attractive to the Communist Party, because it wants people, essentially, to be stable and ordered.

But there are other ideas – such as individual self-development or self-cultivation, which could lead more to the idea that people should have individual rights – that are less popular with the party.

China’s political culture since 1949 has been heavily shaped by the Marxism and Leninism that underpins the Chinese Communist Party.

Many of the ideas are still there and you can hear them in the language of Xi and other top leaders. Even while they are praising traditional Chinese culture and wisdom, they are also pointing out that Marxism and Leninism still have significance.

How are these two things compatible? Actually, it’s not easy.

There was a TV show broadcast in Hunan province that got a lot of criticism on Chinese social media. It was called When Marx Met Confucius and was a way of trying to talk about the difficulties in combining these ideas.

There is actually quite an interesting and difficult tension in the way that these two thought systems operate in China today, but I think that they are both very much part of the debate.

How has the Chinese intellectual landscape changed in the past 10 years? Do you share the view that it can be summarised as a rise in nationalism, Sinification of ideas and declining critical voices? What other trends are you seeing and what are their effects?

In some ways, China’s intellectual sphere has narrowed, at least in public, but in other important ways, it has expanded.

The narrowing is real, and probably the biggest obstacle that China places in its own path to developing new ideas at home and being able to exert influence abroad. It’s difficult to persuade the wider world that you’re a force for new thinking if new thinking at home is heavily restricted.

In terms of subjects, including history, most people would say that the room for publication and discussion is much more limited than it was 10, 15 or 20 years ago. Many aspects of modern history are harder to research and write about in China today than in the past.

The most productive recent time intellectually in China was the late 1990s and early 2000s, when there was the most capacity to be able to speak more freely. That time will need to come again as China comes to grips with its new role in the world. It’s not possible to have a very narrowed intellectual sphere and a very wide influence.

But there are some areas where I think things are broader, and I’m particularly thinking about social media and the way it has expanded and grown so significantly in China in the past decade.

Lots of ideas actually are discussed at a popular level, even when there’s censorship a lot of ideas still get out there – not about top-level politics as that’s too sensitive to permit – but if you think about things like concerns about economic change, people’s concerns about their own financial situation, ideas about the position of women, society, feminism, those are quite visible in Chinese social media.

That is not the same thing as two or three scholars sitting in a think tank writing some big paper, but in terms of understanding social trends and how they are shaping China today, social media has been very valuable to reflect those changes.

How has the China studies community been affected by the changes of recent years? What will the subject look like, with a growing percentage of scholars outside the country unable to conduct interviews and on-the-ground research in China?

You have put your finger on one of the most problematic issues – the number of students studying Chinese languages and doing higher-level research in the West on China is going down significantly. It was never very high, but it was going up, and now the numbers are shrinking.

One reason is the sense that doing serious research in China – particularly for social scientists but also for researchers who need to use archives and libraries – is much more difficult than it used to be.

What real China researchers need is to be able to travel and set up their own agendas, to be able to do interviews at the local level that enable them to understand how local government works, or to collect large amounts of data that enables them to see how effective or ineffective particular policies are.

This is the work of real social science, and it involves transparency and openness on data and a willingness to welcome the gathering of data, rather than assuming that it has to be banned for security reasons.

So, although more scholars are coming back to China, opening up more capacity to be able to do real research in China is the next barrier that needs to be overcome.

There are a lot of brilliant Chinese students in many countries in the West who are doing significant social science and humanities research. But their Western equivalents who study China can’t do that kind of work in China, so it becomes very unbalanced.

What about your own experience with the Asia studies and Chinese history students you taught at Oxford and now Harvard?

When it comes to postgraduate students doing PhDs, a significant number are Chinese. We do still have some Westerners, but the problem is that they have to be enthusiastic about China, willing to learn its language and culture, and then be able to find a meaningful project to research.

It’s harder now to assure students that they can find a pathway to doing really good social science research inside China, so a lot of students just leave China out. If people say China is a very difficult place to do research and South Korea is easy, maybe people just decide they want to learn Korean instead.

The sense among Western researchers that it’s hard to do serious research in China has transmitted to students finding it difficult to find a career path if they do study China. I think that’s a great shame.

item.title: [SCMP] China’s ‘stolen’ cultural relics: why the numbers just don’t add up
item.description:
More than 150 years after British and French troops sacked and razed the Summer Palace, in Beijing, the incident is regularly revisited in the Chinese press. Articles usually appear around the October anniversary of the destruction, after yet another announcement of plans to catalogue looted antiquities now overseas, or when Summer Palace items appear at foreign auction houses.

As well as their incomplete and inaccurate descriptions of the palace and its destruction, these stories often contain transparently false accusations against foreign institutions holding collections of Chinese treasures, as well as unsustain­able claims of a legal right to them and demands for their uncompensated return.

Even the most outrageously distorted claims often go unrefuted by timid governments and cultural institutions, perhaps for fear of complicating more important diplomatic negotiations or voiding loan arrangements and cultural exchanges.
item.content:encoded:
More than 150 years after British and French troops sacked and razed the Summer Palace, in Beijing, the incident is regularly revisited in the Chinese press. Articles usually appear around the October anniversary of the destruction, after yet another announcement of plans to catalogue looted antiquities now overseas, or when Summer Palace items appear at foreign auction houses.

As well as their incomplete and inaccurate descriptions of the palace and its destruction, these stories often contain transparently false accusations against foreign institutions holding collections of Chinese treasures, as well as unsustain­able claims of a legal right to them and demands for their uncompensated return.

Even the most outrageously distorted claims often go unrefuted by timid governments and cultural institutions, perhaps for fear of complicating more important diplomatic negotiations or voiding loan arrangements and cultural exchanges.

Museum public relations departments keep curators away from the press and mention of the Summer Palace is omitted from catalogue and cabinet label alike. Requests for a response to the Chinese campaign for repatriation of just about anything Chinese, with its insinuation that even legally purchased items are loot, are answered slowly, if at all.

As a result, it’s easy to conclude that museums, particularly those in the English-speaking world, must indeed have a lot to hide, although just how much is hidden away is itself the subject of considerable distortion. The French are more outspoken about both their possessions and their plans to retain them, yet receive less criticism.

For many years it has been claimed in the mainland Chinese press (as well as the South China Morning Post), with minor variations, that 1.64 million Chinese antiquities reside in 200 museums in 47 foreign countries.

On a 1998 visit to Beijing, Britain’s then prime minister Tony Blair was asked by a local journalist how he could justify the British Museum’s continued possession of 23,000 of these antiquities, a question still being posed when successor David Cameron visited 15 years later.

The China Centre for International Economic Exchanges, a “super think tank” headed by former vice-premier Zeng Peiyan, took up the invitation to ask Cameron questions via his newly created Sina Weibo microblog account.

“When will Britain return the illegally plundered artefacts?” was the inquiry, with the implication that the museum’s entire Chinese collection had been acquired by military force.

How an old palace and a historic railway station lay bare China’s conflicted relationship with its past

By last year, the source for these figures was repeatedly claimed to be “a Unesco study”, although in fact an information pack by the UN’s heritage body on the illicit trafficking of cultural property merely quoted a 2009 article in the magazine Art Antiquity and Law, by author Ji Ling. There is no such Unesco study.

In 2009, the Summer Palace’s then director, Chen Mingjie, claimed that 1.5 million antiquities had been looted in 1860 alone, and that they were in 2,000 museums, 10 times as many as previously suggested. By last year, the China Cultural Relics Academy was estimating that 10 million Chinese items were overseas, including those in private collections.

Among public institutions, London’s British Museum is often said to be the chief culprit, with its holdings now sometimes magically increased tenfold to 230,000 items, all now claimed to be from the Summer Palace. Eventually, the museum meekly responded to Post Magazine, claiming that, among its 23,000-item Chinese collection, purchased from or donated by myriad sources over a long period, just 15 pieces might possibly be of Summer Palace origin.

The French are typically more forthright. When asked in a 2011 interview how many items in Paris’ Château de Fontainebleau collections were from the plundering of the Summer Palace, the then director of patrimony and collections at the French museum, Xavier Salmon, answered immediately and unblushingly, “We think between 600 and 800.”

With an eye to national identity, Beijing vows to stem loss of cultural treasures

As the ponderous shutters of Fontainebleau’s Chinese Museum are unbarred and swung open, gleams of gold in the dark interior swell into a display of dazzling magnificence. Jades, porcelains and bronzes jostle for shelf space around a jewel-encrusted golden stupa flanked by two upright elephant tusks. The walls are lined with landscapes in gold and black lacquer, and the ceiling is draped with silk tapestries. The chamber buzzes with beauty, and it is difficult for the eye to know where to rest.

Here, then, is the magnificence that otherwise exists only in the imaginations of those keen to magnify for political purposes the wonders of the now-vanished Summer Palace.

The complex’s decay was already apparent in 1793, when it was visited by Lord Macartney, King George III’s ambassador to the Qianlong emperor. The best of the palaces, wrote Macartney, “is so much out of repair that I already see it will be impossible to reside in it comfortably during the winter”.

The looting and destruction of 1860 was intended, according to official and much personal correspondence, as a reprisal for the torture and murder of British and French envoys who had been under a prearranged flag of truce (a fact always omitted from Chinese accounts).

The French boxed up the best of the treasures they plundered from the Summer Palace and shipped them to Emperor Napoléon III. The Empress Eugénie is said to have been present in person at the opening of the crates.

She selected items to display in a purpose-built museum, mixing them with gifts from other parts of Asia, purchases from Parisian antiques shops and treasures confiscated from aristocratic families during the French revolution. She commissioned the building of display cabinets inset with Chinese panels and gave pieces of Chinese cloisonné to a master craftsman to incorporate in a vast chandelier that, 150 years on, still glitters overhead.

“She didn’t have an historic or artistic vision for these objects, she had a very personal vision,” said Salmon. “It is she who created this ambience, mixing up techniques and colours in a manner to which her eye responded and which was of the China of her imagination.”

Eugénie’s creation, he firmly asserted, was now part of French patrimony and “to return the objects would be to destroy a little bit of French history”.

But if the items were stolen, is this a sufficient defence?

“The question of plunder in war remains a question with a history as long as that of the planet,” said Salmon. “The history of the world has been regularly marked by these events, and the Chinese with their politics of conquest have also taken objects from their proper culture.”

In fairness, wild claims about the grandeur of the Summer Palace and the quality of the items stored therein began not with the Chinese but with Jesuit missionaries keen to justify the costs of maintaining their mission in the Manchu empire’s capital, and who compared the Summer Palace to Versailles.

There were also conflicting overestimates of the Summer Palace’s size from foreign travellers anxious to impress their readers.

Official descriptions of the now-much-built-over site continue this tradition in order to exaggerate the losses, increase criticism of foreign powers and enhance support for the Communist Party as the only bulwark behind which the Chinese can effectively unite and resist foreign exploitation.

The truth is, the number of surviving Summer Palace antiquities is unknowable, although no expert credits the figure of 1.5 million looted items overseas. There are no records of the palace’s original contents, much was destroyed on site and several eyewitnesses describe extensive looting by both local Chinese and the 2,500 coolies from southern provinces who were aiding the foreign forces (information also omitted from Chinese accounts).

Those forces were welcomed with open arms by Peking shopkeepers and items both with palace provenance and without were purchased and mixed together. Chinese traders in Canton and Hong Kong were willing purchasers of loot from the French troops who passed through on their way home.

The French expeditionary force provided lists of what it had packed, but these contain very little in way of description: “A vase, a vase, a vase,” quoted Salmon, from one of these lists, which makes individual identification impossible.

Furthermore, little in the Summer Palace was unique to its collection and, according to those present, the most easily identifiable items were of foreign manufacture, such as the field guns given by Macartney’s late-18th century embassy and French clocks and watches in such numbers that French looters sold them for pocket money to British soldiers, whose own looting opportunities had been relatively limited.

Chen never contacted the institutions he had accused of holding the largest collections, according to Salmon and other museum officials. Instead, a visit to museums in nine American cities in 2009 was deemed a success for the “discovery” of several previously unknown items. Chen declined to provide details except for those of a single Song-dynasty painting at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, which bore 18 seals, including those of the Chun Hua Xuan, a hall in the Summer Palace complex.

At first, the museum claimed difficulty in identifying the painting in question, and gave a carefully anodyne response: “We have many strong connections to cultural institutions in China and look forward to continued collaborations.” It eventually emerged that the painting had been purchased from a Chinese seller within China in December 1913. And while the museum is apparently shy of labelling the painting in English as being of Summer Palace origin, Herd-boys with Water Buffaloes Under Willow Trees can clearly be seen on its website complete with identifying seals.

Peking University accused of not protecting Summer Palace relics

Chen’s “discovery” could have been made from a comfortable chair anywhere in the world, including Beijing. The painting had not been on public display since 1997, and a museum spokeswoman said in an e-mailed response that she could find no record of Chen’s visit.

In recent years, auctions of Jesuit-made bronze animal heads from the 1860 looting have brought ever more strident demands for their return. There have been futile legal attempts and the intervention of state actors willing to pay any price for national pride. This has driven up bidding for other Summer Palace items to well beyond what the state is willing to pay, leading to claims in Chinese media that prices are “unfair”.

When acquired instead by Chinese nouveaux riches, these pieces sometimes disappear into private collections and remain as invisible to ordinary Chinese as they were in Europe – or were back in 1860. Foreign museums are willing to lend items for exhibition but a willingness to accept them would also suggest acceptance of foreign ownership, and the political campaign has made this impossible, even where antiquities were legally purchased from Chinese sellers. Rather than achieving its aim of acquiring Chinese treasures, the carefully orchestrated brouhaha has put them further out of reach.

As Anglo-French forces progressed towards Beijing in 1860, Henry Loch, secretary to British plenipotentiary Lord Elgin, was one of the parley party imprisoned and tortured, and so did not participate in the looting. According to the accounts of various witnesses, the British watched the French carry off the largest part of the loot but subsequently pooled their finds of art, costumes and silks for auction, producing a fund of £8,000 – nearly US$1 million in today’s money – for distribution among the British forces.

Eighteen of his party were murdered but Loch survived to bid successfully for a pair of cloisonné double crane censers. In 2010, these were auctioned again and their Summer Palace connections helped push their sale price to US$16.7 million, a new record for cloisonné and roughly 17 times the value of the entire original British haul.

This was not a quirk. A month earlier, a gaudy Qing-dynasty porcelain vase from the Summer Palace had been sold by a small English auction house to a Beijing-based bidder for US$85.9 million, including tax and fees – 50 times its estimate.

While many museums now shy away from discussing the Summer Palace provenance of items in their collections, Chinese cataloguers and foreign auctioneers claim it wherever they can because it adds both political and financial value.

In May 2011, Bonhams promoted the auction of a white jadeite seal sold by the descendants of a 19th-century medical missionary to China, William Lockhart. The auction house sought to add Summer Palace lustre by mentioning the entirely irrelevant “unequivocal support” for British actions shown in Lockhart’s memoirs, and stating that he was “possibly” in Beijing during the sacking.

Norwegian art museum to return seven columns from Old Summer Palace to Beijing

Lockhart’s concise chapter of history on Anglo-Chinese relations from 1839 to 1860 contains not even a hint that he was at the Summer Palace. He moved to Beijing only in 1861. The price obtained was only double the estimate, suggesting that bidders found Bonhams’ claims no more credible than those of Chen.

In April 2011, complaints about unfair auction prices gave way in the official China Daily to the headline “Asian art market sizzles”. A surprisingly outrage-free article oozed with national pride because there were now Chinese sufficiently wealthy to pay record-breaking sums for Summer Palace jade, cloisonné and ceramics, while still avoiding any suggestion that state interference had increased the need for such deep pockets.

This was finally acknowledged in assorted articles in November last year that quoted Song Xinchao, deputy director of the State Administration of Cultural Heritage (SACH), as decrying the private purchase of “lost relics”, because “purchasing them will, in a way, confirm the legitimacy of such thefts, and make the prices of these items even higher in the international market”.

As with the inquiries made to the British prime ministers, there was also the implication that all Chinese treasures “lost” overseas must be, in some sense, stolen.

The main purpose of the 2016 articles was to trumpet SACH’s success in suppressing an auction in Japan of frescoes and manuscripts taken from a cave-temple site outside Dunhuang, on the Silk Road, as part of China’s supposedly growing success in repatriating treasures using diplomatic and legal persuasion rather than purchase. But Chinese propaganda has elevated Silk Road artefact prices also and, without it, there might be more to see in China’s museums.

Around the rim of the lens-shaped Taklimakan Desert, signs at cave-temple sites condemn by name the foreign explorers who plundered frescoes, paintings and manuscripts during an Indiana Jones-style archaeological free-for-all in the early 20th century.

At Dunhuang, where sheer cliffs are pitted with hundreds of hand-carved caves dating back as far as 366CE, it is again the British and French who come in for most criticism. In 1907, Britain’s Marc Aurel Stein purchased thousands of documents recently discovered in a hidden library cave. The following year, France’s Paul Pelliot did the same, as did subsequent Russian and Japanese expeditions.

The seller was a Taoist monk, Abbot Wang, the caves’ self-appointed guardian, who had been unable to interest local officials in the documents he had discovered and who wanted funds for the preservation of the caves and their frescoes.

The sums paid by foreigners were large for what local people regarded as useless papers in assorted scripts they could not read, but derisory in terms of their cultural significance. The Chinese authorities now cry foul.

Amazing journey: how China hid palace artefacts from Japanese invaders

The November 2016 articles, in assorted Chinese media and a paid-for soft-power supplement to The Washington Post, claimed China had triumphed by suppressing a Yokohama International Auction sale of Tang-dynasty frescoes and manuscripts from Dunhuang “stolen by Otani Kozui, a Japanese abbot who was part of expeditions to China between 1902 and 1913”, according to SACH.

Accuracy is once again of little interest here. The records of the exhibitions financed by Otani make it clear he did not travel to Dunhuang in person but those he’d sponsored did purchase the scrolls directly from Abbot Wang.

These Dunhuang manuscripts were catalogued before financial trouble led Otani to sell the remainder of his collection in 1915, but take the Dunhuang items to Lüshun, in Japanese-occupied northeast China. After Japan’s 1945 defeat, these manuscripts ended up in museums in Lüshun and Beijing, except for 49 later discovered in Japan, which are now at the Ryukoku University, in Kyoto, and not for sale.

It is not entirely clear, then, what Yokohama International Auction intended to sell at the suppressed auction, but this is one of the exports of antiquities about which China has least to complain, since almost all are already back in the country.

It’s not impossible that other manuscripts may turn up, but these will most likely not be from Dunhuang, says Cambridge University Otani expert Dr Imre Galambos.

“[Otani] is often vilified for his acquisition of antiquities, even though his collection was quite modest in comparison to that of Aurel Stein, but he was Japanese and, on top of that, related by marriage to the imperial house, all of which have a very bad resonance with the Chinese public.”

Records of three Otani-sponsored expeditions show that frescoes were acquired not from Dunhuang but from Miran, hundreds of kilometres further west, and these are now in the National Museum of Korea, in Seoul.

“We are not conditioned by guilt,” said a forthright Jacques Giès, when interviewed at the Musée Guimet in Paris in 2011. Giès had spent more than 30 years curating the museum’s magnificent Silk Road displays. “Our duty is to present the best of the Chinese creation, to testify to the excellence of this civilisation, and to let our public have respect for Chinese history and civilisation.”

China bans looted antiques from going under hammer at mainland auction houses

Indeed, Giès points out that Silk Road studies were a foreign invention. It was the 1890 discovery by a British Indian Army officer of ancient texts on birch bark in an unknown language that sparked multiple arduous desert expeditions to discover more of the same.

It was principally European, Russian, Japanese and American scholars who pieced together the history of the trade routes, deciphering scripts and translating forgotten languages.

“We, who have worked for almost one century on these materials, represent the best of the best of the scholarship in all these countries, and these materials were essential not only for the history of China, but also for all High Asia and the Indian subcontinent,” said Giès.

In other words, there are many other Asian cultures that might lay claim to the Silk Road treasures, including those of the local minority and the Tibetans who controlled Dunhuang for centuries and compelled the local Chinese to wear Tibetan clothing and speak Tibetan.

Of the Otani Dunhuang documents already back in China, it’s the Chinese-language ones that have been taken to Beijing, with those in other languages left tucked away in distant Lüshun.

“History is not made of ‘if’,” said Giès. Due to the French revolution, the most important French royal furniture collections are in England. “But that’s history. I am very grateful because they preserved these pieces which could have been destroyed.”

Dr Frances Wood, formerly head of Chinese collections at the British Library, says she is familiar with that sentiment.

“In private, most Chinese scholars are much happier that the material is in England,” she says. The Dunhuang scrolls remaining in Japan are dwarfed in number by those in the British Library’s collection, purchased by Stein from 1907.

“There are about 7,000 fairly complete scrolls, so they’re reasonably substantial. Six thousand of those are rolls of paper anything from five to 30 feet long, mostly Buddhist. And then when you get towards the other end, they’re very tiny fragments because they’re really the bottom of the sacks.”

No sooner had China begun to open up in the 1970s than Chinese scholars were invited to work on this “Stein debris”, carefully flattening pieces for analysis.

Continuing cooperation by members of the British Library-based International Dunhuang Project has seen thousands of documents from collections around the world digitally photographed and made freely available online. The British Library’s entire Dunhuang collection is now being published in a 150-volume catalogue by the Guangxi Normal University Press.

In private, most Chinese scholars are much happier that the material is in England

Dr Frances Wood

In 2014, China drafted an international rule on the return of cultural property – China’s first such effort, reported the China Daily, in November. “The Dunhuang Recommendation has led to more success in China’s efforts since then.”

However, this home-made “international rule” is merely wishful thinking and China has been party to a 1970 Unesco convention on the illicit transfer of stolen cultural property since 1989. It is this that provides a proper legal basis for reclaiming stolen antiquities, but it doesn’t apply to those taken before 1970, and the Dunhuang Recommendation, as the 2014 rule is known, changes nothing.

Yokohama International Auction is registered in Hong Kong and its owner is reportedly a Japanese national of Chinese descent. On its Japanese webpages – although not those in Chinese – the company makes clear that its very purpose is the return of Chinese antiquities to China.

Before being cancelled, the November auction had been won by a Japanese national, but the items were returned to their owner, not passed to China. This was, in fact, the opposite of progress, and nothing to do with any “international rule”.

Threats against foreign auction houses with Chinese connections have been seen before, such as in another quoted example of “more success in China’s efforts”, the 2013 return of two bronze animal heads originally from a fountain in the Summer Palace.

These were returned free of charge by French billionaire François-Henri Pinault, whose Kering group owns luxury brands such as Gucci and Saint Laurent that now rely on China for a significant portion of their income.

Through the holding company Groupe Artemis, Pinault also owns auction house Christie’s. The heads had appeared in a Christie’s-run auction of the late Yves Saint Laurent’s effects in Paris in 2009, leading SACH to threaten “serious effects” on Christie’s’ future in China. It was widely reported that the company began to experience difficulties with Chinese customs inspections.

Pinault was accompanying then French president François Hollande on a trade visit to China at the time of the announcement of his donation. It may only be coincidence that Christie’s became the first international fine-art auction house to receive a licence to operate independently in China that very same year.

Return of Old Summer Palace statues seen as Kering group PR exercise

Other claimed Chinese successes concern antiquities stolen recently by Chinese themselves and smuggled overseas, their repatriation subject to existing conventions and not to any newly coined domestic rule. But the Communist Party ensures that only its own version of events is heard domestically, and stories of foreign destruction and looting certainly help to distract from the infinitely greater ruination brought about by the party itself.

During the 1966-76 Cultural Revolution, Red Guards confiscated 613,600 antiques and jade pieces from their Beijing owners in just one month, according to the book Mao’s Last Revolution (2008), few of which were ever seen again. More than 70 per cent of 6,843 officially designated places of cultural or historical interest in the city were destroyed, and what remained or had been rebuilt of the Summer Palace sustained further damage.

According to SACH itself, destruction in recent times has continued apace. Of about 225,000 historic sites in China on an incomplete list compiled in 1982, 30,995 had disappeared by 2009.

That foreign destruction, looting and purchase of China’s cultural heritage is statistically insignificant compared with the towering catastrophe the Chinese have achieved for themselves does not provide any excuse for it.

The Greeks, the Egyptians and the people of Benin in West Africa are among others pressing more honestly for the return of “stolen” antiquities, and engaging in debate. It’s long past time certain museums also stood up for their own reputations and against Chinese propaganda, and demanded that accurate and complete accounts be given of both historical events and existing collections.

item.title: [SCMP] What Indonesia’s warnings of energy cuts mean for Asean
item.description:
Indonesia’s warnings of curbing energy exports to countries it deems disrespectful amid regional tensions have put Singapore and other Southeast Asian buyers on notice, exposing the risks of relying on a neighbour increasingly protective of its resources.

But analysts see little chance of Jakarta following through on the threat, given its own economic interests and the mutual benefits of regional energy cooperation, including the long-planned Asean Power Grid.

On Thursday, Coordinating Minister for Downstreaming and Energy Transition Bahlil Lahadalia said he would not hesitate to consider halting exports to countries that did not respect Indonesia.
item.content:encoded:
Indonesia’s warnings of curbing energy exports to countries it deems disrespectful amid regional tensions have put Singapore and other Southeast Asian buyers on notice, exposing the risks of relying on a neighbour increasingly protective of its resources.

But analysts see little chance of Jakarta following through on the threat, given its own economic interests and the mutual benefits of regional energy cooperation, including the long-planned Asean Power Grid.

On Thursday, Coordinating Minister for Downstreaming and Energy Transition Bahlil Lahadalia said he would not hesitate to consider halting exports to countries that did not respect Indonesia.

“Don’t come asking for help only when you’re in need, but when other issues that can actually be discussed arrive, act like you have no sense of propriety, like someone who doesn’t know how to conduct yourself properly,” said Bahlil at the launch of a gas facility, as reported by local media.

A day earlier, he told reporters that Indonesia was considering not renewing natural gas export contracts with neighbouring countries to prioritise domestic energy needs. Bahlil, who is also the minister of energy and mineral resources, did not name any countries on either occasion.

Mirza Huda, a senior research fellow at the climate and sustainability programme at think tank ODI Global, said Indonesia’s remarks were likely to put neighbouring countries who imported natural gas from Jakarta – such as Singapore, Thailand and the Philippines – on notice.

But while the warnings “warranted attention”, they should not be interpreted as a decision to disrupt supplies, he added.

Among member states of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), Singapore was the largest importer of natural gas from Jakarta last year at 3.22 million tonnes, according to statistics agency BPS. Thailand and the Philippines imported 291,000 tonnes and 138,000 tonnes respectively.

Victor Nian, founding co-chairman of the Centre for Strategic Energy and Resources, cites Singapore as arguably the most exposed to potential non-renewal of natural gas contracts, given that its deal with Indonesia is set to expire at the end of 2028.

But the city state had diversified supplies through liquefied natural gas imports for global markets, and losing the Jakarta pipeline was likely to risk higher energy costs rather than a supply crisis, he said.

Dinita Setyawati, senior Asia energy analyst at Ember, pointed out that breaching gas contracts before expiry would lead to losses for Indonesia.

The warnings underscored the vulnerability of being dependent on imported gas, she said, urging investments in renewable energy and relevant technologies to serve as buffers. “Fossil fuels are molecules that cannot be reproduced.”

Resource nationalism

Bahlil’s remarks come as Indonesia grapples with a stock-market rout and its worst haze episode in over a decade.

Jakarta has responded to the crises with public shows of nationalism. President Prabowo Subianto this week called out global index MSCI, which warned that Indonesia’s economy could be downgraded from emerging-market to stand-alone-market status. “MSCI wants to scare us, but I say to them: Indonesia fears no one and will not be intimidated!”

During a cabinet meeting on Wednesday, Prabowo also slammed countries he said liked to snub his nation over intensifying wildfires. “Indonesia is a polite and patient nation. Our country is often insulted, but believe me, our nation does not want to be insulted all the time,” he said.

Jakarta has reportedly held off accepting offers of help from Singapore and Malaysia to tackle the fires, which have plagued many countries in the region.

Melinda Martinus, a fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute’s Asean Studies Centre, noted that the current transboundary haze situation might lead to the perception that Indonesia was targeting Singapore with its latest warnings.

She said resource nationalism was not new in Indonesia, citing recent moves such as the establishment of Danantara Sumber Daya Indonesia by the Indonesian government to supervise commodity exports.

The mineral-rich country has also banned the export of unprocessed nickel, bauxite and raw copper to encourage companies to refine minerals domestically and boost the local economy. Jakarta has also restricted palm oil exports on several occasions to safeguard domestic supply and prevent excessive price rises.

“This form of resource nationalism is often framed by politicians as a means of helping Indonesia achieve its ambition of becoming a high-income country,” she said.

Jakarta’s warnings reflected a broader and intensifying trend towards resource sovereignty among commodity producers, said Kaho Yu, head of energy and resources research at Verisk Maplecroft.

“Southeast Asian countries reliant on Indonesian gas will need to strengthen supplier engagement and diversify their energy sources,” he said, urging states to vary suppliers and start early negotiations for long-term contracts.

Nian cautioned that Bahlil’s remarks risked setting the precedent of attaching prerequisites to energy exports.

On Thursday, the minister said Indonesia remained open to signing energy export agreements with countries that treated it as an equal, even if they did not have existing contracts with Jakarta.

“Indonesia has every right to prioritise domestic energy security and maximise the economic benefits of its natural resources,” Nian said. “But making energy exports conditional on political ‘respect’ goes beyond legitimate resource nationalism and raises the troubling prospect of weaponising strategic resources.”

Impact on Asean cooperation

Observers say while Indonesia’s warnings are unlikely to hinder progress on regional frameworks such as the Asean Power Grid, they highlight the need for stronger dispute resolution mechanisms.

The regional grid, first conceptualised in 1997, aims to connect the electricity networks of all 11 member states through overland and undersea links. It is expected to boost the economy of exporters while strengthening the energy security of those who receive the supply.

“The fundamental premise of the power grid remains strong,” Martinus said. “Under such arrangements, everyone should benefit.”

But Nian said Jakarta’s warnings risked impeding the advancement of the regional grid, which required substantial investment and mutual confidence in the long term. “The prospect of politically motivated supply disruptions could increase investment risks, financing costs and hesitation over deeper regional energy integration.”

Mirza said the incident highlighted the need for long-term agreements, continued dialogue and a regional dispute resolution mechanism to address potential disagreements over electricity trade.

The grid has seen gradual progress – only eight of 18 planned interconnection projects were operational in 2024, according to the Asean Power Centre – but leaders of member states seem to be pushing it up the agenda list. The Asean summit in May set out a new target of full operationalisation across all member states by 2045.

Dinita was confident that discussions on the power grid would continue as usual. “As long as Indonesia stands to benefit, be it from electricity exports or toll rates for transmission lines, negotiations will continue,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] ‘Opportunistic’: experts weigh Manila’s minilateral agenda ahead of Trump-Xi meeting
item.description:
The Philippines’ dual push for stronger “minilateral” defence links and a more robust Asean security role is dividing analysts, with one calling the move “opportunistic”.

Some experts view Manila’s advocacy for the “Squad” alliance as a strategic opportunity to deepen core security partnerships while chairing the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. Others question how much actual weight is carried by this informal defence grouping – comprising the United States, the Philippines, Japan and Australia – which aims to counter China’s influence in the region.

They also caution that a flurry of US-led small-group diplomacy could undermine Asean’s centrality in a coming summit and leave Manila with less strategic leeway ahead of next month’s Trump-Xi talks.
item.content:encoded:
The Philippines’ dual push for stronger “minilateral” defence links and a more robust Asean security role is dividing analysts, with one calling the move “opportunistic”.

Some experts view Manila’s advocacy for the “Squad” alliance as a strategic opportunity to deepen core security partnerships while chairing the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. Others question how much actual weight is carried by this informal defence grouping – comprising the United States, the Philippines, Japan and Australia – which aims to counter China’s influence in the region.

They also caution that a flurry of US-led small-group diplomacy could undermine Asean’s centrality in a coming summit and leave Manila with less strategic leeway ahead of next month’s Trump-Xi talks.

In an exclusive interview with the South China Morning Post, Philippine ambassador to the US Jose Manuel Romualdez indicated that the Squad could meet on the sidelines of next month’s Asean summit in Manila.

If realised, the talks would come just days before US President Donald Trump meets Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on the Apec forum sidelines, in what would be their third summit meeting this year.

In the interview, Romualdez also expressed hope that Asean could one day take greater responsibility for its own security, much like Nato.

Meanwhile, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has confirmed that the Quad will hold its first summit in more than two years during the Manila gathering.

Characterised as a “diplomatic partnership” by the US, the informal bloc with Japan, Australia and India – aimed at “fostering a free and open Indo-Pacific” – has not held a summit since Trump returned to power in 2025. As reported by the SCMP, Trump refused to travel to India for a Quad meet last year after the two sides failed to strike a trade deal to his liking.

The timing of the meetings has led analysts to question whether the US and its allies were seizing an opportune window to highlight minilateral security cooperation and how this push might affect Asean unity and regional flexibility towards Beijing.

Arrizal Jaknanihan, a researcher with the Asean Studies Programme at The Habibie Centre in Jakarta, said the prospect of Squad meetings signalled “the Philippines’ long-standing pursuit of expanding and deepening its network of security partnerships across the Indo-Pacific”.

Given the recurring maritime clashes with rival claimant Beijing in the South China Sea and limited guarantees from other Asean members, “it is only natural that leaders in Manila eye the US, Japan and Australia as trusted partners”, he added.

Hosting the meetings while chairing Asean, Jaknanihan contended, offered “a strategic opportunity to show its commitment to both deepening security partnership with extra-Asean countries, while remaining committed to the regional grouping in Southeast Asia”.

Maritime tensions between China and the Philippines have escalated under President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr, who has been more assertive regarding Philippine claims compared with his predecessor.

Beijing claims most of the islands and rocks in the South China Sea and rights over their adjacent waters, with rival claimants including Malaysia, Vietnam and Brunei, in addition to the Philippines.

Manila also asserts sovereign rights within its exclusive economic zone, a position upheld by a 2016 international arbitral ruling that China rejects.

Chinese coastguard and militia vessels have repeatedly used water cannons and blocking manoeuvres against Philippine resupply missions to Second Thomas Shoal and around other disputed features, resulting in a series of collisions and injuries.

Manila has responded by expanding US military access under the Enhanced Defence Cooperation Agreement, while increasing joint patrols with Squad members.

He Xianqing of the Haikou-based National Institute for South China Sea Studies described the proposed Squad meetings as “both opportunistic and deliberate”.

“It’s simply convenient to hold this gathering on the sidelines of the Asean summit, with so many key officials already in town,” he said. “But it also shows Manila clearly favours a smaller, tighter group built on formal US alliances, different from the Quad.”

The format of the Squad grouping was “far more military-focused and centred on deterrence”, He said, noting that the Philippines, Japan and Australia were all formal US treaty allies.

He added that scheduling the talks just before the Trump-Xi meeting in southern China allowed Manila to “show it stands with US security support” without looking “like a troublemaker ahead of the crucial bilateral summit”.

Jennifer Kavanagh of Defence Priorities, a think tank in Washington, questioned the actual geopolitical weight of the Squad.

“Despite reports of a meeting of the Squad on the sidelines of Asean, I see no evidence the Trump administration has prioritised or is investing in this vehicle,” she said.

“It is not mentioned in any US strategic documents issued in recent years,” Kavanagh added, cautioning that without sustained joint training and institutional work, “the Squad will remain most irrelevant to Asian security, as it has been since it was announced under the [Joe] Biden administration”.

Pointing to Trump’s preference for bilateral engagement, she said: “A meeting of regional powers without the US would send a stronger signal to Beijing than a formulaic meeting of the Squad at this point.”

Commenting on the Quad meeting confirmed by Rubio, Ken Moriyasu of the Hudson Institute said: “If the leaders of the US, Japan, India and Australia were in the same venue and they didn’t hold a Quad, that would send quite the negative signal.”

But he cautioned against reading too much into a meeting alone, urging observers to focus instead on “the length and substance of the discussion, including the wording used in the joint statement”.

On the Squad, he said a gathering of US treaty allies “would provide an important opportunity for the Trump administration to demonstrate to the world that America’s alliance network in Asia remains ironclad”.

Ambassador Romualdez’s suggestion that Asean could evolve towards a Nato-style security alliance drew the sharpest scepticism from analysts.

Jaknanihan called the idea “both unrealistic and unnecessary”, as members held “differing perceptions regarding what they consider as a security threat, including China”.

An alliance built around a single threat “will be the complete opposite of Asean’s approach for decades”, he noted.

He of the National Institute for South China Sea Studies said an Asean Nato was “simply not realistic strategically”, pointing to the Asian group’s diverse political systems, non-aligned tradition and resistance to binding collective defence.

Manila is trying to walk a very fine line ... but right before the Trump-Xi summit, this delicate balance can easily break down

He Xianqing, National Institute for South China Sea Studies

Kavanagh was more blunt in her assessment. “Asean will never function like Nato,” she said, noting that Nato was a US-led collective defence alliance organised around blocs, while Asean operated on consensus and had no collective defence role.

On Asean centrality, Jaknanihan said the grouping had long accommodated differing external alignments as long as it did not “directly harm the security interest of other Asean members”.

Provided the Philippines continued to engage Asean-led processes during its chairmanship, deeper minilateral ties “will not substantially undercut Asean centrality”, he contended.

But He took the opposite view, saying that concurrent Quad and Squad activity alongside talk of an Asean Nato “looks like US-led small group diplomacy [is] taking over regional security” and this “weakens Asean’s central role”.

From Beijing’s perspective, Jaknanihan said that given the proximity of the Trump-Xi summit, it would be less likely to “express frontal opposition or punitive measures in response to the potential Squad meeting to avoid escalating tension, but China will definitely signal displeasure towards the development”.

According to Kavanagh, Beijing “sees the Philippines as a US puppet and will interpret the ambassador’s comments as either directed by Washington or motivated by a desire to tell Washington what it wants to hear”.

Looking ahead to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meetings in Shenzhen and potential talks on the sidelines between Marcos and Xi, analysts expect a familiar Philippine hedging posture complicated by the surrounding optics.

Jaknanihan said the meetings “offer an opportunity to find the pathway towards a more stable relationship, while still maintaining a mitigation through deeper security partnerships with Indo-Pacific partners”.

He in Haikou called the dual approach “exactly the Philippines’ hedging style”, but cautioned that if Squad coordination dominated the narrative, “the Marcos-Xi meeting will end up being nothing more than a symbolic photo opportunity, with little chance for real tension reduction”.

“Manila is trying to walk a very fine line: it wants both military deterrence and diplomatic dialogue with China,” He said. “But right before the Trump-Xi summit, this delicate balance can easily break down.”

item.title: [SCMP] What Beijing’s 2-to-1 shipbuilding lead means for the US in war over Taiwan
item.description:
Mainland Chinese shipyards delivered more than twice as much naval tonnage as their US counterparts in 2024 and 2025, according to a new survey, exposing a growing production gap that analysts say could weigh heavily in a prolonged conflict over Taiwan.

Tonnage alone is an imperfect measure of naval power, specialists cautioned, pointing to ongoing US advantages in submarine technology, aircraft carriers and operational experience. They also highlighted China’s ability to draw on commercial shipyards, unmanned systems and dual-use civilian vessels during a conflict. But they differed on how far the balance between the two had already shifted.

The Chinese mainland turned out 636,208 tonnes of military, paramilitary and auxiliary vessels over the two years, against 270,509 tonnes from American builders, the survey showed.
item.content:encoded:
Mainland Chinese shipyards delivered more than twice as much naval tonnage as their US counterparts in 2024 and 2025, according to a new survey, exposing a growing production gap that analysts say could weigh heavily in a prolonged conflict over Taiwan.

Tonnage alone is an imperfect measure of naval power, specialists cautioned, pointing to ongoing US advantages in submarine technology, aircraft carriers and operational experience. They also highlighted China’s ability to draw on commercial shipyards, unmanned systems and dual-use civilian vessels during a conflict. But they differed on how far the balance between the two had already shifted.

The Chinese mainland turned out 636,208 tonnes of military, paramilitary and auxiliary vessels over the two years, against 270,509 tonnes from American builders, the survey showed.

The survey, compiled by maritime intelligence publication Flottes de Combat and the French Naval Industry Association, found China accounted for more than 43 per cent of global naval production tonnage in the two years, compared with just over 18 per cent for the US.

Chinese yards delivered 84 vessels, up from 31 in 2022 and 2023, while American deliveries rose from 32 to 38, said the report, which was presented in Paris on Tuesday ahead of next month’s Euronaval defence exhibition.

While the US Navy’s combat fleet remains more than double the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) by tonnage, China is catching up. But analysts have questioned whether total tonnage alone would prove decisive in a war fought near China’s coast.

China has had the world’s largest navy by number of ships since at least 2020, according to the Pentagon, with the new survey counting 418 PLA Navy combat vessels on January 1. But at 1.44 million tonnes, they displaced less than half the 3.11 million tonnes of the US Navy’s 283 ships. The US had 11 aircraft carriers to China’s three.

Still, China is rapidly renewing its fleet. More than 40 per cent of the PLA Navy’s combat ships have entered service since 2018. Chinese yards delivered 10 destroyers in 2024 and 2025 to America’s four, while the PLA Navy commissioned 26 combat vessels against the US Navy’s nine.

Retired Royal Australian Navy vice-admiral Peter Jones attributed that pace to consistent shipbuilding practices. Designs appeared to be developed through Chinese naval research bodies and state-owned shipbuilder CSSC, avoiding repeated commercial tenders, he said.

Chinese destroyers and frigates followed a process of “incremental development”, with “modest upgrades between batches” reducing production risks, Jones said. A “steady drumbeat of work” at five specialised shipyards helped build workforce expertise.

By contrast, the US had “only some elements of this”, he added. Its Arleigh Burke destroyer programme was a success, but other projects suffered from “turbulence in decision-making”. Washington, he said, “just needs to return to the proven approach to shipbuilding across the fleet’s programmes”.

China’s commercial shipyards reinforce that advantage. Brian Hart, deputy director of the China Power Project at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, said builders had “intentionally blurred the boundaries” between naval and commercial production. Because the same yards built cargo ships and tankers, Beijing could “ramp up production of naval vessels in a protracted war”, he noted.

Chinese civilian ships that are not currently counted in combat-fleet totals could serve as military transports – since 2015, national standards have required certain cargo ships to be able to meet military needs. Hart cited “dual-use barges and ferries” that could boost amphibious transport capabilities, along with unmanned systems outside traditional counts.

Vessel types could distort shorter-term comparisons, said Bradley Martin, a senior policy researcher at the Rand Corporation and retired US Navy captain. American warships were often “large and complicated ships” that took years to build, so the delivery of a single carrier, such as China’s Fujian in 2025, could skew the figures.

China is also catching up in firepower. Hart pointed out it “has been rapidly closing the gap” in vertical launch system cells, which fire missiles from warships and submarines. Still, Hart said, the US had nuclear-powered carriers, unlike China. It also has more capable submarines and, crucially, experience gained through decades of global operations and combat.

Yet China is trying to close the undersea gap. The survey estimates that expanded facilities at Huludao – a coastal city in northeast China’s Liaoning province – can produce three nuclear-powered attack submarines annually, exceeding current US output. Martin argued that nuclear submarine warfare was not an area where “quantity can reasonably overcome quality”, though more Chinese boats could increase demands on anti-submarine forces.

A war over Taiwan, however, would be fought close to mainland China’s shores, where Martin said US warships would face land-based strike forces, so ship-to-ship engagements “might not be the most relevant consideration”. The longer a conflict lasted, the more Beijing’s industrial depth would matter, particularly its ability to keep producing “landing craft and logistics support forces”.

Lyle Goldstein, Asia programme director at Washington-based think tank Defence Priorities, called China’s shipbuilding lead “not an anomaly, but rather a persistent trend”. The western Pacific naval balance, he argued, “has been tilting decidedly in Beijing’s favour for some time”.

In a mid-Pacific encounter, the US would “almost certainly prevail”, he said, but fighting around Taiwan or in the South China Sea “would radically favour China”. In waters close to the Chinese mainland, such as the Taiwan Strait, “size can actually be a disadvantage”, making smaller diesel submarines preferable to nuclear-powered ones.

To keep pace, Washington would likely need allies. Martin said partners could supply smaller warships and auxiliaries and undertake “battle damage repair”. But Goldstein warned that air and missile strikes could make western Pacific yards unusable, urging stronger rear-area defences across the second and third island chains.

Losses could be severe. Given the lethality of modern anti-ship weapons, “many ships and even whole fleets would be sunk or badly damaged” in a high-intensity naval war, Goldstein said.

In such a conflict, starting fleets could matter less than how quickly they were replaced – and as the survey’s figures show, China is building faster.

item.title: [SCMP] Thailand has had enough of foreign tourists behaving badly
item.description:
At a zoo a short drive south of Bangkok, Charoon Youngprapakorn has spent a lifetime taking the pulse of Thailand’s tourism industry from an unlikely vantage point: the open jaws of crocodiles.

Handlers at his Samut Prakan Crocodile Farm & Zoo have long thrilled onlookers by coaxing tips from the audience and carefully placing the money into the mouths of animals capable of taking off an entire hand.

The crocodiles at this open-air, fan-cooled throwback to 1980s showmanship still take their tips at the end of every show. But these days, the notes are almost all Thai baht, handed over by Thai visitors. The busloads of overseas tour groups have largely disappeared.
item.content:encoded:
At a zoo a short drive south of Bangkok, Charoon Youngprapakorn has spent a lifetime taking the pulse of Thailand’s tourism industry from an unlikely vantage point: the open jaws of crocodiles.

Handlers at his Samut Prakan Crocodile Farm & Zoo have long thrilled onlookers by coaxing tips from the audience and carefully placing the money into the mouths of animals capable of taking off an entire hand.

The crocodiles at this open-air, fan-cooled throwback to 1980s showmanship still take their tips at the end of every show. But these days, the notes are almost all Thai baht, handed over by Thai visitors. The busloads of overseas tour groups have largely disappeared.

Tourism accounts for roughly one-fifth of the Thai economy, from the five-star resorts of Phuket and Koh Samui to the jet-ski operators and massage parlours of Pattaya.

The industry has never been immune to external shocks, however – and Charoon, who is in his seventies, has felt each one register at the ticket office of a business his father founded nearly 90 years ago to sell crocodile leather to tourists.

Sars, bird flu and the global financial crisis of 2007-08 all took their toll on visitor numbers, interspersed with boom years as mass tourism from China, an emerging Russian middle class and increasingly affluent Southeast Asian travellers pushed up attendance.

Then came a three-year closure amid the Covid-19 pandemic and – as with so much else in this world – nothing at Charoon’s zoo has been quite the same since.

“We used to have maybe 100, 200 big tour buses a day,” he told This Week in Asia. “But they stopped and we had to close because of the lockdown.”

By the time the business was able to reopen, tourism trends had changed. “People stopped travelling as big groups and instead they came as FITs,” Charoon said, using the industry acronym for “free, independent tourists”.

The zoo’s ample car park now welcomes only a handful of buses at a time. Across from it, a turreted wall built for elaborate performances once staged for Chinese tour groups stands as a chipped and faded monument to the high-water mark of Thai tourism.

Nearly 40 million people visited Thailand in 2019, the final year before the pandemic’s onset and still a Southeast Asian record.

Last year’s total of 32.9 million fell well short of that peak, despite a 60-day visa-free scheme introduced in 2024 to lure travellers back.

The Tourism Authority of Thailand has now trimmed its 2026 forecast to between 30 million and 34 million international visitors, as this year’s US-Israel war on Iran and Russia’s 4½-year-old war with Ukraine conspire to drive up oil prices and, with them, international airfares to Southeast Asia.

Years of a strong baht, meanwhile, have nudged budget-conscious international travellers towards cheaper alternatives in Vietnam and Malaysia.

Money, geopolitics and changing tastes tell only half the story, however. The rest is down to patience – and Thailand’s is wearing thin.

Misbehaving tourists

Long known as the “land of smiles”, Thailand has for years prided itself on its easy-going approach to hospitality that asks little of guests beyond good manners.

But scroll through Thai social media on any given morning nowadays and the previous night’s transgressions are laid out for all to see: unpaid bills, drunken brawls and arrests for theft or vandalism among them.

Each post gets shared and reshared until the obvious disrespect for a proud local culture starts to sour public opinion on the costs of welcoming millions of strangers every year.

“Thai people are pragmatic. We do like the money [tourism brings],” said Voranai Vanijaka, a prominent political and social commentator. “But at the same time, we are highly nationalistic and we don’t like tourists acting the fool.”

This year alone, tourists have been caught performing sex acts in public, assaulting locals, trespassing on private property and vandalising local landmarks. Recent crackdowns have also revealed dozens of bars and restaurants run by foreigners but masquerading as Thai-owned enterprises.

Other crimes are far more grave. In June, Australian national Simon Peter Carman, 45, was arrested on suspicion of murdering a teenage Thai girl, stuffing her body into a suitcase and disposing of it in the undergrowth near Pattaya.

Authorities have separately uncovered Chinese and Korean cyberscam operators holed up in luxury villas, an Indian national flaunting firearms on social media and a steady stream of British cannabis mules.

All the while, public attitudes against foreigners have been hardening – a sentiment Voranai said had also been fuelled by global nativist trends, nationalism stirred up by the recent border conflict with Cambodia and grievances over foreign nationals buying up land and businesses.

“There is an anti-foreigner, anti-immigrant feeling sweeping the world; it’s not just in Thailand,” he said, describing a “mood and tone” within which every viral episode of misbehaviour now played out, and a “lower tolerance” for such actions.

The steady drumbeat of bad news pushed Thailand to end its 60-day visa-free stays for tourists from September 15. Days later, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul told reporters he thought misbehaving foreigners had “gone too far”.

Not for the first time, Thailand has said it will step back from playing the numbers game to focus on attracting fewer, higher-spending tourists instead.

Officials describe 2027 as “the year of transformation”, aiming to attract wealthier travellers willing to stay a week or two at a time.

A proposed flat fee of 450 baht (US$13.50) on all foreign visitors to fund tourism infrastructure upgrades is also being actively considered.

But this soul-searching over who Thailand wants to welcome, and for how long, comes as hotel bookings during the current low season have disappointed and as travellers appear to be waiting until the last minute to book their stays in the crucial high season that begins in November.

On the upside, Thai tourism authorities are anticipating 200,000 Chinese tourist arrivals during next month’s “golden week” holiday from October 1 to 7, just as a the baht’s recent retreat is offering travellers better value.

Against this uncertain backdrop, Charoon’s crocodile farm has enjoyed something of social media-spurred revival.

In its 1980s heyday, when his father welcomed dignitaries including Singapore’s founding prime minister Lee Kuan Yew, the business made headlines for encounters with reptiles that visitors elsewhere might only see behind glass.

But as the novelty of live-animal shows began to wear off and tastes changed, the zoo’s weekday crowds thinned to a trickle.

Then, in late August, a TikTok video showing a single visitor sitting alone in the stands at one of the zoo’s elephant shows found an audience all of its own, garnering more than 1 million likes and sending a flood of visitors streaming back through gates.

“I was shocked. I didn’t expect that. I never thought one video could communicate to so many people,” Charoon said.

“People are coming in their thousands. I just hope they keep coming.”

Show respect, or go

Thailand is far from alone in pausing to reconsider its relationship with visitors.

In Indonesia’s Bali, a foreign-led running club accused of barring locals from taking part suspended operations this summer; in Sri Lanka, Buddhist monks held a violent protest outside a newly opened Jewish community centre known as a Chabad house last month, questioning its legality; and in Vietnam, authorities have vowed zero tolerance for foreign misconduct after recent drunken rampages and a deadly shooting linked to foreign nationals.

Social media, as ever, amplifies both the insults delivered and how they are received.

One Phuket business owner, who asked not to be named to protect his livelihood, told This Week in Asia that the types of tourists now visiting Thailand were more entitled, demanding unreasonable discounts and firing off insults at the slightest whiff of not getting their own way.

“I don’t think Thais are xenophobic,” he said. “But my mindset has changed, like a lot of people on Phuket. Customers are customers, but if they’re not nice and don’t respect the culture and the people, we are happy to see them go.”

This change in public sentiment appears to have influenced the government’s decision to halve the 60-day visa free-entry. It has also produced unusually blunt warnings from ministers who normally pull their punches when addressing foreign embassies.

In August, Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told the Chinese ambassador to “come out and explain” when sensitive issues arise “instead of speaking only to protect Chinese interests” – remarks that followed a viral confrontation between Chinese passengers and Thai officials at Bangkok’s main airport.

His comments also came amid mounting evidence of Chinese nationals illegally owning land and companies in Thailand, in some cases via officials bribed with as little as 500 baht to issue fraudulent birth certificates conferring land-ownership rights.

A small but vocal protest movement against official corruption and the influence of so-called grey money has since emerged, fronted by veteran conservative agitator Sondhi Limthongkul, who has rallied tens of thousands to take to the streets in the past.

Prime Minister Anutin, who himself rode a wave of nationalist sentiment to victory in February’s election, has responded to the backlash by fast-tracking deportations of foreign criminals and opening a wider investigation into “nominee” arrangements that allow foreign business owners to hide behind Thais.

Chinese, French, British, Indian and Russian nationals have all come under scrutiny, but it has been Israeli nationals – many of them military-aged and arriving in the wake of the war in Gaza – who have attracted the most intense attention, accused of building extensive “nominee”-business networks across southern Thai islands and of operating an illegal cemetery in Chachoengsao province.

“This has gone too far,” Anutin told officials on September 17 in response to the outrage.

“If they want to use our existing facilities, we have no problem with that. We have no objection whatsoever,” he said. “But they cannot come here, take our land, and then bury their dead here.”

Anutin’s point man on the “nominee” scandal, Deputy Interior Minister Polapee Suwunchwee, has since said he is investigating several Chabad houses across the country, warning that any found to have been built unlawfully could be torn down.

Following a meeting with Thailand’s foreign minister earlier this month, Israeli Ambassador Alona Fisher-Kamm told local media that bad behaviour was not unique to citizens of her country, adding that Hebrew-language pre-departure awareness campaigns were being introduced outlining Thai laws and cultural norms.

Nationalist commentators with large online followings have seized upon the anti-Israeli rhetoric, some veering into outright antisemitism.

“There is a risk of this getting out of hand,” Voranai said, referring to growing anti-Israeli “paranoia” stoked by hardline conservatives chasing clicks and the political spotlight.

Yet he doubts the swirling public anger will cost Anutin’s government much in the long run.

“There is no risk to the government at all – except for bad press, which they don’t care about,” Voranai said. “Nor should they, they hold all the power and they can just ride it out.”

Meet the neighbours

Amid the blizzard of bad publicity, some are determined to build bridges between foreigners and their Thai hosts.

John Ho, who was born and raised in Hong Kong but swapped a career in hospitality for a new life in Chiang Mai with his Thai wife a decade ago, this month launched CosmoLocal CNX – a government-backed “pop-up village” offering workshops, talks and communal meals to draw the Thai city’s digital-nomad population into closer contact with their Thai neighbours.

“There’s a transitional period where you’re travelling as a tourist, when you may not care that much about the local culture and language,” Ho said.

“But then, if you want to stay longer and set up a base, it naturally comes to a question of: ‘OK, let’s make friends’. It’s better to learn some Thai, and learn some of the laws around business and work.”

His pop-up, which offers discounted tickets for Thai attendees to keep it accessible, trades on Chiang Mai’s slower pace of life, distinctive northern Lanna culture and small-town feel – qualities that have attracted legions of remote workers since the pandemic.

It is a world away from the raucous party scene of Thailand’s southern islands, where many of the recent cultural clashes have occurred.

“We see the tensions,” Ho said. “But the majority of nomads do care – maybe they need more facilitation to meet the locals. This is the first attempt to do that.”

As for the seemingly endless churn of viral confrontations between Thais and foreigners?

“News cycles are news cycles,” Ho said. “I think a lot of it is out of proportion. Everyone in Thailand welcomes foreigners.”

item.title: [SCMP] How Japan’s innovative Nakagin Capsule Tower is finding new life
item.description:
In 1988, upon moving to Tokyo, British architect Mark Dytham made a pilgrimage to Ginza to see one building he believed encapsulated everything he had imagined Japan to be: Nakagin Capsule Tower. “It was one of the first proper hi-tech buildings in the world, like a machine or a robot, and represented a vision where things don’t have to be static,” the co-founder of Klein Dytham architecture says. “I thought it was the future.”

So in 2022, it was with mixed feelings that Dytham stood on a street in the Japanese capital and watched the Metabolist building come down. After cranes gingerly hoisted capsules off the two interconnected towers that accommodated them, roughly one in five were loaded onto trucks destined for temporary shelters, where they would be rehabilitated and shipped to new homes.

Given that Metabolism was an architectural movement founded on the ability of buildings to move with the times, its radical poster child seemed to be exhibiting normal vital functions. Or was it metastasis? In the past two years, newly revitalised since the dismantling of their 50-year-old mother ship, Nakagin cells have spread throughout Japan and beyond. Hong Kong is part of that advance.
item.content:encoded:
In 1988, upon moving to Tokyo, British architect Mark Dytham made a pilgrimage to Ginza to see one building he believed encapsulated everything he had imagined Japan to be: Nakagin Capsule Tower. “It was one of the first proper hi-tech buildings in the world, like a machine or a robot, and represented a vision where things don’t have to be static,” the co-founder of Klein Dytham architecture says. “I thought it was the future.”

So in 2022, it was with mixed feelings that Dytham stood on a street in the Japanese capital and watched the Metabolist building come down. After cranes gingerly hoisted capsules off the two interconnected towers that accommodated them, roughly one in five were loaded onto trucks destined for temporary shelters, where they would be rehabilitated and shipped to new homes.

Given that Metabolism was an architectural movement founded on the ability of buildings to move with the times, its radical poster child seemed to be exhibiting normal vital functions. Or was it metastasis? In the past two years, newly revitalised since the dismantling of their 50-year-old mother ship, Nakagin cells have spread throughout Japan and beyond. Hong Kong is part of that advance.

Nakagin’s scattered course would have pleased its avant-garde architect Kisho Kurokawa (1934-2007), who conceived the design to emancipate what he called Homo movens (mobile humans). Many fans still demonstrate their unbridled enthusiasm for the building by donning zany get-ups inspired by its form – often described as a stack of front-loading washing machines.

In my mind’s eye, however, Nakagin had always been a colony of barnacles. That analogy borrows from the free movement of these crustaceans before anchoring themselves in place. But unfortunately, it was the unexpected immobility of Kurokawa’s capsules during their first phase of life that ultimately thwarted his vision that they be modular, interchangeable and recyclable.

That idea of impermanent permanence remains irresistible, however – at least in Japan. Which was one reason Metabolism captured the imagination of many during the country’s buoyant post-war expansion, making its name and ethos heard at the 1960 World Design Conference in Tokyo. Adaptable buildings and cities – with renewable nodes fed by circulation systems – sparked interest. Adding excitement was the promise of Expo ’70, whose theme was “progress and harmony for mankind”.

At that landmark event in Osaka, futuristic pavilions, including several by Kurokawa, allowed the forward-thinking to see for themselves the biomimetic potential of a movement whose proponents included other eminent architects, Kenzo Tange and Fumihiko Maki among them.

Nakagin, however, earned the kind of cult status accorded few other buildings in Japan. One reason was the charisma of Kurokawa, also a media personality and, towards the end of his career, a politician. His building was among the few examples of Metabolist architecture ever realised.

In late 2022, Ikko Yokoyama visited a warehouse in Chiba, near Tokyo, where salvaged Nakagin capsules, resembling pet Cyclops, awaited adoption. As lead curator of design and architecture at M+, she was there to see one of 23 pods that had been saved by the Nakagin Capsule Tower Preservation and Restoration Project, founded by former resident Tatsuyuki Maeda.

Hong Kong’s museum of contemporary visual culture was prepared for this inevitable moment, according to Yokoyama. Debate had raged for years about whether to preserve Nakagin whole, with Kurokawa himself shifting from yes to no. Ultimately, land value outweighed legacy, says Dytham, who had tried without success to persuade developers and hospitality groups to turn Nakagin into a boutique hotel. “It wasn’t sustainable to keep it there,” he says.

The decision to tear it down was made despite its uniqueness. Unlike anything the West had produced – except, perhaps, in the minds of Britain’s Archigram group of architects – Nakagin consisted of capsules “plugged” into the building’s towers, or cores, one 11 storeys high, the other two floors taller. Tight spaces between each pod impeded access and meant that repairs were difficult because “you couldn’t get in”, says Dytham. Worse, owners were unwilling to pay the high cost of detaching their capsules for upkeep every 25 years, as Kurokawa had warned they must. Decay set in, leaks appeared and damage from Japan’s frequent earthquakes saw the building’s exterior netted for safety. Additionally, the presence of asbestos complicated matters.

But M+’s capsule speaks volumes about their enduring appeal. A806 now stands beside another of the museum’s inspired acquisitions, Kiyotomo (1988), the sushi bar designed by Shiro Kuramata. Unlike that 656 sq ft restaurant – which was disassembled in Japan, shipped to Hong Kong and later put together again by the original contractors and an M+ team of restorers – Kurokawa’s capsule was purchased fully reconditioned.

The 2.78 metre x 2.69 metre x 4.21 metre capsule in the East Galleries is one of six standard units, complete with their famous round window at one end accommodating a circular blind that folds open like a hand fan. Also included within the 121.9 sq ft space are mod cons and a dinky unit bath, those tiny waterproof rooms sold as a single product in Japan.

“Like organ donation”, as Yokoyama puts it, parts for the capsule were harvested from others in the building because none of the pods survived with all of its original fittings intact. Kiyotomo’s neighbour now also boasts a new blue carpet and mattress, in addition to a fold-down desk, television and reel-to-reel tape deck, among other integrated features. Combine the service and payload modules of a spaceship and you get the idea.

Of the capsules plucked to safety by Maeda’s group, 14 have been sold to companies and museums, including M+ and the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, which purchased Kurokawa’s prized personal unit. Of the nine remaining, he says, four are to stay in Japan while five will head abroad.
