Some have already been turned into display modules and mobile units and, next year, hotel-room conversions are expected, which should come as no surprise: in 1979, Kurokawa’s ideas also gave birth to the world’s first capsule hotel. New Japan Umeda continues to offer budget accommodation in Osaka.

Maeda’s is not the only group intent on giving the (in) famous corner building a second life. The Nakagin Capsule Tower A606 Project is named after the pod that another ex-resident helped restore several years before the building came down. This group, which owns seven units, has even more ambitious, albeit firmly parochial, aims.

“We plan to reconstruct a mini-tower using several capsules we own,” the group reveals via core member, architect Akiko Ishimaru.

“We aim to keep the reconstructed ones for 50 years [100 years after their completion] by continuing to use them ourselves. We want to utilise the capsules that were born in Japan and rebuild them in Japan.”

Crowdfunding has helped pay for the work so far. “The cost of asbestos control and investigation during the survey and dismantling, transportation and storage of seven capsules, storage of original parts, printing of a book with records, restoration of the interior of capsule A606, crowdfunding gifts [such as the aforementioned book], and fees consumed most of the total 8,673,000 yen [HK$443,000],” the group says.

Ishimaru’s efforts to keep Nakagin from history’s scrapheap underscores the passion in the project. But that’s not to say she fully enjoyed her year living in the building (and seven more working in two other capsules).

“One of my fond memories is drawing the actual survey plan for Nakagin Capsule Tower on my laptop at the original desk of Capsule A606 in August 2021,” she recalls, adding, “The 1.3-metre-diameter round window meant that the small room didn’t feel cramped.”

Having been designed as “hotel-like second homes” – or crash pads for salarymen – none of the capsules came with a kitchen. It was “very quiet”, Ishimaru recalls. The prefabricated steel modules didn’t share walls and, by 2013, when she moved in, there were only a few residents left. “Since it was so old and there was no hot water, I couldn’t even take a shower inside the capsule, so I stopped living there and used it as a shared office.”

Other assessments were bleaker. “From outside, the tower looked like a dying animal, sweating and greasy in the heat, trapped inside its wire netting,” reads an account by The Paris Review of Nakagin’s condition in 2016. “Looking up, you could see that some capsules had been half-filled with rotting garbage, a rippling line of trash drawn across their single windows. Inside, panels peel from the ceilings and mold crawls underneath; grime and seepage scorches the concrete with strange, bubbling forms.”

The reviewer added: “Kurokawa’s masterpiece was an utter, unsalvageable failure.”

And there’s the rub.

On whether Metabolism remains relevant in the 21st century, few can deny the importance of urban development that hews closely to principles of sustainability and flexibility. “The idea that buildings can change, grow and regenerate over time within a city may be increasingly needed to adapt to urban population growth and environmental issues,” the A606 group argue.

But how to label Kurokawa’s achievement remains as polarising as the fractious debates about whether the building should have been protected for posterity.

“It was an amazing success because he made it happen,” says Yokoyama, referring to how Kurokawa turned theory into reality and created a prototype. “It wasn’t just imagination.”

Dytham also believes Kurokawa got it “pretty right”, explaining that Nakagin was an early model. “If you’re building 10 of them, you get it. That was the first one.”

He adds that, for him, the building’s success had much to do with a design so simple that even a child could read and recognise it. “That would be a totally protected building if it was in the UK,” he posits. “Traditionally, here [in Japan], things are built in a temporary way.”

However, the recent wide dispersal of Nakagin capsules underscores the fact that Kurokawa’s vision has come to fruition. As Dytham says, “How many buildings have been taken apart and put all around the world?

“Taking [Nakagin] to the rest of the world is as important as just being all in one place.”

Metabolism was simply operating at its own pace.

item.title: [SCMP] What Beijing’s two-to-one shipbuilding lead means for the US in war over Taiwan
item.description:
Mainland Chinese shipyards delivered more than twice as much naval tonnage as their US counterparts in 2024 and 2025, according to a new survey, exposing a growing production gap that analysts say could weigh heavily in a prolonged conflict over Taiwan.

Tonnage alone is an imperfect measure of naval power, specialists cautioned, pointing to ongoing US advantages in submarine technology, aircraft carriers and operational experience. They also highlighted China’s ability to draw on commercial shipyards, unmanned systems and dual-use civilian vessels during a conflict. But they differed on how far the balance between the two had already shifted.

Yards on the Chinese mainland turned out 636,208 tonnes of military, paramilitary and auxiliary vessels over the two years, against 270,509 tonnes from American builders, the survey showed.
item.content:encoded:
Mainland Chinese shipyards delivered more than twice as much naval tonnage as their US counterparts in 2024 and 2025, according to a new survey, exposing a growing production gap that analysts say could weigh heavily in a prolonged conflict over Taiwan.

Tonnage alone is an imperfect measure of naval power, specialists cautioned, pointing to ongoing US advantages in submarine technology, aircraft carriers and operational experience. They also highlighted China’s ability to draw on commercial shipyards, unmanned systems and dual-use civilian vessels during a conflict. But they differed on how far the balance between the two had already shifted.

Yards on the Chinese mainland turned out 636,208 tonnes of military, paramilitary and auxiliary vessels over the two years, against 270,509 tonnes from American builders, the survey showed.

The survey, compiled by maritime intelligence publication Flottes de Combat and the French Naval Industry Association, found China accounted for more than 43 per cent of global naval production tonnage in the two years, compared with just over 18 per cent for the US.

Chinese yards delivered 84 vessels, up from 31 in 2022 and 2023, while American deliveries rose from 32 to 38, said the report, which was presented in Paris on Tuesday ahead of next month’s Euronaval defence exhibition.

While the US Navy’s combat fleet remains more than double the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) by tonnage, China is catching up. But analysts have questioned whether total tonnage alone would prove decisive in a war fought near China’s coast.

China has had the world’s largest navy by number of ships since at least 2020, according to the Pentagon, with the new survey counting 418 PLA Navy combat vessels on January 1. But at 1.44 million tonnes, they displaced less than half the 3.11 million tonnes of the US Navy’s 283 ships. The US had 11 aircraft carriers to China’s three.

Still, China is rapidly renewing its fleet. More than 40 per cent of the PLA Navy’s combat ships had entered service since 2018. Chinese yards delivered 10 destroyers in 2024 and 2025 to America’s four, while the PLA Navy commissioned 26 combat vessels against the US Navy’s nine.

Retired Royal Australian Navy vice-admiral Peter Jones attributed that pace to consistent shipbuilding practices. Designs appeared to be developed through Chinese naval research bodies and state-owned shipbuilder CSSC, avoiding repeated commercial tenders, he said.

Chinese destroyers and frigates followed a process of “incremental development”, with “modest upgrades between batches” reducing production risks, Jones explained. A “steady drumbeat of work” at five specialised shipyards helped build workforce expertise.

By contrast, the US had “only some elements of this”, he added. Its Arleigh Burke destroyer programme was a success, but other projects suffered from “turbulence in decision-making”. Washington, he said, “just needs to return to the proven approach to shipbuilding across the fleet’s programmes”.

China’s commercial shipyards reinforce that advantage. Brian Hart, deputy director of the China Power Project at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies, said builders had “intentionally blurred the boundaries” between naval and commercial production. Because the same yards built cargo ships and tankers, Beijing could “ramp up production of naval vessels in a protracted war”, he noted.

Chinese civilian ships that are not currently counted in combat-fleet totals could serve as military transports: since 2015, national standards have required certain cargo ships to be able to meet military needs. Hart cited “dual-use barges and ferries” that could boost amphibious transport capabilities, along with unmanned systems outside traditional counts.

Vessel types can distort shorter-term comparisons, said Bradley Martin, a senior policy researcher at the RAND Corporation and retired US Navy captain. American warships were often “large and complicated ships” taking years to build, so the delivery of a single carrier, such as China’s Fujian in 2025, could skew the figures.

China is also catching up in firepower. Hart pointed out it “has been rapidly closing the gap” in vertical launch system cells, which fire missiles from warships and submarines. Still, Hart said, the US had nuclear-power carriers, unlike China. It also has more capable submarines and, crucially, experience gained through decades of global operations and combat.

Yet China is trying to close the undersea gap. The survey estimates that expanded facilities at Huludao – a coastal city in northeast China’s Liaoning province – can produce three nuclear-powered attack submarines annually, exceeding current US output. Martin argued that nuclear submarine warfare was not an area where “quantity can reasonably overcome quality”, though more Chinese boats could increase demands on anti-submarine forces.

A war over Taiwan, however, would be fought close to mainland China’s shores, where Martin said US warships would face land-based strike forces, so ship-to-ship engagements “might not be the most relevant consideration”. The longer a conflict lasted, the more Beijing’s industrial depth would matter, particularly its ability to keep producing “landing craft and logistics support forces”.

Lyle Goldstein, Asia programme director at Washington-based think tank Defense Priorities, called China’s shipbuilding lead “not an anomaly, but rather a persistent trend”. The western Pacific naval balance, he argued, “has been tilting decidedly in Beijing’s favour for some time”.

In a mid-Pacific encounter, the US would “almost certainly prevail”, he said, but fighting around Taiwan or in the South China Sea “would radically favour China”. In waters close to the Chinese mainland, such as the Taiwan Strait, “size can actually be a disadvantage”, making smaller diesel submarines preferable to nuclear-powered ones.

To keep pace, Washington would likely need allies. Martin said partners could supply smaller warships and auxiliaries and undertake “battle damage repair”. But Goldstein warned that air and missile strikes could make western Pacific yards unusable, urging stronger rear-area defences across the second and third island chains.

Losses could be severe. Given the lethality of modern anti-ship weapons, Goldstein said, “many ships and even whole fleets would be sunk or badly damaged” in a high-intensity naval war.

In such a conflict, starting fleets could matter less than how quickly they are replaced – and as the survey’s figures show, China is building faster.

item.title: [SCMP] ‘Saved my mum’s life’: Chinese cancer drug on sale in US after Americans travel to buy it
item.description:
Global pharmaceutical firm AstraZeneca on Thursday said it would start selling a cancer drug after coming under criticism for failing to bring it to the US market faster, prompting some Americans to fly to Shanghai to procure the potentially life-saving medicine first developed by China.

In recent months, desperate Americans have travelled to China to obtain the Chinese-made cancer drug that was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration but remained unavailable in the country for more than a year, according to a cancer-treatment awareness advocate who made the journey while his mother was battling the disease.

“I’m very thankful to all the development that companies in China have done because it saved my mum’s life,” Max Doppelt, chief executive of Patient Data Vault, a consultancy that connects cancer patients to clinical trials, told the South China Morning Post.
item.content:encoded:
Global pharmaceutical firm AstraZeneca on Thursday said it would start selling a cancer drug after coming under criticism for failing to bring it to the US market faster, prompting some Americans to fly to Shanghai to procure the potentially life-saving medicine first developed by China.

In recent months, desperate Americans have travelled to China to obtain the Chinese-made cancer drug that was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration but remained unavailable in the country for more than a year, according to a cancer-treatment awareness advocate who made the journey while his mother was battling the disease.

“I’m very thankful to all the development that companies in China have done because it saved my mum’s life,” Max Doppelt, chief executive of Patient Data Vault, a consultancy that connects cancer patients to clinical trials, told the South China Morning Post.

Developed by China’s Dizal Pharmaceutical, sunvozertinib is a targeted lung cancer drug designed to treat adults with an advanced form of the illness, offering another treatment option for patients.

“Being in China physically, when I was there, I felt a very strong presence of connection between two very foreign, two very different places,” Doppelt said.

“We are all human beings, and health transcends it all. There are no political biases or sides when it comes to health.”

He added that he knew of at least 30 other Americans who had made the same trip.

Doppelt said he decided to travel to Shanghai to obtain the drug after his mother’s lung cancer spread to her brain in January 2025, when she had about 10 tumours.

At a lung cancer conference, a doctor told him that if his mother “happened to have lived in China, she could just get it”, as the country had approved the drug in 2023.

“I became pretty obsessed over it because my first reaction was, well, why don’t we go to China?”

However, at the time, he grew increasingly concerned about the escalating trade war between Washington and Beijing, marked by tit-for-tat tariffs and export controls.

“I was reading that in the news every day. So my main concern was: in six months, will there still be an avenue and a route for my mum to get this medicine?”

Despite the geopolitical tensions, he flew to China and returned home with 26 boxes of the China-made drug.

The Washington Post first reported the story on Tuesday.

AstraZeneca said on Thursday that sunvozertinib would be commercially available in the United States under the brand name Zegfrovy, after securing worldwide rights to develop and sell the drug from China’s Dizal Pharmaceutical.

While the FDA granted an “accelerated approval” to the drug in July 2025, AstraZeneca announced its “exclusive license agreement” with China’s Dizal Pharmaceutical in July of this year.

“AstraZeneca will acquire worldwide rights to develop and commercialise Zegfrovy,” the company said in a press release.

The deal included a US$600 million upfront payment to Dizal, with a further US$900 million potentially payable upon meeting specific regulatory clearances, as well as tiered royalties on global sales of Zegfrovy.

“The transaction is expected to close in the second half of 2026, subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory clearances,” the statement added.

In an email response to the SCMP, an AstraZeneca spokesperson said the global licensing agreement was “completed” only on September 1, 2026, and that the firm “has been working to make Zegfrovy available to patients in the US as quickly as possible”.

“By making Zegfrovy available in the US, we are bringing an oral, mutation-specific treatment option to a distinct patient population with substantial unmet need,” the spokesperson added.

Doppelt said he initially chose not to speak publicly but became “increasingly frustrated” that the drug remained unavailable in the US despite an FDA approval.

“Every single quarter, we have been told as a community, of all the lung cancer patients who have this mutation, that it’s going to be ready next quarter. It’s going to be next quarter.”

However, Doppelt said he would not blame the drug maker for the 15-month delay.

“Without AstraZeneca, we wouldn’t even have the drug today.”

Kyle Concannon, a doctor-scientist at the University of Colorado, said Washington needed to change its approach to developing and adopting new treatments.

“If the US wants to remain competitive and ensure patients don’t have to travel across the world for treatments, we need to both accept greater risk, recognising that for many patients the alternative is no treatment,” he wrote on social media.

Anne Wojcicki, CEO and founder of the 23andMe Research Institute, noted that China had transformed from a country known for producing raw materials into a global force in drug discovery, contrasting its position with that of the US in the early 2000s.

“The world has flipped. It’s remarkable how China has become a powerhouse in drug discovery and is now leading,” she said on social media.

She added that artificial intelligence would bring another shift in the industry, with large-scale data initiatives and “nimble regulatory oversight” key to driving progress.

China has rapidly expanded its pharmaceutical sector, taking the lead in clinical trial registrations between January 2024 and June 2025 with 24 per cent of the world total, according to World Health Organization data compiled by the British Medical Journal.

China’s share of global early-stage drug-development programmes rose from 8 per cent in 2015 to 32 per cent in 2024, closing the gap with the US, whose share fell from 48 per cent to 37 per cent over the same period, according to a study published in the Journal of the American Medical Association in March 2026.

Doppelt called for FDA reforms, including greater transparency around clinical trials and data reporting, as well as greater openness to testing new cures.

He also pointed to China’s approach to cellular therapy research, saying the US could adopt some of its practices.

“In China, I think we could learn something from them because there are dozens of cellular therapy trials that are spun up all the time.”

item.title: [SCMP] Who blinked first? Fragile EU-China trade peace sparks new war of words
item.description:
Less than two weeks after Brussels and Beijing struck a surprise deal to avert an escalating trade dispute, their fragile rapprochement has descended into a battle over who blinked first.

In Brussels and Berlin, officials are emboldened by what they consider proof that collective EU pressure can force Chinese concessions. Rather than resting on their laurels, they are cooking up a fresh batch of trade restrictions.

Beijing, on the other hand, has bristled at the idea that it can be strong-armed into yielding to Europe’s demands, even more so the suggestion that further concessions may be coming. State media has carried numerous warnings against European hubris.
item.content:encoded:
Less than two weeks after Brussels and Beijing struck a surprise deal to avert an escalating trade dispute, their fragile rapprochement has descended into a battle over who blinked first.

In Brussels and Berlin, officials are emboldened by what they consider proof that collective EU pressure can force Chinese concessions. Rather than resting on their laurels, they are cooking up a fresh batch of trade restrictions.

Beijing, on the other hand, has bristled at the idea that it can be strong-armed into yielding to Europe’s demands, even more so the suggestion that further concessions may be coming. State media has carried numerous warnings against European hubris.

It has resulted in an awkward, terse trade peace: an agreement that was supposed to defuse a trade war has led to both sides, rhetorically at least, hardening their positions. With verbal volleys flying back and forth, doubts are already surfacing over whether this delicate ceasefire can hold until the next round of negotiations in January.

“I can tell you that the French-German paper you refer to was clearly seen from China as ‘OK, now it’s becoming serious’. For the first time, France and Germany agreed on this,” Pascal Canfin, the ranking member on China in the European Parliament’s trade committee, told reporters on Wednesday.

Canfin was referring to a now-famous joint paper between the EU’s biggest powers, which proposed a kill switch that could kick Chinese companies out of the EU market overnight, which has now become an official policy to be proposed in December.

His comments reflected a new-found confidence in Europe on how to conduct relations with China.

“If you just negotiate without the credible possibility to do something differently, then negotiation is not credible at all. If we have the two legs and one voice, I think we are much stronger than we thought, because China is also dependent on the access to our market,” said Canfin, who will join a delegation of trade MEPs visiting China next week.

In Berlin on Wednesday, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he was “surprised” at the “unanimous support” from EU members at the summit, even as he said Germany did not want a trade war with China.

“The first indication that this could really have an effect on our relations is that obviously the government in Beijing is willing to accept a limited number of car imports to the European Union, which was not the case in the last couple of weeks and months. So we are making progress,” Merz said.

In the run-up to last week’s summit of EU leaders, more than a dozen diplomatic and official sources suggested the bloc had landed on a “two-track” formula of intense dialogue, backed by hard trade action.

The suggestion has been met with fury in Beijing, where official organs have been pushing back strongly against the idea that China could be managed in such a way.

“China’s willingness to make a strategic compromise should not be confused with a willingness to accept an endless series of concessions. Mistaking the former for the latter could turn Beijing’s goodwill into the next source of confrontation,” fumed Brussels Tea House, a newsletter written by Xinhua journalists in the Belgian capital, on Wednesday.

The comments echoed an official commerce ministry statement on Friday, which warned the bloc not to “fantasise” that its pressure had worked. The EU should “harbour no illusions about extracting concessions through pressure, still less underestimate China’s determination and ability to defend its own interests”, the ministry said.

On Wednesday, however, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen doubled down on the strategy, promising further trade restrictions and new instruments to defend European industries against Chinese competition.

“We see jobs lost in our industrial heartlands. So last week, at the European Council, we agreed a clear approach. First, dialogue where it delivers. Second, action where needed. And third, stronger tools to defend our interests,” von der Leyen said, adding that the commission was “already working closely with our chemicals and machinery sectors”, where further quotas were expected.

The deal will cap the import of Chinese hybrid cars at 350,000 per year from December 1.

The South China Morning Post has been told that quotas will also be applied to South Korea, Japan, Turkey, Britain and Morocco, calculated using last year’s volume of exports plus an additional 15 per cent. The commission would, sources said, be examining these flows for evidence of circumvention by Chinese companies looking to fill out quotas elsewhere.

In her address to the European Parliament on Wednesday, von der Leyen spoke of “the removal of certain EU companies from Chinese control lists”.

The SCMP understands this refers to the German company Sindlhauser, an important supplier to ASML which was added to a Chinese blacklist in July and removed in a tit-for-tat delisting. Bloomberg previously reported that, unable to access Chinese inputs, the company was at risk of going bust.

Some are hoping that the Beijing agreement can be the bedrock of something more substantive.

Bernd Lange, who will lead the European Parliament delegation to China next week, called for further agreements “quite soon”, adding that “negotiations forever make no sense”.

“I remember the negotiation on the so-called CAI, the investment agreement, which is deep in the freezer,” Lange told reporters, referring to the Comprehensive Agreement on Investment, frozen by the parliament after a row over human rights sanctions in 2021.

Lange suggested revisiting the investment provisions of the frozen agreement, including whether Brussels and Beijing could ease restrictions on each other’s investors.

Behind the scenes, however, the triumphalism was less apparent. A well-placed official worried that public remarks last week overhyped what negotiators see as a first step, potentially harming the next rounds of negotiations.

Some also wonder if the shift came too late. A deal to cap the import of Chinese hybrid cars is a “pyrrhic victory”, said one senior diplomat, noting that it covered a minute portion of overall trade.

“Look at what is going on in France, [far-right leader Marine] Le Pen could be in next year – I am not sure any of this China hawkishness outlasts [President Emmanuel] Macron in Paris,” they said, with an eye on presidential elections in April 2027, likening the mood in Brussels to a football team celebrating a consolation goal when they are already 6-0 down.

item.title: [SCMP] Quad confirmed, Manila envoy signals likely ‘Squad’ talks before Trump-Xi summit
item.description:
The Philippine ambassador to the United States signalled possible meetings of the “Squad” bloc ahead of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations gathering in Manila, as Washington confirmed that the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue would hold its first leaders’ summit in more than two years on the sidelines of the regional talks.

An informal defence grouping, the “Squad” forms part of a US-led regional strategy to counter China’s growing influence in the Asia-Pacific region. It comprises the US and three of its treaty allies: the Philippines, Australia and Japan. The Quad, by contrast, includes India in place of the Philippines and is not a formal military alliance.

Speaking exclusively with the South China Morning Post in a recent interview, Jose Manuel Romualdez also voiced hope that Asean would evolve into a Nato-like alliance capable of handling its own security.
item.content:encoded:
The Philippine ambassador to the United States signalled possible meetings of the “Squad” bloc ahead of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations gathering in Manila, as Washington confirmed that the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue would hold its first leaders’ summit in more than two years on the sidelines of the regional talks.

An informal defence grouping, the “Squad” forms part of a US-led regional strategy to counter China’s growing influence in the Asia-Pacific region. It comprises the US and three of its treaty allies: the Philippines, Australia and Japan. The Quad, by contrast, includes India in place of the Philippines and is not a formal military alliance.

Speaking exclusively with the South China Morning Post in a recent interview, Jose Manuel Romualdez also voiced hope that Asean would evolve into a Nato-like alliance capable of handling its own security.

The “Squad” and Quad meetings are expected to take place in the Philippines just days before US President Donald Trump is set to meet Chinese leader Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen next month.

“This type of meetings regularly happen, and if it’s an opportunity that is there, I’m sure that they will do it,” Romualdez said when asked about a possible “Squad” defence ministers’ meeting.

On whether the grouping would be raised to the leaders’ level, Romualdez – who is also President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr’s second cousin – said it would depend on “what kind of an agreement” or meetings that officials “will have on the sidelines of the Asean summit”.

A source familiar with the discussions said the probability of the “Squad” meetings was “very high” and added that since many US allies and partners would be in the Philippines, the “pretence” of US diplomatic commitment could be “cheaply done”.

Before the leaders’ summit from November 16 to 18 in Manila, the Philippine Department of National Defence will host the defence ministers’ meeting and related engagements on October 28 and 29 in Cebu.

Manila’s ambassador to Washington stressed that Marcos had consistently pursued a “multilateral approach” to the Asia-Pacific region, backed by a network of defence agreements with other countries.

“We’re counting now about seven or eight of them, but more importantly, between Japan, Australia, the United States and the Philippines,” he said.

Romualdez confirmed, however, that Marcos would attend the Apec summit in Shenzhen, expressing hope that he could at least have a “possible good conversation” with Xi even if no formal meeting took place.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced on Tuesday that the Quad leaders would meet in the Philippine capital next month, marking the group’s first summit in more than two years.

“It’s been agreement now that we’re going to do it; we’re going to do it in Manila, at the Asean conference,” Rubio said in an interview with Indian news channel CNN-News18.

“We don’t have the specific date yet, but that’s going to happen, and we’re very enthusiastic about it.”

The Squad and the Quad were part of the previous Joe Biden administration’s strategy of building a “latticework” of coalitions to counter China’s clout.

The first meeting of “Squad” defence ministers took place on the sidelines of the Shangri-La security dialogue in Singapore in June 2023, followed by a series of interactions.

The Trump administration has continued the dialogue, with the most recent engagement between defence chiefs taking place on the sidelines of the Asean summit in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, last November.

Military officials of four countries also convened for a defence cooperation council meeting in May in Singapore.

Beyond deepening security ties with regional powers, the Philippine envoy to Washington also floated the idea of an “Asean Nato”, reviving a proposal rejected by the country’s defence secretary, Gilberto Teodoro Jnr, in 2024.

“I’m even hoping that Asean will become like a Nato, that it can take care of its own security,” Romualdez told the SCMP.

He added that “having an integrated security” is more efficient as the Asean countries are “all together” and “live in the same neighbourhood”.

“Then we can make agreements with countries like China as a whole, agreements with the United States,” he said.

“I hope that one day we will be able to have not only our economies integrated, but even our defence and military.”

Teodoro in November 2024 had dismissed the prospect, saying that Asean’s complex “dichotomies and divergence in country interests” would make it challenging to set up a unified military alliance.

The ambassador’s statements come as the Trump administration recalibrates its priorities in the Asia-Pacific, prompting concerns among regional partners over the durability of US security commitments and Washington’s strategy for competing with China.

In June, the US renamed the Indo-Pacific Command as Pacific Command, reversing a change made in 2018. In August, Trump ordered the annual US-South Korean military exercise be cut from 11 days to five.

Washington has redeployed the Japan-based USS George Washington to the Middle East for operations against Iran, leaving no US aircraft carrier permanently stationed in the Indo-Pacific.

The Trump administration has also pressed regional allies and partners to shoulder more of their own defence costs.

Romualdez argued that he saw no sign of US commitments weakening for now, but stressed that Manila had to be “ready for any kind of eventuality”.

“We remain focused on strengthening our armed forces to where we want it to be, so that we would be able to defend ourselves.”

He also ruled out any possible involvement in a Taiwan crisis, saying the Philippines was not part of any security arrangements related to the island and that his country adhered to the one-China policy.

“The only role that Philippines right now has in Taiwan is the fact that we have 250,000 workers. We obviously are concerned about that,” he added, referring to Filipino migrant workers living on the island.

The ambassador’s stance is in sharp contrast to that of defence chief Teodoro, who has rejected Beijing’s warnings over Manila’s engagement with Taiwan.

“We define the one-China policy. We define it. Not them,” Teodoro said in September.

Under an expanded defence pact, the Philippines has granted the US military rotational access to strategic sites in northern Luzon, including bases in Cagayan province near Taiwan.

The two countries have also expanded joint military exercises in the northernmost Batanes islands, where Manila is strengthening its own military infrastructure.

Beijing views Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the island’s main international partner, the United States, do not recognise self-ruled Taiwan as an independent state. Washington is opposed to any attempt to take it by force and is legally bound to supply it with weapons to defend itself.

item.title: [SCMP] Can Prabowo’s economic nationalism save Indonesia from potential MSCI downgrade?
item.description:
In the wake of Indonesia’s worst stock-market rout since the 1998 Asian financial crisis, President Prabowo Subianto’s administration has turned to appeals to economic nationalism to shore up confidence, urging citizens to rally behind the country’s battered stock market.

The government has promised reforms in response to warnings from global index provider MSCI that Indonesia could be downgraded from emerging-market to stand-alone-market status.

But analysts say its patriotic appeals will do little to restore investor confidence without concrete steps to improve market transparency and governance, while potentially exposing retail investors to further losses.
item.content:encoded:
In the wake of Indonesia’s worst stock-market rout since the 1998 Asian financial crisis, President Prabowo Subianto’s administration has turned to appeals to economic nationalism to shore up confidence, urging citizens to rally behind the country’s battered stock market.

The government has promised reforms in response to warnings from global index provider MSCI that Indonesia could be downgraded from emerging-market to stand-alone-market status.

But analysts say its patriotic appeals will do little to restore investor confidence without concrete steps to improve market transparency and governance, while potentially exposing retail investors to further losses.

After the Jakarta Composite Index (JCI) plunged 11 per cent on Friday, further sell-offs followed in the ensuing days, prompting a defiant Prabowo to address the market turmoil at a cabinet meeting five days later.

“MSCI wants to scare us, but I say to them: Indonesia fears no one and will not be intimidated!”

Prabowo also claimed Indonesia’s dispute with MSCI was among the “hurdles and obstructions” continuing to harry his administration. “But the nation has the strength, courage and willingness to make the necessary sacrifices.”

The president’s defiance was accompanied by calls from senior figures in his administration and allies in the business community for Indonesians to support the domestic stock market.

Sufmi Dasco Ahmad, deputy speaker of the House of Representatives and a senior leader in the ruling Gerindra party, launched a Buy Indonesia campaign on Tuesday, urging citizens to buy domestic shares to prevent further declines.

“Through collective pan-Indonesia efforts, we can turn our bourse around. Buy Indonesia!” Dasco said on social media, reaffirming his confidence in the resilience of the local economy.

He was among the first officials to visit the Jakarta Stock Exchange on the day of the October 16 crash.

Mufti Nurlatifah, a lecturer in the Department of Communication Science at Yogyakarta’s University of Gadjah Mada, said while Dasco’s public appeal attempted to maintain optimism about Indonesia’s economic future, “it’s hardly enough without giving the public concrete reasons and measurable indicators why they should remain upbeat”.

She said it would be a grave error to conflate citizens’ patriotism with indiscriminate investment in Indonesian stocks.

Indonesian tycoon Jusuf Hamka, recently made one of Prabowo’s presidential advisers, also tried to support the market by announcing on Sunday that he was setting up a consortium to inject 5 trillion rupiah (US$277 million) into the bourse.

“Our blue chips can yield between 8 and 9 per cent annually, higher than term deposits,” he claimed.

Hamka described MSCI’s downgrade threat as a “shakedown” by a foreign force seeking to destabilise Indonesia, and urged local entrepreneurs to “step up and defend our sovereignty by buying up our domestic stocks”.

Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara, executive director of Jakarta-based think tank the Centre of Economic and Law Studies, called the patriotic appeals made by Dasco and Hamka “dangerously misleading”.

“They could put retail investors in jeopardy as stock prices could tank further if and when institutional investors take a hike,” he said.

An MSCI downgrade could remove Indonesian stocks from global indexes tracking emerging markets, potentially prompting funds that follow those benchmarks to reduce their exposure to the country.

To calm market nerves, the Indonesia Stock Exchange met MSCI on Monday and outlined further measures to improve transparency, including identifying affiliated shareholders and excluding highly concentrated stocks from the JCI’s calculation. Authorities have also pledged broader capital-market reforms.

MSCI has said, however, that investors want evidence of the measures being consistently implemented and having a meaningful impact.

MSCI’s consultation on Indonesia’s proposed reclassification remains open until April 30, 2027, with a final decision expected by the end of June that year, giving the government time to demonstrate progress on the reforms.

Bhima argued that the central issue was how the Indonesian stock market was administered, rather than a lack of patriotic support for domestic shares.

“Instead of enacting the necessary reforms in the capital market, the government and its cohorts have opted for a narrative steeped in economic nationalism.”

For Vedi Hadiz, a political sociologist at the University of Melbourne, the market turmoil also reflected tensions arising from Prabowo’s efforts to recentralise political and economic power.

These include the creation of Danantara, a sovereign wealth fund designed to consolidate management of state-owned enterprises, and plans to channel exports of key commodities such as coal and palm oil through a single state-owned company, giving the government greater control over the movement of resources and capital.

“His efforts to change the rules of the game to suit his own political and economic agenda will inevitably cause problems for established business groups who have to adapt to his agenda,” Hadiz said.

Dasco’s Buy Indonesia plea also exposed the tensions emerging from Prabowo’s bid to bring big businesses under tighter political control, Hadiz said. “But an appeal based on economic nationalism glosses over these tensions by suggesting that everyone shares the same interests.”

Hadiz observed that patriotic appeals have featured in previous administrations’ responses to economic turmoil, often with limited results.

He cited former president Joko Widodo’s 2015 appeal to Indonesians to buy local products to counter rupiah depreciation.

In January 1998, amid the rupiah’s collapse, presidential daughter Siti Hardijanti Rukmana launched the Love the Rupiah Movement and tried to set an example by publicly selling US$50,000 of her own money.

Her initiative failed to arrest the currency’s slide, with the rupiah reaching almost 17,000 to the US dollar in June 1998, Bhima noted. “It happened because the appeal was made when the government had lost all public credibility and trust.”

For investors, the concerns extend beyond the immediate MSCI dispute.

Ricky Ho, chief investment officer and portfolio manager at Jakarta-based family office Four Capital, said he remained “bearish on Indonesia”.

In his assessment, the Indonesian equity market faces a daunting combination of headwinds, including higher global discount rates, a stronger US dollar, expensive oil, weaker purchasing power among the middle class, continued pressure on banks’ asset quality, uncertain commodity margins and the unresolved MSCI issue.

“That is simply not the environment in which I’d want to take large risks,” Ho said.

For Hadiz, however, the stock-market turmoil did not in itself demonstrate that big businesses were resisting Prabowo’s economic agenda, often referred to as Prabowonomics.

“Resistance can take the form of lobbying, holding back investment, demanding concessions or pushing for changes in policy.”

The upheaval nevertheless presents a dilemma for the president.

“Prabowo wants to exercise greater control over the conglomerates, yet still needs their investment and cooperation to make his economic and political agenda work,” Hadiz said.

item.title: [SCMP] Haze forces Malaysian fitness groups to swap outdoor runs for shopping mall laps
item.description:
Runners in Malaysia are swapping their usual routes through parks and city streets for laps around shopping malls, commandeering air-conditioned corridors to keep up their training as a stubborn blanket of haze makes exercising outdoors increasingly hazardous.

The switch comes as smoke from forest and peatland fires continues to foul the air across parts of Southeast Asia, with Malaysia’s capital Kuala Lumpur and its surrounding districts among the hardest-hit areas.

By 9am on Thursday, 15 of Malaysia’s 68 air quality monitoring stations were recording unhealthy pollution levels. Readings reached 163 in Negeri Sembilan, while parts of Kuala Lumpur and neighbouring Selangor remained above 150, according to data from the Department of Environment.
item.content:encoded:
Runners in Malaysia are swapping their usual routes through parks and city streets for laps around shopping malls, commandeering air-conditioned corridors to keep up their training as a stubborn blanket of haze makes exercising outdoors increasingly hazardous.

The switch comes as smoke from forest and peatland fires continues to foul the air across parts of Southeast Asia, with Malaysia’s capital Kuala Lumpur and its surrounding districts among the hardest-hit areas.

By 9am on Thursday, 15 of Malaysia’s 68 air quality monitoring stations were recording unhealthy pollution levels. Readings reached 163 in Negeri Sembilan, while parts of Kuala Lumpur and neighbouring Selangor remained above 150, according to data from the Department of Environment.

At Atria Shopping Gallery in Petaling Jaya, just outside Kuala Lumpur, dozens of runners spent Wednesday evening weaving through the mall’s upper-floor corridors, clocking up laps past shops and escalators in a workout that would ordinarily have taken place on the streets.

The free event, organised by fitness studio The Active Chimp with the mall’s approval, attracted nearly 200 registrations – far exceeding the 50 to 60 participants organisers had anticipated.

“We were actually expecting the first run to attract around 50 to 60 people, but it was actually overwhelming,” The Active Chimp founder Keith Tan said.

Organisers eventually limited participants to around 150, with running coaches setting the pace along a roughly 500-metre circuit and helping participants avoid shoppers.

Tan, 40, came up with the idea after struggling to find somewhere to run without exposing himself to the haze. He approached the mall’s management after noticing how much space was available during quieter hours.

“I was watching, I was teaching classes, and I was like, ‘Oh, the mall’s so empty,’” he recalled. “I was wondering, can we actually run inside the mall when there’s not so many people?”

He pitched the idea to management, arguing that runners needed somewhere to train while the air outside remained hazardous. “It’s hazy and no one can run outside,” he said.

The mall agreed, moving benches to widen the route and providing security personnel to help manage foot traffic. Tan’s coaches also tested the circuit at different times of the day before launching the first organised run.

The fitness entrepreneur, who has worked in the industry for more than a decade, wants the runs to become a regular fixture if the arrangement proves manageable.

“I know the treadmill is a choice, but running on a track is different,” he said. “Personally, it’s my own pain because I wanted to run and I had nowhere to go.”

Retail ‘run’ therapy

Fitness groups across the Klang Valley, which includes Kuala Lumpur and its surrounding cities, have also begun organising indoor mall runs as the haze disrupts outdoor training.

At The Starhill, an upscale shopping centre in Kuala Lumpur’s bustling Bukit Bintang district, the Worst Pace Run Club held its first indoor mall run on Wednesday, promoting the event on social media with a cheeky declaration: “The haze can have the streets, we’ll take the mall!”

Other events advertised this week include a mall run at United Point in Kepong, a session at Sunway Square Mall on Saturday and a 3km (1.9-mile) indoor run at 1 Utama on Sunday, according to running community directory runclubs.my.

These makeshift running tracks follow a similar experiment across the border in Singapore, where the worst haze since 2015 has disrupted outdoor exercise and forced the cancellation of sporting events, including the Great Eastern Women’s Run and the Singapore Half Marathon.

Last Saturday, about 15 runners from X-Run Singapore took over sections of Marina Square shopping centre before opening hours, covering distances of between 9km and 21km with permission from management.

Back in Malaysia, Amirul Hakim, 32, was among those who signed up for the Atria run after missing his usual outdoor routine.

“We haven’t been able to run like we used to for a long time,” he said, explaining that the opportunity to try something new encouraged him to join. “It won’t be the same as running outside because the surface can be slippery … but at least we can have fun and work up a sweat.”

With his office nearby, Amirul said he would consider joining future sessions if the mall allowed them regularly.

No clear skies

Malaysia’s Ministry of Health has urged the public to avoid outdoor exercise when the air pollutant index exceeds 100, warning that fine particles in the haze can penetrate the respiratory system and pose serious health risks. It has recommended N95 masks for those who must venture outside.

The prolonged pollution has also disrupted school activities, with education authorities suspending outdoor sports in affected areas and ordering temporary closures when air quality deteriorates. Under government guidelines, educational institutions must close when the API exceeds 200.

The transboundary haze remains a perennial diplomatic headache in Southeast Asia, where smoke from forest and land-clearing fires regularly drifts across national borders.

Malaysia and Indonesia were exploring closer cooperation on fire prevention and hotspot monitoring, Deputy Minister of Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Syed Ibrahim Syed Noh told parliament on Wednesday.

“Malaysia and Indonesia will continue to work together through the Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution,” he said, outlining plans to strengthen regional prevention and monitoring efforts.

For 50-year-old Steven Ho, who works in Kuala Lumpur’s KL Sentral district, completing an estimated 5km around Atria on Wednesday proved surprisingly challenging due to the air conditioning.

“When we run outside, our body temperature will go up because it’s outside. But here it’s a bit cold,” he said. “I probably need a few more laps to warm up.”

Still, Ho sees great potential in the concept. “Malls that are a bit empty, or floors that are a bit more empty, could open up space for people to run, especially during the haze,” he said.

The coming monsoon season offered another reason to keep the corridors open, Ho added, given how frequently heavy downpours interrupt outdoor running towards the end of the year.

Organiser Tan is already looking beyond the two sessions at Atria, noting that around 180 people had signed up for the next event by the time he spoke to This Week in Asia.

But turning shopping centres into regular running venues will require more than just enthusiastic participants – especially when regular shoppers are going about their day.

“We cannot just accommodate the runners and neglect the shoppers. We have to find a balance,” Tan said. “If safety, traffic and all the benefits can be secured, hopefully it gives the confidence for the mall to actually allow people to run here.”

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong’s Apec meetings give Beijing a venue to pitch the virtues of its system
item.description:
As Hong Kong hosts the Apec finance ministers’ meeting on Tuesday, this two-part series examines the summit’s significance and its implications for Beijing on the global stage. In part two, Frank Chen explores how the event could help Beijing pitch its philosophies and urge cooperation in digital infrastructure financing.

China’s hosting of this year’s Apec meetings, including a finance ministers’ gathering in Hong Kong, will see a more confident Beijing seek to pitch its economic and financial governance philosophies to other countries, analysts say.

That desire – and ambition – to showcase the feats and experience of the world’s second-largest economy to member nations of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum was bolstered by perceived “inadequacies” in the ability of Western doctrines to address challenges, they added.
item.content:encoded:
As Hong Kong hosts the Apec finance ministers’ meeting on Tuesday, this two-part series examines the summit’s significance and its implications for Beijing on the global stage. In part two, Frank Chen explores how the event could help Beijing pitch its philosophies and urge cooperation in digital infrastructure financing.

China’s hosting of this year’s Apec meetings, including a finance ministers’ gathering in Hong Kong, will see a more confident Beijing seek to pitch its economic and financial governance philosophies to other countries, analysts say.

That desire – and ambition – to showcase the feats and experience of the world’s second-largest economy to member nations of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum was bolstered by perceived “inadequacies” in the ability of Western doctrines to address challenges, they added.

“China has evolved from a participant in global governance to a real architect … Beijing knows the delegates will spend three days in Hong Kong, and a month later leaders will be in Shenzhen. The message is in the setting: come see how this works, come see what we’ve built,” said Zak Dychtwald, founder and CEO of Young China Group, a Shanghai-founded market advisory consultancy.

About 500 guests, including some finance ministers from Apec’s 21 economies, are set to congregate in Hong Kong from Monday to Wednesday. Finance Minister Lan Foan will deliver a keynote address and China will also present a policy statement on enhancing cooperation in digital infrastructure financing across the Asia-Pacific region.

“When some Western governance principles are unravelling and becoming inadequate to resolve economic and financial challenges and as America retreats from its leadership role, China is proposing its visions as a solution to the complexities,” said Wang Yong, a professor at Peking University’s school of international studies. “The hope is that Chinese initiatives can become Apec consensus.”

Dychtwald said China would be deft in peddling its vision.

“Beijing will look to create economic dependencies and continue positioning itself as a reliable partner, which has been a successful policy amid continued unpredictability from America and Europe,” he said.

One indication of China’s effort to lead this year’s discussion and how well Chinese proposals are heeded and adopted will be the finance ministers’ joint statement, the most significant outcome of the gathering.

“Governments in this region are pragmatic. They’ll take the parts of China’s offer that help them and, within the constraints of maintaining a positive relationship, ignore the parts that don’t,” Dychtwald said.

Beijing has set four key themes for talks between financial officials: fiscal policies supporting livelihoods, financing for digital infrastructure, inclusive finance tailored to local conditions and exchange and cooperation among young finance professionals.

China’s finance ministry last week said these topics would address “both immediate priorities and longer-term considerations”.

“Economies across the region now face common tasks of stabilising growth, fighting risks and safeguarding livelihoods,” said a ministry spokesperson, referring to the changes brought about by artificial intelligence. “There is an urgent need to strengthen communication and coordination on macroeconomic policies and to adopt appropriate measures to support innovation.”

The spokesperson called the finance ministers’ meeting one of the most important ministerial exchanges in the Apec grouping – demonstrating the significance Beijing attaches to the Hong Kong event – as it will help “build financial-sector deliverables” for the leaders’ summit next month.

Beijing also aimed to continue to champion values of a multipolar world.

“China stands ready to work with all Apec economies to uphold multilateralism [and] safeguard stability and industrial supply chains for the region’s long-term, sustainable growth,” said the spokesperson.

The conversation that matters most this fall is the one between Washington and Beijing

Zak Dychtwald, Young China Group

In a sign of Beijing’s efforts to back multilateralism and the role of international agencies, representatives from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank and Asian Development Bank would present their global and regional economic and financial outlooks to Apec financial policymakers, according to the meeting agendas.

On Saturday, China’s central bank governor Pan Gongsheng also said in Bangkok that Beijing supported the IMF in boosting the surveillance of fiscal risks in “major advanced economies” and their spillover effects.

Meanwhile, the likely absence of the US’ top finance official might make discussions smoother and give Beijing more room to boost its influence, according to Peking University’s Wang.

The South China Morning Post has reported that US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent may skip Hong Kong to focus on preparations for US President Donald Trump’s visit to Shenzhen and his talk with President Xi Jinping at next month’s Apec leaders’ summit. The two countries aim to secure a more durable trade truce, which is due to expire in January.

Dychtwald said the outlook for a third Trump-Xi summit this year might dominate discussions in Hong Kong.

“Everyone at the finance ministers’ meeting understands that the conversation that matters most this fall is the one between Washington and Beijing, and that one is happening just across the border,” he said.

Dychtwald added that Bessent’s absence could be a reminder that only one superpower was a regional partner.

That said, China’s recent slowdown in gross domestic product growth, with a 4.3 per cent year-on-year rate reported in the second quarter – lower than Beijing’s full-year target of 4.5 to 5 per cent – may draw attention to some issues afflicting the Chinese economy even as Beijing touts the outlook and applicability of its approach.

“China as the host may still face different voices from other countries on certain issues concerning China, like market access, subsidies, transparency, industrial policy, exports and debt, as well as insufficient consumption,” Wang said.

He said the country’s bulging trade surplus, with outbound shipments rising 36.3 per cent year on year to US$447.18 billion last month, might also spark debate at the gathering.

Dychtwald said other countries might seek to use Apec to gain some leverage over China.

“The idea that Beijing wants continued access to export markets, and will work to protect that access, isn’t novel,” he said. “Everyone at Apec knows it. What’s interesting is whether it becomes a bargaining chip for other participants.

“China’s export reliance isn’t going away due to the softness in domestic consumption. I’d expect the smart governments at Apec to use that leverage in the way they work with Beijing.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why is Hong Kong hosting the Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting? There is another agenda
item.description:
As Hong Kong hosts the Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting on Tuesday, this two-part series examines the summit’s significance and its implications for Beijing on the global stage. In part one, Simpson Cheung and Alfred Lam explore how the event could elevate the city’s status as an international financial centre at a pivotal moment.

Beijing’s decision to have Hong Kong host the Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting this week is a deliberate move to galvanise the city’s standing as an offshore renminbi hub and showcase it as a safe harbour amid continuing geopolitical tensions, analysts have said.

About 500 guests, including finance chiefs and senior officials from the 21 member economies, are expected to attend the annual meeting on October 20 and 21, which Hong Kong will host for the first time. It will take place at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai.
item.content:encoded:
As Hong Kong hosts the Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting on Tuesday, this two-part series examines the summit’s significance and its implications for Beijing on the global stage. In part one, Simpson Cheung and Alfred Lam explore how the event could elevate the city’s status as an international financial centre at a pivotal moment.

Beijing’s decision to have Hong Kong host the Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting this week is a deliberate move to galvanise the city’s standing as an offshore renminbi hub and showcase it as a safe harbour amid continuing geopolitical tensions, analysts have said.

About 500 guests, including finance chiefs and senior officials from the 21 member economies, are expected to attend the annual meeting on October 20 and 21, which Hong Kong will host for the first time. It will take place at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai.

Lau Siu-kai, a consultant for the semi-official Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies think tank, said Beijing’s choice of venue showed it deliberately intended to promote Hong Kong’s international status, especially as a financial centre. The event would bolster its standing as an offshore renminbi hub and a wealth management capital, support the city’s economic development and underscore its importance to China’s development, he said.

“The Apec meeting … will allow Hong Kong to present itself to the world in grand style and refute false, negative portrayals by hostile external forces,” he added.

Data from Swift – the Belgium-based cooperative formally known as the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication – showed the city handled about 76 per cent of the world’s renminbi payments as of August. Offshore yuan lending reached a record 935 billion yuan (US$140 billion) last year.

Lau said hosting more international events such as Apec would strengthen the city’s global profile and status, particularly as a gateway to China’s vast economy.

He added that the city’s international image and reputation had suffered considerably since the 2019 anti-government protests, the enactment of the national security law and the negative narratives about Hong Kong purveyed by the West.

Lau said the meeting would bring many key officials, media representatives and businesspeople to China, giving them a chance to see Hong Kong’s robust, growing economy and investment opportunities, particularly in financial services and wealth management.

The theme for Apec this year is “Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together”, with openness, innovation and cooperation identified as the three priorities.

China is hosting the Apec leaders’ meeting for the third time. The summit to be held in Shenzhen in November comes after earlier meetings hosted in Beijing in 2014 and Shanghai in 2001.

Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu told the South China Morning Post in an exclusive interview on Thursday that the finance ministers’ gathering was timely as regional cooperation was increasingly vital given the state of geopolitical tensions around the world.

He said Hong Kong was in the right position to organise the event, a rare occasion that would allow major representatives and finance ministers of the 21 member economies to see first-hand the city’s latest developments such as financial services, information technology and fintech, as well as to enjoy its natural landscape and heritage.

Hui said the 2026 Apec year underlined China’s contribution to regional stability.

China’s Ministry of Finance said on Wednesday that Beijing was willing to work with all Apec economies to stay committed to multilateralism, deepen macroeconomic policy communication and coordination, maintain stable and smooth regional industrial and supply chains, jointly promote the long-term sustainable growth of the Asia-Pacific economy and contribute to building a regional community.

Lee Shu-kam, director of Hong Kong Shue Yan University’s business, economic and public policy research centre, said the city’s role as host would solidify its position as an irreplaceable offshore financing hub for Chinese companies and a buffer against geopolitical tensions as a separate customs territory.

Lee noted that the expiration of the US trade truce with China on January 10 next year and the future direction of tariffs would have a significant impact, creating a period of uncertainty and sensitivity amid the ongoing geopolitical and technological rivalry between the two superpowers.

“If Hong Kong can use this Apec meeting to gather finance ministers from the Asia-Pacific region to reach practical consensus on digital finance, it will prove to the world that even with many changes or potential crises in US-China relations, Hong Kong still has independent political mediation capabilities and can reach consensus with various countries,” he said.

Institutions, including the International Monetary Fund, will give presentations during the meeting. Lee said the continuous and deep engagement of international multilateral institutions, which are extremely strict on compliance and legal risks, could effectively dispel doubts in the West about the rule of law in Hong Kong.

“If major multinational institutions participate in the meeting, give speeches and conduct high-level substantive dialogues in Hong Kong, to a certain extent, it already reflects that Hong Kong’s rule of law and compliance environment are validated,” he said.

“[They] send a very strong signal that Hong Kong’s common law system, contract enforcement capability and commercial arbitration mechanisms still possess complete legal validity and international credibility in multilateral financial cooperation.”

The Apec leaders’ summit will be held in Shenzhen next month. Lee said Hong Kong and Shenzhen would play complementary roles, with Shenzhen positioned as a competitive innovation and technology hub amid the ongoing technological rivalry with the United States, while Hong Kong would handle global capital markets to support mainland China’s continued opening up.

Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po told a programme on Saturday that the Hong Kong meeting would serve as an opportunity for regional decision-makers and enterprise representatives to understand the city on the ground and build mutual trust, rather than just being an international conference.

Chan added that closer cooperation among regional economies was extremely important under the shadow of geopolitics and trade protectionism.

He said the city encouraged enterprises looking to develop their mainland businesses to list and raise capital in Hong Kong.

“Hong Kong’s professional services have a great advantage in this regard, and we can also act as their consultants to open up the mainland market hand in hand with them,” Chan said.

Jeffrey Lam Kin-fung, a member of the key decision-making Executive Council, said he believed the Hong Kong meeting would help attract more foreign investment to the city.

He said he had hosted many foreign businesspeople over the past two years from the West and emerging markets such as the Middle East, and they had shown interest in investing in Hong Kong, as the city’s low taxes, common law system and recent development as an international arbitration centre were attractive to them.

“After visiting Hong Kong, every one of them said they found the city different from what they heard in their hometown,” he said. “They find Hong Kong a stable city, politically, economically and socially. They discovered so many opportunities for future development.”

Lam said he had passed on information to them about the Greater Bay Area, Northern Metropolis and Hung Shui Kiu Industrial Park Company. Lam is the chairman of the company’s board of directors.

Latest government figures showed a record 11,070 companies from the mainland and overseas were operating in Hong Kong last year, an 11 per cent rise year on year.

A drafting session for the finance ministers’ joint statement will take place on Monday, followed by two days of meetings.

Chinese Finance Minister Lan Foan will deliver an opening speech on Tuesday afternoon. Ambassador Chen Xu, who chairs the Apec Senior Officials’ Meeting, will speak about Apec’s priorities for the year.

There will be eight sessions during the two days of meeting. On the first day, there will be three sessions covering the global and regional macroeconomic and financial outlook, fiscal policies supporting households and digital infrastructure financing.

On the second day, another three sessions will cover financial access and opportunities for all, a young financial talents dialogue and the Apec finance ministers’ 2027 process priorities. These will be followed by the signing of the joint statement drafted on Monday. The meeting will end with closing remarks by Lan, followed by a press conference.

China’s Ministry of Finance said on Wednesday that various visits would be arranged for the delegates after the meeting.

“Hong Kong … will fully demonstrate its recent development achievements and urban charm, inviting everyone to jointly experience the diverse vibrancy and growth opportunities of Asia’s World City,” it said.

Additional reporting by Denise Tsang

item.title: [SCMP] Robin Xing on how China’s ‘two-speed’ economy can solve contrasting problems
item.description:
Robin Xing is chief China economist at Morgan Stanley. A famed economist and Peking University graduate, Xing has a PhD in economics from the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and previously worked at Goldman Sachs and China International Capital Corp.

In his second Open Questions interview, Xing dissects China’s K-shaped economic divergence and why he remains convinced that the “top half of the K” can offset challenges such as deflation and weak consumption. He also discusses Beijing’s real priorities, the “fallacy of composition” and why helping consumers will sustain and accelerate China’s tech advance.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.
item.content:encoded:
Robin Xing is chief China economist at Morgan Stanley. A famed economist and Peking University graduate, Xing has a PhD in economics from the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and previously worked at Goldman Sachs and China International Capital Corp.

In his second Open Questions interview, Xing dissects China’s K-shaped economic divergence and why he remains convinced that the “top half of the K” can offset challenges such as deflation and weak consumption. He also discusses Beijing’s real priorities, the “fallacy of composition” and why helping consumers will sustain and accelerate China’s tech advance.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump have met twice and are expected to meet two more times this year. Will the meetings deliver stability in trade, investment and broader economic ties? Can businesses now proceed with their trade and investment plans with greater clarity and confidence? Is the two-month extension of the tariff truce a disappointment?

The successful meetings this year could help steer the US-China relationship towards managed competition: modestly expanding cooperation in non-sensitive areas such as trade, agriculture and other commercially practical sectors, while important strategic differences – particularly around technology and national security – are likely to persist.

Deep economic interdependence gives both sides an incentive to maintain a floor under the relationship and reduces the potential for broader escalation. That should make bilateral ties more predictable, even as de-risking, localisation and restrictions in sensitive areas continue.

We expect the improvement in clarity and confidence to be concentrated in non-sensitive sectors. Recent progress around the Board of Trade, including reciprocal tariff reductions on around US$30 billion of non-sensitive goods, suggests that both sides are willing to offer incremental stability where national-security concerns are less prominent.

However, in technology, critical minerals and other strategically sensitive areas, we believe the broader direction remains towards localisation and tighter controls.

Amid the slowdown, Beijing has rolled out new measures recently, including mortgage loan subsidies and rate reductions. Are they enough? Has Beijing become more tolerant of the slowdown while remaining convinced of long-term prospects?

China is undergoing a challenging economic transformation, as old growth drivers face diminishing returns. Deflation pressures have persisted, and domestic demand remains weak.

But in the meantime, there is a structural transformation taking place in the country towards what we call the Industrial Revolution 5.0.

This transition will require a lot of spending and capital expenditure. We estimate around US$6 trillion factory upgrade investment in areas like robotics, smart machinery, industrial software, power grids and related infrastructure. In addition, we see another US$6 trillion investment being directed towards strategic new capacity. In total, this represents about US$12 trillion in incremental capex over the next 10 years.

China is now in a two-speed, K-shaped economy. The top half of the K is showing some bright spots

The hope is that this decade-long capex supercycle in advanced manufacturing can help offset the drag from deflation and gradually replace old growth drivers like housing and infrastructure investment.

China is now in a two-speed, K-shaped economy. The top half of the K is showing some bright spots in manufacturing, artificial intelligence and in different emerging sectors.

But you also have a huge bottom half of the K: an “old economy” like housing, consumption, a job-intensive services sector and so on. They are now under a cyclical, very painful adjustment.

Beijing has stepped up targeted easing to cushion the downside. This signals a greater willingness to deploy central fiscal resources directly to support housing demand.

Yet, the overall package remains modest, unlikely to reverse confidence-driven household deleveraging due to a weak job market outlook while the existing mortgage rate is still at 3 per cent. There is still the risk of continued pro-cyclical policy tightening amid structurally lower land sales and elevated local government debt.

We thus expect full-year real GDP growth to remain near the lower end of the 4.5 to 5 per cent target range.

So, what is your take on this two-speed, K-shaped economy?

My view is that the top half of the K will be stronger in the future, leading to the next industrial revolution, contributing to US$12 trillion in new capex, and that’s going to be very powerful in offsetting the drag from old sectors.

Housing investment as a share of GDP will decline to only 3 per cent, and the share for traditional infrastructure will also decline to 4 per cent. Industrial capex right now is 17 per cent of GDP. We think it will increase to close to 20 per cent in 10 years.

That being said, 10 years is a very long horizon. For now, we are seeing deflationary pressure lasting longer than expected.

At the end of last year, some observers assessed that China was gradually reflating, with housing prices stabilising and [consumer price index] and [producer price index] showing signs of improvement. They argued that maybe China was ‘out of the woods’. We disagree. China’s deflationary pressure remains quite prolonged.

Another key issue is the ongoing household deleveraging cycle, which began around 2021, when the housing market peaked. Nearly five years on, households are still deleveraging.

Household debt growth has now turned negative, marking the first absolute contraction on record. This suggests that precautionary savings remain very high, with households prioritising debt repayment while the housing sector continues to adjust.

Even though households have not borrowed much in the past five years, the issue is that asset prices have also been falling. In other words, the denominator is shrinking as well. This creates a typical deflation trap: asset prices decline, sometimes faster than households can pay down debt. Thus, household leverage remains relatively high.

People still feel the need, the urgency, to continue to deleverage. Deleveraging, in turn, is bad for consumption.

In this environment, I think a typical approach should be much more aggressive countercyclical central government borrowing: the central government widens the deficit to support consumers and corporates.

But I think policymakers appear to remain cautious about a much larger demand-side stimulus. They likely view a broad consumption transfer as unsustainable, which will not contribute to long-lasting productivity growth.

Instead, the strategic priority remains firmly anchored on the supply side: self-sufficiency, manufacturing resilience, national energy security and related objectives. These remain the real priorities.

That’s why, in my view, the bottom line for near-term policy is that it will likely defend the growth floor, rather than deliver a meaningful consumption or housing-led reflation package.

Deflationary pressure may persist until the housing market finds a structural bottom and until the productivity benefits from AI are more fully unleashed as part of the transition towards a new industrial revolution. Over time, that could contribute to stronger potential GDP growth – but that will take time.

Various government departments have recently made regulatory moves, including controls on cross-border capital flows and taxing offshore products, that have been seen by some as a signal of tightening. What is your view? How do they compare with the curbs seen in 2021?

There are currently two contrasting narratives. The first is that there is growing discussion and hope for another pivot like September 2024: a larger demand-side stimulus package or a “bazooka,” aimed at reflating consumption and stabilising housing prices.

Many argue that such support is needed because the economy is still in deflation, second-quarter GDP fell short of the target and high-frequency data is tracking at a subdued level.

But on the other side, a lot of corporate leaders and foreign investors are asking a very different question: do recent policy moves signal a return to the 2021 playbook – that is, another round of broad-based regulatory tightening?

My answer is “neither”.

The 2021 tightening cycle was unique. It was a proactive, top-down regulatory reset across multiple sectors, including internet and tech, after-school tutoring, property, gaming, healthcare and others. It also took place against a different macro backdrop: China had been first into the initial Covid-19 shock, and among the first to recover from it.

China’s growth was more robust back then. Against that backdrop, policymakers proactively initiated this broad regulatory reset.

Today, however, I do not think what we are seeing is another policy reset. It looks more like stricter enforcement of existing regulations, because the overarching regulatory framework has already been in place for some time.

In a deflationary environment, the housing market remains under adjustment, which means new project launches and land sales are likely to remain weak. At the same time, subdued nominal GDP growth weighs on corporate revenue growth. The result is growing pressure on government revenues from land and corporate value-added tax.

The macro challenge is the “fallacy of composition”. Each micro-level action may be rational on its own – controlling risk, collecting revenue, closing fiscal gaps or maintaining stability. But if many agencies tighten enforcement at the same time, the aggregate effect can become macro tightening.

That is essentially pro-cyclical tightening. This means when the economy is already under deflationary pressure, policy should arguably be moving in the opposite direction: widening the deficit, supporting households and easing pressure on corporates. Instead, we are now seeing pro-cyclical tightening due to micro-level enforcements.
