Pro-cyclical tightening can occur when governments enforce contradictory policies during an economic turndown, which can worsen the slump. What types of enforcement policies are currently in place that may contribute to this effect?

There are three areas of recent enforcement.

First, in housing, the shift from presales towards completed-home sales will slow developers’ asset turnover.

Second, social pension contributions are being tightened. In the past, many small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) contributed based on the minimum salary; but starting this year, they need to contribute based on a higher real wage.

The third is taxation. Tax authorities are now paying closer attention to higher-income individuals. And lastly, some companies that previously benefited from local tax rebates or preferential treatment are also facing tax clawbacks.

Based on our estimate, the tax and social security contribution measures could create a fiscal and cash-flow drag equivalent to around 1 to 2 per cent of GDP. This may not sound large, but in a deflationary environment, the last thing corporates and households need is an additional burden.

In fact, there has been a de facto fiscal consolidation in the last 12 months, with the augmented fiscal deficit narrowing by 2.5 percentage points of GDP.

The bigger issue is confidence. While this could further weaken private-sector sentiment and capex, more broadly, this kind of micro-level tightening runs counter to the need for more proactive reflationary policy.

In September, Beijing unveiled a capital injection of 360 billion yuan (US$53.7 billion) into state-owned banks and insurers. What is your take?

That was already part of the 2024 plan, which widened the deficit for a few purposes: partly to support consumers through trade-in programmes and partly to stabilise the financial system. So this is not new.

The key issue is the trade-off between state-owned financial sector stability and household balance sheet stability.

If we look at other countries, policy has often supported household deleveraging more directly, for example through aggressive rate cuts. In China, however, policymakers appear to have placed greater emphasis on financial-sector stability. As a result, while rates have been lowered, the reduction in household debt-servicing burdens has been more modest than in many other economies.

The trade-off is that household deleveraging may take longer. Households are trying to pay down debt, but their mortgage burdens have not fallen meaningfully, especially as income growth has also slowed.

So the risk is that the harder households try to deleverage, the more demand weakens – reinforcing a classic deflationary trap.

Over the longer run, China needs to address unbalanced growth and weak consumption, which means shifting from a supply-led growth model to a more consumption-driven one.

We believe more aggressive central government fiscal policy is needed – with a larger deficit aimed at supporting demand and consumption

This can be realised by building a stronger social safety net. Better access to public housing, education, healthcare, pensions and unemployment protection would reduce precautionary savings and help unlock household spending.

If China’s priorities remain as technology self-sufficiency, supply chain resilience, energy security and geopolitics, then fiscal and financial resources available to support consumers will be limited.

That said, there is still a great deal China can do to gradually rebalance the economy, but this will take time and the risks of a deflationary trap may need to become more fully recognised.

We believe more aggressive central government fiscal policy is needed – with a larger deficit aimed at supporting demand and consumption.

US government debt continues to breach successive ceilings, triggering significant sell-offs that have driven up borrowing costs. What are the implications? What lessons should China, as a major holder of US Treasuries, draw from these developments?

If we look at how the US uses government borrowing, the majority is on welfare-related spending, including healthcare. By contrast in China, it’s more on capital formation, capex and investment.

These are two very different approaches. In my view, both economies need some form of rebalancing.

For the US, the priority should probably be gradual fiscal consolidation, reducing the deficit over time while redirecting spending towards reinvestment. For China, given its large manufacturing base and extensive infrastructure, fiscal policy may be more effective if it is directed towards consumption, household welfare and social support.

For investors, the near-term uncertainties are clear. There is still debate over the path of US monetary policy, including where the Fed’s terminal rate will settle, as well as how the US government may respond to pressure on Treasury yields.

But my sense is that most global investors still view corporate America as profitable and innovative. While concerns about US government debt exposure may lead to some hedging, confidence in US assets remains broadly intact.

A key reason is fundamentals: US companies continue to be seen as strong, profitable and innovation-driven, which helps support the broader appeal of American assets.

In this part of the world, many still argue that US government debt is too high and without fiscal consolidation, sovereign credit risks could eventually emerge.

When you speak with global investors, the picture is more nuanced. Many may adjust their exposure to US government debt or demand a higher long-term risk premium on Treasuries. Yet they remain broadly confident in corporate America. Thus, there are almost “two Americas”.

China faces a different challenge. Global investors generally view the central government’s fiscal position and the state-owned financial system as quite robust, largely because China has prioritised financial sector resilience, especially the profitability and stability of state-owned financial institutions.

Few investors are seriously concerned about Chinese sovereign risks, systemic financial risk or China’s long-term national competitiveness.

If anything, China’s industrial strength and supply-chain advantages remain clear. The bigger concern is corporate profitability. Foreign investors are less certain whether Chinese companies can deliver sustainable earnings growth.

This is also a challenge for China to attract more foreign capital and FDI. Yes, China’s supply chain advantages and geopolitical competitiveness are all well recognised, but the key question is whether these strengths can be translated into visible, predictable and sustainable improvements in corporate profitability.

The yuan has been on a steady path upwards, despite Beijing reiterating it has neither the need nor the intention for competitive trade advantages through currency depreciation. What is your take?

There are market voices talking up the possibility of further yuan appreciation, with some even predicting significant strengthening in the next few years. Their argument is largely based on China’s trade surplus. Given the sheer scale of that surplus, they argue that the yuan is likely undervalued.

I am not fully convinced. If we look at other East Asian economies, such as Japan and South Korea, large trade surpluses have not automatically translated into sustained currency appreciation.

A trade surplus is just one side of the story. The other side is the capital account. The key question is what happens to the surplus – is it reinvested domestically or deployed offshore in search of better returns?

In the cases of South Korea and Japan, a sizeable portion of their trade surplus has been reinvested overseas – usually in US assets, like bonds or the stock market because their domestic yields are lower than offshore ones.

China is facing a similar challenge. Yes, China does run a large trade surplus, but persistent deflationary pressure means domestic yields and assets remain relatively unattractive. Government bond yields have been hovering below 2 per cent, while the stock market has recovered from two years ago but is largely muddling through.

Against this backdrop, it’s natural that many exporters, after receiving their export proceeds, may prefer to park their funds offshore and invest in overseas assets instead.

If we look at the broader balance-of-payments picture, it does not clearly support the view that the yuan is undervalued.

What would support a much stronger, sustainable yuan appreciation would be a genuine rebalancing of China’s economy, driven by faster and more effective domestic reflation.

When nominal GDP growth recovers, corporate revenue and profit growth should also improve. In turn, bond yield and equity earnings will likely be higher too, making Chinese assets more attractive, which will provide a more durable foundation for yuan strength.

This year, the yuan may even break 6.7 against the US dollar, but we don’t believe China is actively seeking a significantly stronger currency at this stage.

In our previous interview in March 2025, you highlighted “green shoots” in the tech sector. With China’s AI boom and the rise of new players, from robotics to chipmaking, can green shoots evolve into a new growth driver? Can technology alone sustain – or even accelerate – growth?

I think what we’re seeing now is more than just “green shoots”. In a K-shaped economy, the upper arm of the K is becoming stronger, supported by a profound structural transformation taking place underneath the surface of deflation, something we call the Industrial Revolution 5.0.

Historically, there have been four major industrial revolutions: mechanisation; then electrification; then automation; and fourth, digitalisation, which broadly unfolded from the 1970s through the early 2000s.

Now, China may be among the first economies to move meaningfully into a fifth industrial revolution, one enabled by industrial intelligence and the large-scale deployment of physical AI.

This is not limited to humanoid robots. It is about the broader integration of AI-native operating systems into the physical economy – drones, EVs and robotics in different forms.

Right now, China has 8 million such systems deployed across factories, transport and logistics. That number could rise tenfold to roughly 80 million by 2035. This large-scale deployment of next-generation AI in the real economy could help address China’s labour constraints.

China’s population is ageing and shrinking, but the deployment of physical AI may be sufficient to offset much of the resulting labour shortage. That’s the first key enabler; we call it intelligence.

The second enabler is resilience. Under the 15th five-year plan, China is trying to address all key chokepoints across its domestic technology stack, including areas such as semiconductor equipment, industrial design software and very high-end computer numerical control machines.

China is entering this next industrial revolution from an unmatched starting point

China has historically relied on foreign technology in several of these critical areas, and it is now trying to reduce that dependence with localisation.

Finally, there is leadership. China is moving beyond just exporting finished goods assembled domestically to exporting a full-stack industrial ecosystem, including global standards.

Taken together, intelligence, resilience and leadership suggest that China is entering this next industrial revolution from an unmatched starting point.

China already accounts for 28 per cent of global manufacturing value added and the country covers all of the 666 industrial categories and subcategories defined by the United Nations. That breadth gives China extraordinary scale, depth and flexibility across the industrial system.

China also has a large and expanding base of smart manufacturing capacity, including tens of thousands of smart factories supported by 5G and Internet of Things infrastructure. That’s why it can move away from just a factory country to something broader – an industrial operating system for the world.

In conversations with international investors, China’s industrial story is often too quickly dismissed simply as a narrative of overcapacity, low margins or even trade war-induced decline.

These narratives do not fully capture what is happening. We believe a more important story lies in what’s coming next: China transitioning from being the world’s factory to the world’s industrial operating system.

This could help China address key chokepoints across supply chains. This is also a story about leadership.

A lot of sectors could benefit, such as industrial automation, semiconductor equipment, robotics components, industrial ecosystem software and so on.

If China can accelerate this technology revolution while adopting a more effective approach to economic rebalancing, for example, by using government financial resources to support consumption and welfare, its growth model could become much more sustainable.

Importantly, the capex cycle associated with embodied AI does not have to be value-destructive. It could drive fundamental improvements in productivity, margins and potential GDP growth, creating a more durable foundation for long-term economic expansion.

Through deeper reform and rebalancing, China could also break the deflation trap, which in turn will reinforce its technological progress. Stronger domestic demand is essential because firms need the ability to sell products and services at healthy prices in the home market.

Ultimately, China would benefit from a demand-driven ecosystem, one that gives companies the confidence to invest, hire and spend more on research and development. If policymakers continue to deepen their understanding of this dynamic and deliver the reforms required, China’s Industrial Revolution 5.0 could become not only a technological transformation, but also a more sustainable growth model.

item.title: [SCMP] Does Singapore’s tougher stance on haze mark an inflection point?
item.description:
Singapore has warned it will go after companies responsible for the forest fires in Indonesia causing the regional haze, but cross-border challenges remain stumbling blocks to solving a problem that has plagued the city state for decades.

Analysts point to long-standing obstacles hampering the country’s decade-old haze legislation, such as complex corporate ownership and opaque transboundary supply chains. To date, no company has been prosecuted under the law.

Beyond legal threats, greater accountability is needed from corporate boards and investors, observers add. The renewed push has reignited tensions over state ownership, with a former Indonesian minister challenging Singapore to take hard action against companies with business links to the city state.
item.content:encoded:
Singapore has warned it will go after companies responsible for the forest fires in Indonesia causing the regional haze, but cross-border challenges remain stumbling blocks to solving a problem that has plagued the city state for decades.

Analysts point to long-standing obstacles hampering the country’s decade-old haze legislation, such as complex corporate ownership and opaque transboundary supply chains. To date, no company has been prosecuted under the law.

Beyond legal threats, greater accountability is needed from corporate boards and investors, observers add. The renewed push has reignited tensions over state ownership, with a former Indonesian minister challenging Singapore to take hard action against companies with business links to the city state.

On Monday, Singapore’s Coordinating Minister for National Security K. Shanmugam told local media the country would use “every legal and regulatory lever” at its disposal to “exert pressure where it matters – including on [companies’] bottom lines, including on their access to financing, and including on their standing with investors”.

Shanmugam, who is also home affairs minister, said the city state would change or introduce laws on an urgent basis to ensure further cooperation.

“Companies cannot claim to be environmentally responsible while refusing to subject themselves to scrutiny. Their claims must be backed by evidence, not just words. They cannot greenwash their behaviour,” he said.

Companies would not be able to simply wait for the haze to clear and return to business as usual, he added. “We will pursue this matter for as long as it takes.”

As of Monday, Singapore sent notices under its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act (THPA) to 10 companies with plantations in South Sumatra and Kalimantan.

Felicia Liu, a senior lecturer in sustainability at the University of York, called the issuance a “significant step”, but said “the real test is whether this translates into meaningful investigations and enforcement where accountability can be established”.

THPA, which came into force in 2014, allows authorities in Singapore to hold companies responsible for causing or contributing to haze pollution in the city state even if the activities take place overseas.

It allows the state to require a person to provide documents or information, and can issue preventive notices. Citizens or businesses badly affected by the haze can also hold the haze-linked companies to account under the Act. If found guilty, firms can be fined up to S$100,000 (US$78,245) a day, capped at a total of S$2 million.

But an increasingly complex structural setting and the ambiguity of accountability made it fundamentally difficult for Singapore to take action, said Lawrence Loh, director of the Centre for Governance and Sustainability at the National University of Singapore Business School.

“Responsibility attribution is made even more difficult when there are subsidiaries, special-purpose vehicles, nominee ownerships, joint ventures and independent suppliers,” he said.

No company has been fined or sued under the law. In 2015, Singapore issued notices to six companies under THPA and subsequently closed two cases. In response to queries, the National Environment Agency said investigations into four companies – Bumi Andalas Permai, Bumi Mekar Hijau, Sebangun Bumi Andalas Woods Industries and Rimba Hutani Mas – remained ongoing.

Tan-Soo Jie-Sheng, director of the Institute for Environment and Sustainability at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, underscored Singapore’s inherent limitations in tackling the haze due to its cross-border nature. “Even within national boundaries, pollution crossing state or provincial borders can be difficult to address,” he said.

Other challenges include identifying forest fires, the companies behind them, and establishing that pollutants from the blazes contributed to the haze in Singapore, he said. “Quantifying the damages attributable to each company introduces further complexity.”

Loh said it was challenging to implement the THPA, acknowledging that it was hard to gather evidence across borders. “It is even more difficult to enforce the law as external parties in other countries cannot control investigations and legal processes in the country where forest-burning occurs,” he said.

Shanmugam said in his press conference that manufacturing giant Asia Pulp and Paper (APP) bought from three of the companies that received notices.

This Week in Asia has contacted APP for comment.

The minister also noted that some of the fires or smoke-source points seemed to be associated with Singapore-listed palm oil producers First Resources and Bumitama Agri, and First Borneo Plantations, and said authorities would be asking more questions of these companies.

Former Indonesian trade minister Muhammad Lutfi addressed Singapore leaders in a social media post on Tuesday, saying: “Don’t write letters just to make your constituents and voters happy.”

He noted that of the seven companies listed, Bumi Andalas Permai, Bumi Mekar Hijau, SBA Wood Industries and Bangkanesia were “suppliers to conglomerate groups with massive corporate holdings and listings” in Singapore and urged authorities to take action against those with offices in the city state.

“Singapore has no jurisdiction in Indonesia, and you know it. So, if you truly believe you have jurisdiction over these groups, then just charge them. No need to threaten and announce at a press conference. Prosecute their headquarters in Singapore and show us what Singapore is really made of,” Lutfi said.

His remarks struck a nerve among Singaporean social media users, with many accusing him of shirking responsibility and pushing blame to the city state.

Calvin Cheng, a former Singapore nominated member of parliament, fired back on social media that Indonesia was “turning the narrative” onto Singapore. “Indonesia officials use Singapore as the bogeyman whenever something bad happens.”

Loh said the perennial problem was less a policy inadequacy than a failure in business incentive and corporate governance.

“Boards of directors and senior management must play critical roles beyond passive oversight,” he said. “Statements are not enough and they do not absolve the companies from responsibility in the forest burning and haze situation.”

Liu said while Singapore’s individual efforts were not sufficient to solve the systemic crisis, it had an “important opportunity” to lead in corporate environmental accountability.

“The Transboundary Haze Pollution Act alone will not improve accountability in the agroforestry sector overnight,” she said.

“Singapore’s financial sector must also step up on its demands for disclosure and accountability in investment chains to ensure that Singapore, as the region’s financial hub, is not bankrolling haze.”

item.title: [SCMP] For Filipinos, virtual assistant trumps doctor as ‘dream job’. But what’s the reality?
item.description:
When Mark Ifurung left his 18-year career as an IT professional in May, he was happy to ditch his two-hour commutes from his home in Cavite province south of Manila to his office in Makati City.

So for his fresh start, the 40-year-old father of four wanted something that would allow him to work from home. “After being unemployed for five months, I decided to explore freelancing,” he said. “With my background in IT operations and application support, I realised I already have transferable skills that I can offer to clients.”

While job hunting online, he came across information on the “virtual assistant” industry and was lured by the idea of flexibility and attractive pay.
item.content:encoded:
When Mark Ifurung left his 18-year career as an IT professional in May, he was happy to ditch his two-hour commutes from his home in Cavite province south of Manila to his office in Makati City.

So for his fresh start, the 40-year-old father of four wanted something that would allow him to work from home. “After being unemployed for five months, I decided to explore freelancing,” he said. “With my background in IT operations and application support, I realised I already have transferable skills that I can offer to clients.”

While job hunting online, he came across information on the “virtual assistant” industry and was lured by the idea of flexibility and attractive pay.

Ifurung is one of a growing number of Filipinos gravitating to virtual assistant work, a booming sector of the Philippines’ offshore labour industry that has steadily risen post-pandemic.

Virtual assistants provide administrative, technical or creative services to businesses and individuals, often overseas. Unlike traditional office workers, they typically work from home and may serve multiple clients on a freelance basis – handling tasks ranging from scheduling and customer support to social media management and IT services.

VA Masters, a virtual assistant placement agency, estimates there are more than 1 million virtual assistants in the Philippines. Filipinos make up about 38 per cent of the global market, often for clients and companies based in the US, the UK and Australia, according to the agency’s estimates.

A survey based on online job searches from May 2025 to May 2026 by remittance agency Remitly found that the role is now the top “dream job” among Filipinos, overtaking doctors.

“Virtual work in the Philippines is a fast-rising source of employment for Filipinos,” said Verna Dinah Viajar, an assistant professor at the University of the Philippines School of Labour and Industrial Relations.

Viajar said virtual assistant work had attracted Filipinos branching out from the business process outsourcing sector, after AI replaced many tasks in IT and communication such as call centres. “With adequate skills in IT communications, many [business process outsourcing] workers have shifted to VAs,” she said.

Work from home, earn abroad

Many virtual assistants in the Philippines are independent contractors who are not tied full time to a particular employer. This allows them to take on several clients at once and increase their income potential.

Erica Marie Ebrona, 29, manages seven clients from her home in Dumaguete City in central Philippines. “I work as a social media and content strategist, handling content planning, captions, strategy and analytics. I have flexible hours, so I can choose when I work as long as I meet deadlines,” she said.

Ebrona started as a virtual assistant in 2023, transitioning from human resources, and earned her first client through a referral.

While her monthly income varies, she earns at least 100,000 pesos (US$1,580) a month – over five times the minimum wage in Metro Manila. Virtual assistant work, she said, “offers flexibility and opportunities to work with international clients”.

Phu Huynh, a labour analyst for the International Labour Organization (ILO), said the strong interest in virtual assistant work “reflects the appeal of relatively accessible remote work that can connect Filipinos directly to international clients and potentially higher earnings without having to migrate abroad”.

A young, digitally connected, and English-speaking workforce made the Philippines an attractive location for outsourced labour – but did not necessarily guarantee decent working conditions, he added.

The industry’s unregulated nature leaves many workers open to abuse, according to experts. Most have no contracts, no social protection benefits, and are vulnerable to health issues due to working in different time zones. This lack of regulation could make some assistants “work like slaves in the cyberworld”, Viajar said.

Their geographical location also means they do not have redress from the head office. “Being in remote work, it is difficult to follow up work grievances, and their isolated work formats … robs them of the opportunity to exercise their rights as workers,” she said.

Most people are drawn to virtual assistant work because of “the prospect of building a better livelihood while remaining connected to their families and communities”, according to Alistair Mercado, CEO and founder of Kasama Connect, a technology platform focused on transparent agreements, payments and accountability for remote work.

But the dream should not stop there, he added. “It should include getting paid reliably, developing expertise and having a meaningful say in the terms of your work.”

To protect independent contractors, “we need to stop treating ‘be careful’ as a worker-protection system”, he said. “Professionals have responsibilities, but clients, platforms, intermediaries and government have responsibilities too.”

AI intervention

Artificial intelligence is another challenge to the industry.

“[The] work is exposed to AI because many routine tasks such as scheduling, data entry, drafting and basic customer support can increasingly be automated through AI technologies,” Huynh said. “However, ILO research suggests AI is more likely to transform many jobs than eliminate them entirely.”

Virtual assistant roles may shift towards more complex tasks requiring judgment, problem solving, managing client relationships and the ability to use AI effectively, he said. “The challenge will be ensuring workers are well equipped with these complementary skills.”

Viajar said that AI has become a necessity for virtual assistants. “AI can easily replace tasks that are repetitive but if the work still requires human cognitive abilities, AI becomes a tool for higher productivity and precision work,” she said.

Virtual assistant Dani Gregorio, 25, does not see AI fully replacing her job just yet.

“I can definitely see why people are worried. We’ve already seen how AI is changing the way different industries operate, and some roles … are being automated or reduced,” she said.

“But I also think we need to look at what AI can actually replace and what it can’t fully replicate … You can automate certain processes, but managing people, building trust, understanding human behaviour, and making decisions that consider the bigger picture require more than simply generating an answer. Emotional intelligence and accountability matter, too.”

Not everyone would have such skills – “and that’s OK”, Gregorio said. “We shouldn’t romanticise one kind of work just because it looks good on social media.”

item.title: [SCMP] Brazil’s family farming backbone embraces Chinese AI to reverse vital sector’s decline
item.description:
The family farmers who produce the lion’s share of Brazil’s staple foods are opening their arms to cutting-edge Chinese artificial intelligence in a bid to modernise operations and secure their future.

Brazil and China agreed to a five-year cooperation programme in September aimed at giving smallholders – the backbone of the Brazilian agricultural sector – an AI boost after a decade of declining employment and limited access to affordable technology.

Representatives of the Brazilian Agricultural Research Corporation (Embrapa) and four Chinese institutions signed the memorandum of understanding in Nanjing, capital of Jiangsu province.
item.content:encoded:
The family farmers who produce the lion’s share of Brazil’s staple foods are opening their arms to cutting-edge Chinese artificial intelligence in a bid to modernise operations and secure their future.

Brazil and China agreed to a five-year cooperation programme in September aimed at giving smallholders – the backbone of the Brazilian agricultural sector – an AI boost after a decade of declining employment and limited access to affordable technology.

Representatives of the Brazilian Agricultural Research Corporation (Embrapa) and four Chinese institutions signed the memorandum of understanding in Nanjing, capital of Jiangsu province.

The Chinese parties were the state-owned Sinomach Digital Technology Corporation, Nanjing Agricultural University, the Jiangsu Academy of Agricultural Sciences and the International Association for People’s Cooperation.

The agreement includes the establishment of the Brazil-China Cooperation Centre for the Application of AI in Agriculture, aimed at strengthening this key sector of the Brazilian economy by developing new technologies and tools.

“The idea is to combine complementary skills from both countries … to develop and adapt technologies to Brazilian production, social, and environmental conditions,” said Luciana Romani, a researcher at Embrapa Digital Agriculture.

According to Romani, these complementary skills include “agronomic knowledge, artificial intelligence, computer vision, automation and smart agricultural machinery”.

The World Bank has reported that family farming accounts for around 77 per cent of Brazil’s five million rural establishments, producing 87 per cent of the country’s cassava and 70 per cent of its beans – a foundational and essential staple of the Brazilian diet.

Family farms are also responsible for 60 per cent of Brazil’s milk, half of its poultry and 34 per cent of its rice.

In its 2017 census of agriculture, the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics (IBGE) found that family farms employed around 10.1 million people – 67 per cent of the agricultural workforce and around 5 per cent of the total population.

Cristhiane Amancio, general head of Embrapa Agrobiology, said “an important milestone is expanding access to digital technologies that reduce arduous labour in the production of healthy and sustainable food. That is an important step to help keep workers in rural areas as well.”

Under the agreement, Smart Agricultural Machinery Centres will be established in pilot family farming areas of Brazil where small and medium-sized machines, sensors, Internet of Things devices and AI will support crop monitoring and management.

“The technologies integrated into agricultural machinery have evolved significantly in recent years and are being adopted in Brazil,” said Jayme Barbedo, another researcher at Embrapa Digital Agriculture.

However, he noted that in many cases “those machines are too expensive or have dimensions that do not suit the conditions found in family farming”.

According to Romani, China and Brazil will work together “to identify needs, develop technology and validate artificial intelligence solutions and other digital technologies aimed at family farming”.

However, the Chinese technologies identified as offering potential applications in Brazil were developed for specific agricultural conditions and must be proven, tested and adapted to Brazil’s diverse production systems and local environments, she said.

Amancio added that Sinomach in particular “has an integrated platform that supports decision-making at different management levels, adding value for both farmers and managers within associations, cooperative unions or in the public sector”.

Romani also highlighted the expertise of the Brazilian research team in artificial intelligence, computer vision and automation, which will be essential to testing and adapting the technologies to local conditions in Brazil.

The initial phase is expected to include an assessment of equipment and systems already being tested at the Brazil-China Centre of the University of Brasilia, alongside technical exchanges with Chinese researchers.

Romani said potential applications included “artificial intelligence-based systems for pest and disease diagnosis, crop monitoring, decision-making support, more efficient use of inputs and natural resources, as well as the integration of those tools with smart agricultural machinery and equipment”.

The history and tradition of China in developing technologies for smallholders and medium-scale farmers, together with its advances in automation and robotics, were an important factor in choosing Chinese partners for the project, she said.

“This knowledge complements what has been developed in Brazil and fits very well with the current needs of smallholders and midscale farmers.”

The researchers said the cooperation was intended to go beyond technology transfer, establishing a continuing process of joint development, adaptation, validation and knowledge exchange to deliver practical solutions for family farming.

According to Barbedo, the use of AI does not represent a new model of farming. Instead, it will “play a central role as a tool to support decision-making, automation and the adaptation of technologies to real family farming conditions”.

By combining data from sensors, machines and other digital tools, these technologies could be used to interpret, identify patterns, optimise resources, support the diagnosis of agricultural problems and improve the use of inputs and natural resources, he said.

“Artificial intelligence should not be seen as an end in itself, nor as a substitute for agronomic knowledge and the experience of farmers, but as a technology that can expand such capabilities.”

According to Barbedo, the project will focus mainly on adapting existing AI models rather than developing new ones. The researchers will need to account for Brazil’s diverse production systems, crops, environmental conditions and producer profiles.

“Consistent data collection, adjustment, testing and validation efforts will be essential, ensuring that each developed solution is reliable and suitable for real-world use,” he said.

Romani added: “The project aims to transform advances in AI and automation into concrete, affordable and reliable tools with the potential to increase efficiency, reduce costs, improve sustainability and expand the management capacity of smallholders and midscale farmers.”

The project will also need to consider how to make these technologies affordable. “One possible approach is the involvement of farmers’ associations and cooperative unions to allow for quicker adoption,” Barbedo said.

Silvia Massruha, Embrapa president, said that “if we don’t digitally include smallholders and midscale farmers in family agriculture, the gap between them and large-scale farmers will grow”.

Family farming in Brazil declined by 9.5 per cent between 2006 and 2017, according to the IBGE, while employment in the sector decreased by around 2.2 million people. Over the same period, employment in non-family farming increased by around 703,000.

Embrapa Agrobiology’s Amancio highlighted the importance of South-South scientific and technological cooperation in strengthening national capabilities and autonomy as well as supporting economic and social development.

The cooperation is also expected to include scientific and technical exchange, training and capacity-building activities, such as giving Chinese scientists the opportunity to learn more about the Brazilian Agricultural Research Corporation’s experience, while gaining a better understanding of the sociocultural conditions of family farming.

“Raising awareness of the importance of investing in science and technology to promote national development is fundamental so that partnerships like this one can increasingly qualify Brazilian scientists and strengthen both the national industrial and agricultural sectors,” Amancio said.

Passionate about science? Dive deeper with the Dark Matters newsletter, a weekly in-depth analysis on China’s rise in science, technology and military that goes beneath the surface. Sign up for free now.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong touts key advantages over London in bid to become global gold hub
item.description:
Distinctive features will set Hong Kong apart from London, a major bullion hub, as the city accelerates efforts to develop an international gold and precious metals trading ecosystem covering the entire value chain, a minister has told the South China Morning Post.

item.content:encoded:
Distinctive features will set Hong Kong apart from London, a major bullion hub, as the city accelerates efforts to develop an international gold and precious metals trading ecosystem covering the entire value chain, a minister has told the South China Morning Post.

In an exclusive interview on Thursday, Secretary for Financial Services and the Treasury Christopher Hui Ching-yu said the city would officially launch a central gold clearing platform in the first quarter of next year. It would handle both physical delivery and payments, with the latter linked to the real-time gross settlement system.

Hui said the ultimate aim was to connect regional liquidity with international market standards, giving participants a venue in the Asian time zone for trading, storage, clearing, refining and risk management.

“We are confident [of] achieving [this] because in the Asia time zone, we see Hong Kong as uniquely positioned to do that,” he said.

In the wide-ranging interview, Hui also discussed the city’s efforts to promote the international use of the yuan, the development of China’s digital currency, the e-CNY, and next week’s Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting in Hong Kong.

Asked about the Saudi Central Bank’s departure from mBridge – a China-led multilateral central bank digital currency platform seen as an alternative to the traditional US dollar-dominated payments system – Hui said the project would still press ahead.

The Saudi Central Bank, a key participant, confirmed last month that it had left the project after completing what it described as a limited proof-of-concept trial in May last year.

“Fundamentally, what we try to do is, through Hong Kong, at the same time through these measures, to engage different players across the industry in such a way that they can work on some live cases or new cases to test out this technology,” Hui said.

“So technology as it is, people still see the benefit. At the same time, what Hong Kong should do is continue contributing our expertise and also our relevance here.”

Hong Kong is a founding member and co-developer of mBridge.

The city is also accelerating the development of its gold trading ecosystem as a key part of its first five-year plan, which runs to 2030. The initiative is intended to support the development of mainland China’s gold economy, which boasts the world’s largest domestic production and consumption of the precious metal.

Hui said that government ownership and backing, integrated delivery-versus-payment settlement and cooperation with Shanghai would distinguish Hong Kong’s offering. The cross-border cooperation would allow eligible gold stored in the city to be used to settle trades in both markets.

Asked about competition with Singapore as a regional gold trading hub, Hui said Hong Kong was focused on improving its own performance.

“What Hong Kong tries to do is always to compete against ourselves, because fundamentally we have to focus on areas that are within our control,” he said.

The minister expressed confidence in Hong Kong’s competitive advantages.

“What sets a global commodities market [apart] from the other markets is that it is really a market that is not just about financials but also close to the real economy,” he said.

“It has to be about also storage, about logistics, and also, at the same time, about trading, of course. And also when it comes to disputes, there could also be some legal issues.

“So actually, it’s a whole value chain in terms of the potential composition of this industry association to be set up before the end of this year.”

Hui added that following a trial in July, the system with integrated delivery-versus-payment settlement service was due to launch officially in the first quarter of next year.

“The clearing system now in the UK is run by the London Bullion Market Association, which is an industry association,” he said. “But the clearing house in Hong Kong is owned and run by the government. So I think this government backing sets us apart in terms of credibility.

“Another thing that is different between Hong Kong and London in that context is the fact that our current system will not just do physical delivery but also money settlement.”

Hui said 11 banks were already taking part in the payment settlement arrangements and others had expressed strong interest in joining, adding that the city would discuss cooperation on delivery standards with the London association.

Hui, who chairs the board overseeing the clearing facility, said a representative of the Shanghai bourse served as deputy chair. Under the cross-border delivery connect arrangement, physical gold stored in certified Hong Kong vaults can be used to settle contracts traded in the local market and on Shanghai’s international board.

“If there is gold that is going to satisfy both the settlement in the Hong Kong contract and the Shanghai contract, they can use the vaults in Hong Kong, catering for both the Hong Kong market and the Shanghai market to do that,” he said. “It is an area that is uniquely Hong Kong.”

He added that the government was aiming to increase Hong Kong’s gold storage capacity to more than 2,000 tonnes within three years, with half at the airport and the remainder expected to come from the private sector.

Some gold refineries have also been established in the city.

Asked how Hong Kong could help the mainland gain greater influence over gold pricing, Hui said this would come once the city had attracted enough market participants and built sufficient liquidity.

“I see pricing more as an outcome, in the sense that once we build up a sufficient liquidity, [and] at the same time a quantum of gold here ... it will eventually come,” he said, stressing the importance of creating a critical mass of market participants.

On products, Hui highlighted the relaunch of a US dollar-denominated gold futures contract and said details of a yuan-denominated contract would be announced before the end of this year.

With this work under way, Hui hoped to share the latest developments in Hong Kong’s gold trading ecosystem when the city hosted the London Bullion Market Association Asia Forum in April next year.

Reflecting on this month’s conference in Sorrento, Italy, which he attended, he said industry stakeholders had responded positively to Hong Kong’s plans.

“First of all, they are quite impressed in terms of the timeliness of this project, in a sense that in this world of changing geopolitics,” he said, adding that they were also impressed with the city’s ecosystem approach, its “concrete” plans and “Hong Kong speed”.

Hui said the initiative had progressed rapidly since its announcement in the October 2024 policy address.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong aims for share of HK$350 billion yacht industry as travel scheme launches
item.description:
Hong Kong can capture a share of the global yacht industry, which is expected to reach HK$350 billion (US$44.6 billion) in six years, a senior official has said as the city launched a scheme to welcome leisure vessels from mainland China.

Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan also announced fresh measures to attract overseas captains and draw superyachts to the city on Friday.

The new Southbound Travel for Yachts from Guangdong scheme is part of the government’s broader plan to develop Hong Kong’s yacht economy, as outlined in the city’s first five-year plan and the latest annual policy address.
item.content:encoded:
Hong Kong can capture a share of the global yacht industry, which is expected to reach HK$350 billion (US$44.6 billion) in six years, a senior official has said as the city launched a scheme to welcome leisure vessels from mainland China.

Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan also announced fresh measures to attract overseas captains and draw superyachts to the city on Friday.

The new Southbound Travel for Yachts from Guangdong scheme is part of the government’s broader plan to develop Hong Kong’s yacht economy, as outlined in the city’s first five-year plan and the latest annual policy address.

Under the scheme, mainland vessels can register through the Marine Department’s Electronic Business System to sail in Hong Kong waters.

Speaking at the launch ceremony, Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong Wai-lun said the global yacht market was expected to reach HK$350 billion by 2032 and that Hong Kong could capture a slice of the market.

He noted that there were about 6,000 superyachts in the world exceeding 30 metres (98.4 feet). More than 90 of them were in Hong Kong and the government planned to roll out more measures to boost the yacht economy.

“The outline of the national 15th five-year plan clearly calls for developing leisure consumption such as cruises and yachts, and Hong Kong’s first five-year plan also stated that we will actively develop it,” he said.

“Our vision for the yacht economy also reflects the global trend.”

Wong said they are also pushing to build four new yacht clubs at the airport, Lamma Island, Aberdeen and Hung Hom, which would provide more than 1,100 berths.

The new yacht clubs would also have four “very attractive” clubhouses to improve and complete the infrastructure and ecosystem of the city’s yacht economy, he added.

Wong also revealed that three of the five registered vessels were from Shenzhen, one was from Zhuhai and one from Guangzhou’s Nansha.

The five vessels all moored at facilities in Discovery Bay provided by Lantau Yacht Club, which organised the launch ceremony.

Transport minister Chan also said the Marine Department would coordinate with local training institutions to offer online courses for overseas captains, with the aim of turning the city into a hub for superyachts.

Chan said the five yachts had varied itineraries, including sea tours and visits to urban areas, and that many of their passengers had booked hotels for stays of three to four days, reflecting “a new model of high-end tourism consumption”.

Director of Marine Wong Sai-fat said on Thursday that 23 individuals or groups had registered under the new travel scheme as of this week.

Max Teng, secretary general of the Shenzhen Boating Industry Association, was one of the five mainland yacht owners arriving on the first day.

He said he came to Hong Kong specifically for an “ice-breaking journey to witness the historic moment”, and would stay only one night in the city.

Teng was cautious, however, about his willingness to return. “Just the cost this time, not counting fuel, we already spent up to HK$40,000,” he said.

Entry and exit clearance fees were 14,500 yuan, he said, which included a processing fee of 2,000 yuan per trip, port berthing fee of 2,000 yuan per hour and customs declaration fee of 1,000 yuan per vessel.

He praised the smooth application through the official system, although he said some technical details still needed work.

“There are some things that don’t quite match, for example, the shore power interfaces,” he said.

“Freedom of navigation is the most important thing for mainland yacht owners.

“Many mainland businessmen buy boats and register companies in Hong Kong for its international endorsement and tax incentives.”

Teng said that he saw the scheme boosting Hong Kong’s yacht trading and benefiting nearby cities such as Shenzhen.

Another Shenzhen yacht owner, surnamed Sheng, said he had come to Hong Kong with several friends for a three-day free and easy trip, and planned to shop in Central and Tsim Sha Tsui.

“Shenzhen is very close to Hong Kong. Now that the government has made the process more automated and standardised, the more convenient it becomes, the more willing we are to come,” he said.

“If this scheme had come into effect before National Day, we might have stayed a couple more days – during holidays the roads are congested, but the sea is not.”

Sheng added that he would be more interested in sailing his yacht to Victoria Harbour to watch the fireworks during holidays.

Franklin Mak, executive vice-president of hospitality at HKR International, the developer behind the Lantau Yacht Club, welcomed the “long-anticipated” scheme, saying the club had prepared for more mainland yachts coming to Hong Kong since 2019.

“We have special rates for our berths, and we purposely reserve space for people who come in on a transient basis, so we can accommodate yachts, unlike other yacht clubs that usually sell all that space to long-term owners,” he said.

Apart from berthing, the club also offers both long- and short-term service package discounts, including hotel accommodation and golf sessions, which are more cost-effective than a long-term membership.

Mak also noted that 10 mainland yachts had registered for the Lantau Yacht Club Boat Show early next month and would start arriving from next week. They represented the largest number in years, up from just two or three previously.

David Norton, commodore of the Royal Hong Kong Yacht Club, said one boat from Zhuhai was set to spend the night at its Causeway Bay headquarters on Friday.

Acknowledging that the club was quite full and could only offer berthing and hospitality on a case-by-case basis, Norton stressed the demand was real.

“There is a big demand in mainland China for participation in water sports, 60 per cent of entries in Hong Kong Race Week at the beginning of the year came from the mainland,” he said, adding he was excited to see if the scheme could bring more mainland entries to water sports events in Hong Kong.

Five designated berthing areas at Tai O, Repulse Bay, Tai Tam Bay, Stanley Bay and Three Fathoms Cove in Sai Kung will provide 115 berths, in addition to those at private yacht clubs.

There are also seven kiosks supplying water to vessels and eight designated bunkering areas, according to the Water Supplies Department and the Marine Department.

While saying the five anchorage areas were well located, Norton noted “there is a lack of facilities” around the areas.

“It’s very hard to get water and find someone to dump some trash or empty the tanks from the toilet,” he said.

He also added that tourists needed an easy way ashore: “They need a landing station, or maybe a water taxi service that will get them on and off the boat. So that’s what’s missing.”

Lawmaker Roy Chu Lap-wai described the registration of five yachts on the first day as “encouraging”.

“In the initial stage, I believe the five yachts that come here will go back and spread the word about how convenient and good Hong Kong is, if everything goes smoothly,” he told a radio programme.

Chu said Hong Kong had many distinctive islands for visiting yachts to explore. He hoped tourists would go island-hopping during the day, then dine and shop in urban areas at night.

“The government also held many successful big events regularly, and they could get more involved in different aspects, so these relatively high-end, big-spending yacht tourists can really spend more money in Hong Kong and contribute to our economy,” he said.

Chu said the city could also develop a “one-day tour” and other services, such as chauffeur-driven cars with professional guides, adding that the Tourism Board could do more to promote these offerings and increase the economic benefits.

item.title: [SCMP] Huang Qifan, China’s political tumbler, falls after a decade of close corruption calls
item.description:
For a decade, former Chongqing mayor Huang Qifan stood out as a political survivor while colleague after close colleague fell in China’s far-reaching anti-corruption campaign.

Throughout that time, including his seven years as the megacity’s mayor from 2009 to 2016, Huang was seen as a “tumbler” in Chinese politics – a weighted doll that wobbles but never falls over.

The nickname was well-deserved – he served under six municipal Communist Party secretaries, watching two of them – Bo Xilai and Sun Zhengcai – jailed for corruption.
item.content:encoded:
For a decade, former Chongqing mayor Huang Qifan stood out as a political survivor while colleague after close colleague fell in China’s far-reaching anti-corruption campaign.

Throughout that time, including his seven years as the megacity’s mayor from 2009 to 2016, Huang was seen as a “tumbler” in Chinese politics – a weighted doll that wobbles but never falls over.

The nickname was well-deserved – he served under six municipal Communist Party secretaries, watching two of them – Bo Xilai and Sun Zhengcai – jailed for corruption.

Bo and Sun were both members of the Politburo, the pinnacle of the party’s power, and their downfalls were two of the biggest political earthquakes the country has seen in recent decades. Yet Huang survived.

Huang, 74, was also very visible after he left public service in 2018. Rather than retreat to retired obscurity, Huang kept up a busy schedule of interviews and conferences across the country, firing hot takes on China’s economic issues.

So when news of the corruption investigation into Huang finally came on Tuesday, it was a surprise to many – not only because it involved one of China’s most celebrated economic technocrats, but also because it came so long after the political tremors around him appeared to have stopped.

“Subjecting someone like Huang, who had emerged from many previous rounds, to a formal corruption investigation, before the fifth plenum sends a very serious message to the whole party: corrupt officials should not harbour any illusions of escaping detection,” said a Beijing-based political scientist, who declined to be named due to sensitivity of the matter.

“There is no political ‘tumbler’ and no safe landing for corrupt officials in the anti-corruption fight.”

The fifth plenum is a party meeting scheduled for October 26-29 in Beijing at which the organisation’s inner circle will discuss and adopt a landmark document to “deepening party self-governance”.

The event is expected to focus on tackling systemic corruption, tightening internal political oversight, and eliminating organisational loopholes across the bureaucracy and state sectors.

While many anti-corruption investigations into retired senior officials go unnoticed and unannounced, Huang’s unusually heavy speaking schedule made his downfall difficult to hide from the public.

The South China Morning Post understands that Huang was originally scheduled to deliver a keynote speech in Beijing on October 25 and another in Hangzhou the next day.

Before Tuesday’s announcement, word got out that he would miss the Hangzhou event. An employee at AIA Group – the organiser of the October 25 speech in Beijing – said they had not been able to reach Huang or his secretary since Monday.

Huang’s reputation as a tumbler goes back to his relationship with Bo, the charismatic and swashbuckling Politburo member who ran Chongqing from 2007 to 2012.

As Bo rolled out his ideologically charged “singing red songs and smashing the dark forces” campaign, Huang was the administrative and economic brain behind the policies that became known as the “Chongqing model”.

The model combines state-led capitalism, aggressive public-welfare provision, and foreign direct investment with a populist revival of revolutionary Maoist culture and a heavy-handed public security crackdown.

Positioned as an alternative developmental path to China’s coastal, market-driven consensus, the model gained national and international attention as a potential blueprint for addressing rising wealth inequality, regional imbalances and social stratification.

The two men projected an image of an unshakeable governing duo. During the national parliamentary “two sessions” in Beijing in March 2010, Huang famously described his working relationship with Bo as “like a duck to water”. He was also a magnet for reporters at the annual meetings, readily answering questions about the economy and Chongqing.

That alliance faced a critical test in February 2012, when Bo’s estranged police chief, Wang Lijun, fled to the US consulate in Chengdu, triggering one of China’s biggest political scandals in decades.

Following the diplomatic stand-off, Bo was removed from the party’s leadership. He was later sentenced to life in prison on charges of bribery, embezzlement and abuse of power.

The aftershocks hit many of Bo’s subordinates in Chongqing, as the municipality’s new leadership headed by caretaker party chief Zhang Dejiang, repeatedly pledged to “eradicate” Bo’s “toxic influence”. Despite the chaos, Huang remained in position.

In November 2012, Sun took over from Zhang, becoming Huang’s new partner and direct supervisor.

Like Bo before his fall, Sun was also seen as a political rising star. He relied on Huang to maintain the city’s administrative machinery and drive double-digit economic growth. Huang, it seemed, had weathered the Bo saga unaffected, and was among six regional officials to be part of President Xi Jinping’s delegation to the United States in 2015.

The political ground shook beneath Chongqing again in 2017, just months after Huang stepped down as the city’s mayor. Sun was rounded up in anti-corruption investigation during a trip to Beijing for a top-level meeting, and ultimately sentenced to life imprisonment on corruption charges.

The southwestern metropolis again pledged to clean up the negative influence of a disgraced party boss and again Huang appeared to sail through the controversy. Huang stayed on in his semi-retired role in the national legislature as vice-chairman of the National People’s Congress Financial and Economic Affairs Committee, finally stepping down in March 2018.

Even after his retirement, Huang, respected as a capable economic manager, remained an influential intellectual heavyweight. Affiliated with prestigious platforms including the China Centre for International Economic Exchanges, the China Finance 40 Forum and Fudan University, he had a towering media profile, offering perspectives on a wide range of economic issues.

In 2021, he warned that the business models of Chinese internet firms would no longer work in the coming decade, slamming them as “taking advantage of weaknesses in human nature to entice purchases”.

In 2022, Huang warned that China’s property market had reached a turning point, questioning whether the country could sustain its decades-long construction boom.

As recently as May this year, he described China’s record US$1.2 trillion trade surplus in 2025 as “shocking”, urging Beijing to rebalance trade through a combination of gradual yuan appreciation, tariff cuts and improved benefits for workers.

He is known among various lecture organisers as exceptionally proactive and eager to take the podium, and is said to have told organisers that he is willing to talk on any issue.

He is also believed to be in good health for his age, with a fondness for steak and cigars.

His confidence was built on decades of economic policy experience.

Born in Zhuji in Zhejiang province in 1952, Huang rose through Shanghai’s industrial bureaucracy.

Entering the municipal party and government apparatus in 1983, he was deeply involved in the early development and opening of the Pudong New Area.

In October 2001, he was transferred to Chongqing as a vice-mayor, overseeing the city’s industrial policy, state-owned assets, taxation and financial sectors before becoming mayor in January 2010 – a post he held for nearly seven years.

Under his stewardship, Chongqing logged consecutive years of double-digit GDP growth, routinely outpacing the rest of the country.

Huang promoted the Chongqing-Xinjiang-Europe freight railway, and attracted Hewlett-Packard and Foxconn to build an electronics manufacturing hub in the city.

He also pioneered the municipal investment vehicle modelled on Singapore’s state fund Temasek and kept runaway property speculation in check through strict land-supply management and an expansive public rental housing programme.

Huang’s downfall follows a smaller earthquake in Chongqing. Since 2022, the anti-corruption drive has sped up, targeting more and more senior officials across the country.

Chongqing was hit hard, with seven other high-ranking provincial officials coming under investigation since then. The most senior of the seven was then-mayor Hu Henghua, who came under the microscope in March, triggering another shake-up across the administration.

The investigation into Huang comes less than two weeks before the party’s fifth plenum, which brings together the hundreds of full and alternate members of the Central Committee.

The Central Committee’s ranks have been thinned by the anti-corruption campaign, with 34 of its 205 full members under investigation or stripped of their status as deputies to the National People’s Congress.

The Beijing-based political scientist said Chongqing had been the epicentre of China’s most disruptive political tremors over the past two decades and the investigation of Huang nearly a decade after retirement showed Beijing’s resolve to clean up Chongqing’s factional legacy, allowing no perceived seniority to impede its continued organisational housecleaning.

Not all are that surprised by Huang’s fall.

His family’s commercial dealings cast a persistent shadow over his administration. In Chongqing, the extensive business footprint of his son was “an open secret” among political and business circles, according to sources familiar with the situation.

“Many in Chongqing’s government and financial circles know his son very well, as Huang Qifan is widely regarded as the ‘godfather’ of Chongqing’s state-driven financial vehicles, which can mobilise a lot of resources,” said a source who worked with Huang.

The source said the younger Huang quickly immersed himself in China’s capital market deals.

item.title: [SCMP] China’s rocket boom has made Hainan a space hub. Can launches fuel wider growth?
item.description:
As technological developments augur an era of renewed space exploration, China is aiming to become a major player. In the first part of this two-part series, Wency Chen and Mia Nurmamat examine how the southern island province of Hainan is betting on a growing aerospace cluster to rewrite its economic playbook beyond tourism.

On Hainan’s northeastern coast, launch towers rise abruptly from a flat landscape of coconut palms and open sky. At Pad 1 of the commercial spaceport in Wenchang, an 83-metre (272 feet) service tower stands surrounded by four slender, steel lattice towers, designed to protect the launch site from lightning during the island’s frequent tropical storms.

No mission is scheduled, but an orange flame flickers from a gas vent at one facility.
item.content:encoded:
As technological developments augur an era of renewed space exploration, China is aiming to become a major player. In the first part of this two-part series, Wency Chen and Mia Nurmamat examine how the southern island province of Hainan is betting on a growing aerospace cluster to rewrite its economic playbook beyond tourism.

On Hainan’s northeastern coast, launch towers rise abruptly from a flat landscape of coconut palms and open sky. At Pad 1 of the commercial spaceport in Wenchang, an 83-metre (272 feet) service tower stands surrounded by four slender, steel lattice towers, designed to protect the launch site from lightning during the island’s frequent tropical storms.

No mission is scheduled, but an orange flame flickers from a gas vent at one facility.

Long known for its coconuts, its namesake chicken and generations of emigrants who left for Southeast Asia in search of a living, Wenchang has been thrust onto the frontier of national development. Beijing’s space ambitions have turned the city into a showcase for rocket launches – and given Hainan a catalyst to reshape an economy long reliant on tourism and consumer services.

Today, the island province is working to build a more diversified and sustainable growth model and, together with its ambition to host a premier free-trade port, is embracing a hi-tech future increasingly centred on the space economy.

From coconuts to rockets: Hainan’s economic reboot

“Commercial space flight could give Hainan a clearer manufacturing focus while complementing its traditional strengths in tourism and consumer services,” said Peng Peng, executive chairman of the Guangdong Society of Reform, a prominent think tank affiliated with the provincial government.

Home to more than 10 million people and comparable in size to Belgium, Hainan now boasts a growing industrial cluster known as Wenchang International Aerospace City. At its centre are two state-owned rocket launch facilities: one serving national programmes and another handling commercial missions.

The Wenchang Space Launch Site staged its first launch in 2016 and focuses mainly on lunar exploration and human space flight. Just a few miles away sits the Hainan Commercial Space Launch Site, China’s first dedicated commercial launch platform.

Since its inaugural mission in November 2024, the commercial site has completed 21 launches and has sent 221 satellites into orbit, according to Xu Xikai, deputy head of the development department at Hainan International Commercial Aerospace Launch, the site’s operator.

Two more general-purpose liquid-fuel launch pads were also under construction and could host their maiden missions by the end of this year, Xu noted. Longer-term plans envision as many as eight large coastal launch pads, together with tracking facilities and systems for recovering rockets at sea.

We want to attract more companies to Hainan, using the launch site to drive the wider industry and bringing in companies across the rocket, satellite and data chains

Xu Xikai, Hainan International Commercial Aerospace Launch

Wenchang’s coastal geography gives it a major advantage. Massive rockets can be delivered directly by sea, bypassing the road, tunnel and bridge constraints faced by inland facilities. And at about 19 degrees north latitude, rockets gain an extra momentum boost from the Earth’s rotation, reducing fuel requirements or allowing heavier payloads, Xu explained.

“For large-diameter, heavy-lift rockets in the future, coastal launch sites will increasingly have an advantage,” he said.

Geography, however, is also one of Hainan’s economic weaknesses. The island has historically lacked a heavy industrial base, meaning much of the specialised hardware and construction materials required for space manufacturing must be shipped in.

Inside Wenchang’s manufacturing ambitions

The challenge for Hainan is transforming launch sites into the nucleus of a wider industrial ecosystem – and early signs are encouraging.

Wenchang International Aerospace City recorded a surge in revenue amid an “unprecedented” pace of rocket launches, according to a June report by Nanhai Net, a state-run news portal operated by the Hainan Daily Press Group.

The aerospace park’s revenue jumped 85 per cent in 2025 to 23.53 billion yuan (US$3.5 billion), while manufacturing output from its rocket supply chain more than doubled to over 8 billion yuan, the report stated.

Under a provincial action plan from 2025 to 2027, Hainan also aims to raise annual operating revenue at Wenchang’s aerospace cluster to 10 billion yuan by 2027, while building an integrated supply chain spanning rockets, satellites and data services.

The expansion comes as Beijing presses ahead with reforms to open the island further and develop new sources of growth – though competition is intensifying. Two other commercial launch sites have already begun operating in Gansu and Shandong provinces, while at least four more are under development nationwide.

To stay ahead, Hainan’s strategy is to push further up the industrial chain. Its action plan prioritises a “super factory” next to the launch pads, designed to produce up to 1,000 satellites annually. The location would allow freshly assembled satellites to move straight from production line to launch pad with very little transit time, the Star Market Daily, a Shanghai-based financial news outlet focused on technology and capital markets, reported in December.

Described by local authorities as Asia’s largest satellite-manufacturing facility, the industrial complex is also expected to support China’s Qianfan low-Earth-orbit constellation. A planned special bonded zone for satellite data would further leverage Hainan’s free-trade policies to attract data from overseas, according to the report.

“We want to attract more companies to Hainan, using the launch site to drive the wider industry and bringing in companies across the rocket, satellite and data chains,” said Xu of Hainan International Commercial Aerospace Launch.

The infrastructure buildout is already reshaping launch activity. After more than two years of development, the Hainan Commercial Space Launch Site has moved from experimental testing to routine operations. It handled more than 30 per cent of China’s commercial satellite launches in 2025 and successfully carried out the country’s first offshore rocket booster recovery.

Business beyond the launch pad

Putting a rocket into orbit, however, is only one part of the emerging space economy. Ye Shiyang, a Wenchang native who chairs the company behind the Aerospace Supercomputing Centre in Wenchang International Aerospace City, argued Hainan must capture a larger share of the value generated after a rocket launches.

“Over the past few years, we have connected the entire chain – from collecting and receiving satellite data to storing, processing, applying and trading it,” Ye said.

Completed in 2023, the supercomputing centre occupies about 40,000 square metres (about 431,000 square feet), with about 22,400 square metres of floor space. A guide at the centre said it offered peak computing power of 100 petaflops – a measure of processing capacity – and was designed to accommodate about 2,000 server racks.

Meanwhile, three of the centre’s remote-sensing satellites operate as part of Jilin-1, which is described by its developer as the world’s largest commercial sub-metre Earth-observation constellation. The centre has also built 13 ground stations, according to a guide there.

The practical applications could be numerous. Satellite images processed in Wenchang can distinguish food crops from cash crops, identify fallow land and monitor crop growth, assess pest outbreaks and track the effects of typhoons. Such imaging tools can also help to detect water pollution, illegal logging and unauthorised land use.

These services, Ye argued, could generate steady demand from agricultural, environmental and land-management authorities, giving Hainan a revenue stream that is less dependent on the schedule of rocket launches.

The aerospace city is also developing a space tourism business. The Jixing Meteorite Museum, for instance, displays more than 400 specimens gathered from around the world, while exhibitions introduce visitors to satellite data and supercomputing.

“We are developing space tourism in response to market demand,” Ye said. “Visitors should not only watch a launch or see a rocket or satellite. They should also understand the industry and technology behind them.”

In 2025, tourism, modern services, hi-tech industries and tropical agriculture – Hainan’s four pillar sectors – accounted for 65.9 per cent of the province’s gross domestic product, according to the provincial government.

“The Wenchang launch site has already become a tourist attraction, and this could give Hainan an economic model built around tourism, consumer services and aerospace manufacturing – and give its manufacturing sector a much clearer direction,” said Peng of the Guangdong Society of Reform.

For a Wenchang native surnamed Xie, the transformation has been drastic. Growing up in a village in Longlou town, he once walked barefoot along unpaved red-earth tracks. Today, working as a taxi driver, he has watched the sprawling aerospace complex reshape the place he calls home.

As the launch site and surrounding projects expanded, local families were relocated and farmland acquired. While some households received hundreds of thousands of yuan in compensation, Xie noted how traditional livelihoods were quickly fading, leaving coconut processing as one of the few legacy industries remaining.

“Farmers around here barely farm any more,” he said.

In Longlou, the coconut palms still remain – quiet reminders of a past that existed before the rockets arrived, even as a new economy takes shape around them.

item.title: [SCMP] Inside scorching Pakistani factories making clothes for global fashion brands
item.description:
Machines whirred around Siddiqui as her vision blurred and her heart hammered. The garment factory on the outskirts of Karachi was sweltering. The room was packed with sweating fellow workers and huge industrial equipment that radiated heat. The air felt thick with the humidity of this summer’s monsoon.

Siddiqui, who asked to be identified only by surname, felt like she was suffocating. Concerned colleagues called over her supervisor. “The supervisor said, ‘Just complete this work,’” the 28-year-old said. “Suddenly darkness came before my eyes.”

Exhausted by the heat, she collapsed.
item.content:encoded:
Machines whirred around Siddiqui as her vision blurred and her heart hammered. The garment factory on the outskirts of Karachi was sweltering. The room was packed with sweating fellow workers and huge industrial equipment that radiated heat. The air felt thick with the humidity of this summer’s monsoon.

Siddiqui, who asked to be identified only by surname, felt like she was suffocating. Concerned colleagues called over her supervisor. “The supervisor said, ‘Just complete this work,’” the 28-year-old said. “Suddenly darkness came before my eyes.”

Exhausted by the heat, she collapsed.

Extreme heat – intensified by climate change – is creating dangerous conditions for factory workers in Pakistan.

From blue jeans to homeware, these factories produce goods for global companies that have pledged to protect workers’ safety. But experts and labour rights advocates say those promises remain unfulfilled, as temperatures rise and workers pay the price with their health and safety.

Of the more than a dozen workers interviewed in Karachi, all described scorching workplaces, absent heat protocols and negative health effects, including fainting. They spoke on the condition that their identities be protected out of fear of retaliation by their employers.

All but one said they lost wages when heat-related illness forced them to miss work. Ten of the workers made goods for global brands sold in the United States and Europe.

For workers like Siddiqui, extreme heat – temperatures at or above 32 degrees Celsius (90 degrees Fahrenheit) combined with high humidity – is not just a workplace hazard. Living with her six children in a small room with no air conditioning on the outskirts of Karachi, temperatures routinely exceed 37.8 degrees during heatwaves.

Inside the garment factory where she stitches clothes for Spanish brands like Zara and Mango, it is even hotter. Huge machines churn heat into the air. There are fans, but they’re often broken or small. Windows are slitlike and set high, or even closed to deter theft, further trapping the heat, workers said.

“Smoke, heat, you face it,” said a 34-year-old male factory worker.

Silent killer

Extreme heat is a silent killer. It can show few outward symptoms while causing severe internal damage and worsening conditions, including cardiovascular disease, diabetes and asthma. Studies have linked it to dehydration, heatstroke, organ failure and death.

“The longer you work in the heat, the less that you’re protected from it and the health risks rise,” said Andreas Flouris, the founder of FAME Lab, which researches heat’s impact on health.

The number of people exposed to extreme heat is growing exponentially due to climate change. Heat stress is a leading cause of weather-related deaths, according to the World Health Organization. Studies by World Weather Attribution say that climate change has also drastically increased the frequency, intensity and risks of extreme heatwaves in Pakistan.

Workers interviewed described temporary muscle paralysis, swollen limbs, blood pressure swings, breathing problems, blurred vision and exhaustion that peaked in the hottest months. One worker showed scaly skin rashes on her arms from routine chemical exposure, saying how the pain intensified during summer.

All said they had seen colleagues faint from the heat. Several said they had fainted themselves, some multiple times. Those who fainted were often offered only a short break or sugary drink before being told to resume work.

They said complaining to supervisors led to no changes. Only one worker had paid sick leave. The rest said that missed hours – even from fainting on the job or from heat-related illnesses – meant slashed wages.

Siddiqui wept on the floor of her home as she described fainting and being sent to the hospital. As she earned 15,000 rupees (US$54) a month, the hospital visit cost, which her employer refused to pay, left her unable to buy food for her children.
