After completing a master’s degree in data science at Pace University in New York in May last year, Tarun returned to India in October, saying frequent changes in US visa rules and employer sponsorship requirements had made it difficult for him to find a job in the world’s largest economy.

Tarun, who is from the southern Indian city of Tirupati, felt returning home was a more prudent move than pursuing a job in the US indefinitely.

“I got a job within one month here [Bengaluru] with an American engineering company,” he said, without giving further details about his job. “At the end of the day, my decision is about my happiness. I am close to my friends and family.”
item.content:encoded:
After completing a master’s degree in data science at Pace University in New York in May last year, Tarun returned to India in October, saying frequent changes in US visa rules and employer sponsorship requirements had made it difficult for him to find a job in the world’s largest economy.

Tarun, who is from the southern Indian city of Tirupati, felt returning home was a more prudent move than pursuing a job in the US indefinitely.

“I got a job within one month here [Bengaluru] with an American engineering company,” he said, without giving further details about his job. “At the end of the day, my decision is about my happiness. I am close to my friends and family.”

Tarun’s experience mirrors a debate over whether growing uncertainty surrounding US immigration rules could spur more Indian professionals to return home, with prominent figures in India’s tech industry weighing in on the issue.

In a viral social media post, Sridhar Vembu, co-founder and chief scientist of Chennai-headquartered cloud software company Zoho Corporation, urged Indian professionals in the US to return, arguing that India could turn the increasingly hostile climate in Washington towards foreign talent into a valuable opportunity to grow its technological capabilities.

“Indians have made a major contribution to America’s technological prowess. Yet, a big part of America no longer wants us. Indians who are on a visa in the US face the painful prospect of uprooting the life you have built with hard work,” Vembu wrote on October 9.

“Let this be the birth pains of a bold new future. Come back, let’s build India,” he said.

Indians have made a major contribution to America's technological prowess. Yet, a big part of America no longer wants us.

Indians who are on a visa in the US face the painful prospect of uprooting the life you have built with hard work.

Let this be the birth pains of a bold…

— Sridhar Vembu (@svembu) October 9, 2026

The US is home to the world’s largest Indian diaspora, estimated at between 5.8 million and 6.1 million people as January, many of whom hold senior positions at global technology companies.

Former Indian education minister Dharmendra Pradhan has backed Vembu’s call to contribute to India’s tech growth, emphasising the need to strengthen local capabilities and foster innovation.

“With confidence in our talent and a commitment to building indigenous capabilities, we can help shape the future of technology,” he wrote on social media.

The posts have raised expectations of Indian tech talent to accelerate innovation in India.

“It would be great if the government took more initiative to support professionals because there are a lot of highly talented Indians who are in the US. Many of them are struggling with visa pressures,” said Tarun.

On October 8, the US administration suspended the Permanent Labour Certification programme, a key step for foreign professionals to work in the US and potentially obtain permanent residency under an employer-sponsored process, affecting Indian companies such as Tata Consultancy Services and Wipro, as well as US giants including Microsoft and Adobe.

Speaking on the move on the same day, US Vice-President J.D. Vance accused major companies of fraudulently bringing in lower-paid foreign workers whom he described as “indentured servants” instead of employing Americans.

India’s Ministry of External Affairs slammed his remarks as “deeply offensive” the following day.

“We believe that such descriptions are unwarranted and ignore the fact that Indian professionals in the United States are highly educated and skilled contributors to its economy and innovation ecosystem,” it said in a statement.

Vance later clarified that his remarks were criticism of American companies and the visa system rather than of workers.

Indian professionals said that his remarks showed a lack of respect towards them.

“A professional is not ‘cheaper’ because they were born in India, China, Brazil or anywhere else. Their salary may be different. Their immigration status may be different. But their education, experience, expertise, ambition and dignity are not cheaper,” Dhananjay Ramakrishnappa, a manager of operations at Bengaluru-based software firm Flexara, said in a social media post, which also mentioned that he had previously worked in the US for 13 years.

“What worries me even more is the fear that many immigrants now feel about simply travelling home to see their families,” he said.

He said that a US-based family friend did not travel to India to attend her mother’s last rites because she feared that she would not be able to come back.

Washington’s curbs against foreign professionals could tighten further as it is reportedly examining a proposal to levy a US$70,000 fee on international students seeking post-graduation work authorisation.

Ramakrishnappa, who returned to India in 2017 after working in senior US-based executive roles with Microsoft, told This Week in Asia that Indian-origin professionals who had spent a decade or two working in the US tech sector could become successful entrepreneurs in India.

Subbu K., head of technology at New York-based start-up Trust Guard AI, however, said he was torn between whether to stay in the US or return to India. His daughter, who is studying in a US high school, might not be keen to head home, he added.

“I would love to do that [return to India] because it gives me the best of both worlds,” said Subbu, who still holds an Indian passport after spending over two decades working in the US tech sector.

Nonetheless, tech professionals and analysts say India has to take steps to lure more tech talent home.

Subbu worried about red tape in India, citing how a friend of his spent around eight months to get clearance from Indian regulators to start a business, compared with as fast as within a day in the US.

Vivek Mishra, deputy director of the strategic studies programme at the Observer Research Foundation, said the significant salary gap between what Indian tech professionals could earn in the US and India could be a deterrent.

“There has to be a calculated outreach to these people. Otherwise it will be just a slogan,” he said.

Uday Chandra, professor of political science at India’s Ashoka University, said appealing to Indian talent to return home based on “innate patriotism” alone would not work.

“Ultimately, highly skilled professionals will go wherever their talents are valued and they can pursue their ambitions. India will need to compete for such talent,” he added.

item.title: [SCMP] Sydney opens US$4 billion second airport with few flights
item.description:
After more than half a century of political procrastination, environmental protests and funding shortfalls, Sydney finally has a second airport. But the new A$5.6 billion (US$4 billion) site’s commercial prospects are already in question.

Western Sydney International, 50km (31 miles) inland from the city centre, will handle its first passenger flight on Sunday – a Jetstar service to the Gold Coast. But the facility has attracted only a handful of airlines and has half a dozen or fewer scheduled flights a day for the next 12 months, according to aviation data company Cirium.

Australia’s biggest aviation infrastructure development in decades is opening just as the global travel industry endures its toughest period since the pandemic. Around the world, airlines are sounding the alarm on rising fuel costs and fares as the Iran war drags on. Many, including dominant Australian carrier Qantas, are cutting back on domestic capacity rather than laying on more flights.
item.content:encoded:
After more than half a century of political procrastination, environmental protests and funding shortfalls, Sydney finally has a second airport. But the new A$5.6 billion (US$4 billion) site’s commercial prospects are already in question.

Western Sydney International, 50km (31 miles) inland from the city centre, will handle its first passenger flight on Sunday – a Jetstar service to the Gold Coast. But the facility has attracted only a handful of airlines and has half a dozen or fewer scheduled flights a day for the next 12 months, according to aviation data company Cirium.

Australia’s biggest aviation infrastructure development in decades is opening just as the global travel industry endures its toughest period since the pandemic. Around the world, airlines are sounding the alarm on rising fuel costs and fares as the Iran war drags on. Many, including dominant Australian carrier Qantas, are cutting back on domestic capacity rather than laying on more flights.

Airlines are also struggling to get their hands on new jets, leaving few spare aircraft to send to start-ups like Western Sydney International where passenger demand is unproven.

Compounding the government-owned airport’s challenges, a planned rail link would not open until 2027 at the earliest, while a shuttle bus to the centre of Sydney costs A$55 and takes about one hour. That means Sydney Kingsford Smith, 20 minutes by taxi or train from the central business district and Australia’s primary gateway, remains a more practical option for most people.

“The main airport is much more convenient to almost all travellers,” said David Levinson, a professor of transport at the University of Sydney. Western Sydney International’s passenger forecasts look “a bit optimistic,” he said.

Named for pioneering Australian aviator Nancy Bird Walton, the new airport expects to handle 8.4 million passengers a year by the end of the decade, and almost 20 million annually by 2045, according to its master plan. Both figures are fractions of the numbers handled by the city’s main airport.

Western Sydney International is built on old farmland at Badgerys Creek. The government settled on the site in 2014, ending a debate about the need and location for a second airport that stretches back to 1946. Construction started in 2018 and the airport opened for cargo flights in July.

The surrounding population is key to the facility’s commercial fate. By 2030, half of Sydney’s 6.1 million people will live in the city’s west, according to the airport’s master plan. Some 40 per cent of Greater Western Sydney’s population was born overseas, which should generate demand for flights to countries such as India, China and Vietnam, the document says.

Yet Qantas plans to operate little more than one domestic flight a day, on average, from March next year, according to Cirium data through September 2027. Virgin Australia, the country’s second-largest carrier, has no flights scheduled. The new airport’s main customer is Jetstar, the leisure-focused, low-cost carrier owned by Qantas.

“We are looking closely at the Western Sydney opportunity and assessing whether it would fit into a network and schedule that best serves the needs of our customers,” Virgin Australia said in a statement.

Qantas referred to a speech by Chief Executive Officer Vanessa Hudson in June, when she described Western Sydney as “such an important market”, specifically highlighting its relevance to Jetstar. “We expect demand will grow, and when we see that, we’ll put more frequency in,” she said at the time.

Other airlines that will use the new airport are Air New Zealand, VietJet, Fiji Airways and Singapore Airlines.

In an interview, Western Sydney International Chief Executive Officer Simon Hickey said more airlines would use the airport in time, and talks were taking place with several other carriers. “Right now, I’m really happy with where we’re sitting,” he said.

But Hickey also needs the local population to give the airport a chance, which would help him persuade other carriers that there’s demand to capture. “It’s use it or lose it,” he said. “That will mean that we continue to grow and other airlines will come and join the pack.”

To be sure, long-term appetite for air travel is relentless. Worldwide passenger demand was expected to more than double by 2050, according to the International Air Transport Association.

And while it may be off to a slow start, Western Sydney International has some advantages over Sydney’s main airport. Most importantly, it has no overnight curfew like at Kingsford Smith, allowing international airlines to schedule departures that connect with other flights at their own hubs. The new airport expects to handle 82 million passengers a year by 2063 and ultimately become Sydney’s primary air-travel hub.

It takes time for a new airport to establish itself, said Stephen Beckett, CEO of Airlines for Australia & New Zealand, which represents Qantas, Jetstar, Air New Zealand and Virgin Australia.

“Some airlines will sit back and make their own commercial assessments based on passenger demand,” he said.

For now, Western Sydney International is already drawing unfavourable comparisons with airports elsewhere that ultimately failed to live up to expectations.

Levinson, the transport professor at the University of Sydney, compared Western Sydney International to Mirabel Airport outside Montreal. Mirabel opened in 1975 in time for the Montreal Olympics but handled its last commercial passenger flight in 2004. The airport now operates chiefly as a freight hub.

Right now, Western Sydney International is trying to serve a market that does not yet exist, Levinson said. The new airport’s opening is “early, given actual demand,” he said.

There was a risk Sydney’s secondary airport would end up with a similar status as Avalon Airport, which is more than 50km outside Melbourne, according to Peter Forsyth, an aviation economics consultant who’s a former professor at Monash University. Avalon, where Jetstar has operated flights since 2004, has never broken through as a genuine alternative airport to Melbourne’s main airport, he said.

Growth at Sydney’s new airport would be a slow burn, said Forsyth. “There is a market there,” he said. “But exactly how big it is, I don’t know.”

item.title: [SCMP] India needs more fighter jets. It cannot build them fast enough
item.description:
India has a soaring ambition to modernise its air force, built around a fleet of domestically developed fighter jets. Yet production of these aircraft has been hampered by engine delays and other bottlenecks that defence analysts say could limit its ability to fight future air wars.

On October 11 at an airbase in Jodhpur, Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh strapped into a Tejas jet for the last time. It was his final fighter sortie before retiring later this month and he flew it in an Indian-built jet to show support for the country’s domestic defence industry.

A week earlier, he had warned that the Indian Air Force (IAF) faced a critical shortage of fighter squadrons. “We need to induct two fighter squadrons every year,” Singh said on October 3, noting that “between 36 and 40 aircraft” would need to be produced annually to meet India’s target of having 42 fighter squadrons in service.
item.content:encoded:
India has a soaring ambition to modernise its air force, built around a fleet of domestically developed fighter jets. Yet production of these aircraft has been hampered by engine delays and other bottlenecks that defence analysts say could limit its ability to fight future air wars.

On October 11 at an airbase in Jodhpur, Air Chief Marshal A.P. Singh strapped into a Tejas jet for the last time. It was his final fighter sortie before retiring later this month and he flew it in an Indian-built jet to show support for the country’s domestic defence industry.

A week earlier, he had warned that the Indian Air Force (IAF) faced a critical shortage of fighter squadrons. “We need to induct two fighter squadrons every year,” Singh said on October 3, noting that “between 36 and 40 aircraft” would need to be produced annually to meet India’s target of having 42 fighter squadrons in service.

“Actually, we need even more than that,” he said.

The Tejas programme, which dates back to the 1980s, has become emblematic of India’s drive to build up its domestic defence industry. A Mark 1A variant of the light combat aircraft was unveiled last year and a Mark 2 is still under development.

Induction of the Mark 1A is only now about to begin, 2½ years late, after the F404 engines needed from US manufacturer GE Aerospace arrived late and the various radar, weapons and software systems took longer to integrate than planned.

Vice-Chief of the Air Staff Air Marshal Ashutosh Dixit said in late September that induction was expected to begin within one or two months, following a protracted development cycle and exhaustive operational evaluations of the aircraft’s avionics suite.

GE Aerospace, the Tejas programme’s only engine supplier, recently stepped up deliveries to principal manufacturer Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL), shipping three F404-IN20 engines in August and another four engines in September. That makes 14 engines delivered so far, against the 20 that are due to arrive by the end of this year.

State-run HAL aims to produce 24 Tejas fighters annually. The IAF has already ordered 83 Mark 1As, wants to add 97 more and is also actively considering the Mark 2 variant.

Projections indicate at least 350 – and potentially more than 400 – Tejas will eventually be built, with the aircraft expected to form the backbone of India’s air force in future.

However, “repeated delays in certification, weapons/radar integration and engine supply show that indigenisation still needs execution, not just policy”, said Gurcharan Singh Bedi, a retired IAF air marshal.

“Having acquired the capability to produce the aircraft, we are then just talking of scale, which can be boosted. But it will take a very strong focus by the government and a very hard commitment by HAL or whosoever produces these aircraft.”

Fleet depletion

India’s air force badly needs replacements for the ageing aircraft that are leaving active service.

The IAF officially retired the last of its Cold War-era Soviet-designed MiG-21 jets in September last year – 36 in total – with another six squadrons of Anglo-French Sepecat Jaguar ground-attack fighters due to be phased out between 2028 and 2031.

To keep the remainder of its Jaguar fleet flying, India is buying nine of the aircraft that Britain’s Royal Air Force retired in 2007 to use for spare parts.

Three MiG-29 squadrons and three squadrons of the French-designed Mirage 2000 are set to also be retired through the mid-to-late 2030s.

Each IAF squadron contains about 18 active aircraft, plus three or four in reserve.

Bedi agreed with outgoing air force chief Singh’s assessment that roughly two new squadrons per year would be needed simply to maintain the number of aircraft India had in service.

HAL’s target of 24 Tejas fighters a year would fall short of that goal, but a second programme could help close the gap, he said.

In February, India cleared the purchase of 114 Rafales from France, under a government-to-government deal as part of its Multi-Role Fighter Aircraft programme.

Taken together, Bedi said this would bring annual deliveries close to the 32 or 36 aircraft required.

Final talks on price and production arrangements for the Rafales are still pending, though local media reports indicate manufacturer Dassault Aviation has agreed to 50-60 per cent “Make in India” content for the aircraft, as well as technology transfers and the integration of Indian weapons and systems.

Bedi said a “genuine acceleration” of India’s fighter jet production would depend on HAL meeting or beating its target of 24 combat aircraft per year, the timely delivery of multi-role fighters from France and retirements not outpacing inductions.

“The chief has spelled out the requirement, but it’s difficult to meet in the near future,” he said of Singh’s assessment. “At the same time, I believe anything is possible.”

‘The real constraint’

Several new aircraft are on the way. The first flight of the Tejas Mark 2 is expected between June and September 2027, with initial induction planned for 2030-31 if development stays on track.

India also wants to have a prototype of its fifth-generation stealth fighter, the Advanced Medium Combat Aircraft (AMCA), airborne for a test flight by September 2028.

Bids to develop and produce the AMCA prototype have come in from India’s Tata Advanced Systems and domestic consortiums led by Larsen & Toubro and Bharat Forge, while France’s Safran is competing with a partnership formed by India’s Reliance and Britain’s Rolls-Royce to supply AMCA’s engine.

Sanjay Iyer, a retired Indian Army brigadier, said these overlapping programmes were likely to hit another bottleneck: the fact that they had to draw from the same pool of test pilots, certification staff and integration engineers.

“That is the real constraint, not shop-floor space,” he said. “And even if every Tejas [production] line ran flat out, you would still fall short of 36 to 40 a year.”

Iyer argued that India’s aircraft production problems could best be tackled through increased domestic engine manufacturing, design discipline and boosting private industry’s role.

Much time was lost on the Mark 1A’s development because of design changes, he said, adding that private companies – some of which already made fuselages and wings for HAL – should also be allowed to assemble aircraft.

“As long as one American supplier decides when your fighters fly, your output figures are really their output figures,” Iyer said regarding the Tejas’ GE engine. “And geopolitical considerations matter too. The US is not beyond twisting India’s arm if its other interests are affected.”

Holding buffer stocks of engines could serve as a costly stopgap solution, he added, further calling the opening of AMCA development and manufacturing to domestic private industry a “good sign”.

item.title: [SCMP] The China decoupling paradox: why the world still needs its manufacturing machine
item.description:
Talk of global decoupling from China has persisted for years, as has speculation that emerging economies such as India and Vietnam could soon replace it as the “world’s factory”.

But for Indian hardware engineer Neeraj Arora, the growth of India’s electronics manufacturing industry has not eliminated the need to source components from China. Instead, it has changed the nature of those imports.

A decade ago, Arora imported finished phone chargers from the world’s second-largest economy. Today, more of these products can be made in India, even as manufacturers there still rely on Chinese parts for assembly.
item.content:encoded:
Talk of global decoupling from China has persisted for years, as has speculation that emerging economies such as India and Vietnam could soon replace it as the “world’s factory”.

But for Indian hardware engineer Neeraj Arora, the growth of India’s electronics manufacturing industry has not eliminated the need to source components from China. Instead, it has changed the nature of those imports.

A decade ago, Arora imported finished phone chargers from the world’s second-largest economy. Today, more of these products can be made in India, even as manufacturers there still rely on Chinese parts for assembly.

“They don’t have a single industry; they have created an ecosystem,” said Arora, who has travelled repeatedly to Shenzhen, Dongguan and Guangzhou – southern China’s manufacturing hubs that offer a wide range of competitively priced parts, from power-switching transistors to charging chips.

Arora’s experience, together with broader economic data, illustrates the challenge facing countries seeking to diversify their supply chains: shifting production out of China does not necessarily mean reducing reliance on Chinese industry. A recent report by investment bank Morgan Stanley examined this pattern, arguing the country had strengthened its role in global supply chains despite trade tensions.

“China has continued to deepen its presence in global supply chains by capturing value-added content in global imports and increasing exports to [emerging markets],” the bank’s analysts, including chief Asia economist Chetan Ahya and chief China economist Robin Xing, wrote in the note, published earlier this month.

The world’s second-largest economy was “well-positioned” to deepen that presence, the analysts argued, citing its focus on high-growth sectors, integrated supply chains, a financial system aligned with strategic goals and a large pool of skilled workers.

The upstream advantage

The challenge facing the likes of India and Vietnam is whether they can develop the industrial expertise and networks required to make more inputs at home. But a closer look at the data suggests that as manufacturing expands in these economies, Chinese supplies remain essential.

These developments indicate broader regional supply-chain integration, centred around China

Morgan Stanley analysts

“While India has made significant headway in electronics manufacturing, it still imports a large part of its intermediate and capital goods from China,” the Morgan Stanley analysts wrote, noting that 52 per cent of India’s imported Chinese content went into domestic investments.

Looking beyond where products are finally assembled, they tracked “value-added content” – the value contributed by a country through the goods and services used along the chain. A product assembled in Vietnam, for instance, may still contain Chinese parts or rely on Chinese machinery.

Using this measure, the analysts found that China’s share of value-added content in global imports rose from 12.6 per cent in 2017 to 14.3 per cent in 2024. The report also found that Chinese inputs are playing a growing role in Asian economies often touted as manufacturing rivals.

In Vietnam, 55 per cent of imported Chinese content is channelled towards exports, according to the analysts. “We also find that Chinese value-added content has not just increased in the rest of Asia’s exports to the US, but also to non-US markets as well,” they wrote.

“Overall, these developments indicate broader regional supply-chain integration, centred around China.”

Arora’s experience illustrates how difficult mainland China’s manufacturing ecosystem is to replace. Taiwan’s higher-end products, he said, were less suited to the low-cost goods his Indian customers needed while Vietnam offered fewer options.

“Only China has that ecosystem,” he said.

Nevertheless, Arora said he believed India was making headway. He cited the expansion of home-grown electronics giant Dixon Technologies into television and phone assembly, as well as the growing ability of Indian firms to design and develop circuit boards and prototypes that once required trips to Shenzhen. Despite the progress, however, local manufacturers continue to rely on China’s extensive network of component suppliers.

Arora estimated that China had gained 20 to 25 years of electronics manufacturing experience, compared with India’s push that gathered pace only around 2015. He argued India could reach the current capabilities of the world’s second-largest economy within five to seven years, although he expected China to have moved further ahead by then.

New Delhi is also pushing to develop more of its inputs at home. The government’s Electronics Component Manufacturing Scheme, launched in 2025 and expanded to 400 billion rupees (US$4.2 billion) in the 2026-27 budget, supports local production of parts and partially assembled products. By August, 106 projects had been approved and 38 plants had begun production, according to the Indian government.

But the government also acknowledged that India remained dependent on imports for critical components, including printed circuit boards, camera and display modules, connectors and capacitors.

Vietnam is pursuing a similar goal of strengthening its domestic supplier base. A revised industrial policy that took effect in September 2025 provides support for technology transfer, training and certification, as well as programmes intended to help local companies supply multinational manufacturers.

The limits of Western decoupling

For the United States and Europe, where the decoupling narrative has arguably been most pronounced, efforts to reduce dependence on China have transformed where products are sourced and how they reach their destinations. But the Morgan Stanley analysts found that lower direct imports from the world’s factory do not necessarily translate into less Chinese content in those goods.

They estimated that the US and EU together accounted for about 80 per cent of the increase in global reliance on Chinese value-added content. While China’s share of direct US imports plunged from 22 per cent in 2017 to about 8 per cent currently, the share of Chinese value-added content in US imports has remained broadly stable in recent years, standing at 15.4 per cent in 2024.

The analysts found that more US sectors had increased their reliance on China than reduced it, with only five of 13 manufacturing sectors recording a material decline in the share of Chinese value-added content in their imports since 2016.

“The US is still importing just as much value-added content from China, just not directly,” they wrote.

The report identified extensive re-routing of goods. About 25 per cent of Chinese content in US imports now reached the country indirectly through third economies, up 10 percentage points from 2017, according to the analysts. Nearly half of this indirect value passed through just three economies: Mexico, Taiwan and Vietnam, with the latter standing out for a much higher share of Chinese content in its exports to the US.

The analysts said the greater use of indirect channels, particularly from 2022 onwards, was “unique to US-China trade” and consistent with production moving to other countries to serve the American market while continuing to rely on Chinese inputs.

“We do not observe a similar shift towards indirect channels in imports of the rest of the world outside the US, nor for EU imports,” they said, estimating that the share of Chinese value-added content in Europe’s imports had edged up from 6.9 per cent in 2017 to 8.3 per cent in 2024.

Why China’s manufacturing machine endures

The stubborn persistence of Chinese inputs in overseas supply chains reflects the country’s unrivalled strength across a wide range of industries.

The Morgan Stanley report found that China’s share of value-added content in global imports increased in 10 of 13 manufacturing sectors over the past decade, with gains in both lower-value-added industries such as textiles, leather and footwear and more technologically advanced sectors.

In 2024, for instance, China accounted for 33 per cent of the value-added content in global imports of electrical and optical equipment, 24 per cent in machinery and equipment and 10 per cent in transport equipment.

“These patterns are consistent with China retaining higher-value production processes even as final assembly moves elsewhere, while China continues to supply the equipment and inputs needed by new manufacturing hubs,” the analysts said.

Meanwhile, China’s exports surged 36.3 per cent year on year to US$447.18 billion last month, customs data showed on Wednesday. The momentum – driven by strong global tech demand and a pre-holiday shipping rush ahead of the “golden week” break – logged a monthly high for its trade surplus in 2026 and put the country on course for another record gap this year.

A separate report from Goldman Sachs last week examined China’s rising proportion of global exports. According to the bank’s analysis, that share increased from 4 per cent in 2000 to 15 per cent in 2025, outpacing the peaks previously reached by Germany in the 1970s and Japan in the 1980s.

“Our benchmarking exercise implies that robust real export growth [in China] can continue over the next few years,” the bank’s analysts said. “The runway is therefore clear for now – but eventually will depend on stronger economic growth in importing economies.”

The Morgan Stanley report also highlighted emerging technologies as a potential source of further growth. “China is increasingly playing a critical role in global supply chains, not just in low-cost component supplies but also in high-end capital goods as well,” the analysts wrote.

“Our China team also believes China’s advantage in global manufacturing will be strengthened as it enters a new phase of industrial development in the form of ‘Industry 5.0’”, they added, referring to manufacturing enabled by artificial intelligence and robotics.

An earlier report by Morgan Stanley released in May argued humanoids and other robotics technologies could help China consolidate its dominance over global manufacturing, building on its decade-long expansion in electric vehicle manufacturing.

The bank’s analysts projected that China’s share of global exports would reach 16.5 per cent by 2030, up from about 15 per cent at the time of the report.

For countries pushing to become alternative manufacturing hubs, the findings suggest they would also need to develop the suppliers, expertise and networks that China has spent decades building. “Diversification is achievable, but decoupling will be challenging,” the analysts argued.

item.title: [SCMP] Nobel Peace Prize: the message behind Navi Pillay’s win
item.description:
The awarding of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to South African jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay matters for reasons that go well beyond the laureate herself.

The award does three things at once. First, it restores credibility to the prize. Second, it rejects in unambiguous terms the Thrasymachian doctrine that might is right, which has become the operating philosophy of major powers. Third, it highlights a warning of what happens when a hegemon decides it is above the law.

The correction was overdue. Last year, the Norwegian Nobel Committee gave the Peace Prize to Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, in what was widely read as a political signal. Machado, however, then gave her prize to US President Donald Trump.
item.content:encoded:
The awarding of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to South African jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay matters for reasons that go well beyond the laureate herself.

The award does three things at once. First, it restores credibility to the prize. Second, it rejects in unambiguous terms the Thrasymachian doctrine that might is right, which has become the operating philosophy of major powers. Third, it highlights a warning of what happens when a hegemon decides it is above the law.

The correction was overdue. Last year, the Norwegian Nobel Committee gave the Peace Prize to Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, in what was widely read as a political signal. Machado, however, then gave her prize to US President Donald Trump.

Whatever one’s view of Venezuelan politics, that act made a mockery of an institution founded on Alfred Nobel’s will: that the prize go to the person who has done the most for fraternity between nations, for the abolition or reduction of standing armies, and for the promotion of peace congresses. A Nobel Prize cannot be re-gifted like a souvenir. As the organisers made clear, “a medal can change owners, but the title of a Nobel Peace Prize laureate cannot”.

In choosing Pillay this year, the Nobel Committee cited “her efforts to promote peace and international law” and her work showing that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide can and must be prosecuted.

It said: “The system of international law is under tremendous pressure, and its institutions are under attack. We see a shift towards power politics at the expense of legal frameworks and global respect for law and justice. Whenever might overtakes right, it undermines stability, trust and peaceful coexistence.”

2026 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career. Born into a family of Indian Tamil origin under apartheid in Durban, South Africa, Pillay became a lawyer and legal pioneer, confronting deep structural discrimination, segregation and exclusion. A common thread runs from her early work defending Nelson Mandela and others who stood up against apartheid to her service as a judge in some of the key international court cases of our time. This year’s laureate has significantly enlarged the scope and impact of international law. She has served as a judge on the High Court in South Africa, the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court. She was the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights and, until recently, she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. Today Navi Pillay is a judge on the International Court of Justice in the case where Myanmar stands accused of genocide. In historic international court cases, she has shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence. Navi Pillay has also contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law. Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time. Learn more about the 2026 #NobelPeacePrize: https://t.co/JMjpp1jPKc #NobelPeacePrize #NobelPrize

— The Nobel Prize (@NobelPrize) October 9, 2026

Honouring Pillay is therefore not only about her biography; it is about upholding a principle.

In the West, it is the refutation of Thrasymachus’ contention in Plato’s Republic. In response to Thrasymachus’ declaration that “justice is nothing other than the advantage of the stronger”, Socrates answers that this cannot be justice at all. As Socrates puts it: “No physician, in so far as he is a physician, considers his own good in what he prescribes, but the good of his patient.”

In the East, the same contest is wangdao vs badao: the kingly way vs the hegemonic way. According to Mencius, he who uses force under the pretence of humaneness is a hegemon while he who uses his virtue to practice humaneness is a true king. The message is clear: a king dispenses benevolence with virtue; a hegemon appropriates benevolence by force.

Confucius also rejected rule by force: a ruler must govern by virtue and humaneness, holding the mandate of heaven by moral rectitude, not coercion. His great antagonist, Han Feizi, China’s Machiavelli, argued the opposite: man is selfish, order comes only from shi (positional power), fa (the law as an instrument of the state) and shu (techniques of reward and fear).

For Han, the first principle of political theory was the reality of human nature. This was the legalist doctrine favoured by China’s first emperor, Qin Shi Huang, who unified the country in 221BC. I place Pillay firmly in the Socratic-Confucian lineage – might may prevail but that does not make it right, and even the strongest state is bound by law.

The third reason is more immediate, and it concerns Trump. His petulance at not receiving the Nobel Peace Prize – last year and, again, this year – would be comical if it were not consequential. Earlier this month, he argued that he should win the Nobel Peace Prize for having settled “eight wars”.

What is consequential is how American power has been deployed against the very institutions that Pillay, a former judge of the International Criminal Court (ICC), helped to build.

In February last year, Trump issued an executive order announcing sanctions on 13 ICC officials. On October 9 this year – hours after Pillay’s prize was awarded – the US Treasury added the ICC itself to its sanctions list, with Secretary of State Marco Rubio saying: “We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate.”

For China, this moment carries a particular lesson. As a major power, China will be judged not only by its growth but by its rectitude.

Pillay’s career suggests what that choice requires. Her most controversial work was as the chair of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on ‌the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which concluded last year that Israel was failing to prevent and actively committing genocide.

The commission found that four of five acts defined under the 1948 UN Genocide Convention had been committed, and that Israel’s President Isaac Herzog, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defence minister Yoav Gallant had incited genocide. Israel dismissed the report as a “libellous rant” and “scandalous”.

Pillay, who in 1967 became the first woman to establish a law practice in South Africa’s then Natal province, who in 1973 won a case for Robben Island prisoners including Nelson Mandela to have access to lawyers, and who served as a judge at the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda that investigated the 1994 genocide, in which about 800,000 people were killed, knows that the law is fragile.

The world needed to understand that the alternative is the situation Thrasymachus and Han described. The 2026 prize is a reminder that we can still choose the normative path.

item.title: [SCMP] Why did Hong Kong’s 11 Skies fail and can the megaproject be rescued?
item.description:
The roar of plane engines and the hustle and bustle at Hong Kong International Airport’s Terminal 2 present a stark contrast to the pin-drop silence at the adjacent 11 Skies commercial complex.

A South China Morning Post reporter who travelled between the two places in early October found minimal footfall at the shopping centre, with the bright and airy environment of the airport terminal replaced by dim, stuffy and boarded-up corridors, and poor air conditioning amid the simmering outdoor heat.

Occupying a gross floor area of 3.8 million square feet, 11 Skies is a mammoth project at the airport. Seventy per cent of the space was originally earmarked for a mall with 800 stores and 120 food and drink concepts, and the rest equally divided between experiential entertainment facilities and grade A office spaces.
item.content:encoded:
The roar of plane engines and the hustle and bustle at Hong Kong International Airport’s Terminal 2 present a stark contrast to the pin-drop silence at the adjacent 11 Skies commercial complex.

A South China Morning Post reporter who travelled between the two places in early October found minimal footfall at the shopping centre, with the bright and airy environment of the airport terminal replaced by dim, stuffy and boarded-up corridors, and poor air conditioning amid the simmering outdoor heat.

Occupying a gross floor area of 3.8 million square feet, 11 Skies is a mammoth project at the airport. Seventy per cent of the space was originally earmarked for a mall with 800 stores and 120 food and drink concepts, and the rest equally divided between experiential entertainment facilities and grade A office spaces.

But only one of its three office towers currently houses some companies running businesses at the airport.

The rest of the space sits in gloomy darkness.

After months of market speculation, the fate of 11 Skies was decided in early October when Hong Kong’s Airport Authority and developer New World Development signed an agreement to end the latter’s nearly 50-year contract for the project.

With the authority back at the helm, the mall’s management plans to tear down the existing 11 Skies signature logo, reconfigure the retail space into an entertainment hub, bring in tenants and investors, and relaunch the project under a new name and identity.

New World, which has been mired in a debt crisis since 2023, relinquished its control of the property and paid a HK$2.3 billion (US$293 million) break-up fee. It will spend an additional HK$1.05 billion on works and services before handing operations over to the authority by April next year.

The majority shareholder, the Cheng family’s private investment vehicle Chow Tai Fook Enterprises, will grant the authority an option to buy New World shares. Although the call option gives the authority the right to buy 750 million shares at HK$3 each from Chow Tai Fook Enterprises within the next three years, it comes with conditions that call its feasibility into question.

This rare break-up in Hong Kong’s public works sector raises questions of moral hazard and the risks of setting a precedent.

Wei Lai, head of Lingnan University’s department of finance, said the surrender appeared to be a negotiated restructuring involving a substantial termination payment, asset transfer and other contractual obligations.

“On the question of moral hazard, I would be cautious about characterising the arrangement as allowing a private developer to return a project ‘at will’,” Wei said, stressing that the arrangement was different from an unconditional exit option.

“From an economic perspective, the more relevant moral-hazard question is whether this arrangement changes the ex ante incentives of developers in future projects.”

Debt-ridden partner in an ambitious project

New World’s exit had been under discussion for months.

As a key step in taking over, the authority set up a new subsidiary, IEC Holdings, to spearhead the Skytopia project, a HK$100 billion megadevelopment that will turn the airport into a destination for yachting, shopping, dining, wellness, culture and entertainment. The 11 Skies project is part of it.

The authority’s executive director for commercial, Cissy Chan Ching-sze, became CEO of IEC on October 1.

“We will soon rename 11 Skies and change its style in a cost-effective way to reflect a new identity so that we can go recruiting for tenants and investors,” Chan said shortly after New World announced the deal on September 30.

On the same day, the developer’s financial results and debt levels were also a focal point.

In 2023, signs of New World’s financial distress prompted it to seek ways to reduce or refinance its debts to boost liquidity.

The 11 Skies project was also a factor in the debt crisis. Under the original terms of the contract, the developer was required to pay a guaranteed rent or a revenue rent representing 20 per cent of the gross revenue from the project, whichever was higher. New World was due to pay the rent from 2027 until the end of the contract in 2066.

The early termination allowed the developer to shed the contract’s financial obligations.

As of June 30, the developer’s total debt stood at HK$143.3 billion. Net debt amounted to HK$126.3 billion, an increase of HK$6.2 billion during the financial year.

To ease its financial burden, the developer implemented seven measures to reduce debt, including asset disposals, capital expenditure optimisation and a decade-long suspension of dividend payments that ended last year.

Julian Lee Pui-hang, the authority’s executive director for finance, conceded that it had to bring forward the 11 Skies project by parting with the “debt-ridden partner”.

“How can we work with a debt-ridden partner as we need to bring forward the project?” he said. “The deal represents the best efforts of the controlling shareholder.”

Exit deal triggers moral hazard?

Wei of Lingnan University said she did not think the existence of one exceptional and costly exit mechanism by itself established an expectation for developers to bid more aggressively or take greater risks.

“Where difficulties arise partly from unusually adverse market conditions rather than simply from poor project execution, an orderly restructuring may in some circumstances preserve more economic value than allowing the situation to deteriorate further,” she said.

Market financing introduced an additional layer of market discipline because lenders and institutional investors would assess the financial position, risk exposure and expected returns of the authority.

“That market discipline can reduce, though not eliminate, governance and moral-hazard concerns,” Wei said.

Ervi Liusman, senior lecturer at the hotel and tourism management school at the Chinese University of Hong Kong Business School, said allowing a private developer to surrender a contracted commercial property would theoretically constitute a moral hazard if the developer could avoid the commercial risks it originally agreed to bear without facing a penalty.

“Allowing a developer to exit at will without penalty will encourage aggressive bids, knowing that there is an exit option if the market conditions deteriorate,” she said.

Liusman said that, based on what was revealed to the public, the developer had to bear significant financial losses upon returning 11 Skies, which meant the project was not surrendered at will and therefore did not constitute a moral hazard or set a bad precedent.

The surrender of the infrastructure, the break-up fee and other related expenses dealt a blow to New World’s balance sheet.

It resulted in HK$18.32 billion in net impairment losses and provisions relating to 11 Skies in the year ending June 30, contributing to New World’s HK$26.8 billion net loss. The net loss widened from HK$16.35 billion a year ago.

“Because the Airport Authority remains accountable to lenders and investors, it has strong incentives to ensure that any decision to take back the development is commercially justified and capable of generating long-term value,” Liusman said.

If the developer incurred substantial losses and contractual penalties, the focus shifted from who absorbed the loss to which party was best placed to unlock the future value of the asset, she explained.

“The Airport Authority’s intervention may then be seen as a realistic restructuring of a strategically important asset rather than a transfer of risk from private sector to the public sector,” Liusman said.

Despite being wholly owned by the government, the authority has primarily funded its infrastructure, such as the HK$141.5 billion three-runway system, through issuing debt, charging departure taxes and drawing on internal resources. The authority also retained the dividend payments the government agreed to forgo for a decade until last year.

It rarely directly taps the public coffers.

Ken Ip Man-hon, associate director of Saint Francis University’s Innovative Incubation Centre, said whether private developers should be allowed to exit large public-facing projects when commercial assumptions deteriorated was a legitimate policy question.

“The bigger lesson is that long-term projects need both accountability and flexibility,” Ip said.

He said a long-term project could not realistically be based on the assumption that its original business model would remain optimal for decades.

The project was tendered in 2018, a record year for tourist arrivals in the city before unexpected disruptions arose amid the social unrest of 2019 and the Covid-19 pandemic between 2020 and 2023.

After the borders reopened, another unexpected trend emerged, with mainland Chinese visitors – the city’s largest group of inbound travellers – spending less and Hongkongers choosing to cross the border for leisure spending.

Chan of the authority said her team would reposition and reconfigure the 11 Skies retail space into an entertainment hub, offer more unique experiences for visitors and bring in new features from overseas.

Win-win arrangement?

Ip said the authority was moving in the right direction by expanding the project beyond conventional retail to include aviation activities, arts and culture, tourism and experiential entertainment.

“The more important question remains – that is, what activities benefit most from being next to an international airport?”

Tourism and entertainment were part of the answer, but Ip suggested that the site could also include higher education, executive education, professional training, research and innovation.

“If 11 Skies can become a mixed-use international gateway rather than simply a better shopping and entertainment complex, the new strategy could give the project a much stronger foundation,” he said.

Li King-king, a professor at Hang Seng University of Hong Kong’s department of economics and finance, said the early termination was a very special case and was potentially a win-win arrangement.

The break-up was driven by factors such as location, airport design, trends in the Hong Kong retail market, changes in consumer behaviour due to the internet and residents travelling to the mainland for leisure, he said.

“The focus is whether the whole of society, the entire Airport Authority, the whole of Hong Kong, benefits from this agreement,” Li said.

Delaying the project could incur costs and affect overall airport planning, and the parties had to make a choice, taking society’s overall interests into consideration, he added.

The authority is now racing to reconfigure and relaunch the 11 Skies complex in 2028, with plans to align the project with the ambitious Skytopia megadevelopment at the airport.

Skytopia is a strategic blueprint that aims to create a new landmark for Hong Kong that will serve as a major growth engine for the economy.

The ecosystem will include a 20,000-seat arena for world-class performances at AsiaWorld-Expo next to the airport, a yacht bay providing 500 berths, a water recreation area, art galleries and storage facilities.

It will also feature a promenade with leisure facilities and an autonomous transport system connecting Skytopia, the Hong Kong border crossing of the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge and Tung Chung railway station.

“We expect the entertainment hub to serve as a platform for mainland companies to market their products to an international audience, and for international businesses to make inroads into the mainland market,” Chan of the authority said.

The authority aims to recruit top-notch entertainment operators and business partners globally to be a part of major Skytopia components in the 2028-29 financial year.

“It will be an attraction for locals, transit passengers and visitors,” she said.

Additional reporting by Lo Hoi-ying and Denise Tsang

item.title: [SCMP] Slain model Abby Choi called ‘birthing machine’ by ex-father-in-law, court hears
item.description:
The former father-in-law of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung called her a “birthing machine” and tried to assault her before he allegedly plotted with his two sons to kill her three years ago, a court has heard.

Choi’s partner, Chris Tam Fong-chun, recounted on Tuesday a bitter argument between the influencer and her former in-laws in what he said was a watershed moment leading to a breakdown in the relationship in mid-2022.

Choi was previously married to Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, who is standing trial on a joint count of murder alongside his brother Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, and his father Kwong Kau, 68.
item.content:encoded:
The former father-in-law of slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung called her a “birthing machine” and tried to assault her before he allegedly plotted with his two sons to kill her three years ago, a court has heard.

Choi’s partner, Chris Tam Fong-chun, recounted on Tuesday a bitter argument between the influencer and her former in-laws in what he said was a watershed moment leading to a breakdown in the relationship in mid-2022.

Choi was previously married to Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31, who is standing trial on a joint count of murder alongside his brother Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, and his father Kwong Kau, 68.

Testifying for the first time in the High Court, Tam also said Choi had given his family a false impression that her former in-laws were leading a good life, because she feared her two children from her previous marriage would be disparaged in their new home due to their background.

Tam said he was not surprised initially to find out that Kwong Kau was the registered owner of a HK$72 million (US$9.17 million) flat at the Kadooria residential complex in Ho Man Tin, before she told him the flat was in fact bought using her money.

“When I saw the Kadooria flat was in Kwong Kau’s name, I did not deliberately ask [Choi] about it because she had been telling me all along that this family was doing OK,” Tam said.

Kwong allegedly resented Choi for trying to sell the upscale property and enlisted his two sons to help kill the 28-year-old on February 21, 2023. Prosecutors argued the flat was only registered in his name to avoid paying HK$9 million in double stamp duty.

The elder Kwong, a retired police sergeant, has also denied preventing the burial of Choi’s body, an offence to which his two sons pleaded guilty before the trial began last month.

Tam said his family’s wealth grew significantly after his father, who founded the popular restaurant chain TamJai Yunnan Mixian, received part of the profit from selling the brand to a Japanese company for HK$1 billion.

He said he first met Choi around the end of 2013 and early 2014, when he briefly returned from Australia during a break in his studies to meet up with her then-husband Alex Kwong, his former classmate.

He said Alex Kwong “totally disappeared” after one day in 2015, the same year he began the process to divorce Choi and absconded from criminal proceedings arising from his alleged involvement in a HK$6.3 million theft case.

Tam said he did not probe further after Choi said her then-partner was safe, because he thought she had somehow managed to find a way to contact him.

“I came out very often with Abby afterwards. We took care of her children together, and love grew between us as time went by,” he added.

The court heard Tam and Choi formally started dating in December 2015 and held a wedding banquet a year later, although they never registered their marriage. The model gave birth to their daughter in September 2016, and their son was born three years later.

Choi lived with her partner’s family at a luxurious residence on Begonia Road in Kowloon Tong and received up to HK$300,000 monthly from Tam’s father to cover the couple’s expenses.

Tam said the two children Choi had with Alex Kwong lived separately with two domestic helpers initially at a flat in the Laguna Verde estate in Hung Hom, before the socialite decided to move them to the Kadooria development in 2019 because it was closer to her Kowloon Tong home.

The witness highlighted a heated argument between Choi and her former mother-in-law, Jenny Li Sui-heung, on a day when the influencer’s elder daughter had a fever at the Kadooria home in June or July 2022.

According to Tam, the model was angry at Li for telling Alex Kwong to stay away from the child because she could infect him.

“My understanding is that Abby was at that time accusing Li Sui-heung of preferring sons to daughters,” he said.

Kwong Kau, who joined the row, reportedly lunged at Choi and hurled curses at her after he accused the influencer of assaulting his wife.

“And then Kwong Kau said: ‘Who do you think you are? You’re just a birthing machine’,” Tam continued.

Tam said the elder Kwong attempted to attack Choi a second time, but he intervened to prevent the former police officer from hitting the model.

He said Choi then barred Kwong Kau from visiting the residence. She also told Tam they needed to cut ties with the Kwong family, whom she described as horrible and ungrateful.

Defence lawyers also grilled a police officer helping to lead the investigation of the case.

Detective Constable Ko Yan-ki, who was originally not expected to take the witness box, was cross-examined over his text conversations with Choi’s mother, Cheung Yin-fa, in the months preceding the trial.

The messaging logs were produced as evidence after the officer contacted Cheung while she was giving evidence last week about her purported ownership of a flat at Whampoa Garden. She later clarified that she did not own the property.

Ko rejected the prosecution’s suggestion that he should have avoided contact with Cheung while her testimony was ongoing, saying he needed to make prompt inquiries on new information regarding her property ownership.

The messaging records also showed that Cheung had a monetary dispute with a friend she met at a mahjong parlour earlier this year.

Cheung said she was alleged to have owed HK$1.6 million, but she insisted the debt was settled seven years ago. She also revealed that she once lost “a few tens of millions of dollars” while gambling at a mahjong parlour in Jordan.

Ko said Cheung’s alleged debts did not catch his attention when he investigated the case, adding that he could not ascertain whether her claims about gambling millions of dollars away were true or exaggerated.

The trial continues before Deputy Judge Brian Keith and a nine-member jury.

item.title: [SCMP] Dr Ron Roukema on education, leadership and life at Hong Kong International School
item.description:
I WAS BORN in October 1972, in New Jersey, in the United States. My parents were both immigrants – young adults who migrated during World War II, in the early 1940s. My father is Dutch and my mother is Italian, from Sicily. As children, we were always told that if we worked for the state, we’d be well taken care of.

MY MUM WAS a nurse and she met my father in New York. She worked in a hospital, and he was a police officer. My father retired when he was in his 40s after he broke his back. We then moved to North Carolina, which we chose because it was the exact halfway point between my two sets of grandparents (in New Jersey and Florida).

MY FAMILY IS made up of educators. I’m the youngest of five siblings. I have three older sisters, and my parents adopted the son of my father’s friend, when I was about 12. My eldest sister is a university professor and runs a business that does training with government departments. My middle sister retired in one state, moved to another and continues to teach in public schools. My youngest sister is a psychologist and also runs a business working with the government. My brother’s birth father was also in the police force; they were having problems at home, so he lived with us until he was 20. It was just like having a bigger brother, but also a friend who was a role model in some ways. I know he’s a firefighter now in the mountains, but I haven’t seen him in 15 or 20 years.
item.content:encoded:
I WAS BORN in October 1972, in New Jersey, in the United States. My parents were both immigrants – young adults who migrated during World War II, in the early 1940s. My father is Dutch and my mother is Italian, from Sicily. As children, we were always told that if we worked for the state, we’d be well taken care of.

MY MUM WAS a nurse and she met my father in New York. She worked in a hospital, and he was a police officer. My father retired when he was in his 40s after he broke his back. We then moved to North Carolina, which we chose because it was the exact halfway point between my two sets of grandparents (in New Jersey and Florida).

MY FAMILY IS made up of educators. I’m the youngest of five siblings. I have three older sisters, and my parents adopted the son of my father’s friend, when I was about 12. My eldest sister is a university professor and runs a business that does training with government departments. My middle sister retired in one state, moved to another and continues to teach in public schools. My youngest sister is a psychologist and also runs a business working with the government. My brother’s birth father was also in the police force; they were having problems at home, so he lived with us until he was 20. It was just like having a bigger brother, but also a friend who was a role model in some ways. I know he’s a firefighter now in the mountains, but I haven’t seen him in 15 or 20 years.

I LOVE SCHOOLS in general. I grew up in a family where everybody enjoyed going to school. I was in about 20 organisations and clubs in secondary school, playing sports and joining activities to make friends. I was voted “Most Involved” and I was also the lead in the school musical, captain of the wrestling and baseball teams, and field conductor for the marching band. Every now and then, I’d choose classes to be with friends, only to regret it when the classroom turned into more play than study.

GROWING UP, WE didn’t really have the funds to pay for university. I got a full scholarship as a teaching fellow, to teach in the state of North Carolina for four years after graduation, in exchange for tuition. During university (at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill), I continued to play baseball and also did cheerleading. I got my master’s at East Carolina University and my doctorate at North Carolina State University.

MY WIFE AND I went to the same secondary school, but we didn’t meet until university – which is good, because I grew up a lot between the time that I met her and the time that I graduated. I was a fourth-year student, and she was a first-year student. She’s an accomplished photographer and has taught photography at different levels. We’ve been married for 28 years.

MY FIRST JOB was as a fill-in teacher of kindergarten classes at Southern Pines Elementary; that lasted about three months before I realised that was the wrong age group for me. I had kids tell me, “I have to go to the bathroom.” I’d reply, “Well, just go down the hall and go to the bathroom.” But they were like, “No, no, no. We have to walk as a class.” Learning to teach kindergarten was very different. After that, I went back to Pinecrest High School to teach secondary-school history.

MY FIRST ADMINISTRATIVE job was the last year that Southern Pines Middle School existed (2000). I was tasked with converting the academic framework into an International Baccalaureate Primary Years Programme and helping my former colleagues transition, either to other schools or to different areas of education.

ACTUALLY, I NEVER wanted to go into administration. I love teaching. But Joyce Edwards, my associate principal at the time, wanted me to go along with her because she thought I asked good questions. Joyce gave me two options: be the middle-school principal at the new school we’d just built, or move to Durham, in North Carolina, and get a doctorate and go to work at this new school out there.

SO, I MOVED to Durham, in 2000. I helped introduce technology programmes at Eno Valley Elementary School as an administrator, where they told me it would take three to five years to build a technology programme. We built it in seven months.

IN 2007, AROUND the time that my wife and I were expecting our first child, I was offered a job at an international school in Beijing. But instead of going there, we headed to Shanghai American School, where I served as the founding principal of the middle school at the Pudong campus. I worked there for several years before taking my first headship, reporting directly to the board, at Marymount International School, in Paris, France.

WE WERE HAPPY in Paris. We stayed for four years. It was a great school that aligned with my beliefs and philosophies. When our second daughter was born, we started thinking about moving back to Asia. One of the things that drew me towards Hong Kong International School (HKIS) is my Christian faith and the way the school embraces Christianity.

WHAT’S THE PURPOSE of knowledge? I think that’s why religion is important to me, because to understand and to learn – it has to be for a greater purpose, and that greater purpose, in the end, is understanding God’s word and what he hopes for us. In the meantime, it’s also about using your knowledge to serve others and develop a culture that people want to be part of, and to understand that everything we do and everything that happens is for a greater purpose.

MY FIRST IMPRESSION of Hong Kong was in 2007 – right here in this very office, purely by chance. HKIS was hosting a meeting for middle-school principals, and this office I’m in was previously a boardroom. I joined HKIS as the upper-primary principal in 2014. About a year later, they asked me to move into a larger role, as the associate head of school, or what they called the provost at the time, because of my background in education and the knowledge that I had built up over 20-plus years of experience, which was what the school was hoping for and needing at the time. So, I supported them in that role.

DURING THAT FIRST visit, we brought Eva, our oldest, and went to Hong Kong Disneyland. On a trip to Stanley, I ran into the then-head of school, Richard Mueller. We were having lunch at Pizza Express with my wife’s cousins when Richard and his wife walked by and we started chatting. That brief encounter showed me how close and open people in Hong Kong are across both the expat and local communities. It made me feel that I would be happy here, both on an academic and personal level.

I AM HORRIBLE with raising my own children, in the sense of being a parent and an educator at the same school where they go and I work. My oldest graduated two years ago, my youngest is in Year Five and my second daughter is in Year Seven. Whenever I go to an open house or a play to support my kids, I usually get pulled away. It’s hard to just be a dad there, because other parents don’t see me for my kids – they see me for them.

STILL, FOR THE most part, my kids have loved having me around. I walk my son to school every day, and he’s very happy to do it. Whenever my oldest saw me in secondary school, she’d run over, give me a hug and make sure her friends got to say hello.

I WORK IN Hong Kong, but I live in North Carolina. Every summer and Christmas, we go home and see family and friends that we went to school and university with. We have a nice home there – the kind of place people want to be. No dates, no deadlines, but we know that’s eventually what we’ll go back to. It’s just exciting to be around people who have the same origins that I have.

I’M PART OF what we call the “US Gourmet Eating Club”, where we go eat fast food in Hong Kong. It’s just a bunch of people; some are associated with the school, some are not. We get together for new restaurant openings. We’re looking forward to the opening of (American fast-food restaurant) Dairy Queen here in Hong Kong – we joke around and call it “gourmet”.

MY JOY OF working in schools started before I had kids, and it will continue after they have grown up. I feel like I’ve made an impact in each role I’ve held. When I was a teacher, it was daily conversations to help people make decisions that were impactful. Most of my conversations today are about helping students develop lifelong skills, so that they can be successful in the future. I’m interested in seeing how communities come together and grow.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

This story was made possible with support from Hong Kong International School

item.title: [SCMP] Macau’s opulent fine dining scene is using AI to tackle sustainability: how restaurants in Galaxy Macau, Sands China and Grand Lisboa are leading the green march forward
item.description:
In a city as vibrant and fast-paced as Macau, the hungry need not look far to find a fine dining institution worthy of a visit. The city’s leading restaurants are known for their high quality produce and innovative twists on classic cuisines.

Now, increasingly, attention is being paid to sustainability – no easy feat in a territory that, by necessity, imports most of its ingredients and where much hospitality is focused on clients expecting only the very best.

In one sense at least, local traditions provide a head start.
item.content:encoded:
In a city as vibrant and fast-paced as Macau, the hungry need not look far to find a fine dining institution worthy of a visit. The city’s leading restaurants are known for their high quality produce and innovative twists on classic cuisines.

Now, increasingly, attention is being paid to sustainability – no easy feat in a territory that, by necessity, imports most of its ingredients and where much hospitality is focused on clients expecting only the very best.

In one sense at least, local traditions provide a head start.

“Cantonese cuisine has always been curated based on sustainability. We fully utilise every part of the ingredient,” explains chef Tam Kwok-fung of the eponymous one-Michelin-starred establishment Chef Tam’s Seasons, located at Wynn Palace.

Keith Lei, senior vice-president of human resources and sustainability at MGM Macau, says adopting a traditional nose-to-tail approach has granted chefs a sense of culinary liberty. “[This] has challenged chefs to be more creative in their use of less common cuts of meat, leading to a resurgence of diverse cooking techniques and a broader appreciation for the entire animal, discovering new flavours and textures.”

While nose-to-tail and farm-to-table dining are popular trends, chef Tam explains how fish and poultry are prepared. Bones are put aside for flavoursome broths, while vegetables take centre stage or accent dishes as garnishes. “All of this puts our sustainable beliefs and theories into an actual dish,” he says.

Recognising the geographic limitations of a pure farm-to-table approach in Macau, Galaxy Macau’s sustainability and technical services facilities management team sees the success of this approach most in its seasonal menus.

Andre Lai, executive chef of Galaxy’s Andaz Kitchen at the Andaz Macau, sees identifying sustainable sources as the most important component of an all-round sustainable approach to fine dining, and balancing this with “maintaining the identity of our own cuisine”. “Local sourcing is the priority, but we must also look to sustainable initiatives in native cuisine countries,” he says.

Galaxy Macau introduced a Central Production Kitchen in 2021 in a bid to improve energy efficiency and further reduce waste. Feedback on portion sizes and unconsumed food has helped to facilitate menu adjustments and improve future planning. Brand-specific partnerships include a deal with Nespresso that allows for their single-use coffee capsules to be recycled.

Lai shares plans for an urban garden, currently in the development phase, to grow more items to encourage self-sufficiency. “In the future, once we have our urban garden, we aim to introduce our own produce at Andaz Kitchen and our own fermented beverages at Andaz Bar,” he adds.

Julien Tongourian, executive chef of Michelin three-star Robuchon au Dôme – situated atop SJM’s Grand Lisboa hotel – champions a zero-waste philosophy. In an interview with the Michelin Guide, Tongourian explained that the restaurant’s produce is never ordered in bulk, maximising freshness and reducing the risk of excess and waste.

“We never keep our fridge stocked with ingredients. Yes, it’s a challenge for our team to have to work from scratch with new ingredients that arrive every morning, but that’s also how we ensure we get the best flavours from our produce,” he said.

Melco Resorts, which counts City of Dreams, Altira Macau and Studio City among its portfolio in Macau, has been steadily growing its green credentials. Among its many reputable dining establishments are Jade Dragon and Alain Ducasse at Morpheus, both of which featured in last year’s 100 Top Tables guide. The philosophy of small batch ordering is echoed across Melco Group’s establishments and the group has announced a goal of zero waste by 2030, including food waste.

In 2019, Melco announced it would trial the use of dedicated Winnow AI technology, explaining this decision in its sustainability report: “Being the most advanced food waste measurement technology on the market, this initiative will allow us to maximise operational efficiency and data accuracy, with the ability to reduce food waste by up to 50 per cent by value.”

Wynn already uses Winnow technology across its outlets, including at Chef Tam’s Seasons. “[We are] applying computer vision-based monitoring technology powered by AI and machine learning to track and measure what food is being wasted. The system then delivers data-driven insights, enabling us and also other Wynn dining outlets to take an analytical approach to food production that enhances efficiency without compromising on quality,” says Tam.

Wynn Group has also installed a Nordaq water bottling plant, enabling high-quality filtered water to be produced locally and served in reusable glass bottles. Producing around 2,000 bottles per hour, Tam says this will save an estimated eight million plastic bottles every year.

Similarly, at MGM, the implementation of a zero-plastic programme has resulted in the elimination of an estimated 4.5 million pieces of single-use plastic.

Lei and Adam Mathis, culinary director at MGM, emphasise the importance of education in ensuring sustainable practices are adhered to throughout the organisation. They explain that e-learning on sustainability practices is offered to all new food and beverage employees in the organisation. MGM additionally relies on advanced technologies to minimise food waste, including a food digester, composter and food dehydrating machines.

Chef Alex Gaspar, executive director of culinary at Sands China, sees a truly sustainable approach as one that is “multifaceted, using sustainably sourced products, with a zero-waste mindset, to extract as much flavour as possible from the product, utilising as much of it as possible”.

Unable to rely solely on local agriculture, Gaspar places a strong emphasis on working with speciality producers around the region. Winnow AI has also informed Sands China’s approach to food waste, leading them to create live cooking stations instead of using chafing dishes, and portioning up food presented in buffets.

Gaspar urges the importance of sustainable approaches to fine dining without compromising on quality. The proof lies in dishes such as the artichoke risotto at The Londoner’s Churchill’s Table. “We use the artichoke in three different ways: braised, puréed and even using the skin, which is normally discarded – through a special technique we turn it into a crispy and delicious garnish for our risotto,” he says.

“As chefs, we must challenge ourselves to highlight our ingredients and pay respect to all the work that was involved in our dishes.”

item.title: [SCMP] China’s youth draw upon Long March spirit to navigate modern uncertainties
item.description:
As China marks the 90th anniversary of the Red Army’s victory in the Long March, some young Chinese are looking to the historic journey for guidance as they face uncertainty in their lives and future.

For Lyu Leiyiyi, a 22-year-old student at the Communication University of China, the spirit of the Long March offers a sense of stability at a time when people and the environment around her are changing at a dizzying pace.

“People in their 20s are going through a period of uncertainty,” Lyu said. “The spirit of the Long March can help us build a more stable inner core.”
item.content:encoded:
As China marks the 90th anniversary of the Red Army’s victory in the Long March, some young Chinese are looking to the historic journey for guidance as they face uncertainty in their lives and future.
